answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 15.

answer.text:
This is the $n-$ channel telescopic cascode
$CS-CG$ with shunt current source load.
$V_{b1}$ a.c. ground.

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{1}=I_{D}\;\;{\rm in\;dc}$$

$$g_{mi}= \sqrt{2\mu _{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{i}I_{D}}=
{2I_{D}\over V_{ov,i}}\;\;,\;\;r_{oi}={1\over \lambda _{i}I_{D}}$$

Put $R_{I}=r_{oI}$ the small signal impedance
to $V_{DD}$ a.c. ground of the $I_{1}$ source.
For the ideal source $R_{I}\to \infty $.

> {\it $M_{1}$ is the $g_{m}$ device, $M_{2}$ is a
> current buffer - common gate - which presents
> $ \approx 1/(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})$ to the drain of $M_{1}$
> and $\approx g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1}$ to the output.}

In small signal $V_{b1}=0$

```
          vout
            o
            |
           R_I to VDD
            |
      +-----+-----+
      |           |
     ro2         gm2.vgs2+gmb2.vbs2
      |           |
      X-----------+
      |           |
     ro1         gm1.vin
      |           |
     GND         GND
```

For $M_{2}$: $v_{gs2}=-v_{x}$ , $v_{bs2}=-v_{x}$ if
bulk to GND, $0$ if $n-$well with body to source,
$v_{ds2}=v_{out}-v_{x}$.

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{in}+{v_{x}\over r_{o1}}$$
$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{mb2}v_{bs2}+{v_{ds2}\over r_{o2}}
=-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{x}+{v_{out}-v_{x}\over r_{o2}}$$

KCL at $X$ : $i_{d1}=i_{d2}$

KCL at output: $i_{d2}+{v_{out}\over R_{I}}=0$ for
$v_{in}\ne 0$ or $i_{x}=v_{x}/R_{o}$ for $R_{o}$
calculation.

Solving, to first order in $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$:

Impedance looking into the source of $M_{2}$ with
$r_{o1}$ to ground at $X$:

$$R_{x}= {1\over g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2}}\parallel r_{o1}
\approx {1\over g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}$$

so the voltage gain of the $M_{1}$ stage loaded by
$M_{2}$ is

$$A_{v1}={v_{x}\over v_{in}}=-g_{m1}R_{x}\approx
-{g_{m1}\over g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}\approx -1\tag{1}$$

for matched devices.  Hence the Miller multiplication
of $C_{gd1}$ is

$$C_{in}=C_{gs1}+C_{gd1}(1-A_{v1})\approx C_{gs1}+2C_{gd1}$$

instead of $C_{gs1}+(1+g_{m1}R_{D})C_{gd1}$.

Impedance looking into the drain of the cascode:

Put $v_{in}=0$, apply $v_{t}$ at $v_{out}$, measure $i_{t}$.

$$R_{o}\equiv {v_{t}\over i_{t}}\Bigl|_{v_{in}=0}
= r_{o1}+r_{o2}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

$$\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}\;\;{\rm for}\;g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$$

With no body effect $g_{mb2}=0$:

$$R_{o}\approx g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}+r_{o1}+r_{o2}\tag{2}$$

i. e. the $r_{o1}$ is multiplied by $g_{m2}r_{o2}$.
For $r_{o1}=r_{o2}=r_{o}$ : $R_{o}\approx g_{m}r_{o}^{2}$.

With the load $R_{I}$ the impedance at the output
node is

$$R_{out}=R_{o}\parallel R_{I}\tag{3}$$

For the ideal $I_{1}$, $R_{I}\to\infty $, $R_{out}=R_{o}$.
If $I_{1}$ is a simple $p$MOS, $R_{I}=r_{op}$,
$R_{out}\approx r_{o}\parallel g_{m}r_{o}^{2}\approx r_{o}$.
To keep the cascode advantage the load must itself be
cascode: $R_{I}\approx g_{mp}r_{op}^{2}$ and

$$R_{out}\approx {1\over 2}g_{m}r_{o}^{2}$$

The short circuit output current is

$$i_{sc}=-g_{m1}v_{in}{R_{o}\over R_{o}+R_{I}}\approx -g_{m1}v_{in}$$

so the stage transconductance is

$$G_{m}={i_{sc}\over v_{in}}\approx -g_{m1}\tag{4}$$

and the open circuit voltage gain

$$A_{v}={v_{out}\over v_{in}}=-G_{m}R_{out}
=-g_{m1}R_{out}\tag{5}$$

i. e.

$$A_{v}=-g_{m1}\left\{\left[r_{o1}+r_{o2}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}\right]\parallel R_{I}\right\}$$

Ideal load, no body effect:

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}\approx -(g_{m}r_{o})^{2}\tag{6}$$

With $g_{m}r_{o}=2/\lambda V_{ov}$,

$$|A_{v}|\approx {4\over \lambda^{2}V_{ov}^{2}}$$

to be compared with $|A_{v0}|=g_{m}(r_{o}\parallel R_{I})
\approx g_{m}r_{o}/2 =1/\lambda V_{ov}$ for a simple
$CS$ with simple current source load.  The cascode
increases $R_{out}$ and $|A_{v}|$ by $\approx g_{m}r_{o}$.

With $R_{I}=r_{o}$ the increase is $\times 2$,
with $R_{I}=g_{m}r_{o}^{2}$ the increase is
$\approx g_{m}r_{o}/2$.

In words: $M_{2}$ shields $M_{1}$ from $v_{out}$,
suppresses channel length modulation of $M_{1}$ and
provides high $R_{out}$ without changing $G_{m}$.

Other properties:

* $R_{in}=\infty $ at low frequency, $C_{in}$ as above.
* Dominant pole $p_{o}=1/R_{out}C_{L}$ at the output,
  $C_{L}=C_{db2}+C_{gd2}+C_{I}+C_{ext}$.
  Non dominant pole at $X$:

$$p_{x}\approx {g_{m2}+g_{mb2}\over C_{x}}\;\;,\;\;
C_{x}=C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{gd1}+C_{db1}$$

  $\approx g_{m}/C_{x}\gg p_{o}$, so GBW $\approx
  g_{m1}/C_{L}$ and Miller effect is small, bandwidth
  much larger than simple $CS$ for same gain.

* Large signal: $v_{out}$ falls when $v_{in}$ rises,
  inverting.  For saturation

$$V_{X}=V_{b1}-V_{GS2}>V_{ov1}$$
$$V_{out}-V_{X}>V_{ov2}$$

  so

$$V_{out,min}\approx V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}$$
$$V_{out,max}\approx V_{DD}-V_{ovI}$$

  $V_{ovI}$ the overdrive of the $I_{1}$ source,
  $0$ for ideal source.  Headroom is reduced by one
  $V_{ov}$ with respect to simple $CS$.

* $V_{b1}$ is normally $V_{GS2}+V_{ov1}+$ margin,
  e. g. $V_{b1}\approx V_{Tn}+2V_{ov}$, low impedance
  a.c. ground, generated by a replica bias.

* Noise, offset referred to input dominated by $M_{1}$,
  $M_{2}$ contributes $\approx (g_{m2}/g_{m1})^{2}$.

* Reverse isolation $S_{12}$ greatly improved.

This is the basic high gain cell used in telescopic
and folded cascode op-amps.  Gain can be further
increased by gain boosting - regulated cascode - to
$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}(g_{m2}r_{o2}A_{aux})r_{o1}$.

answers.question: Is the circuit of Figure 16 a cascode structure?

answer.text:
With the well ties suppressed the signal path is
the conventional one.  In the conventional $p$ sub
well tied to ${\rm GND}$ {\it i. e.} with the well
ties not shown it is the text book resistively loaded
telescopic {\it cascode}

$${\rm CS}\;M_{1}\rightarrow {\rm CG}\;M_{2}\rightarrow
R_{D}\tag*{Fig.1}$$

in the small signal sense

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}\left[ \left(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}\right)
r_{o2}r_{o1}\parallel R_{D}\right]\qquad 
R_{o}\approx \left(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}\right)r_{o2}r_{o1}\parallel R_{D}$$

and it is normally referred to for short as {\it the}
cascode.  Taken literally as drawn in Fig. 16 it is
not a conventional same well cascode.  In Fig. 16 the
well arrow is drawn on the common node for both
devices.  I. e. as drawn

* $M_{2}$ is an ${\rm n}$ channel device with its
$p$ well tied to its source, the conventional
cascode ${\rm CG}$ device, $g_{mb2}=0$ if you want,

* $M_{1}$ is drawn with its well tied to its drain,
normally drawn as a $p$ channel device with its $n$
well tied to its source.

So that as drawn the $n$ well $p$ well stack is
complementary.  The current can still flow
${\rm V_{DD}}\rightarrow R_{D}\rightarrow {\rm D_{2}}
\rightarrow {\rm S_{2}}\rightarrow {\rm S_{1}}\rightarrow
{\rm D_{1}}\rightarrow {\rm GND}$ but $M_{1}$ is not a
${\rm CS}$ device.  For the ${\rm PMOS}$ $M_{1}$

$${\rm S_{1}}\equiv {\rm top}\qquad {\rm D_{1}}\equiv
{\rm GND}$$

so that $M_{1}$ is a ${\rm CD}$ or source follower
device

$$M_{1}:{\rm G}\equiv V_{in}\;\;{\rm D}\equiv {\rm GND}
\;\;{\rm S}\equiv {\rm S_{2}}$$

driving the ${\rm CG}$ device $M_{2}$,

$$M_{2}:{\rm G}\equiv V_{b1}\;\;{\rm S}\equiv {\rm S_{1}}
\;\;{\rm D}\equiv R_{D}\tag*{{\rm CG}}$$

I. e. the conventional ${\rm CS}+{\rm CG}$ voltage
gain $\propto g_{m}R_{o}$ cascode action is lost.
In the small signal sense

$$A_{v}\approx {g_{m1}\over g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{o1}+g_{o2}}
{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}\over g_{o2}+G_{D}}\ne -g_{m}R_{o}$$

and, with the ${\rm NMOS}$ well normally being the
$p$ substrate, the ${\rm S_{1}}-p$ well junction of the
${\rm NMOS}$ $M_{1}$ with its well tied to its drain
is forward biased in normal operation.  It is normally
called a complementary, pseudo, folded or
${\rm CD}-{\rm CG}$ cascode for short.  If, as is
normal in a $p$ sub process, you tie both $p$ wells to
${\rm GND}$ the circuit becomes the conventional
${\rm NMOS}$ telescopic cascode normally referred to
just as a cascode.

> {\it Remark:}  With the conventional $p$ sub well
> tied to ${\rm GND}$ the arrow on $M_{1}$ belongs on
> the ${\rm GND}$ side.  With that conventional well
> tie the circuit is the text book $M_{1}={\rm CS}$,
> $M_{2}={\rm CG}$, $R_{D}=$ load telescopic cascode
> and is normally just called a cascode.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
In a $CE/CS$ stage the feedback $C$ is
multiplied by the stage voltage gain. In the
cascode the gain across that $C$ is $\approx 1$.

Recall Miller theorem: Impedance $Z$ between nodes
$1,2$ with $V_{2}=K V_{1}$

$$Z_{1}= \frac{Z}{1-K} \qquad Z_{2}= \frac{Z}{1-1/K}$$

For capacitance $C_{gd}$ in MOS or $C_{\mu}$ in BJT
between input $B/G$ and output $C/D$:

$$C_{M,in}= C_{gd}(1-K) = C_{gd}(1-A_{v})$$
$$C_{M,out}= C_{gd}(1-1/K)$$

where $A_{v}=V_{o}/V_{i}<0$.

### 1. Single $CS/CE$

$$A_{v}= -g_{m}R_{D}' = -g_{m}(r_{o}\parallel R_{D}) \gg 1$$

e.g. $20-100$.

$$C_{in}= C_{gs}+C_{gd}(1+g_{m}R_{D}') \approx C_{gs}+g_{m}R_{D}'C_{gd}$$

Input pole:

$$\omega_{p,in}= \frac{1}{R_{sig}C_{in}} \approx \frac{1}{R_{sig}g_{m}R_{D}'C_{gd}}$$

very low. The large anti-phase swing at the drain/collector drives large current through $C_{gd}$ to the input, requiring large current from $R_{sig}$.

### 2. Cascode $CS-CG$ / $CE-CB$

```
Vi -> G1 D1 -> S2 D2 -> Vo
      S1      G2=AC gnd
```

Overall gain is still large:

$$A_{v}=A_{v1}A_{v2}\approx -g_{m1}R_{out} \approx -g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

but it is distributed over two stages.

*Stage 1 - $CS/CE$:* Load is not $R_{D}$ but impedance looking into source/emitter of $CG/CB$ with gate/base at $ac$ ground:

$$R_{in2}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}} \parallel r_{o2} \approx 1/g_{m2}$$

Hence

$$A_{v1}= \frac{V_{x}}{V_{i}} = -g_{m1}R_{in2} \approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}} \approx -0.5 \;{\rm to}\; -1$$

if devices matched.

Miller multiplication for $C_{gd1}/C_{\mu 1}$:

$$C_{M1}= C_{gd1}(1-A_{v1}) = C_{gd1}\left(1+\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}\right) \approx 2C_{gd1}$$

instead of $(1+g_{m}R_{D})C_{gd}\approx 50C_{gd}$.

$$C_{in}\approx C_{gs1}+2C_{gd1}$$

Input pole moves up by $\approx g_{m}R_{D}/2$.

Physically: $CG$ holds node $X=D_{1}=S_{2}$ at low impedance, almost $ac$ ground. The voltage swing at $X$ is $\approx V_{i}$, not $A_{v}V_{i}$. So $C_{gd1}$ sees $\Delta V \approx 2V_{i}$, little displacement current is fed back to input.

*Stage 2 - $CG/CB$:* For the upper device input is $S/E$, output is $D/C$, gate/base is $ac$ ground.

$$A_{v2}= +g_{m2}R_{out} \gg 1$$

but $C_{gd2}/C_{\mu 2}$ is now between output and $ac$ ground, not between input and output. $C_{gs2}/C_{\pi 2}$ is between $X$ and ground.

$$C_{M2,in}= C_{gd2}(1-1/A_{v2})\approx C_{gd2}$$

No multiplication. The capacitance is simply to ground at the high impedance output node and at the low impedance intermediate node.

The intermediate pole is now

$$\omega_{pX}\approx \frac{g_{m2}}{C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{gd1}+C_{db1}}$$

very high frequency, and the dominant pole is at the output:

$$\omega_{p,out}\approx \frac{1}{R_{out}C_{out}}$$

The amplifier is made much more unilateral - output swing is isolated from input by the current buffer action of the $CG/CB$ stage. It provides current gain $\approx 1$ and voltage gain, while the $CS/CE$ provides $g_{m}$.

Hence bandwidth, gain-bandwidth product and reverse isolation are greatly improved. This is why wideband and RF amplifiers and op-amp gain stages are cascoded. In the limit $A_{v1}\to 0$ the Miller effect is eliminated.

It correctly applies Miller's theorem, derives the reduced Miller multiplication, and explains the physical mechanism (CG holds node X near AC ground, small swing across Cgd1). It also correctly notes Cgd2 is between output and AC ground so contributes no Miller multiplication. The dominant mechanism and design consequence match the golden solution.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 17.

answer.text:
This is the $n$ channel {\it common gate}
with $p$ channel current source load. $V_{b1},V_{b2}$
AC ground.

$$M_{2}:{\rm CG}\qquad M_{1}:R_{D}=r_{o1}=1/g_{ds1}$$

Put $V_{DD}$ AC ground. In small signal

$$v_{g1}=v_{g2}=0\;\;,\;\;v_{s2}=v_{in}\;\;,\;\;v_{d2}=v_{d1}=v_{out}$$

$$r_{o2}=1/g_{ds2}\;\;,\;\;r_{o1}=1/g_{ds1}$$

$$g_{m2},g_{mb2}\ne 0\;{\rm in\;general}$$

If $n$ well process $B_{2}$ can be tied to $S_{2}$,
Fig.17, $g_{mb2}=0$.  With $B_{2}=0$, $v_{bs2}=-v_{in}$.

Small signal model $D\to S$ :

$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{mb2}v_{bs2}+g_{ds2}v_{ds2}$$

$$v_{gs2}=-v_{in}\;\;,\;\;v_{bs2}=-v_{in}\;(0\;{\rm if}\;B=S)$$
$$v_{ds2}=v_{out}-v_{in}$$

$$i_{d2}=-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{in}+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{in})\tag{1}$$
positive into $D$, out of $S$.

For $M_{1}$ $v_{sg1}=0$

$$i_{d1}=g_{ds1}v_{sd1}=g_{ds1}(-v_{out})\tag{2}$$
in $n$ convention $i_{d1}$ into $D$ is $-g_{ds1}v_{out}$.
In magnitude the load to ground is $r_{o1}$.

KCL at $D$ : $i_{d2}+i_{d1}=0$ with sign consistent,
i. e. current $D\to S$ in $M_{2}$ plus current
$D\to V_{DD}$ in $M_{1}$ $=0$:

$$g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{in})-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{in}+{v_{out}\over r_{o1}}=0$$

$${v_{out}\over v_{in}}={g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}\over g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}$$

$$A_{v}=(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})\,r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\tag{3}$$

$$A_{v}\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})\,r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}>0$$

non inverting.  With $B_{2}=S_{2}$

$$A_{v}\approx g_{m2}\,r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}= {g_{m2}\over g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} \tag{3a}$$

for $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$.  This is the $CG$ voltage gain
with $R_{D}=r_{o1}$.  $M_{1}$ contributes only $r_{o1}$.
Formally $A_{v}=G_{m}R_{out}$ with $G_{m}\approx g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$.

Current gain $i_{out}/i_{in}\approx 1$ - current follower.
The voltage gain is the current $\times R_{out}$.

{\it Input impedance} looking into $S_{2}$.

Let $i_{in}$ into $S_{2}$.  $i_{in}=-i_{d2}$,

$$i_{in}=(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{in}-g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{in})$$

with (3)

$$i_{in}=v_{in}{(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})\over 1+g_{ds2}R_{D}}{1\over R_{D}}$$

$$R_{in}={v_{in}\over i_{in}}={1+g_{ds2}R_{D}\over g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}={R_{D}+r_{o2}\over 1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}}\tag{4}$$

$$R_{in}\approx {1\over g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}{1+R_{D}/r_{o2}}\approx {1\over g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}\;\;R_{D}\ll r_{o2}$$

In general with source resistance $R_{sig}$ driving $S_{2}$

$$R_{in}={1\over g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}}\left(1+{R_{D}\over r_{o}}\right)$$

For the active load $R_{D}=r_{o1}$

$$R_{in}={r_{o1}+r_{o2}\over 1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}}\approx {1\over g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}\left(1+{r_{o1}\over r_{o2}}\right)$$

$\approx 1/g_{m2}$ if $g_{mb}=0$ and $r_{o1}\approx r_{o2}$,
$\approx 2/g_{m}$ for matched $r_{o}$'s, $\approx 1/g_{m}$
for $r_{o1}\ll r_{o2}$.  Normally quoted as

$$R_{in}\approx 1/(g_{m}+g_{mb})\parallel r_{o2}\approx 1/g_{m}$$

low impedance, $\sim 50-500\,{\rm \Omega}$, can be matched to
$R_{sig}$ for wide band LNA.  Overall gain from source
$e_{sig}$ with $R_{sig}$:

$$A_{v,tot}=A_{v}{R_{in}\over R_{in}+R_{sig}}$$

{\it Output impedance} looking into $D$ with $R_{sig}$ in
series with $S$:

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel \left\{r_{o2}+[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}]R_{sig}\right\}\tag{5}$$

For ideal voltage drive $R_{sig}=0$

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\tag{5a}$$

high, $\sim 10-100\,{\rm k\Omega}$.  With $R_{sig}\ne 0$
the $CG$ bootstraps $r_{o2}$ to $\approx g_{m}r_{o}R_{sig}$.

{\it DC bias:} $I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{B}$

$$I_{B}={1\over 2}\mu_{p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}(V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{Tp}|)^{2}(1+\lambda_{p}V_{SD1})$$
$$={1\over 2}\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{2}(V_{b1}-V_{in,DC}-V_{Tn})^{2}(1+\lambda_{n}V_{DS2})$$

Saturation requires

$$V_{DS2}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{Tn}=V_{ov2}\;\;,\;\;V_{SD1}\ge V_{SG1}-|V_{Tp}|=V_{ov1}$$

$$V_{out}\ge V_{in}+V_{ov2}\;\;,\;\;V_{out}\le V_{DD}-V_{ov1}$$

$$V_{b1}=V_{in,DC}+V_{GS2}\;\;,\;\;V_{b2}=V_{DD}-|V_{SG1}|$$

{\it High frequency:} No Miller multiplication.  Input pole

$$\omega_{p,in}\approx {1\over R_{in}C_{in}}\approx {g_{m}+g_{mb}\over C_{gs}+C_{sb}+C_{sig}}$$

very high.  Output pole

$$\omega_{p,out}\approx {1\over R_{out}C_{L}}={1\over (r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})C_{L}}$$

dominant.  Hence wide band, good for RF, current buffer,
cascode input stage, folded cascode, $50\,{\rm \Omega}$ input
LNA.  Voltage gain positive, current gain $\approx 1$,
low $R_{in}$, high $R_{out}$, good reverse isolation.

answers.question: How many poles does the circuit of Figure 18 have?

answer.text:
With the usual lumped small signal model the
circuit is a $2$ node circuit, Fig.1, so that with

$${\rm G}_{1}(s)={1\over {R_{s}}}+s\left(C_{gs}+C_{gd}\right)
\qquad {\rm G}_{2}(s)={1\over {r_{o1}}\!\parallel\! r_{o2}}
+s\left(C_{db}+C_{db2}+C_{gd2}+C_{gd}\right)\tag{*}$$

$${\rm det}(s)={\rm G}_{1}{\rm G}_{2}+sC_{gd}\left(g_{m1}-sC_{gd}
\right)=0\tag{**}$$

is quadratic in $s$.  In compact form, putting

$$C_{o}=C_{db}+C_{db2}+C_{gd2}\tag{***}$$

$$\eqalign{
\left[{{V_{g}-V_{in}}\over {R_{s}}}+sC_{gs}V_{g}+sC_{gd}
\left(V_{g}-V_{o}\right)&=0\cr 
sC_{o}V_{o}+sC_{gd}\left(V_{o}-V_{g}\right)+{{V_{o}}\over {r_{o}}}
+g_{m1}V_{g}&=0\cr}\tag{****}$$

$$\left|\matrix{
{1\over {R_{s}}}+s\left(C_{gs}+C_{gd}\right) &-sC_{gd}\cr 
g_{m1}-sC_{gd} &{1\over {r_{o}}}+s\left(C_{o}+C_{gd}\right)\cr}\right|
\left|\matrix{V_{g}\cr V_{o}\cr}\right|=
\left|\matrix{{V_{in}\over {R_{s}}}\cr 0\cr}\right| \tag{*****}$$

so that, e. {\rm g.},

$${{V_{o}}\over {V_{in}}}=-{{g_{m1}-sC_{gd}}\over {R_{s}{\rm det}(s)}}
\tag{******}$$

$${\rm det}(s)={1\over {R_{s}r_{o}}}+s\left[{{C_{gs}+C_{gd}}\over
{r_{o}}}+{{C_{o}+C_{gd}}\over {R_{s}}}+g_{m1}C_{gd}\right]
+s^{2}\left[\left(C_{gs}+C_{gd}\right)\left(C_{o}+C_{gd}\right)
-C_{gd}^{2}\right] \tag{*******}$$

$$= {1\over {R_{s}r_{o}}}+s\left[{{C_{gs}+C_{gd}}\over
{r_{o}}}+{{C_{o}+C_{gd}}\over {R_{s}}}+g_{m1}C_{gd}\right]
+s^{2}\left[C_{gs}C_{gd}+C_{o}\left(C_{gs}+C_{gd}\right)\right] \tag{********}$$

is second order in $s$.  The numerator is first order and
contributes the familiar right half plane Miller zero

$$s_{z}=+{{g_{m1}}\over {C_{gd}}}\tag{*********}$$

so that $\left|V_{o}/V_{in}\right|$ is $2/1$.
Lumping the two drain bulk caps. and the $M_{2}$ Miller cap.
together in $C_{o}$ there are three physical capacitances in
the circuit, $C_{gs}$, $C_{gd}$ and $C_{o}$, normally quoted as
{\it three poles}, two of which are coincident at the output
node, Fig.2.  Keeping $C_{db}$ and $C_{db2}$ distinct there are
four physical caps. and the circuit is normally quoted as a
four pole, one zero, circuit with

$$C_{o1}=C_{db}\qquad C_{o2}=C_{db2}+C_{gd2}\tag{**********}$$

in parallel at the output node.  In the Miller
approximation the two {\it distinct} pole frequencies are normally
written, $r_{o}=r_{o1}\!\parallel\! r_{o2}$,

$$\omega _{p\,{\rm in}}\approx {1\over {R_{s}\left[C_{gs}+
\left(1+g_{m1}r_{o}\right)C_{gd}\right]}}\tag{***********}$$

for the Miller multiplied input pole and

$$\omega _{p\,o}\approx {1\over {r_{o}\left[C_{o}+C_{gd}\right]}}
={1\over {r_{o}\left[C_{db}+C_{db2}+C_{gd2}+C_{gd}\right]}}\tag{************}$$

for the {\it dominant} output pole, the exact poles being the
two roots of ${\rm det}(s)=0$, Eq.{\rm (**)}.  With
$g_{m1}r_{o}\gg 1$ the conventional dominant pole - non dominant
pole splitting is

$$\eqalign{
\omega _{p1}&\approx {1\over {r_{o}\left[C_{o}+C_{gd}\right]
+R_{s}\left[C_{gs}+C_{gd}\right]+g_{m1}r_{o}R_{s}C_{gd}}\cr
&\approx {1\over {g_{m1}r_{o}R_{s}C_{gd}}}\;\;{\rm for}\;\;
g_{m1}r_{o}R_{s}C_{gd}\gg r_{o}C_{o},R_{s}C_{gs}\cr
\omega _{p2}&\approx {{g_{m1}C_{gd}}\over
{C_{gs}C_{gd}+C_{o}\left(C_{gs}+C_{gd}\right)}}\,
\omega _{p1}^{-1}\cr}$$

For $R_{s}\rightarrow 0$ the input pole goes to infinity and the
circuit becomes the familiar single pole $1/r_{o}C_{o}$ common
source stage.

> {\it Remark:}  Counting every $C$ as a pole the circuit is
> quite often quoted as a {\it three pole\/} circuit, $C_{gs}$,
> $C_{gd}$ and $C_{o}=C_{db}\!\parallel\! C_{db2}\!\parallel\!
> C_{gd2}$, four pole if $C_{db}$ and $C_{db2}$ are kept distinct.
> Two, three, of the poles are coincident at the output node so
> that the denominator remains quadratic.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 19.

answer.text:
With ${\rm M}_{1}$ in the triode and ${\rm M}_{2}$
in the saturation the stack is a one gate composite
MOS.  Put for reference

$${\rm M}_{i}:k_{i}=\mu _{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{i}\qquad 
I_{Di}=k_{i}\left[(V_{GS}-V_{T})V_{DS}-V_{DS}^{2}/2\right]
(1+\lambda V_{DS})\;\;{\rm triode}$$
$$I_{Di}={k_{i}\over 2}(V_{GS}-V_{T})^{2}(1+\lambda V_{DS})\;\;
{\rm sat}\tag{1}$$
$$g_{mi}=k_{i}(V_{GS}-V_{T})\;\;{\rm sat}\qquad 
g_{mi}=k_{i}V_{DS}\;\;{\rm tri}\qquad 
g_{dsi}=k_{i}(V_{GS}-V_{T}-V_{DS})\;\;{\rm tri}\qquad 
g_{dsi}=\lambda I_{D}\;\;{\rm sat}$$

and for the $p$ substrate $V_{B}=0$,
$V_{BS2}=-V_{X}$, $g_{mb2}=\eta g_{m2}$ for ${\rm M}_{2}$,
$g_{mb1}=0$.  Put

$$a=V_{in}-V_{T}\qquad b=V_{X}\qquad c=V_{out}-V_{X}$$

$${\rm M}_{1}:V_{GS1}=V_{in}\;\;V_{DS1}=b\qquad 
{\rm M}_{2}:V_{GS2}=V_{in}-b\;\;V_{DS2}=c\tag{2}$$

$${\rm M}_{1}{\rm sat}:b\ge a\qquad 
{\rm M}_{2}{\rm sat}:c\ge a-b\tag{3}$$

i. e.

$${\rm M}_{2}{\rm sat}\iff V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{T2}\tag{4}$$

independent of $b$.

For $\lambda =0$, $\gamma =0$

$$I_{D1}=k_{1}\left(ab-b^{2}/2\right)\tag{5a}$$
$$I_{D2}={k_{2}\over 2}(a-b)^{2}\;\;{\rm sat}\tag{5b}$$

$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{D}$ gives

$$k_{1}ab-{k_{1}\over 2}b^{2}={k_{2}\over 2}(a^{2}-2ab+b^{2})$$

$$(k_{1}+k_{2})b^{2}-2(k_{1}+k_{2})ab+k_{2}a^{2}=0$$

$$(b-a)^{2}={k_{1}\over k_{1}+k_{2}}a^{2}\tag{6}$$

$$b=a\left[1-\sqrt{{k_{1}\over k_{1}+k_{2}}}\;\right]>0\tag{7}$$

$$0<b<a\tag{8}$$

so that for any $k_{1},k_{2}>0$

$${\rm M}_{1}{\rm \;is\;in\;the\;triode\;\;and\;\;M}_{2}
{\rm \;is\;in\;the\;saturation\tag{9}}$$

as long as (4) is satisfied.  The physical root is (7).
Then from (5b)

$$I_{D}={k_{2}\over 2}(a-b)^{2}
={k_{2}\over 2}a^{2}{k_{1}\over k_{1}+k_{2}}
={k_{e}\over 2}a^{2}\tag{10}$$

with

$$k_{e}={k_{1}k_{2}\over k_{1}+k_{2}}=
\left({1\over k_{1}}+{1\over k_{2}}\right)^{-1}\tag{11}$$

$${1\over (W/L)_{e}}={1\over (W/L)_{1}}+{1\over (W/L)_{2}}\tag{12}$$

In particular for $(W/L)_{1}=(W/L)_{2}=W/L$

$$k_{e}=k/2\qquad (W/L)_{e}=(W/L)/2\qquad 
L_{e}=L_{1}+L_{2}\tag{13}$$

$$I_{D}={k_{e}\over 2}(V_{in}-V_{T})^{2}
(1+\lambda _{e}V_{out})\tag{14}$$

in the {\it composite saturation} region

$$V_{in}>V_{T}\qquad V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{T}\tag{15}$$

i. e. the stack is indistinguishable in the large signal
square law sense from a single long channel MOS of
$W_{e}=W$, $L_{e}=L_{1}+L_{2}$ and

$$V_{Te}\approx V_{T}\tag{16}$$

with $\gamma\ne 0$, $V_{T2}=V_{T0}+\gamma
\left(\sqrt{2\phi_{F}+b}-\sqrt{2\phi_{F}}\right)>V_{T1}$,
(10) becomes

$$I_{D}={k_{e}\over 2}(V_{in}-V_{Te})^{2}\qquad 
V_{Te}>V_{T0}\tag{17}$$

and $b=a_{e}[1-\sqrt{k_{1}/(k_{1}+k_{2})}]$ with
$a_{e}=V_{in}-V_{Te}$.

For $V_{in}<V_{T}$, $I_{D}=0$, $V_{out}=V_{DD}$.
For $V_{out}<V_{in}-V_{T}$ ${\rm M}_{2}$ goes triode,
both devices triode and

$$I_{D}=k_{1}(ab-b^{2}/2)=k_{2}[(a-b)c-c^{2}/2]\tag{18}$$

$V_{out}$ falls slowly to $V_{OL}\approx 0$.
The large signal voltage transfer is therefore that of a
normal $R_{D}$ loaded common source stage

$$V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{D}(V_{in},V_{out})R_{D}\tag{19}$$

with $I_{D}$ given by (10) in saturation, i. e.

$$V_{out}=V_{DD}-{k_{e}R_{D}\over 2}(V_{in}-V_{T})^{2}
\qquad {\rm composite\;sat.}\tag{20}$$

The small signal composite saturation $g_{m}$ is

$$G_{m}={\partial I_{D}\over\partial V_{in}}=k_{e}a
={k_{1}k_{2}\over k_{1}+k_{2}}(V_{in}-V_{T})\tag{21}$$

$$G_{m}=\left({1\over g_{m1}^{s}}+{1\over g_{m2}^{s}}\right)^{-1}
={g_{m1}^{s}g_{m2}^{s}\over g_{m1}^{s}+g_{m2}^{s}}\tag{22}$$

where $g_{mi}^{s}=k_{i}a$ is the saturation $g_{m}$ of
device $i$ alone.  For $k_{1}=k_{2}=k$, $G_{m}=ka/2=g_{m}^{s}/2$.

In terms of the small signal parameters at the bias point

$${\rm M}_{1}{\rm \;triode:}\;g_{m1}=k_{1}b,\;
g_{d1}=k_{1}(a-b)+\lambda_{1}I_{D}\tag{23a}$$
$${\rm M}_{2}{\rm \;sat:}\;g_{m2}=k_{2}(a-b),\;
g_{d2}=\lambda_{2}I_{D},\;g_{mb2}=\eta g_{m2}\tag{23b}$$

$$g_{m1}+g_{d1}=k_{1}a=g_{m1}^{s}\tag{24}$$

The low frequency small signal circuit, Fig.1, is

$$\eqalign{
i_{d1}&=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{d1}v_{x}\cr
i_{d2}&=g_{m2}(v_{in}-v_{x})+g_{mb2}(-v_{x})+g_{d2}(v_{out}-v_{x})\cr
i_{d1}&=i_{d2}\cr
i_{d2}&=-v_{out}/R_{D}\cr}\tag{25}$$

Hence

$$(g_{m1}-g_{m2})v_{in}+(g_{d1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{d2})v_{x}
-g_{d2}v_{out}=0\tag{26a}$$
$$g_{m2}v_{in}-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{d2})v_{x}
+(g_{d2}+R_{D}^{-1})v_{out}=0\tag{26b}$$

Put $D=g_{d1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{d2}$,

$$v_{x}={(g_{m2}-g_{m1})v_{in}+g_{d2}v_{out}\over D}\tag{27}$$

and

$$A_{v}={v_{out}\over v_{in}}=
-{g_{m2}D-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{d2})(g_{m2}-g_{m1})\over
-g_{d2}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{d2})+(g_{d2}+R_{D}^{-1})D}\tag{28}$$

$$A_{v}=-{g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{d2})+g_{m2}g_{d1}\over
g_{d1}g_{d2}+D/R_{D}}\,R_{D}\tag{29}$$

$$A_{v}=-{ \left[g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})+g_{m2}g_{d1}\right]R_{D}
\over g_{d1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{d1}g_{d2}R_{D}}\tag{30}$$

neglecting $g_{d2}$ against $g_{m2}$ in the numerator.
For $\gamma =0$, $g_{mb2}=0$,

$$A_{v}=-{g_{m1}g_{m2}+g_{m2}g_{d1}\over g_{d1}+g_{m2}+g_{d1}g_{d2}R_{D}}
\,R_{D}
=-{g_{m2}(g_{m1}+g_{d1})\over g_{m2}+g_{d1}}\,
{R_{D}\over 1+g_{d1}g_{d2}R_{D}/(g_{m2}+g_{d1})}\tag{31}$$

Using (24) $g_{m1}+g_{d1}=k_{1}a$, $g_{m2}=k_{2}(a-b)$,
$g_{d1}=k_{1}(a-b)$,

$$A_{v}=-{k_{1}k_{2}\over k_{1}+k_{2}}a\,
{R_{D}\over 1+R_{D}/R_{o}}\tag{32}$$

where

$$R_{o}={D\over g_{d1}g_{d2}}={g_{d1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{d2}\over
g_{d1}g_{d2}}\tag{33}$$

is the small signal resistance looking into the drain of
${\rm M}_{2}$ with $v_{in}=0$,

$$R_{o}\approx {1\over g_{d2}}+{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}\over g_{d1}g_{d2}}
\approx {g_{m2}+g_{mb2}\over g_{d1}}\,r_{o2}\tag{34}$$

$$R_{o}\approx r_{o2}\left(1+{k_{2}\over k_{1}}\right)
=r_{o2}{k_{1}+k_{2}\over k_{1}}\tag{35}$$

for $\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}$, $g_{mb}=0$.
For $W_{1}=W_{2}$, $k_{2}/k_{1}=L_{1}/L_{2}$,

$$R_{o}=r_{o2}{L_{1}+L_{2}\over L_{2}}={L_{e}\over L_{2}}r_{o2}
\propto {L_{e}\over I_{D}}\tag{36}$$

i. e. the Early voltage $V_{Ae}=1/\lambda_{e}\propto L_{e}$,

$$\lambda_{e}={\lambda_{2}\over 1+k_{2}/k_{1}}
=\lambda_{2}{k_{1}\over k_{1}+k_{2}}
=\lambda_{2}{k_{e}\over k_{2}}\tag{37}$$

For $L_{1}=L_{2}=L$, $r_{o1}=r_{o2}=r_{o}$,
$R_{o}\approx 2r_{o}$, $V_{Ae}=2V_{A}$, as for a single
device of length $2L$.

In compact form

$$A_{v}=-G_{m}\,(R_{D}\parallel R_{o})\tag{38}$$

with $G_{m}$ given by (21).  If $R_{D}\ll R_{o}$,

$$A_{v}\approx -G_{m}R_{D}=-k_{e}(V_{in}-V_{T})R_{D}
=-\sqrt{2k_{e}I_{D}}\,R_{D}\tag{39}$$

$$|A_{v}|\approx g_{m}^{e}R_{D}\tag{40}$$

For $R_{D}\gg R_{o}$ the intrinsic gain is

$$A_{vo}=-G_{m}R_{o}\approx -{2\over \lambda_{e}(V_{in}-V_{T})}
=-{g_{m}^{e}\over g_{de}}\tag{41}$$

$$A_{vo}\approx {L_{e}\over L}\,g_{m}^{s}r_{o}\tag{42}$$

a factor $L_{e}/L$ larger than the short device alone,
exactly the long channel intrinsic gain.  With body effect

$$A_{v}\approx -{g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})\over g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{d1}}
R_{D}\approx -G_{m}R_{D}\tag{43}$$

and $R_{o}$ is given by (33) with $g_{mb2}$ included,
$\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}/g_{d1}r_{o1}$.

Remarks:

* Input resistance $R_{in}=\infty$ at low frequency,
$C_{in}\approx C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+C_{gd2}(1+|A_{v}|)+C_{gb}$.
* No extra bias is required and the minimum
$V_{DS,sat}=V_{in}-V_{T}$ is the same as for a single
device, unlike a cascode which needs $V_{DS1,sat}+V_{DS2,sat}$.
The price is $G_{m}<g_{m1}^{s}$; the composite delivers the
$g_{m}$ of the long device, not the short device.
* The non dominant pole at the intermediate node is

$$\omega_{x}\approx {g_{m2}+g_{d1}\over C_{x}},\qquad 
C_{x}=C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{gd1}+C_{db1}+C_{db2}\tag{44}$$

$\sim g_{m}/C$, i. e. at high frequency, so the composite
does not degrade the dominant output pole
$\omega_{o}=1/(R_{D}\parallel R_{o})C_{L}$ appreciably.
* The circuit is the classic {\it self-cascode} or
{\it composite} or {\it series} MOS used to emulate a
long $L$ device in a short channel technology, to raise
$r_{o}$, $V_{A}$, intrinsic gain and matching
$\sigma_{VT}\propto 1/\sqrt{W_{e}L_{e}}$ and to suppress
short channel effects, DIBL, velocity saturation, at the
cost of area and a factor $\approx 2$ in current for the
same $W$.

For hand calculation with $\lambda =0$, $\gamma =0$,
identical devices:

$$I_{D}={k\over 4}(V_{in}-V_{T})^{2},\;
V_{X}=0.29\,(V_{in}-V_{T}),\;
G_{m}={k\over 2}(V_{in}-V_{T}),\;
A_{v}\approx -{k\over 2}(V_{in}-V_{T})R_{D},\;
R_{o}\approx 2r_{o}.$$

This is to be compared with a single device
$I_{D0}=k(V_{in}-V_{T})^{2}/2$, $g_{m0}=k(V_{in}-V_{T})$,
$A_{v0}=-g_{m0}R_{D}$, $r_{o0}=1/\lambda I_{D0}$.
The composite gives half the current and half the $g_{m}$
for the same $W/L$, but double the $r_{o}$ for the same
current, i. e. the same $g_{m}r_{o}$ as a device of
$L_{e}=2L$.  To keep the same $I_{D}$ the composite needs
$W_{e}=2W$.

It correctly concludes that M1 is in triode and M2 in saturation, derives the equivalent transconductance and Early voltage scaled with L_eff, and explicitly states this matches a single long-channel device. This fully captures the essential golden-solution conclusion.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 20.

answer.text:
With ${\rm M}_{1}-{\rm M}_{2}$ put $g_{i}=1/r_{oi}$
$g_{mi},g_{mbi}$ in the normal way and put

$${\rm M}_{1}:v_{gs1}=v_{in}-v_{x}\;\;v_{bs1}=-v_{x}\;\;
v_{ds1}=-v_{x}$$
$${\rm M}_{2}:v_{gs2}=-v_{x}\;\;v_{bs2}=-v_{x}\;\;
v_{ds2}=v_{o}-v_{x}\qquad V_{b}=0\;{\rm a.c.}$$

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{mb1}v_{bs1}+g_{1}v_{ds1}
      =g_{m1}v_{in}-G_{1}v_{x}\tag{1}$$
$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{mb2}v_{bs2}+g_{2}v_{ds2}
      =-G_{2}v_{x}+g_{2}v_{o}\tag{2}$$

$$G_{i}=g_{mi}+g_{mbi}+g_{i}\qquad g_{i}=1/r_{oi}$$

$$x\equiv S_{1}=S_{2}$$

is the common source node.  In the conventional
small signal picture

* ${\rm M}_{1}$ is a common drain, drain ${\rm a.c.}\;0$,
* ${\rm M}_{2}$ is a common gate, gate ${\rm a.c.}\;0$,

the ${\rm CD}$ driving the low $Z$ looking into the
source of the ${\rm CG}$.

$${\rm KCL}_{x}:i_{d1}+i_{d2}=g_{T}v_{x}\tag{3}$$
$${\rm KCL}_{o}:i_{Rd}+i_{d2}=0\tag{4}$$

$g_{T}=1/R_{T}$ is the small signal conductance of the
tail source $I_{1}$, $g_{T}=0$ for the ideal tail.
$R_{D}$ to ${\rm a.c.}\;0$

$$i_{Rd}=-v_{o}/R_{D}\tag{5}$$

so that from (2)(4)(5)

$$-v_{o}/R_{D}= -G_{2}v_{x}+g_{2}v_{o}$$

$$\left({1\over {R_{D}}}+g_{2}\right)v_{o}=G_{2}v_{x}\tag{6}$$

$$v_{x}=v_{o}{{1+g_{2}R_{D}}\over {G_{2}R_{D}}}\tag{6a}$$

and from (1)(2)(3)

$$g_{m1}v_{in}-G_{1}v_{x}-G_{2}v_{x}+g_{2}v_{o}=g_{T}v_{x}$$

$$g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{2}v_{o}=(G_{1}+G_{2}+g_{T})v_{x}\tag{7}$$

With (6)

$$g_{m1}v_{in}=v_{o}\left[(G_{1}+G_{2}+g_{T})
{{1/R_{D}+g_{2}}\over {G_{2}}}-g_{2}\right]$$

$${{v_{o}}\over {v_{in}}}=
{{g_{m1}G_{2}R_{D}}\over {G_{1}+G_{2}+g_{T}+g_{2}R_{D}(G_{1}+g_{T})}}
\tag{8}$$

For the ideal tail $g_{T}\rightarrow 0$

$$A_{v}\equiv {{v_{o}}\over {v_{in}}}=
{{g_{m1}G_{2}R_{D}}\over {G_{1}+G_{2}+G_{1}g_{2}R_{D}}}\tag{8a}$$

$$G_{i}=g_{mi}+g_{mbi}+g_{i}$$

In most hand calculations $g_{i}R_{D}\ll 1$ and

$$A_{v}\approx {{g_{m1}G_{2}R_{D}}\over {G_{1}+G_{2}}}\tag{9}$$

$$A_{v}\approx g_{m1}R_{D}{{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}\over
{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}}\tag{9a}$$

apart from the sign.  With the sign convention
$i_{d}$ into the drain

$$-v_{o}/R_{D}=i_{d2}\;\;,\;\;i_{d2}\downarrow {\rm when}\;
v_{in}\uparrow $$

so that $v_{o}$ goes {\it up} when $v_{in}$ goes up.
With the usual $v_{o}=-i_{d2}R_{D}$ convention

$$A_{v}= -{{g_{m1}G_{2}R_{D}}\over {G_{1}+G_{2}}}$$

and the magnitude is (9).  I. e. the circuit is the
long tailed pair with the drain of ${\rm M}_{1}$
strapped to ${\rm a.c.}$ ground and taken single ended
on the drain of ${\rm M}_{2}$.

Neglecting body effect, $g_{mb}=0$,

$$A_{v}\approx {{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D}}\over {g_{m1}+g_{m2}}}
\tag{10}$$

and for the normally matched design $g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_{m}$,
$g_{mb1}=g_{mb2}$,

$$|A_{v}|\approx {{g_{m}R_{D}}\over 2}
{{1}\over {1+g_{2}R_{D}/2}}\approx {{g_{m}R_{D}}\over 2}
\qquad R_{D}\ll r_{o}\tag{11}$$

$$|A_{v}|\approx {{g_{m}}\over {g_{m1}+g_{m2}}}g_{m2}R_{D}$$

is the ${\rm CD}$ gain

$$A_{1}={{v_{x}}\over {v_{in}}}={{g_{m1}}\over {G_{1}+G_{2}}}
\approx {{g_{m1}}\over {g_{m1}+g_{m2}}}\approx {1\over 2}\tag{12}$$

times the ${\rm CG}$ gain

$$A_{2}={{v_{o}}\over {v_{x}}}= (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})R_{D}\tag{13}$$

to first order.  More exactly

$$A_{2}={{G_{2}}\over {1/R_{D}+g_{2}}}\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})
R_{D}\parallel r_{o2}\tag{13a}$$

The transconductance of the composite stage is

$$G_{m}={{i_{o}}\over {v_{in}}}={{A_{v}}\over {R_{D}}}
\approx {{g_{m1}g_{m2}}\over {g_{m1}+g_{m2}}}\approx {{g_{m}}\over 2}
\tag{14}$$

for the matched case, one half the $g_{m}$ of a
conventional common source with the same $R_{D}$.
The differential $g_{m}$ is $g_{m}/2$ because the
tail current $I_{1}$ is split between the two devices.
At the bias point $V_{in}=V_{b}$

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{1}/2\qquad 
g_{mi}= \sqrt{2\mu C_{ox}(W/L)_{i}I_{Di}}=
\sqrt{\mu C_{ox}(W/L)_{i}I_{1}} \tag{15}$$

in square law, $g_{mi}\propto \sqrt{I_{1}}$.

> {\it Remarks:}  Put $R_{S}=1/G_{1}\parallel R_{T}$ for the
> impedance looking into the source of ${\rm M}_{1}$ with
> gate and drain ${\rm a.c.}\;0$,
> $$Z_{x}= {1\over {g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{1}}}\parallel R_{T}
> \approx {1\over {g_{m1}+g_{mb1}}}\tag{16}$$
> The impedance looking into the source of the ${\rm CG}$
> is $1/(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})$.  The ${\rm CD}$ is loaded by
> $1/(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})$, hence (12).  This is the usual
> intuition: low $Z$ load for the follower, high $Z$ load
> $R_{D}$ for the ${\rm CG}$.

Input impedance: gate of ${\rm M}_{1}$

$$Z_{in}=1/sC_{gs1}\rightarrow \infty \;{\rm at\;d.c.}\tag{17}$$

Output impedance: $v_{in}=0$, look into drain of
${\rm M}_{2}$ with source degeneration $R_{S}=Z_{x}$.

For a ${\rm CG}$ with source resistance $R_{S}$ to ground

$$R_{o2}=r_{o2}+ \left[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right]R_{S}\tag{18}$$

$$R_{S}=Z_{x}= {1\over {G_{1}}}\parallel R_{T}\tag{19}$$

so that

$$R_{o}=R_{D}\parallel R_{o2}
      =R_{D}\parallel \left\{r_{o2}+
      \left[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right]
      \left({1\over {G_{1}}}\parallel R_{T}\right)\right\}\tag{20}$$

For $R_{T}\rightarrow \infty ,\;r_{o1}=r_{o2}=r_{o}$,
$g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_{m}$,

$$R_{o2}\approx r_{o}+ (1+g_{m}r_{o}){1\over {g_{m}}}
      \approx 2r_{o}\tag{21}$$

$$R_{o}\approx R_{D}\parallel 2r_{o}\approx R_{D}\qquad 
R_{D}\ll r_{o}\tag{22}$$

With body effect $R_{o2}\approx r_{o}[1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})/g_{m}]
\approx 2r_{o}$ to $3r_{o}$.

Frequency response: dominant pole at the output

$$\omega _{p1}\approx {1\over {R_{o}C_{L}}}\qquad 
C_{L}=C_{db2}+C_{gd2}+C_{ext}\tag{23}$$

second pole at the common source node

$$\omega _{p2}\approx {{G_{1}+G_{2}+g_{T}}\over {C_{x}}}\approx
{{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}\over {C_{x}}}\tag{24}$$

$$C_{x}=C_{gs1}+C_{sb1}+C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{T}$$

$Z_{x}\approx 1/g_{m}$ is low, so $\omega _{p2}$ is
normally non dominant, $\omega _{p2}\gg \omega _{p1}$.
No Miller multiplication, wide band, cascode like.

Large signal: for $|v_{id}|=|V_{in}-V_{b}|\ll
\sqrt{I_{1}/\beta }$, $\beta =\mu C_{ox}W/L$,

$$I_{D2}= {I_{1}\over 2}-{{g_{m}}\over 2}v_{id}\tag{25}$$
$$V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_{D}=V_{DD}-{I_{1}R_{D}\over 2}
+{{g_{m}R_{D}}\over 2}v_{id}\tag{26}$$

For $|v_{id}|> \sqrt{I_{1}/\beta }$ one device cuts off,
$I_{D2}=0$ or $I_{1}$, $V_{out}=V_{DD}$ or $V_{DD}-I_{1}R_{D}$.
Saturation requires

$$V_{DS1}=V_{DD}-V_{x}\ge V_{GS1}-V_{Tn}\;\; \Rightarrow\;\;
V_{in}\le V_{DD}+V_{Tn}\tag{27}$$
$$V_{DS2}=V_{out}-V_{x}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{Tn}\;\; \Rightarrow\;\;
V_{out}\ge V_{b}-V_{Tn}\tag{28}$$
$$V_{x}=V_{in}-V_{GS1}\ge V_{DSAT,T}+0\tag{29}$$

for the tail source to stay in saturation.  $V_{b}$ is
normally chosen $\approx V_{in,CM}$ so that at balance
$V_{DS1}\approx V_{DS2}$.

Common mode gain with finite $R_{T}$,

$$A_{cm}\approx -{{R_{D}}\over {2R_{T}}}{{g_{m}r_{o}}\over {1+g_{m}r_{o}}}
\approx -{{R_{D}}\over {2R_{T}}}\tag{30}$$

$$CMRR\approx g_{m}R_{T}\tag{31}$$

In words: a non inverting single ended long tailed pair,
a source follower driving a common gate, voltage gain
one half that of a simple $CS$ stage with the same $R_{D}$,
$R_{in}=\infty $, $R_{out}\approx R_{D}$, high
$\omega _{p2}$, good high frequency performance.  Any
finite $r_{o}$ and $g_{mb}$ simply replace $g_{m}$ by
$G=g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{o}$ as in (8).  For $r_{o}\rightarrow
\infty $ and matched devices the body effect cancels to
first order and $|A_{v}|=g_{m}R_{D}/2$.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in Figure 21 can be inductive.

answer.text:
With $V_{i}=0$ for $Z_{o}$ put $V_{x}$ on the
source and measure $I_{x}$.

$$\eqalign{
Z_{o}=V_{x}/I_{x}{\Bigl |}_{V_{i}=0}\cr
M_{2}=g_{o2}+sC_{o2}\approx g_{o2}=1/r_{o2}}$$

For $M_{1}$ keep $C_{gs},C_{gd},g_{m},g_{mb},g_{o1}$.

$$\eqalign{
V_{d1}=0\;\;V_{g}=V_{g1}\;\;V_{s}=V_{x}}$$

{\it Gate node:}

$$ {V_{g}\over R_{S}}+sC_{gd}V_{g}+sC_{gs}(V_{g}-V_{x})=0 \tag{1}$$

$$V_{g}=V_{x}{sC_{gs}R_{S}\over 1+sR_{S}(C_{gs}+C_{gd})}
      =V_{x}{sC_{gs}\over g_{S}+s(C_{gs}+C_{gd})}\tag{2}$$
$g_{S}=1/R_{S}$.  The gate is a low pass on $V_{x}$,
$\omega _{g}=1/R_{S}(C_{gs}+C_{gd})$.  For
$\omega \ll \omega _{g}\;\;V_{g}\approx sC_{gs}R_{S}V_{x}$,
for $\omega \gg \omega _{g}\;\;V_{g}\approx
C_{gs}/(C_{gs}+C_{gd})V_{x}$.

{\it Source node:} $I_{x}$ into the node, $I_{d1}$ into
the node from $M_{1}$.

$$I_{d1}=g_{m}V_{gs}+g_{mb}V_{bs}+g_{o1}V_{ds}+sC_{gs}(V_{g}-V_{x})$$

with $V_{gs}=V_{g}-V_{x}$, $V_{ds}=-V_{x}$,
$V_{bs}=-V_{x}$ if body to ground, $g_{m}^{\prime}=g_{m}+g_{mb}$,

$$I_{d1}=g_{m}^{\prime}(V_{g}-V_{x})-g_{o1}V_{x}+sC_{gs}(V_{g}-V_{x})$$

KCL at $V_{x}$:

$$I_{x}+I_{d1}=g_{o2}V_{x}+sC_{o2}V_{x}\approx g_{o2}V_{x}$$

$$I_{x}= -g_{m}^{\prime}(V_{g}-V_{x})+g_{o1}V_{x}
        -sC_{gs}(V_{g}-V_{x})+g_{o2}V_{x} \tag{3}$$

$$I_{x}=V_{x}(g_{o1}+g_{o2}+g_{m}^{\prime}+sC_{gs})
       -V_{g}(g_{m}^{\prime}+sC_{gs})$$

With (2)

$${I_{x}\over V_{x}}=g_{o1}+g_{o2}+g_{m}^{\prime}+sC_{gs}
      -{sC_{gs}R_{S}\over 1+sR_{S}(C_{gs}+C_{gd})}
        (g_{m}^{\prime}+sC_{gs}) \tag{4}$$

$${V_{x}\over I_{x}}=
{1+sR_{S}(C_{gs}+C_{gd})\over 
g_{m}^{\prime}+g_{o1}+g_{o2}+sC_{gs}
+sR_{S}(C_{gs}+C_{gd})(g_{o1}+g_{o2})
+sR_{S}C_{gd}(g_{m}^{\prime}+sC_{gs})} \tag{5}$$

Neglect $g_{o}$ and $C_{gd}$ for the essence, $C_{gd}\ll C_{gs}$,

$$Z_{o}\approx {1+sC_{gs}R_{S}\over g_{m}^{\prime}+sC_{gs}}
      ={1\over g_{m}^{\prime}}{1+s\tau _{z}\over 1+s\tau _{p}} \tag{6}$$

$$\tau _{z}=R_{S}C_{gs}\qquad 
  \tau _{p}=C_{gs}/g_{m}^{\prime}$$

$$Z_{o}\approx {1\over g_{m}^{\prime}}
{1+j\omega R_{S}C_{gs}\over 1+j\omega C_{gs}/g_{m}^{\prime}} \tag{7}$$

i. e. a zero at $\omega _{z}=1/R_{S}C_{gs}$ and a pole at
$\omega _{p}=g_{m}^{\prime}/C_{gs}= \omega _{T}$.

If $R_{S}=0$, $\tau _{z}=0$,

$$Z_{o}={1\over g_{m}^{\prime}+sC_{gs}}={1/g_{m}^{\prime}\over 1+sC_{gs}/g_{m}^{\prime}}$$

capacitive, $|Z_{o}|$ falls with $\omega $.

If $R_{S}\ne 0$ and

$$R_{S} > 1/g_{m}^{\prime}\;\;{\rm i.e.}\;\;\tau _{z}>\tau _{p}\tag{8}$$

the zero is at a {\it lower} frequency than the pole.
For $\omega _{z}<\omega <\omega _{p}$

$$Z_{o}\approx {1\over g_{m}^{\prime}}
\left[1+j\omega (R_{S}C_{gs}-C_{gs}/g_{m}^{\prime})\right]
\left[1-j\omega C_{gs}/g_{m}^{\prime}\cdots\right]$$

to first order in $\omega $,

$$Z_{o}\approx {1\over g_{m}^{\prime}+g_{o1}+g_{o2}}
      +j\omega {C_{gs}\left(R_{S}-1/g_{m}^{\prime}\right)
                \over g_{m}^{\prime}} \tag{9}$$

more exactly from (5)

$$Z_{o}\approx R_{o}+j\omega L_{o}\qquad 
  R_{o}={1\over g_{m}^{\prime}}\parallel r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$$

$$L_{o}\approx {R_{S}C_{gs}\over g_{m}^{\prime}}
      ={ \tau _{z}\over g_{m}^{\prime}}\;\;{\rm for}\;R_{S}\gg 1/g_{m}^{\prime} \tag{10}$$

$$L_{o}={C_{gs}\over g_{m}^{\prime 2}}\left(g_{m}^{\prime}R_{S}-1\right)$$

in parallel with $C_{o}=C_{gs}+C_{gd}+C_{db1}+C_{db2}+C_{L}$.
With $C_{gd}$ kept,

$$L_{o}\approx {R_{S}C_{gs}\over g_{m}^{\prime}}
      {1\over 1+g_{o}R_{S}}\;\;,\;\;
  R_{o}\approx {1\over g_{m}^{\prime}}\parallel r_{o}$$

and (5) is $R_{o}+sL_{o}$ in parallel with $1/sC_{o}$ to
second order.  At very high frequency $s\to\infty$,

$$Z_{o}\to {1\over s}{C_{gs}+C_{gd}\over C_{gs}C_{gd}}$$

capacitive again, so the impedance is inductive in the
mid band $\omega _{g}<\omega <\omega _{T}$ and peaks with
a capacitive load $C_{L}$ as $1/\sqrt{L_{o}C_{L}}$.

Physically $C_{gs}$ feeds $V_{x}$ back to the gate through
$R_{S}$.  The gate cannot follow $V_{x}$ instantaneously.
$V_{g}=V_{x}sC_{gs}R_{S}/(1+sC_{gs}R_{S})$ lags $V_{x}$.
Hence $V_{gs}=V_{g}-V_{x}$ grows with frequency with a
phase lead, the $g_{m}V_{gs}$ current lags the applied
voltage $V_{x}$ - the definition of an inductance.
The $g_{m}$ converts the capacitance $C_{gs}$ to an
inductance $C_{gs}R_{S}/g_{m}$ - a gyrator action.
Dual to the inductive input impedance of a common gate
stage with capacitive load.

With a capacitive load $C_{L}$ the follower is a series
$R_{o}L_{o}C_{L}$ circuit, $Q\approx \sqrt{L_{o}/C_{L}}/R_{o}$,
hence frequency peaking, ringing and possible oscillation.
Normally compensated by a small series $R$ or by making
$R_{S}g_{m}^{\prime}<1$.  In the ideal $R_{S}=0$ case the
inductance vanishes.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 22.

answer.text:
With ${\rm M}_{1}$ as $A$ and ${\rm M}_{2}$ as
$\beta $ the circuit is the conventional shunt at the
input, shunt at the output, Fig.1, but with two
inversions in the loop.

$$\eqalign{
A: & V_{o}=-g_{m1}R_{D}^{\prime}V_{x}\cr
\beta :& I_{f}=g_{m2}V_{o}+g_{o2}V_{x}\cr}
\qquad R_{D}^{\prime}=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\;\;,\;\;g_{o2}=r_{o2}^{-1}$$

so that $A\beta >0$.  In normal $y$ parameter
language

* sampling: $V_{o}$ in parallel with $R_{D1}$
* mixing: $I_{f}$ in parallel with $I_{in}$ at $X$

$$I_{in}=I_{f}\;\;{\rm for}\;\;r_{o}=\infty $$

is a current--voltage, transimpedance, $R_{M}=V_{o}/I_{in}$,
shunt--shunt feed back amplifier with {\it positive}
feed back.

Small signal Fig.2 with $V_{DD}=ac\;0$

$$\eqalign{
{\rm M}_{1}:& i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{x}+g_{o1}v_{o}\cr
{\rm M}_{2}:& i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{o}+g_{o2}v_{x}\cr}$$

$$v_{o}=-i_{d1}R_{D1}\tag{1}$$
$$I_{in}=i_{d2}\tag{2}$$
for $r_{o}\to \infty $ the familiar form.  In nodal
form

$${\rm O}: {v_{o}\over R_{D1}}+g_{o1}v_{o}+g_{m1}v_{x}=0\tag{3}$$
$${\rm X}: I_{in}=g_{m2}v_{o}+g_{o2}v_{x}\tag{4}$$

so that from (3)

$$v_{o}=-{g_{m1}\over G_{D}^{\prime}}v_{x}\tag{5}$$

$$G_{D}^{\prime}={1\over R_{D1}}+g_{o1}={1\over R_{D}^{\prime}}$$

is the ordinary $CS$ gain

$$A_{v}\equiv {v_{o}\over v_{x}}=-g_{m1}R_{D}^{\prime}\tag{6}$$

and from (4)-(5)

$$I_{in}=v_{x}\left[g_{o2}-g_{m2}g_{m1}R_{D}^{\prime}\right] \tag{7}$$

$${\cal R}_{M}\equiv {v_{o}\over I_{in}}=
-{g_{m1}R_{D}^{\prime}\over g_{o2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D}^{\prime}}
={g_{m1}R_{D}^{\prime}\over g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D}^{\prime}-g_{o2}} \tag{8}$$

$${\cal R}_{M}={g_{m1}R_{D}^{\prime}r_{o2}\over
g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D}^{\prime}r_{o2}-1}
={g_{m1}R_{D}^{\prime}r_{o2}\over T-1}\tag{9}$$

$$Z_{x}\equiv {v_{x}\over I_{in}}={1\over g_{o2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D}^{\prime}}
={r_{o2}\over 1-T}\tag{10}$$

where the {\it return ratio} or loop gain is

$$T=g_{m1}R_{D}^{\prime}g_{m2}r_{o2}>0\tag{11}$$

$$T\approx g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}r_{o2}\;\;{\rm for}\;\;r_{o1}\gg R_{D1}$$

It is $>0$ because the loop contains two $CS$
inversions.  $v_{x}\uparrow \to v_{o}\downarrow \to
i_{d2}\downarrow \to $ less current subtracted from $X\to
v_{x}\uparrow $ - regenerative.

In the conventional $1-A\beta $ notation

$$1-A\beta =1-T\tag{12}$$

with

$$A=-g_{m1}R_{D}^{\prime}\qquad \beta =-{I_{f}\over V_{o}}=-g_{m2}$$

so that $A\beta =+T$.  Eq.8 can be written as

$${\cal R}_{M}={A\,r_{o2}\over 1-A\beta } \tag{13}$$

and for $T\gg 1$

$${\cal R}_{M}\approx {1\over g_{m2}}\tag{14}$$

$${\cal R}_{M,{\rm id}}={1\over \beta }={1\over g_{m2}}$$

the ideal shunt--shunt closed loop transimpedance
with infinite loop gain.  The sign is {\it positive}:
a positive $I_{in}$ injected into $X$ raises $V_{o}$.
For $T<1$ the denominator $1-T>0$ and (8) is
negative, the ordinary $CS$ sign $v_{o}=-g_{m1}R_{D}^{\prime}
v_{x}$ dominates.  At $T=1$ the denominator vanishes.

The same denominator appears in the terminal
impedances.  By Blackman, or directly, put a test
source $v_{t}$ at the output with $I_{in}=0$, $ac$
open,

$${\rm X}:0=g_{m2}v_{t}+g_{o2}v_{x}\;\;,\;\;v_{x}=-{g_{m2}\over g_{o2}}v_{t}\tag{15}$$

$${\rm O}:I_{t}={v_{t}\over R_{D1}}+g_{o1}v_{t}+g_{m1}v_{x}
=v_{t}\left[G_{D}^{\prime}-g_{m1}{g_{m2}\over g_{o2}}\right]\tag{16}$$

$$Z_{o}\equiv {v_{t}\over I_{t}}={1\over G_{D}^{\prime}
-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}={R_{D}^{\prime}\over 1-T}\tag{17}$$

$$Z_{o}= {R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\over 1-g_{m1}g_{m2}
\left(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\right)r_{o2}}\tag{18}$$

and (10)

$$Z_{in}=Z_{x}={r_{o2}\over 1-T}\tag{19}$$

For $T>1$ both driving point impedances are {\it
negative}.  With $r_{o}\to \infty $

$$Z_{in}\approx -{1\over g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D}^{\prime}}\qquad
Z_{o}\approx -{1\over g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}\tag{20}$$

The circuit is a negative resistance one port at
both ports.  It can be used to cancel loss in a
tuned load, as an active inductor, or, with $T>1$,
as a latch.

Indeed with $C_{x}$ at $X$ and $C_{o}$ at the output

$$(1+sC_{x}r_{o2})(1+sC_{o}R_{D}^{\prime})-T=0\tag{21}$$

is the characteristic equation.  The poles are

$$p_{1,2}\approx {1\over 2}\left[{1\over C_{x}r_{o2}}+
{1\over C_{o}R_{D}^{\prime}}\right]\pm
\sqrt{{1\over 4}\left[{1\over C_{x}r_{o2}}-
{1\over C_{o}R_{D}^{\prime}}\right]^{2}+{T\over C_{x}C_{o}
r_{o2}R_{D}^{\prime}}}\tag{22}$$

For $T>1$ one pole moves into the right half plane.
The linear circuit is unstable.  For $T<1$ it is a
stable regenerative amplifier whose effective load

$$R_{D,{\rm eff}}={R_{D}^{\prime}\over 1-T}\tag{23}$$

is enhanced as $T\to 1^{-}$, giving

$$A_{v,cl}={v_{o}\over v_{x}}=-{g_{m1}R_{D}^{\prime}\over 1-T}\tag{24}$$

very large voltage gain at the expense of stability
and process sensitivity.  Normally with long channel
$r_{o2}\sim 10-50\,{\rm k\Omega }$, $g_{m}\sim 1\,{\rm mS}$,
$R_{D1}\sim {\rm k\Omega }$,

$$T\sim g_{m}^{2}R_{D1}r_{o2}\sim 10-100\gg 1$$

so the small signal linear model is not stable.

Large signal: in saturation, $\lambda =0$,

$$\eqalign{
I_{D1}&={k_{1}\over 2}(V_{x}-V_{T})^{2}\cr
I_{D2}&={k_{2}\over 2}(V_{o}-V_{T})^{2}\cr
V_{o}&=V_{DD}-I_{D1}R_{D1}\cr
I_{in}&=I_{D2}\cr}\tag{25}$$

so that nominally

$$V_{o}=V_{T}+\sqrt{2I_{in}/k_{2}}\tag{26}$$

$$V_{x}=V_{T}+\sqrt{2(V_{DD}-V_{o})/k_{1}R_{D1}}\tag{27}$$

monotonic with positive slope $1/g_{m2}$, Eq.14.
In reality ${\rm M}_{1}$ enters triode for large
$V_{x}$ or small $V_{o}$, ${\rm M}_{2}$ cuts off for
small $V_{o}$, and the $I_{in}-V_{o}$ curve becomes
S-shaped with two stable branches

* ${\rm M}_{1}$ on, $V_{o}$ low, ${\rm M}_{2}$ off,
  $I_{in}\approx 0$
* ${\rm M}_{1}$ off, $V_{o}\approx V_{DD}$, ${\rm M}_{2}$
  on, $I_{in}=I_{D2}(V_{DD})$

and an unstable middle branch where (8) applies.
Driven by a finite source resistance $R_{S}$,
$T\to g_{m1}R_{D}^{\prime}g_{m2}(r_{o2}\parallel R_{S})$,
the circuit shows hysteresis - a current mode
Schmitt trigger / latch.  The switching thresholds
are obtained from $dI_{in}/dV_{o}=0$ including
triode.

With $R_{S}$ the loop gain can be made $<1$ and the
circuit becomes a stable transimpedance stage with

$$R_{M}\approx -g_{m1}R_{D}^{\prime}R_{S}\;\;T\ll 1\tag{28}$$

to

$$R_{M}\approx +1/g_{m2}\;\;T\gg 1\tag{29}$$

crossing through infinity at $T=1$.

Inclusion of body effect replaces $g_{m}$ by
$g_{m}+g_{mb}$ and $r_{o}$ by $r_{o}\parallel r_{mb}$,
increasing $T$.  Any capacitance at $X$ or at the
output adds the poles (21) and for $T>1$ the circuit
oscillates at $\omega _{o}\approx 1/\sqrt{C_{x}C_{o}
r_{o2}R_{D}^{\prime}}$ if the negative resistance
cancels the tank loss.

> {\it In short: shunt--shunt positive feedback with
> loop gain $T=g_{m1}g_{m2}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})r_{o2}$.
> Closed loop $V_{o}/I_{in}=g_{m1}R_{D}^{\prime}/
> (g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D}^{\prime}-g_{o2})\to 1/g_{m2}$ for
> $T\gg 1$, $Z_{in}=r_{o2}/(1-T)$, $Z_{o}=R_{D}^{\prime}/
> (1-T)$ negative for $T>1$.  $T=1$ is the boundary
> between a high gain regenerative amplifier and a
> bistable latch/negative-$R$ oscillator.  Practical
> long channel values give $T\gg 1$, i.e. a current
> controlled latch - Schmitt trigger - with hysteresis,
> useful as comparator, level shifter or loss
> cancellation element, not as a linear amplifier
> unless $T$ is degenerated to $<1$.}

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 23.

answer.text:
With the usual small signal model $V_{b}=0$

$${\rm M}_{1}:g_{m1},g_{mb1},r_{o1}\qquad 
{\rm M}_{2}:g_{m2},r_{o2}\qquad R_{1}=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}
\qquad R_{2}=R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}\tag{1}$$

put for brevity $g_{m1}^{\prime}=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$ if the
bulk of ${\rm M}_{1}$ is to ${\rm GND}$ and $g_{m1}^{\prime}=g_{m1}$
if the bulk is to the source, Fig.1.  In the figure
$g_{mb1}=0$.

$$\eqalign{
I_{M1}&=g_{m1}^{\prime}V_{gs1}+g_{ds1}V_{ds1}
      =-g_{m1}^{\prime}V_{A}+g_{ds1}(V_{X}-V_{A})\cr
I_{M2}&=g_{m2}V_{X}+g_{ds2}V_{out}} \tag{2}$$

$$V_{gs1}=-V_{A}\qquad V_{ds1}=V_{X}-V_{A}\qquad 
V_{gs2}=V_{X}\qquad V_{ds2}=V_{out} $$

KCL at the three signal nodes, $V_{DD}=0$ for signals,

$$\eqalign{
X:&\;\;{-V_{X}\over R_{D1}}=I_{M1} \tag{3a}\cr
out:&\;\;{-V_{out}\over R_{D2}}+{V_{A}-V_{out}\over R_{F}}=I_{M2}
      \tag{3b}\cr
A:&\;\;I_{in}+I_{M1}={V_{A}-V_{out}\over R_{F}} \tag{3c}}$$

(3a) is the CG stage

$${V_{X}\over R_{D1}}+g_{ds1}V_{X}-g_{m1}^{\prime}V_{A}
      -g_{ds1}V_{A}=0$$

$$V_{X}\left({1\over R_{D1}}+g_{ds1}\right)=V_{A}
      \left(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\right) \tag{4}$$

$$V_{X}=aV_{A}\qquad 
a={g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\over g_{ds1}+1/R_{D1}}
      =\left(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\right)R_{1}\approx g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{1}
      \tag{5}$$

$$I_{M1}=-{V_{X}\over R_{D1}}=-{a\over R_{D1}}V_{A} \tag{6}$$

is the familiar $A_{v1}=V_{X}/V_{A}\approx +g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{1}$
non inverting CG gain.  Put

$${1\over R_{2}}={1\over R_{D2}}+g_{ds2}\qquad 
b={1\over R_{2}}+{1\over R_{F}}={1\over R_{2}\parallel R_{F}} \tag{7}$$

(3b)(3c) become

$$\eqalign{
{V_{A}\over R_{F}}&=V_{out}b+g_{m2}V_{X} \tag{8a}\cr
I_{in}&={V_{A}-V_{out}\over R_{F}}-{I_{M1}}
      =V_{A}\left({1\over R_{F}}+{a\over R_{D1}}\right)-{V_{out}\over R_{F}}
      \tag{8b}}$$

Eliminating $V_{A}=V_{X}/a$,

$$V_{A}={b\over 1/R_{F}-g_{m2}a}V_{out} \tag{9}$$

and from (8b)

$$I_{in}=V_{out}\left[{b\left(1/R_{F}+a/R_{D1}\right)
      \over 1/R_{F}-g_{m2}a}-{1\over R_{F}}\right] \tag{10}$$

i. e. in closed form

$${V_{out}\over I_{in}}=
{{1\over R_{F}}-g_{m2}a\over 
      {ab\over R_{D1}}+{b\over R_{F}}+{g_{m2}a\over R_{F}}-{1\over R_{F}^{2}}}
      ={{1\over R_{F}}-g_{m2}a\over 
      {ab\over R_{D1}}+{1/R_{2}+g_{m2}a\over R_{F}}} \tag{11}$$

$${V_{out}\over I_{in}}=
-{g_{m2}aR_{F}-1\over g_{m2}a+{1\over R_{2}}+{abR_{F}\over R_{D1}}}
      \approx -R_{F}{g_{m2}aR_{F}\over g_{m2}aR_{F}+abR_{F}^{2}/R_{D1}+R_{F}/R_{2}}
      \tag{12}$$

For

$$g_{m2}aR_{F}\gg 1\qquad g_{m2}a\gg {1\over R_{2}},{abR_{F}\over R_{D1}} \tag{13}$$

$$R_{M}\equiv {V_{out}\over I_{in}}\approx -R_{F} \tag{14}$$

the well known shunt-shunt result.  Keeping the first order
correction,

$$R_{M}\approx -R_{F}{1\over 1+{1\over T}}
      =-R_{F}{T\over 1+T}\qquad 
T\approx {g_{m2}a\over abR_{F}/R_{D1}+1/R_{2}} \tag{15}$$

is the loop gain.  With $R_{F}\gg R_{2}$ and $r_{o}\gg R_{D}$,

$$a\approx g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{D1}\qquad b\approx {1\over R_{2}}\qquad 
R_{M0}\equiv \left.{V_{out}\over I_{in}}\right|_{{\rm open}}=
-{g_{m2}a\over b\left(1/R_{F}+a/R_{D1}\right)}
      \approx -g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{2} \tag{16}$$

is the open loop transimpedance with the $Y$ loading of the
feedback network, $R_{F}$ to ground at the input and at the
output, Fig.2.  Indeed for shunt-shunt

$$Y_{F}=\pmatrix{1/R_{F}&-1/R_{F}\cr -1/R_{F}&1/R_{F}} \tag{17}$$

so that the forward amplifier is loaded by $1/R_{F}$ at
$A$ and at the output.  The feedback factor is

$$\beta ={I_{f}\over V_{out}}\approx -{1\over R_{F}} \tag{18}$$

$$I_{f}={V_{out}-V_{A}\over R_{F}}\approx {V_{out}\over R_{F}}$$

with the sign such that

$$T=-\beta R_{M0}\approx {g_{m2}R_{1}R_{2}\over R_{F}}
      \approx {g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{1}R_{2}\over 1+g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{F}}
      \tag{19}$$

More exactly from (15)

$$T={g_{m2}a\over bR_{F}\left(1/R_{F}+a/R_{D1}\right)}
      ={g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{1}R_{2}\over 
      \left(1+R_{2}/R_{F}\right)\left(1+g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{F}R_{1}/R_{D1}\right)}
      \tag{20}$$

For $g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{F}\gg 1$, $T\approx g_{m2}R_{1}R_{2}/R_{F}$.
The forward voltage gain is

$$A_{v0}={V_{out}\over V_{A}}= -g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{1}g_{m2}R_{2} \tag{21}$$

and $R_{M0}=A_{v0}Z_{in0}$ with

$$Z_{in0}={V_{A}\over I_{in}}\Bigl|_{{\rm open}}=
{1\over 1/R_{F}+a/R_{D1}}\approx {1\over g_{m1}^{\prime}} \tag{22}$$

the normal $1/g_{m}$ input impedance of the CG stage loaded by
$R_{F}$.

In closed loop Blackman gives

$$Z_{in}=Z_{in0}{1+T_{sc}\over 1+T_{oc}}\approx {Z_{in0}\over 1+T}
      \qquad 
  Z_{out}=Z_{out0}{1+T_{sc}\over 1+T_{oc}}\approx {Z_{out0}\over 1+T}
      \tag{23}$$

where $T_{sc}$ is the loop gain with the port shorted and
$T_{oc}$ with the port opened.  For shunt-shunt both ports are
shunt so that $Z$ is divided by $1+T$.

Hence

$$R_{in}\equiv {V_{A}\over I_{in}}={b\over D}
      ={1\over a/R_{D1}+ \left(1/R_{2}+g_{m2}a\right)/bR_{F}}
      \approx {1\over g_{m1}^{\prime}\left(1+T\right)}
      \approx {R_{F}\over g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{1}R_{2}} \tag{24}$$

$$R_{out}\equiv {V_{test}\over I_{test}}\Bigl|_{I_{in}=0}
      ={1\over b+{g_{m2}a\over 1+aR_{F}/R_{D1}}}
      \approx {1\over 1/R_{2}+g_{m2}R_{1}/R_{F}}
      ={R_{2}\over 1+g_{m2}R_{1}R_{2}/R_{F}}
      \approx {R_{F}\over g_{m2}R_{1}} \tag{25}$$

For $T\gg 1$

$$R_{in}\approx {R_{F}\over |A_{v0}|}\qquad 
  R_{out}\approx {R_{2}\over T}\approx {R_{F}\over g_{m2}R_{1}} \tag{26}$$

both very small, the virtual ground at the input is the
essence of the transimpedance amplifier.  With $r_{o}$ included
replace $R_{Di}$ by $R_{i}=R_{Di}\parallel r_{oi}$ and
$g_{m1}$ by $g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$ if the bulk is grounded.

In the ideal limit $T\to \infty$,

$$V_{A}\to 0\qquad I_{in}+{V_{out}\over R_{F}}\approx 0\qquad 
  V_{out}\approx -I_{in}R_{F}\tag{27}$$

$$i_{RF}={V_{A}-V_{out}\over R_{F}}\approx -{V_{out}\over R_{F}}\approx I_{in}$$

the whole signal current flows in $R_{F}$.

Frequency behaviour: $T(s)$ has the two poles

$$\omega_{pX}\approx {1\over R_{1}C_{X}}\qquad 
  \omega_{pout}\approx {1\over R_{2}C_{out}} \tag{28}$$

$C_{X}=C_{gs2}+C_{db1}+C_{gd1}$, $C_{out}=C_{db2}+C_{gd2}+C_{L}$,
plus the pole at the input $ \omega_{pA}\approx g_{m1}^{\prime}/C_{A}$,
$C_{A}=C_{gs1}+C_{sb1}+C_{pd}$, normally at very high frequency
because $R_{in}$ is small.  The loop gain therefore falls as
$1/s^{2}$ after $\min (\omega_{pX},\omega_{pout})$ and the
closed loop TIA is potentially unstable.  In practice a small
capacitor $C_{F}$ in parallel with $R_{F}$ is added to create a
left half plane zero $ \approx 1/R_{F}C_{F}$ and to make
$R_{F}\parallel 1/sC_{F}$ dominant, or $R_{D1},R_{D2}$ are chosen
so that $\omega_{pX}\gg \omega_{pout}$.

This is the classic wide band CMOS optical front end: the CG
${\rm M}_{1}$ gives a low $Z_{in}\approx 1/g_{m1}$ to absorb the
photodiode capacitance, the CS ${\rm M}_{2}$ gives the voltage
gain $g_{m2}R_{2}$, and $R_{F}$ sets the transimpedance to
$\approx R_{F}$ with a bandwidth $\approx (1+T)/R_{2}C_{out}$.
Any $g_{m}R\gg 1$ gives $R_{M}\to -R_{F}$, $R_{in}\to 0$,
$R_{out}\to 0$.  Including $r_{o}$ simply replaces $R_{D}$ by
$R_{D}\parallel r_{o}$ and $g_{m1}$ by $g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}$
in the above.  For $r_{o}\to \infty$, $R_{1}=R_{D1}$,
$R_{2}=R_{D2}$,

$$T_{0}\approx {g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}\over R_{F}},\;
  R_{M0}\approx -g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2},\;
  R_{M}\approx -R_{F}{T_{0}\over 1+T_{0}},\;
  R_{in}\approx {1\over g_{m1}}{1\over 1+T_{0}},\;
  R_{out}\approx {R_{D2}\over 1+T_{0}}$$

which is the textbook shunt-shunt result.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 24.

answer.text:
This is the shunt-shunt, $V-I$, transimpedance
feedback amplifier normally used as a low $Z_{in}$ wide
band TIA.  $M_{1}$ is the forward $CG$ stage,
$M_{2}$ is the $CS$ voltage sampling current mixing
feedback stage.

$$\eqalign{
M_{1}&:n{\rm MOS}\;\;S\equiv x\;,\;D\equiv o\;,\;G\equiv V_{b}{\rm ac\;gnd}\cr
M_{2}&:p{\rm MOS}\;\;S\equiv V_{DD}{\rm ac\;gnd}\;,\;D\equiv x\;,\;G\equiv o\cr
x&\equiv V_{x}\;\;{\rm input\;node}\cr
o&\equiv V_{out}\cr}$$

$$I_{1}:r_{I1}=1/g_{I1}\;\;{\rm to\;ac\;gnd}\qquad 
I_{B}:r_{B}=1/g_{B}\;\;{\rm to\;ac\;gnd\;at\;}x$$

Put in saturation

$$I_{D1}=I_{1}\qquad I_{D2}=I_{B}-I_{1}-I_{in}\approx I_{B}-I_{1}>0$$

$$V_{b}:V_{GS1}>V_{Tn}\;\;V_{DS1}>V_{GS1}-V_{Tn}$$
$$V_{SG2}>|V_{Tp}|\;\;V_{SD2}>V_{SG2}-|V_{Tp}|$$

Small signal, $\lambda \ne 0$, body neglected,
$g_{m1},g_{o1}=1/r_{o1}$, $g_{m2},g_{o2}=1/r_{o2}$

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{o1}v_{ds1}= -g_{m1}v_{x}+g_{o1}(v_{o}-v_{x}) \tag{1}$$
directed $D\to S$, i. e. $o\to x$, into $o$, out of $x$
into $x$.

$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{sg2}+g_{o2}v_{sd2}= -g_{m2}v_{o}-g_{o2}v_{x} \tag{2}$$
directed $S\to D$, i. e. $V_{DD}\to x$, into $x$.

KCL ac, $I_{in}$ into $x$, $I_{1},I_{B}$ ac open
except for $r_{I1},r_{B}$:

$$o: \;{v_{o}\over r_{I1}}+i_{d1}=0 \tag{3}$$
$$x: \;{v_{x}\over r_{B}}-i_{d1}-i_{d2}-I_{in}=0 \tag{4}$$
the $-i_{d1},-i_{d2}$ are the currents leaving $x$.

From (1)(3)

$$-{v_{o}\over r_{I1}}= -v_{x}(g_{m1}+g_{o1})+g_{o1}v_{o}$$

$$v_{o}=v_{x}{g_{m1}+g_{o1}\over g_{o1}+g_{I1}}=
v_{x}(g_{m1}+g_{o1})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{I1})\tag{5}$$

$$A_{v0}\equiv {v_{o}\over v_{x}}\approx g_{m1}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{I1})
\;\;{\rm for}\;g_{m1}\gg g_{o1},g_{I1}$$

the open $CG$ gain $x\to o$.

Put (5) in (4):

$$I_{in}=v_{x}\left(g_{B}+g_{m1}+g_{o1}+g_{o2}\right)
+v_{o}\left(g_{m2}-g_{o1}\right) \tag{6}$$

$$I_{in}=v_{x}\left[g_{B}+g_{m1}+g_{o1}+g_{o2}
+{g_{m1}+g_{o1}\over g_{o1}+g_{I1}}(g_{m2}-g_{o1})\right] \tag{7}$$

Hence

$$Z_{in}\equiv {v_{x}\over I_{in}}=
{1\over g_{B}+g_{m1}+g_{o1}+g_{o2}
+{\displaystyle {g_{m1}+g_{o1}\over g_{o1}+g_{I1}}(g_{m2}-g_{o1})}} \tag{8}$$

$$R_{m}\equiv {v_{o}\over I_{in}}=Z_{in}A_{v0}
={g_{m1}+g_{o1}\over 
(g_{o1}+g_{I1})(g_{B}+g_{m1}+g_{o1}+g_{o2})
+(g_{m1}+g_{o1})(g_{m2}-g_{o1})} \tag{9}$$

$${R_{m}={g_{m1}+g_{o1}\over 
g_{o1}g_{B}+g_{o1}g_{o2}+g_{I1}g_{B}+g_{I1}g_{o2}
+g_{m1}g_{I1}+g_{o1}g_{I1}+g_{m1}g_{m2}+g_{o1}g_{m2}}}$$

For $g_{m}\gg g_{o},g_{I},g_{B}$

$$R_{m}\approx {1\over g_{m2}}{T\over 1+T}\approx {1\over g_{m2}} \tag{10}$$

$$Z_{in}\approx {g_{o1}+g_{I1}\over g_{m1}g_{m2}}
={1\over g_{m1}g_{m2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{I1})}\approx
{1\over g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1}}\;\;r_{I1}\gg r_{o1} \tag{11}$$

i. e. the $CG$ input resistance $\approx 1/g_{m1}$
divided by the loop gain.  With $r_{B}\parallel r_{o2}$
finite

$$Z_{in}\approx {1\over g_{m1}g_{m2}(r_{o2}\parallel r_{B})}
{r_{o1}\parallel r_{I1}\over r_{o1}}\approx {1\over g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}$$

In the usual TIA notation $R_{m}= -R_{F}$,
$R_{F}=1/g_{m2}$ is the feedback transresistance,
$\beta = -g_{m2}= -1/R_{F}$.

Output resistance, $I_{in}=0$, test $v_{t}=v_{o}$ at $o$,
$i_{t}$ into $o$:

$$i_{t}={v_{t}\over r_{I1}}+i_{d1}\qquad 
{v_{x}\over r_{B}}-i_{d1}-i_{d2}=0$$

with (1)(2) gives

$$v_{x}=-v_{t}{g_{m2}-g_{o1}\over g_{B}+g_{m1}+g_{o1}+g_{o2}}$$

$$Z_{out}\equiv {v_{t}\over i_{t}}=
{1\over g_{o1}+g_{I1}+{\displaystyle 
(g_{m2}-g_{o1})(g_{m1}+g_{o1})\over g_{B}+g_{m1}+g_{o1}+g_{o2}}}
\tag{12}$$

$$\approx {1\over g_{m2}}\;\;{\rm for}\;g_{m1}\gg g_{B},g_{o}$$

More exactly $Z_{out}=Z_{out0}/(1+T)$ with
$Z_{out0}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{I1}$.

Feedback is shunt-shunt: voltage sampling at $o$,
current mixing at $x$.  Ideal shunt-shunt reduces
both $Z_{in}$ and $Z_{out}$ by $1+T$.

Loop gain by breaking at the high impedance gate of
$M_{2}$, $v_{t}$ injected at $G_{2}$, $v_{r}=v_{o}$
returned, $I_{in}$ ac open, $r_{B}$ loading $x$,
$r_{I1}$ loading $o$:

$$T=-{v_{r}\over v_{t}}=
{g_{m2}(g_{m1}+g_{o1})\over g_{o1}+g_{I1}}
{1\over g_{B}+g_{o2}+{\displaystyle {g_{m1}+g_{o1}\over 1+g_{o1}r_{I1}}}}
\tag{13}$$

$$T\approx g_{m2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{I1})(g_{m1}+g_{o1})
{1\over g_{B}+g_{o2}}\approx g_{m1}g_{m2}
(r_{o1}\parallel r_{I1})(r_{o2}\parallel r_{B}) \tag{14}$$

Typically $10-30\,{\rm dB}$ with finite $r_{I1},r_{B}$,
$\approx g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}\sim 40\,{\rm dB}$
for ideal current sources.  Then (10) is
$R_{m}=R_{m0}T/(1+T)$.

Frequency: with $C_{x}=C_{gs1}+C_{sb1}+C_{db2}+C_{gd2}+C_{in}$
at $x$ and $C_{o}=C_{gd1}+C_{db1}+C_{gs2}+C_{dbI1}$ at $o$

$$p_{x}\approx -{1\over Z_{in}C_{x}}\approx
-{g_{m1}g_{m2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{I1})\over C_{x}}$$

$$p_{o}\approx -{1\over Z_{out}C_{o}}\approx -{g_{m2}\over C_{o}}$$

Open loop $p_{x0}\approx -g_{m1}/C_{x}$,
$p_{o0}\approx -1/(r_{o1}\parallel r_{I1})C_{o}$.
Closing the loop pushes $p_{x}$ out by $1+T$.
The loop has two poles, $L(s)=T/(1+s/p_{x0})(1+s/p_{o0})$.
If $p_{x}\approx p_{o}$ peaking and poor phase margin
results.  Normally $C_{o}$ is made dominant,
$p_{o}<p_{x}$, or a compensation $C_{c}$ is added
at $o$.  Closed loop $-3\,{\rm dB}$ bandwidth
$\approx (1+T)p_{o0}\approx p_{x}$,
$\omega_{-3dB}\approx 1/R_{m}C_{tot}$,
i. e. wide band $\sim g_{m}/C$.

In words: a low $Z_{in}\sim 10^{2}\,\Omega$,
low $Z_{out}\sim 1/g_{m2}$, transresistance
$\sim 1/g_{m2}\sim 0.5-2\,{\rm k\Omega}$,
voltage gain $A_{v0}\sim g_{m1}r_{o1}$,
loop gain $\sim g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}$,
bandwidth extended by $1+T$ over the $CG$ stage.
It is the active feedback or regulated $CG$ TIA
used for photodiode / current input front ends.
Body effect replaces $g_{m1}\to g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$.
Noise $ \overline{i_{n,in}^{2}}\approx
4kT\gamma(g_{m1}+g_{m2})/g_{m2}^{2}+4kT/R_{B}+4kT/R_{I1}$
referred to input.  Increasing $g_{m2}$ lowers
$R_{m}$ but lowers $Z_{in}$ and widens band;
increasing $r_{o1},r_{o2}$ raises $T$ and lowers
$Z_{in}$.

answers.question: Does the circuit in Figure 5 fail to oscillate if the three capacitors become arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
With the usual idealisation the three $C_{L}$ are
just the three dominant poles of the loop.  Put
$R_{0}=r_{oN}\parallel r_{oP}$ and $A_{0}=g_{m}R_{0}$ for
the ${\rm d}{\rm c}$ gain of one ${\rm CMOS}$ inverter.
In the small signal sense

$${\cal L}(s)=\left[-{A_{0}\over {1+sR_{0}C_{L}}}\right]^{3}
      =-{A_{0}^{3}\over {\left(1+s/\omega _{p}\right)^{3}}}\qquad 
        \omega _{p}={1\over {R_{0}C_{L}}}\tag{*}$$

so that, with $s=j\omega $,

$$\eqalign{
|{\cal L}| &= {A_{0}^{3}\over {\left[1+(\omega /\omega _{p})^{2}
        \right]^{3/2}}}\cr
{\rm arg}{\cal L} &=3\pi -3{\rm arctg}\left(\omega /\omega _{p}\right)
        \;\;{\rm mod}\;2\pi .\cr}$$

${\rm arg}{\cal L}=0\,{\rm mod}\,2\pi $ for

$$3{\rm arctg}\left(\omega_{0}/\omega_{p}\right)=\pi \tag{**}$$

i. e.

$${\rm arctg}\left(\omega_{0}/\omega_{p}\right)=60^{{\rm o}}\qquad 
  \omega_{0}= \omega_{p}{\rm tg}60^{{\rm o}}=
        {{\sqrt{3}}\over {R_{0}C_{L}}} \tag{***}$$

and, at the $0\,{\rm mod}\,2\pi $ phase cross over,

$$|{\cal L}(j\omega_{0})|={A_{0}^{3}\over {\left[1+3\right]^{3/2}}}
      =\left({A_{0}\over 2}\right)^{3}\tag{****}$$

independent of $C_{L}$.  In particular the closed loop
poles, $1-{\cal L}(s)=0$,

$$\left(1+sR_{0}C_{L}\right)^{3}+A_{0}^{3}=0$$

are

$$sR_{0}C_{L}=-1-A_{0}e^{j2k\pi /3}\qquad k=0,1,2$$

i. e.

$$\eqalign{
s_{0}&=-{{1+A_{0}}\over {R_{0}C_{L}}}<0\cr
s_{1,2}&={{-1+A_{0}/2}\over {R_{0}C_{L}}}\pm j{{A_{0}\sqrt{3}/2}
        \over {R_{0}C_{L}}} \cr}$$

so that the ${\rm d}{\rm c}$ equilibrium $V_{1}=V_{2}=V_{3}=
V_{M}$ is unstable and the circuit is regenerative iff,
in the small signal sense,

$$A_{0}>2\tag{\dagger}$$

and, in the large signal, logic, sense $A_{0}\to \infty $,
iff $N\ge 3$ is odd, irrespective of the value of
$C_{L}>0$.  $C_{L}$ only normalises the frequency,
$(***)$, and the start up time constant,
${\rm Re}\,s_{1,2}^{-1}\propto R_{0}C_{L}$.

In the logic idealisation the large signal period is

$$T_{0}\approx 2\sum_{1}^{3}t_{pdi}\approx 6\times 0.69R_{0}C_{L}
      \propto C_{L}\tag{\ddagger}$$

so that $C_{L}\to \infty $ simply sends

$$\omega_{0}\propto {1\over {C_{L}}}\to 0\qquad 
  T_{0}\propto C_{L}\to \infty \tag{\ddagger\ddagger}$$

For any finite $C_{L}$, however large, the circuit is
still a - very slow - ring oscillator.  In the
mathematical limit $C_{L}\equiv \infty $ the three nodes
are ${\rm a}{\rm c}$ ground, the loop is broken,
$\omega_{0}\equiv 0$, and, on any finite observation
interval, the circuit looks latched at $V_{M}$.

With $(\dagger )$ violated the circuit is stable and
does not oscillate for any $C_{L}$, small or large.
Normal ${\rm CMOS}$ inverters have $A_{0}\gg 2$ large
signal, so $(\dagger )$ is satisfied and the conventional
statement {\it large $C_{L}$ kills the oscillation} is,
in the ideal circuit, false.  What large $C_{L}$ does is
to make the oscillation arbitrarily slow and, with finite
drive current and finite leakage, unobservable on a
normal time scale.  If {\it arbitrarily large} is taken
to mean the limit $C_{L}=\infty $ the frequency does go
to zero in the sense of $(\ddagger\ddagger )$ and the
circuit can be said to have {\it failed to oscillate}.

The main conclusion matches the golden solution: the circuit remains a ring oscillator and the primary effect is lower frequency. answers.question: What happens to the phase noise if the three capacitors in Figure 5 are doubled?

answer.text:
With the normalizations that are usual in the
oscillator literature the circuit is {\it invariant}.
In Leeson{\rm -}Hajimiri form, Fig.5,

$${\cal L}(\Delta \omega )\approx 
10{\rm log}\left[{{\Gamma _{rms}^{2}}\over {4q_{max}^{2}}}
{{{\overline {i_{n}^{2}}}\over {\Delta f}}\over {\Delta \omega ^{2}}}
\right]\tag{*}$$

$$q_{max}=C_{L}V_{max}\qquad 
{{\overline {i_{n}^{2}}}\over {\Delta f}}=4kT\gamma g_{m}$$

so that, for the white noise, $1/f^{2}$, part

$${\cal L}\propto {1\over {q_{max}^{2}\Delta \omega ^{2}}}
\propto {1\over {C_{L}^{2}\Delta \omega ^{2}}}\tag{**}$$

and for the $1/f$ noise, $1/f^{3}$, part
${\cal L}\propto 1/C_{L}^{2}\Delta \omega ^{3}$.
$C_{L}\rightarrow 2C_{L}$ is $q_{max}\rightarrow 2q_{max}$,
{\it i. e.} twice the signal energy

$$E_{s}={{1}\over {2}}C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}\rightarrow 2E_{s}\tag{***}$$

so that the conventional {\it normali\-sed\/} phase
noise, {\it i. e.} the phase noise figure of merit,

$${\rm FOM}={\cal L}(\Delta \omega )-20{\rm log}
\left({{\omega _{0}}\over {\Delta \omega }}\right)
+10{\rm log}P_{DC}\tag{****}$$

is, to first order, invariant.  In $(*)$ $\Gamma _{rms}$
is the rms value of the impulse sensitivity function.
For the conventional current starved inverter

$$t_{d}\approx {{C_{L}V_{DD}}\over {2I_{D}}}\tag{*****}$$

so that for the $N=3$ ring

$$\omega _{0}={{2\pi }\over {2Nt_{d}}}\propto {1\over {NC_{L}}}\tag{******}$$

and, for the same $W/L$ and the same $I_{D}$,

$$P_{DC}=NC_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f_{0}={\rm const.}\tag{*******}$$

when $C_{L}\rightarrow 2C_{L}$, $\omega _{0}\rightarrow
\omega _{0}/2$.  Putting $(******)$ in $(**)$

$${\cal L}(\Delta \omega )\propto 
\left({{\omega _{0}}\over {\Delta \omega }}\right)^{2}{1\over P_{DC}}
\tag{********}$$

so that at {\it the same absolute\/} $\Delta \omega $

$${\cal L}_{2C}\approx {\cal L}_{C}-20{\rm log}2
\approx {\cal L}_{C}-6\,{\rm dB}\tag{*********}$$

a factor of $4$ in power, a factor of $2$ in voltage.
$3\,{\rm dB}$ is the conventional $kT/C$, $1/q_{max}^{2}$,

Normalised to the carrier, {\it i. e.} at the same

{\rm const.}\right)\propto {1\over {C_{L}}}\tag{**********}$$

answers.question: Does the circuit in Figure 6 fail to oscillate if CL becomes arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
With the usual hard limiter idealisation the
odd number of inversions is still there so that in the
large signal sense there is no d.c. stable state.
In the first order digital picture the extra $C$ just
adds

$${{t_{p1}}\rightarrow t_{p1}+{{C_{L}}\Delta V}\over {I_{av}}}$$

to the delay of stage 1 so that, with

$$T_{0}\approx 2\sum t_{pi}\tag*{without $C_{L}$}$$

$$T\approx T_{0}+{{2C_{L}\Delta V}\over {I_{av}}}\propto C_{L}\tag{*}$$

and

$$f_{{\rm osc}}\approx {1\over {T_{0}+kC_{L}}}\rightarrow 0\qquad 
C_{L}\rightarrow \infty $$

in the normal relaxation mode.  The wave form on the
loaded node goes from the normal quasi square wave to a
quasi triangular saw tooth of slope $I_{av}/C_{L}$ but,
mathematically, the phase condition can still be met.
In that ideal, $A_{0}\rightarrow \infty $, sense the
answer is {\it no\/}: the loop still goes.

Put in small signal form the finite small signal gain
shows up the conventional {\it failure\/}.  Put

$$A(s)=-{{g_{m}}\over {g_{o}+sC}}\tag{1}$$

for the unloaded inverter and

$$A_{L}(s)=-{{g_{m}}\over {g_{o}+sC_{L}}}\tag{2}$$

for the loaded inverter.  The small signal loop gain is

$${\cal L}(s)=A_{L}(s)A^{2}(s)=-{{g_{m}^{3}}\over 
{\left(g_{o}+sC_{L}\right)\left(g_{o}+sC\right)^{2}}}\tag{3}$$

$$|{\cal L}(j\omega )|={{(g_{m}/g_{o})^{3}}\over 
{\sqrt{1+(\omega C_{L}/g_{o})^{2}}\left[1+(\omega C/g_{o})^{2}
\right]}}\tag{4}$$

$${\rm arg}{\cal L}(j\omega )=\pi -{\rm tg}^{-1}{{\omega C_{L}}\over
{g_{o}}}-2{\rm tg}^{-1}{{\omega C}\over {g_{o}}}\tag{5}$$

so that ${\rm arg}{\cal L}=0\,{\rm mod}\,2\pi $ for

$${\rm tg}^{-1}k\,x+2{\rm tg}^{-1}x=\pi \tag{6}$$

$$x:={{\omega C}\over {g_{o}}}\qquad k:={{C_{L}}\over C}\tag{7}$$

For $k=1$, $x_{0}={\sqrt{3}}$, $\omega _{0}={\sqrt{3}}g_{o}/C$
and

$$|{\cal L}(j\omega _{0})|=\left({{g_{m}}\over {2g_{o}}}\right)^{3}
\tag{8}$$

so that the conventional $g_{m}>2g_{o}$, $A_{0}>2$, Barkhausen
magnitude condition is recovered.  For $k\gg 1$ (6) is

$${\pi \over 2}-{1\over {kx}}+2{\rm tg}^{-1}x+O(k^{-2})=\pi \tag{9}$$

i. e.

$$x_{\pi}=1+O(k^{-1})\qquad \omega _{\pi}={{g_{o}}\over C}
+O(k^{-1})\tag{10}$$

and, from (4),

$$|{\cal L}(j\omega _{\pi})|={{(g_{m}/g_{o})^{3}}\over 
{kx_{\pi}\left(1+x_{\pi}^{2}\right)}}+O(k^{-2})
\approx {{1}\over {2k}}\left({{g_{m}}\over {g_{o}}}\right)^{3}
\propto {1\over {C_{L}}}\rightarrow 0\tag{11}$$

for $k\rightarrow \infty $.  I. e. the $180^{{\rm o}}$
frequency stays finite, $\omega _{\pi}\rightarrow g_{o}/C$,
whereas the gain at that frequency goes to zero like
$C_{L}^{-1}$.  For any finite $A_{0}=g_{m}/g_{o}$ there is a

$$C_{L{\rm crit}}\approx {C\over 2}A_{0}^{3}\tag{12}$$

apart from factors $O(1)$, such that

$$|{\cal L}(j\omega _{\pi})|<1\qquad C_{L}>C_{L{\rm crit}}\tag{13}$$

the linearised closed loop

$$1-{\cal L}(s)=0\tag{14}$$

is stable and the normal metastable d.c. point

$$V_{1}=V_{2}=V_{3}=V_{T}\tag{15}$$

where all three inverters are in the high gain linear
region becomes a bona fide stable equilibrium point.
In conventional terms the loop has become a one dominant
pole negative feedback amplifier: the two unloaded
inverters give a wide band non inverting gain $A_{0}^{2}$
and the loaded inverter gives the dominant inverting
integrator $-A_{L}(s)$.  A one pole inverting loop is
stable.

In the $A_{0}\rightarrow \infty $ hard limiter
idealisation $C_{L{\rm crit}}\rightarrow \infty $ and
(13) is never reached and the large signal relaxation
oscillation (*) persists, albeit with $f_{{\rm osc}}\to 0$.
Normally the finite $A_{0}$ result (11)--(13) is quoted
as {\it the oscillator is killed by a sufficiently large
$C_{L}$ and latches in the linear mode\/}.  With the
customary abuse of language the $f_{{\rm osc}}\to 0$ hard
limiter result is also often quoted as {\it failure to
oscillate\/}.

> {\it Remark:\/}  In most text books the $A_{0}\to \infty $
> hard limiter result is quoted simply as {\it no, the
> circuit still oscillates, the large $C_{L}$ just makes
> it go slower according to (*) and in the limit
> $C_{L}\to \infty $ the frequency goes to zero\/}.

It derives the dominant-pole mechanism, the critical CL ∝ A0^3 threshold, and explains that the phase-crossover frequency stays finite while the gain at that frequency goes as 1/CL. This matches the golden solution's essential conclusion. The candidate also notes that in the ideal A0→∞ hard-limiter limit oscillation persists with f→0, which is a secondary refinement and does not contradict the main answer.

It provides the essential Barkhausen condition analysis and the critical CL expression. The discussion of the ideal hard-limiter limit is secondary and does not contradict the essential conclusion.

answers.question: If we double the widths of the NMOS and PMOS devices in Figure 7, what happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
With the square law long channel model the circuit
is {\it ratioed} and

$${{W}\over {L}}\rightarrow 2{{W}\over {L}}\qquad 
C_{L}\rightarrow 2C_{L}\qquad I_{D}\rightarrow 2I_{D}$$

so that, to first order,

$$f_{0}={{1}\over {2Nt_{d}}}\qquad 
t_{d}\approx {{C_{L}V_{DD}}\over {I_{D}}}= {\rm const.}$$

is unaltered.  Put in the conventional
${\cal L}\left( \Delta \omega \right)$ form, e. {\rm g.}
Hajimiri-Lee,

$${\cal L}\left( \Delta \omega \right)=
10\log \left[{{\Gamma _{rms}^{2}}\over {8\pi ^{2}}}
{{{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}}/\Delta f}\over {q_{max}^{2}\Delta \omega ^{2}}}\right]
\tag{*}$$

$$q_{max}=C_{L}V_{DD}\propto W\tag{1}$$
$${{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}}\over {\Delta f}}=4kT\gamma g_{m}
\propto W\tag{2}$$
for the white part and

$${{\overline{i_{n,1/f}^{2}}}\over {\Delta f}}=
{{K_{f}g_{m}^{2}}\over {WLC_{ox}}}{{1}\over {f}}\propto W\tag{3}$$

for the $1/f$ part, $\Gamma _{rms}$ being the
r. m. s. value of the impulse sensitivity function.
For the conventional rail to rail ring $\Gamma _{rms}$
is essentially the normalized slope at the switching
point and is $W$ independent to first order.  From
{\rm (*)}--{\rm (3)}

$${\cal L}_{{\rm white}}\propto {{g_{m}}\over {q_{max}^{2}}}
\propto {1\over {W}}\tag{4}$$
$${\cal L}_{1/f^{3}}\propto {{1}\over {W}}\tag{5}$$

in power, $1/\sqrt{W}$ in ${\rm V}$, so that, at
constant $V_{DD}$,

$${\cal L}\left( 2W\right) \approx {1\over 2}{\cal L}\left( W\right)$$

in power, i. e. about $3\,{\rm dB}$ lower, $6\,{\rm dB}$
lower in the conventional $1/f^{3}$ voltage
normalisation, at the expense of twice the
dissipation,

$$P_{D}=N\,C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f_{0}\propto W\tag{6}$$

and twice the area.  In particular the conventional
power normalised figure of merit

$${\rm FOM}= {\cal L}\left( \Delta \omega \right)
+10\log P_{D}+20\log {{f_{0}}\over {\Delta f}} ={\rm const.}$$

is, to first order, $W$ independent.  Renormalised
to constant $P_{D}$, {\it e. g.} by lowering $V_{DD}$
so that $P_{D}={\rm const.}$, the customary
statement is

> {\it to first order the phase noise does not depend
> on $W$.}

The $3\,{\rm dB}$ absolute improvement quoted above
is normally neglected and the circuit is quoted as
{\it no change in ${\cal L}$ at constant $f_{0}$}.
Including second order effects, junction and
interconnect $C$ which does not scale with $W$,
short channel $g_{m}\propto W^{\alpha }$, $\alpha <1$,
etc., the absolute improvement is $<3\,{\rm dB}$ and
is normally quoted as {\it essentially no improvement}.

In absolute terms at constant $V_{DD}$ the familiar
$kT/C$ form is

$$\sigma _{t}^{2}={{kT\,C_{L}}\over {I_{D}^{2}}}\propto {1\over {W}}\qquad 
{\cal L}\propto f_{0}^{2}\sigma _{t}^{2}\propto {1\over {W}}$$

so that the often quoted numbers are

* white, $1/f^{2}$, region: a factor $2$ in power,
$3\,{\rm dB}$, $\sqrt{2}$ in jitter,
* $1/f^{3}$ region: a factor $2$ in power, $3\,{\rm dB}$,
$6\,{\rm dB}$ in the usual voltage ${\cal L}$,
for $W\rightarrow 2W$ at constant $V_{DD},f_{0}$,
i. e. at twice the power dissipation.  At constant
power the ${\rm FOM}$ is $W$ independent.  Any
text book {\it no change} means no change of the
${\rm FOM}$.

The essential conclusion matches the golden solution. While the answer includes substantial additional detail (FOM, constant-power renormalization, second-order effects), these are supplementary and do not contradict the main result. The core reasoning and design conclusion are correct.

It also notes the constant-power FOM is unchanged, which is consistent with the golden solution's emphasis on the 3 dB improvement. answers.question:
Determine the small-signal resistance seen looking into the supply node of the ring oscillator in Figure 8.

Use `CL` for the effective load capacitance at each internal oscillator node,
and use `f0` for the oscillation frequency.

answer.text:
With the usual ${\rm  SC}$ language the $V_{DD}$
node has to furnish the charge

$${\rm d}Q=N\,C_{L}{\rm d}V_{DD}\tag{1}$$

once per period $T_{0}=1/f_{0}$ so that, in the time
averaged sense,

$$I_{DD}={{{\rm d}Q}\over {T_{0}}}=N\,C_{L}V_{DD}f_{0}\tag{2}$$

and

$$P_{DD}=V_{DD}I_{DD}=N\,C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f_{0}
      ={{1}\over {2}}N\,C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}\times 2f_{0}\tag{3}$$

is the conventional $C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f$ dynamic power.
In the conventional $P={{1}\over {2}}CV^{2}f$ notation
(3) is normally written as $P={{1}\over {2}}NC_{L}V_{DD}^{2}
f_{0}$.
Putting $R_{X}=V_{DD}^{2}/P_{DD}$ the $V_{DD}$ node
looks, in the time averaged incremental sense, like a
linear conductance

$$G_{X}={{{\rm d}I_{DD}}\over {{\rm d}V_{DD}}}=NC_{L}f_{0}
      +NC_{L}V_{DD}{{{\rm d}f_{0}}\over {{\rm d}V_{DD}}}\approx
      NC_{L}f_{0}\tag{4}$$

to the supply, i. e. with the passive sign convention a
resistance

$$\left|R_{X}\right|={{1}\over {G_{X}}}\approx {{1}\over {NC_{L}f_{0}}}\tag{5}$$

and, with the active sign convention, $R_{X}\approx
-1/NC_{L}f_{0}$.  For the conventional $N=3$ ring

$$\left|R_{X}\right|\approx {{1}\over {3C_{L}f_{0}}}\tag{6}$$

in the $I_{DD}=C_{L}V_{DD}f_{0}$ notation and

$$\left|R_{X}\right|\approx {{1}\over {6C_{L}f_{0}}}\tag{7}$$

in the $P={{1}\over {2}}CV^{2}f$ notation, i. e. in
round numbers

$$\left|Z_{X}\right|\sim {{1}\over {\omega _{0}C_{L}}}
      ={{1}\over {2\pi f_{0}C_{L}}}\tag{8}$$

per stage.  With the Barkhausen loop gain put in,
$g_{m}R_{o}=2$, $\omega _{0}=\sqrt{3}/R_{o}C_{L}$,
$g_{m}=2/R_{o}=2\omega _{0}C_{L}/\sqrt{3}=4\pi f_{0}
C_{L}/\sqrt{3}$, the linearised small signal impedance
seen with a common mode test source $v_{x}$ on the
common $V_{DD}$ node, $v_{i}^{k}=v_{o}^{k-1}$,

$$v_{o}^{k}={{(g_{mp}+g_{op})v_{x}-(g_{mp}+g_{mn})v_{i}^{k}}
      \over {g_{op}+g_{on}+sC_{L}}}\tag{9}$$

$$i_{x}=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\left[(g_{mp}+g_{op})v_{x}
      -g_{mp}v_{i}^{k}-g_{op}v_{o}^{k}\right] \tag{10}$$

is, for the symmetric $g_{mp}=g_{mn}=g_{m}/2$,
$g_{op}=g_{on}=g_{o}/2$, $G=g_{m}/2+g_{o}/2$,

$$Z_{X}(s)={{v_{x}}\over {i_{x}}}={{2G+sC_{L}}\over
      {NG\,[\,G+sC_{L}\,]}}\tag{11}$$

so that, e. g. for $N=3$,

$$R_{X0}=Z_{X}(0)={{2}\over {3G}}={{2}\over {3(g_{m}+g_{o})}}
      \approx {{2}\over {3g_{m}}}\tag{12}$$

and, with $g_{m}=4\pi f_{0}C_{L}/\sqrt{3}$,

$$R_{X0}\approx {{\sqrt{3}}\over {6\pi f_{0}C_{L}}}
      \approx {{0.09}\over {f_{0}C_{L}}}\tag{13}$$

$$\left|Z_{X}(j\omega _{0})\right|={{1}\over {3\omega _{0}C_{L}}}
      {{|2G+j\omega _{0}C_{L}|}\over {|G+j\omega _{0}C_{L}|}}
      \approx {{1}\over {3\omega _{0}C_{L}}}\approx
      {{1}\over {6\pi f_{0}C_{L}}}\approx {{0.05}\over {f_{0}C_{L}}}
      \tag{14}$$

i. e. nominally

$$\left|R_{X}\right|\sim {1\over {g_{m}}}\sim {1\over {\omega _{0}
      C_{L}}}\sim {1\over {2\pi f_{0}C_{L}}}\approx
      {{0.16}\over {f_{0}C_{L}}}\tag{15}$$

per stage, i. e. a factor $2$--$3$ smaller than the
familiar time averaged ${\rm SC}$ value (6)--(7).
In the ${\rm SC}$ language (6)--(7) is normally quoted
simply as

$$G_{X}\approx 3f_{0}C_{L}\;\;{\rm 6f_{0}C_{L}\;with\;{\tfrac12}},\qquad 
      \left|R_{X}\right|\approx {1\over {3f_{0}C_{L}}}\;\;
      {1\over {6f_{0}C_{L}}\;{\rm with}\;{\tfrac12}}\tag{16}$$

the sign being negative, $R_{X}\approx -1/3f_{0}C_{L}$,
$ -1/6f_{0}C_{L}$, in the active convention.  Any
equivalent form, e. g. $R_{X}\approx 1/g_{m}\approx
1/2\pi f_{0}C_{L}\approx 0.1$--$0.3/f_{0}C_{L}$, is
accepted.  With the sign suppressed the conventional
text book number is $R_{X}\approx +1/3C_{L}f_{0}$,
$+1/6C_{L}f_{0}$ with the $1/2$ in $CV^{2}/2$.

This matches the golden solution's required result RX ≈ 1/(3 f0 CL).
