answers.question:
For the ring oscillator in Figure 8, consider the small-signal resistance `RX`
seen looking into the supply node.

Use `CL` for the effective load capacitance at each internal oscillator node,
`f0` for the oscillation frequency, and `TD` for the delay of one inverter stage.

From the dynamic charging and discharging of the three load capacitances, one
can write

```text
RX ~= 1 / (3 f0 CL)
```

Somebody then argues that, because the circuit is oscillating, the path from
`VDD` to ground through the transistors is off for much of the cycle, so the
average resistance should be much higher than the MOS on-resistance or inverse
transconductance scale.

Do you agree with this argument?

answer.text:
With the loop closed the ${\rm V}_{DD}$ current
is not the $d.c.$ short current. It is the
displacement current. In the time average sense

$${\rm V}_{DD}I_{DD}=P_{D}$$

$$P_{D}= N\times {\rm energy\;per\;charge\;per\;period}
      \times f_{0}$$

For ${\rm MOS}$ $E= C_{L}{\rm V}_{DD}^{2}$ per
$0\to 1$ per node, $1/2$ dissipated in the $p$
on the way up, $1/2$ dissipated in the $n$ on the
way down.  With $N=3$

$$P_{D}=3C_{L}{\rm V}_{DD}^{2}f_{0}\tag{1}$$

$$I_{DD,av}=P_{D}/{\rm V}_{DD}=3C_{L}{\rm V}_{DD}f_{0}\tag{2}$$

$${\rm so\;that\;in\;the\;}d.c.{\rm \;or\;time\;average\;
large\;signal\;sense}$$

$$R_{X,av}={{\rm V}_{DD}\over {I_{DD,av}}}={1\over {3f_{0}C_{L}}}
      \tag{3}$$

is the switched capacitor resistor of $N$ capacitors
$C_{L}$ switched at $f_{0}$ in parallel.  For
$f\ll f_{0}$ a small $d{\rm V}_{DD}$ sees the same
time averaged $dI_{DD}$ so that in the low frequency
incremental sense

$${1\over {r_{x}}}={{dI_{DD,av}}\over {d{\rm V}_{DD}}}
      =3C_{L}\left[f_{0}+{\rm V}_{DD}{{df_{0}}\over {d{\rm V}_{DD}}}\right]
      ={{1}\over {R_{X}}}\left[1+{{{\rm V}_{DD}}\over {f_{0}}}
        {{df_{0}}\over {d{\rm V}_{DD}}}\right] \tag{4}$$

$f_{0}=1/T_{0}$, $T_{0}=2NT_{D}$, $N=3$,

$$f_{0}={1\over {6T_{D}}}\tag{5}$$

$$R_{X}={1\over {3f_{0}C_{L}}}={{2T_{D}}\over {C_{L}}}\tag{6}$$

$T_{D}$ is the time to charge $C_{L}$ through the
on device,

$$T_{D}\approx 0.69R_{on}C_{L}\approx {{C_{L}{\rm V}_{DD}}\over {2I_{D}}}
      \approx {{C_{L}}\over {g_{m}}}\tag{7}$$

to within a factor ${\cal O}(1)$ depending on
definition.  I. e.

$$R_{X}\approx 1.4R_{on}\approx {2\over {g_{m}}}\tag{8}$$

$$r_{x}={R_{X}\over {1+{\rm V}_{DD}f_{0}^{-1}df_{0}/d{\rm V}_{DD}}}
      \approx {R_{X}\over 2}\;\;{\rm to}\;\;R_{X}\tag{9}$$

for $I_{D}\propto ({\rm V}_{DD}-V_{T})^{2}$ to
$I_{D}\propto {\rm V}_{DD}-V_{T}$, still
${\cal O}(R_{on})\sim {\cal O}(g_{m}^{-1})$.

The peak current during charge is
$I_{pk}\sim {\rm V}_{DD}/R_{on}\sim g_{m}{\rm V}_{DD}$.
It flows for $T_{D}$.  Averaging current, not
resistance,

$$I_{av}\sim I_{pk}{{T_{D}}\over {T_{0}}}N
      \sim {{{\rm V}_{DD}}\over {R_{on}}}{{T_{D}}\over {6T_{D}}}3
      \sim {{{\rm V}_{DD}}\over {2R_{on}}}\tag{10}$$

so $R_{X}\sim 2R_{on}$.  Averaging $R$,
$\langle R\rangle =T_{0}^{-1}\int R(t)dt\to \infty $,
is meaningless.  What is averaged is $G(t)=1/R(t)$
or $I(t)$.

In particular the ${\rm V}_{DD}$ to ground $d.c.$
short through $n$ and $p$ in series, the crow bar
current, is on only for the cross over time
$\ll T_{D}$ and is indeed high impedance on the
average.  It is not the current in (1)-(2).  The
${\rm V}_{DD}$ current is ${\rm V}_{DD}\to p\to
C_{L}\to {\rm GND}$ on charge and $C_{L}\to n\to
{\rm GND}$ on discharge.  One $p$ is charging at
any time for about $1/2$ the period, $3T_{D}/6T_{D}$,
so $G_{av}\sim G_{on}/2$.

With the loop open and the circuit not oscillating
the small signal impedance looking into ${\rm V}_{DD}$
is indeed the off impedance, very large.  Closing
the loop and letting it oscillate large signal
switches the capacitors and makes the time averaged
large signal and low frequency small signal impedance
(3)-(4) ${\cal O}(g_{m}^{-1})$.  At $f\sim f_{0}$
the impedance is time varying and, with the usual
conversion matrix, has a capacitive/inductive part
and, depending on amplitude limiting, can even exhibit
a small negative real part, but with $|R|\sim R_{X}$.

In short $1/fC$ with $f\sim 1/R_{on}C$ is $R_{on}$.
The circuit is a $3$ phase switched capacitor
resistor.  Formally $R_{X}$ is not a $d.c.$
resistance but a large signal average
${\rm V}/I$ and low frequency incremental $d{\rm V}/dI$
switched capacitor resistance.  Its order of magnitude
is the on resistance that determines $T_{D}$.

answers.question: In the circuit of Figure 9, what happens to the initial voltage gain as the width of M7 increases?

answer.text:
With the usual ${\rm Strong}{\rm Arm}$ jargon the
``linear'' gain is the gain that is sampled on $C_{X}=C_{Y}$
at the moment the ${\rm p}$ latch can go on.
Put $C_{P}=C_{Q}=C_{p}$, $C_{X}=C_{Y}=C_{x}$ and

$${{I_{T}}\over 2}=I_{D1}=I_{D2}\propto W_{7}\tag{*}$$

in saturation.  For $CK=0$

$$V_{P}=V_{Q}=V_{X}=V_{Y}=V_{DD}\tag{1}$$

and $M_{7}$ is off.  For $CK=1$, $S_{1}\dots S_{4}$ are off,
$M_{7}$ goes on and, with $V_{in1}=V_{in2}$,

$$V_{P}(t)=V_{DD}-{{I_{T}}\over {2C_{p}}}t\qquad 
  V_{Q}(t)=V_{DD}-{{I_{T}}\over {2C_{p}}}t \tag{2}$$

until

$$V_{GS3}=V_{Y}-V_{P}>V_{Tn}\qquad V_{GS4}=V_{X}-V_{Q}>V_{Tn}\tag{3}$$

$M_{3}M_{4}$ go on and

$$V_{X}(t)\approx V_{P}(t)\qquad V_{Y}(t)\approx V_{Q}(t) \tag{4}$$

is pulled to ground through $M_{3}M_{1}M_{7}$ and
$M_{4}M_{2}M_{7}$ with the common mode

$$V_{CMX}(t)=V_{DD}-{{I_{T}}\over {2C_{x}}}t \tag{5}$$

The ${\rm p}$ cross coupled pair is off,
$V_{SG5}=V_{DD}-V_{Y}\approx 0$, $V_{SG6}=V_{DD}-V_{X}\approx 0$,
until

$$V_{CMX}(t_{0})=V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|\tag{6}$$

i. e.

$$t_{0}=|V_{Tp}|{{2C_{x}}\over {I_{T}}}\propto {1\over {W_{7}}}\tag{7}$$

is available for linear amplification.
For $0<t<t_{0}$ put $v_{x}=-v_{y}$, $v_{p}=-v_{q}$,
$v_{i1}=-v_{i2}=v_{id}/2$ and, with the tail node ac
ground for the differential signal,

$$\eqalign{
i_{d1}&=g_{m1}v_{i1}+g_{o1}v_{p}\cr
i_{d3}&=g_{m3}(v_{y}-v_{p})+g_{o3}(v_{x}-v_{p})\cr
i_{d5}&=g_{m5}v_{sg5}+g_{o5}v_{sd5}=-g_{m5}v_{y}-g_{o5}v_{x}\cr}$$

$${\rm KCL}_{P}:i_{d3}-i_{d1}-sC_{p}v_{p}=0\tag{8}$$
$${\rm KCL}_{X}:i_{d5}-i_{d3}-sC_{x}v_{x}=0\tag{9}$$

so that, e. g. for $s\to 0$,

$$A_{v0}={{v_{x}-v_{y}}\over {v_{id}}}={{g_{m1}(g_{m3}+g_{o3})}
\over {g_{o1}(g_{m3}-g_{o3})+(g_{m3}+g_{o3}+g_{o1})(g_{m5}-g_{o5})}}
\tag{10}$$

For $t<t_{0}$ the ${\rm p}$ pair is off, $g_{m5}=g_{o5}\approx 0$,

$$A_{v0}\approx {{g_{m1}}\over {g_{o1}}}{{g_{m3}+g_{o3}}\over
{g_{m3}-g_{o3}}}\approx {{g_{m1}}\over {g_{o1}}}\tag{11}$$

the conventional $g_{m}r_{o}$ gain of the $n$ channel
stack, and for $t>t_{0}$, $g_{m5}\ne 0$,

$$A_{v0}\approx {{g_{m1}}\over {g_{m5}+g_{o1}}}\approx
{{g_{m1}}\over {g_{m5}}}\tag{12}$$

In either case, in strong inversion

$$g_{m1}= \sqrt{2\mu _{n}C_{ox}{W_{1}\over L_{1}}I_{D1}}
      \propto \sqrt{I_{T}}\propto \sqrt{W_{7}}\tag{13}$$
$$g_{o1}= \lambda _{n}I_{D1}\propto I_{T}\propto W_{7}\qquad 
  g_{o3}\propto I_{T}\propto W_{7}\tag{14}$$

so that the conventional small signal $g_{m}r_{o}$ gain

$$A_{v0}\propto {g_{m1}\over g_{o1}}\propto {1\over {\sqrt{I_{T}}}}
      \propto {1\over {\sqrt{W_{7}}}}\tag{15}$$

in the square law limit, $\propto 1/I_{T}\propto 1/W_{7}$ in a
velocity saturated short channel technology.  In weak inversion

$$g_{m1}={{I_{D1}}\over {nV_{T}}}\qquad g_{o1}=\lambda I_{D1}\tag{16}$$

so that to first order

$$A_{v0}={1\over {nV_{T}\lambda }}={\rm const.}\tag{17}$$

independent of $I_{T}$ and of $W_{7}$, the $\lambda $ increase
with $V_{DS}$ giving a weak $A_{v0}\propto W_{7}^{-n}$,
$n\approx 0.1-0.3$, decrease in practice.

What is normally quoted as the ``initial'' or ``integration''
gain of the ${\rm Strong}{\rm Arm}$ is the gain sampled at
$t=t_{0}$,

$$\Delta V_{X}(t)={{g_{m1}v_{id}}\over {C_{x}}}t\tag{18}$$

so that at $t=t_{0}$

$$A_{v,int}={{\Delta V_{X}(t_{0})-\Delta V_{Y}(t_{0})}\over {v_{id}}}
        ={{g_{m1}}\over {C_{x}}}t_{0}
        =|V_{Tp}|{{g_{m1}}\over {I_{T}/2}}\tag{19}$$

i. e. with (13)

$$A_{v,int}=2|V_{Tp}|{{g_{m1}}\over {I_{T}}}
        ={{2|V_{Tp}|}\over {V_{ov1}}}\propto {1\over {\sqrt{I_{T}}}}
        \propto \sqrt{{W_{1}\over W_{7}}}\tag{20}$$

in square law, $\propto 1/W_{7}$ velocity saturated and

$$A_{v,int}={{|V_{Tp}|}\over {nV_{T}}}={\rm const.}\tag{21}$$

in weak inversion.  Formally $g_{m1}\propto \sqrt{W_{7}}$ so
that the $s=0$ $g_{m}r_{o}$ gain (11) rises as $\sqrt{W_{7}}$,
but the time (7) available to develop the differential voltage
on $C_{x}$ falls as $1/W_{7}$, so the gain that is actually
presented to the regenerative ${\rm p}$ latch at $t=t_{0}$ falls
as $g_{m1}/I_{T}\propto W_{7}^{-1/2}$, $W_{7}^{-1}$ short
channel, constant to first order in weak inversion.  In round
numbers

$$A_{v,int}\approx 5-10\times {{g_{m1}}\over {I_{T}}}\approx
  10-20\,{\rm dB}$$

for a normal strong inversion design and it goes down when the
tail device is widened.  The circuit gets faster, $t_{0}\propto
1/W_{7}$, at the expense of linear gain, offset and noise.
Pushing $W_{7}$ so far that $M_{1}M_{2}$ go triode for
$t<t_{0}$ collapses the gain altogether.

> {\it Remark:}  If the $s=0$ small signal gain (11) is meant,
> $A_{v0}=g_{m1}r_{o1}\parallel r_{o3}\propto \sqrt{I_{T}}\propto
> \sqrt{W_{7}}$ short channel $\propto W_{7}^{0}$, so it formally
> rises with $W_{7}$.  The usable sampled gain (19) is what is
> normally meant by ``initial gain'' and it falls with $W_{7}$ as
> above.

It appropriately distinguishes this gain from an instantaneous low-frequency gm ro gain that can formally increase with W7. The added strong-, short-channel-, and weak-inversion scaling details do not contradict the required trend.

The essential trend and mechanism match the golden solution.

answers.question: In Figure 9, what happens to the initial voltage gain if we increase the capacitance at nodes P and Q?

answer.text:
With the usual square law short hand the circuit
is an integrator for $0<t<t_{1}$.

$${\cal L}^{-1}\left\{ {g_{m1}\over sC_{P}}\right\} $$

$$C_{P}{dV_{P}\over dt}=-I_{D1}+I_{D3}\tag{1}$$
$$C_{P}{dV_{Q}\over dt}=-I_{D2}+I_{D4}\tag{2}$$
$$C_{X}{dV_{X}\over dt}=-I_{D3}\tag{3}$$
$$C_{Y}{dV_{Y}\over dt}=-I_{D4}\tag{4}$$

$$I_{D3}=k_{n}\left(V_{Y}-V_{P}-V_{Tn}\right)^{2}\qquad 
  I_{D4}=k_{n}\left(V_{X}-V_{Q}-V_{Tn}\right)^{2}\tag{5}$$

for $V_{P}<V_{DD}-V_{Tn}$ and $0$ otherwise.
Put $V_{P}=V_{PCM}+v_{p}$ etc. and linearise

$$i_{3}=g_{m3}(v_{y}-v_{p})\qquad i_{4}=g_{m3}(v_{x}-v_{q})\tag{6}$$

$$g_{m3}(t)=2k_{n}\left(V_{DD}-V_{PCM}(t)-V_{Tn}\right)
      =2k_{n}\left({I_{T}t\over C_{P}}-V_{Tn}\right) \tag{7}$$
for $t>t_{1}$ and $0$ for $t<t_{1}$.

$$\eqalign{
C_{P}\dot {\Delta P}&=-g_{m1}\Delta V_{i}-g_{m3}\Delta P-g_{m3}\Delta X\cr
C_{X}\dot {\Delta X}&=+g_{m3}\Delta P+g_{m3}\Delta X\cr}\tag{8}$$

$$\Delta P=V_{P}-V_{Q}\qquad \Delta X=V_{X}-V_{Y}\tag{9}$$

For $g_{m3}={\rm const.}$

$${C_{P}C_{X}\over g_{m3}}\ddot {\Delta X}+(C_{X}-C_{P})\dot {\Delta X}
      +g_{m1}\Delta V_{i}=0\tag{10}$$

$$\dot {\Delta X}=-{g_{m1}\Delta V_{i}\over C_{X}-C_{P}}
        \left[1-e^{-g_{m3}(C_{X}-C_{P})t/C_{P}C_{X}}\right] \tag{11}$$

$$\Delta X=-{g_{m1}\Delta V_{i}\over C_{X}-C_{P}}
        \left[t-{1-e^{-g_{m3}(C_{X}-C_{P})t/C_{P}C_{X}}\over 
                g_{m3}(C_{X}-C_{P})/C_{P}C_{X}}\right] \tag{12}$$

so that for $t\ll \left|C_{P}C_{X}/g_{m3}(C_{X}-C_{P})\right|$

$$\Delta X\approx -{1\over 2}{g_{m1}g_{m3}\over C_{P}C_{X}}\Delta V_{i}t^{2}
 \tag{13}$$

and, more usefully, for $0<t<t_{1}$, $g_{m3}=0$,

$$C_{P}\dot {\Delta P}=-g_{m1}\Delta V_{i}\tag{14}$$

$$\Delta P(t)=-{g_{m1}\Delta V_{i}\over C_{P}}t\tag{15}$$

i. e. the conventional integrator gain

$$A_{v}(s)={g_{m1}\over sC_{P}}\qquad 
  A_{v}(t)={g_{m1}t\over C_{P}}\tag{16}$$

For a {\it given} $t$ it goes as $1/C_{P}$.
In particular the small signal pole at $P$, $Q$,

$$\omega _{p}= {g_{m3}\over C_{P}}\tag{17}$$

moves down as $1/C_{P}$ and the gain band width
$GBW=g_{m1}/C_{P}$ goes down as $1/C_{P}$.

If the gain is refered to the natural switching time
$t_{1}$ at which $M_{3}$,$M_{4}$ begin to conduct,

$$V_{PCM}(t_{1})=V_{DD}-{I_{T}t_{1}\over C_{P}}=V_{DD}-V_{Tn}\tag{18}$$

$$t_{1}=C_{P}V_{Tn}/I_{T}\tag{19}$$

$$\Delta P(t_{1})=-{g_{m1}\Delta V_{i}\over C_{P}}t_{1}
        =-{g_{m1}V_{Tn}\over I_{T}}\Delta V_{i}\tag{20}$$

$$A_{v0}\equiv {\Delta P(t_{1})\over \Delta V_{i}}={g_{m1}V_{Tn}\over I_{T}}
 \tag{21}$$

nominally $C_{P}$ independent.  The $C_{P}$ in the
denominator of (16) is cancelled by the $C_{P}$ in $t_{1}$.
That is the often quoted {\it to first order the seed
voltage that is presented to the $M_{3}$-$M_{4}$ latch is
independent of $C_{P}$; the extra $C_{P}$ just makes the
comparator wait longer}.

Referred to the output nodes $X$, $Y$ the second
integration has to be included.  With (7)

$$C_{X}\dot V_{XCM}=-k_{n}\left({I_{T}t\over C_{P}}-V_{Tn}\right)^{2}
 \qquad t>t_{1}\tag{22}$$

$$V_{XCM}(t)=V_{DD}-{k_{n}C_{P}\over 3C_{X}I_{T}}
        \left({I_{T}t\over C_{P}}-V_{Tn}\right)^{3}\tag{23}$$

so that $V_{XCM}(t_{2})=V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|$ gives

$$t_{2}= {C_{P}\over I_{T}}\left[V_{Tn}+
        \left({3C_{X}I_{T}|V_{Tp}|\over k_{n}C_{P}}\right)^{1/3}\right]
        \tag{24}$$

$$t_{2}-t_{1}= \left({3C_{X}C_{P}^{2}|V_{Tp}|\over k_{n}I_{T}^{2}}\right)^{1/3}
        \propto C_{P}^{2/3}C_{X}^{1/3}\tag{25}$$

and, e. g. with $\Delta P\approx \Delta P(t_{1})={\rm const.}$
in (8),

$$\Delta X(t_{2})\approx {g_{m3}\over C_{X}}\Delta P(t_{1})(t_{2}-t_{1})
        \propto {g_{m1}V_{Tn}\over I_{T}}{g_{m3}\over C_{X}}
                (t_{2}-t_{1})\Delta V_{i}\tag{26}$$

$$\left|A_{v,{\rm tot}}(t_{2})\right|
        =\left|{\Delta X(t_{2})\over \Delta V_{i}}\right|
        \propto {1\over C_{P}^{1/3}}\tag{27}$$

in the square law model, i. e. for all practical
purposes the usable voltage gain that seeds the
$M_{5}$-$M_{6}$ regenerative latch goes down when $C_{P}$,
$C_{Q}$ are increased.  With $g_{m3}(t)$ from (7) kept
inside (8) the $C_{P}^{2/3}$ growth of $t_{2}-t_{1}$ is
more than compensated by the $1/C_{P}$ fall of $g_{m3}(t)$,
so that $A_{v,{\rm tot}}(t_{2})$ is at best flat and
normally decreasing with $C_{P}$.

In compact form: the incremental gain is $g_{m1}/sC_{P}$.
Double $C_{P}$ and, for the same $\Delta t$, you halve the
integrated differential voltage $\Delta P=g_{m1}\Delta V_{i}
\Delta t/C_{P}$.  At the natural $t_{1}\propto C_{P}$ the
product $g_{m1}t_{1}/C_{P}$ is $C_{P}$ independent to
${\cal O}(V_{Tn})$, but the pole $\omega _{p}=g_{m}/C_{P}$
moves down, the $GBW=g_{m1}/C_{P}$ moves down, the time to
the $PMOS$ threshold $t_{2}$ moves out as $C_{P}^{2/3}$ and
the net small signal gain available at $X$, $Y$ to trip the
cross coupled $M_{5}$-$M_{6}$ pair falls $\propto C_{P}^{-1}$
[$\propto C_{P}^{-1/3}$ with the $t_{2}(C_{P})$ included].
That is why the layout is always done to minimise $C_{P}$,
$C_{Q}$ - and $C_{X}$, $C_{Y}$ - : more $C_{P}$ means less
$GBW$, less effective initial gain, larger input referred
offset and noise and a slower comparator.  In the text book
shorthand: $A_{v0}\propto 1/C_{P}$.

> {\it Remark:}  With the usual abuse of language the
> statement is often phrased as {\it the initial gain is
> inversely proportional to $C_{P}$; to first order the
> differential voltage at $t_{1}$ is $C_{P}$ independent
> because $t_{1}\propto C_{P}$}.  Either phrasing is
> accepted.

The candidate answer reaches the opposite conclusion, claiming the initial gain effectively decreases with increasing C_P (proportional to 1/C_P), which directly contradicts the essential answer. The candidate even states 'A_{v0} ∝ 1/C_P' as the final conclusion, which is the opposite design conclusion from the golden solution. While the analysis contains some relevant circuit reasoning, the final conclusion contradicts the golden solution's central result, warranting a score of 1 per the consistency rules.

While the answer contains extensive small-signal analysis and correctly identifies that larger capacitance slows the transient, it misinterprets the initial gain as inversely proportional to C_P and reaches the opposite design conclusion. answers.question: If we increase the widths of M5 and M6 in Figure 9, does the speed improve or degrade?

answer.text:
With the usual abuse of language the circuit is the
so called Strong Arm.  Put ${\rm CK}=0$ for the
reset and ${\rm CK}=1$ for the evaluate.  For
${\rm CK}=0$

$${\rm S}_{1}-{\rm S}_{4}\;\;{\rm on}\qquad 
M_{7}\;\;{\rm off}\qquad P=Q=X=Y=V_{DD}$$

and for ${\rm CK}=1$

$${\rm S}_{1}-{\rm S}_{4}\;\;{\rm off}\qquad 
M_{7}\;\;{\rm on}$$

$M_{1}-M_{2}$ discharge $P$ and $Q$ with
$\Delta I\propto \Delta V_{in}$, $M_{3}-M_{4}$
discharge $X$ and $Y$ and at $V_{X,Y}=V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|$
$M_{5}-M_{6}$ come on and the $M_{3}-M_{4}-M_{5}-M_{6}$
bistable regenerates to the rail.

In first order, Fig. 9, apart from a logarithmic
factor,

$$t_{d}=t_{0}+t_{r}\tag{*}$$

* $t_{0}$ is the large signal time to get enough
differential signal on $X-Y$ to turn the $p$ latch on,

$$t_{0}\approx {{C_{X,Y}|V_{Tp}|}\over {I_{D1,2}}}
      \propto C_{X,Y}\tag{1}$$

$C_{X,Y}$ is the total capacitance on the
regenerative nodes

$$C_{X,Y}=C_{db3}+C_{db5}+C_{dbS3}+C_{g3}+C_{g5}
        +C_{gd}+C_{w}\tag{2}$$

so that

$$C_{X,Y}=C_{0}+C_{p}^{\prime}W_{5,6}\qquad 
  C_{p}^{\prime}\approx C_{g}^{\prime}+C_{d}^{\prime} \tag{3}$$

* $t_{r}$ is the small signal regeneration time of the
$M_{3}-M_{4}-M_{5}-M_{6}$ latch,

$$t_{r}= \tau _{r}\ln {{V_{DD}}\over {\Delta V_{0}}}\tag{4}$$

$$\tau _{r}^{-1}= \tau _{n}^{-1}+\tau _{p}^{-1}
        ={{g_{m3}+g_{m5}}\over {C_{X,Y}}}\tag{5}$$

$$g_{m5}\propto W_{5,6}\tag{6}$$

so that, apart from the $\ln \Delta V_{0}^{-1}$,

$$t_{r}\propto {{C_{X,Y}}\over {g_{m3}+g_{m5}}}
      ={{C_{0}+C_{p}^{\prime}W_{5,6}}\over
              {g_{m3}+g_{m5}^{\prime}W_{5,6}}}\tag{7}$$

and, from (1),

$$t_{0}\propto C_{0}+C_{p}^{\prime}W_{5,6}\tag{8}$$

is strictly increasing with $W_{5,6}$.

For $t_{r}$ (7) can be made to decrease for small
$W_{5,6}$,

$${{\partial t_{r}}\over {\partial W_{5,6}}}<0\qquad 
  W_{5,6}\to 0\tag{9}$$

if $g_{m5}^{\prime}/C_{p}^{\prime}>g_{m3}/C_{0}$,
normally the case, so that going from $W_{5,6}=0$ to a
finite $W_{5,6}$ the small signal regeneration does get
faster, $\tau _{r}\downarrow $.  In the limit
$W_{5,6}\to \infty $

$$t_{r}\to C_{p}^{\prime}/g_{m5}^{\prime}={\rm const.}\tag{10}$$

so the regeneration time saturates to the intrinsic
$p$ - $C_{p}^{\prime}/g_{m5}^{\prime}$ time and no
more improvement is obtained by making the $p$ device
wider, whereas $t_{0}$ in (1)-(8) goes on increasing
linearly with $W_{5,6}$ and the reset time

$$t_{rst}\approx {{C_{X,Y}V_{DD}}\over {I_{S3,4}}}\propto
C_{X,Y}\tag{11}$$

goes on increasing linearly with $W_{5,6}$.

Hence for the complete comparator, $(*)$,

$$t_{d}(W_{5,6})=A\,(C_{0}+C_{p}^{\prime}W_{5,6})+
B\,{{C_{0}+C_{p}^{\prime}W_{5,6}}\over
{g_{m3}+g_{m5}^{\prime}W_{5,6}}}\ln {{V_{DD}}\over
{\Delta V_{0}(W_{5,6})}}\tag{12}$$

has a shallow minimum for

$$W_{5,6,opt}\approx {{g_{m3}}\over {g_{m5}^{\prime}}}
      \approx W_{3,4}\;\;{\rm to}\;\;2W_{3,4}\tag{13}$$

in most processes, and for any normal design value
${{\partial t_{d}}/{\partial W_{5,6}}}>0$.
In the text book shorthand: {\it the $p$ latch
self loads the regenerative nodes $X-Y$}.

Neglecting the shallow optimum and to first order the
comparator gets slower, the ${\rm CK}\to V_{out}$
propagation delay goes up and the maximum clock rate
that can still precharge $X-Y$ to $V_{DD}$ in (11)
goes down, at essentially constant $g_{m}/C$ regeneration
time.  Normally quoted as: increasing $W_{5,6}$ {\it
degrades} the speed, it just adds capacitance to $X$
and $Y$.

> {\it Remark:} If you start from a minimum size $p$
> latch the small signal $\tau _{r}=C_{X,Y}/(g_{m3}+
> g_{m5})$ does decrease $\propto 1/W_{5,6}$ for a
> very small increase of $W_{5,6}$ and $t_{r}$ in (4)
> can be made a few percent smaller.  The effect is
> normally swamped by the increase of $t_{0}$ in (1)
> and of $t_{rst}$ in (11) so that the net
> ${\rm CK}-V_{out}$ delay is essentially flat to
> increasing with $W_{5,6}$.  With the usual abuse of
> language this is quoted as {\textquotedblleft}the speed
> degrades{\textquotedblright} or {\textquotedblleft}no
> speed improvement{\textquotedblright} on widening
> $M_{5}-M_{6}$.  Up to the optimum (13) the
> regeneration per se does get marginally faster.

The candidate, by contrast, concludes that 'the comparator gets slower' and 'increasing W_{5,6} degrades the speed' as the main result. Although the answer does acknowledge a small initial improvement (regeneration faster for small W) and derives an optimum, it dismisses it as negligible and ultimately frames the answer as degradation. answers.question: In the circuit of Figure 10, does the speed improve or degrade if we increase the widths of the clocked transistors?

answer.text:
With the usual ${\rm min.}\;L$ the circuit is the
${\rm C^{2}MOS}$ master slave of Fig.13.28 of Razavi.
Put $CK=1$ the ${\rm M}$ latch is transparent, the ${\rm S}$
latch is in ${\rm hold}$, put $CK=0$ vice versa.
Neglecting ${\rm Inv_{3}}$ the loop is

$$Z\;\xrightarrow[{CK=1}]{R_{Z}+R_{\bar {CK}}}\;X
 \;\xrightarrow[{CK=0}]{R_{X}+R_{CK}}\;Y
 \;\xrightarrow{{\rm Inv_{3}}}\;Z\tag{*}$$

so that the small signal pole that limits the
${f_{T}}$ of the closed loop, the $CK\to Q$ delay and,
with $Z$ tied to $D$, the $f_{{\rm max}}$ of the
$\div 2$, is the pole at the high impedance storage
nodes $X$ and $Y$.

E. {\rm g.} for the ${\rm M}$ latch, Fig.1a,

$${\rm V_{DD}}\;-\;R_{p}(Z)\;-\;C_{p}\;-\;R_{p}(\bar {CK})
      \;-\;C_{X}\;-\;R_{n}(CK)\;-\;C_{n}\;-\;R_{n}(Z)\;-\;{\rm GND}$$

$$C_{p}=C_{d,p}(Z)+C_{s,p}(\bar {CK})\qquad 
  C_{X}=C_{d,p}(\bar {CK})+C_{d,n}(CK)+C_{g}(S)+C_{w}$$

and, Elmore,

$$\eqalign{
\tau _{X}&\approx R_{p}(Z)C_{p}+\left[R_{p}(Z)+R_{p}(\bar {CK})\right]C_{X}
      \cr
        &\approx R_{n}(Z)C_{n}+\left[R_{n}(Z)+R_{n}(CK)\right]C_{X}
        \quad {\rm for\;the\;other\;edge}} \tag{1}$$

and the same with $X\to Y$, $Z\to X$ for the ${\rm S}$
latch.  $R_{CK}\propto 1/W_{CK}$,
$C_{p},C_{n}\propto W_{CK}$, $C_{X,Y}=C_{0}+C_{1}W_{CK}$,
$C_{0}=C_{g}({\rm next\;stage})+C_{w}$,
$C_{1}\approx C_{d}^{\prime}$,
$R_{Z,X}\propto 1/W_{Z,X}$ is independent of $W_{CK}$.
I. {\rm e.} to first order

$$\tau \approx \left(R_{0}+{R_{1}\over W_{CK}}\right)
            \left(C_{0}+C_{1}W_{CK}\right)
        =R_{0}C_{0}+R_{1}C_{1}+R_{0}C_{1}W_{CK}+{R_{1}C_{0}\over W_{CK}} \tag{2}$$

$$W_{CK,{\rm opt}}=\sqrt{{R_{1}C_{0}\over R_{0}C_{1}}}\tag{3}$$

For the normal design $R_{0}$ is the $R_{on}$ of the
data device $M_{1}$ and of the $p$ device driven by
$Z\;(X)$ and $C_{0}$ is the gate load of the next
stage.  (3) is of the order of $W_{{\rm min}}$ and the
function (2) is very shallow.  In round numbers

$$\tau _{X,Y}\approx \left(R_{D}+R_{CK}\right)C_{X,Y}\tag{4}$$

so that widening the series switch lowers $R_{CK}$ as
$1/W_{CK}$ but raises the load that that same series
combination has to drive as $W_{CK}$.

For $W_{CK}=W_{{\rm min}}$ the $R_{1}C_{0}/W_{CK}$ term
can be made a little smaller by a $10$--$20\%$ increase
of $W_{CK}$; for any appreciable increase the
$R_{0}C_{1}W_{CK}$ term dominates and

$$\Delta \tau \approx R_{D}\Delta C_{d,CK}>0\tag{5}$$

The pole at $X\;(Y)$ moves down, the $CK\to Y\;(X)$
delay goes up, the loop delay $(*)$ goes up and the
$-3{\rm dB}$ frequency, the toggle frequency of the
$\div 2$ connection shown, goes down.  At the system
level the clock load

$$C_{CK}=C_{g,CK}+C_{g,\bar {CK}}\propto W_{CK}\tag{6}$$

goes up proportional to $W_{CK}$ so the clock driver
itself gets slower, its rise/fall time goes up, the
crow bar current in ${\rm Inv_{3}}$ and in the latches
goes up and the charge sharing between $C_{X,Y}$ and
$C_{p,n}$,

$$\Delta V_{X}\approx {C_{p}\over C_{p}+C_{X}}V_{DD}\tag{7}$$

gets worse.  In the limit the latch will fail to hold.

In normal language: keep the clocked devices at
${\rm min.}\;W$, or at most $1.5$--$2\times W_{{\rm min}}$,
and get speed by widening the data devices $M_{1}$ and
the $p$ devices driven by $Z$ and $X$ and by ${\rm Inv_{3}}$.
Widening the $CK,\bar {CK}$ devices alone is normally a
net loss of speed, a large increase of $C_{CK}$ and of
dynamic power $P_{d}=C_{CK}V_{DD}^{2}f_{CK}$ for no
appreciable reduction of $R_{on}$.

> {\it Remark:} If {\it all} devices, data and clocked,
> are widened together $R_{0}\propto 1/W$, $C_{0}\propto W$
> and $\tau \propto RC\approx {\rm const}$ to first order,
> the usual $W/L$ speed up with power penalty is recovered.
> The statement above is for $W_{CK}$ widened with
> $W_{D}$ held constant, the usual interpretation of the
> question.  With $W_{D}$ held constant the optimum (3) is
> essentially $W_{CK,{\rm min}}$; any large $W_{CK}$ degrades
> $f_{{\rm max}}$ by $10$--$30\%$ in a typical $0.18\mu$
> CMOS run.  A small, $\sim 20\%$, increase can be made to
> trade a few ${\rm ps}$ of $R_{CK}C_{0}$ for $R_{D}C_{1}$
> with essentially no change in speed.

answers.question: Does the structure in Figure 10 provide quadrature outputs?

answer.text:
With the usual abuse of language the ${\rm
C^{2}MOS}$ loop is a ${\rm div.2}$ Johnson
counter.  Put $C_{X}$ and $C_{Y}$ on the two
storage nodes.  In the ${\rm delay}=0$ limit

$${\rm Inv}_{1}:Z\to X\;\;{\rm on}\;\;CK=1\tag{1}$$
$${\rm Inv}_{2}:X\to Y\;\;{\rm on}\;\;CK=0\tag{2}$$
$$Z={\bar Y}\tag{3}$$

so that, with $T_{0}=2T_{CK}$,

* $CK=1$ : $X={\bar Z}=Y$, $Y$ floats
* $CK=0$ : $X$ floats, $Y={\bar X}$, $Z=X$

{\it e. g.} with $Y_{0}=0$

$$\eqalign{
CK=1&:\;X_{1}=Y_{0}\cr
CK=0&:\;Y_{1}={\bar X}_{1}={\bar Y}_{0}\cr
CK=1&:\;X_{2}=Y_{1}={\bar Y}_{0}\cr
CK=0&:\;Y_{2}={\bar X}_{2}=Y_{0}\cr}$$

{\it etc.}  $X$ changes on the $0\to 1$ edge of
$CK$, $Y$ changes on the $1\to 0$ edge of $CK$.
In the $t_{d}=0$, $DC=50\%$ limit

$$\eqalign{
X(t)&= {\rm sq}\left( {{\omega _{CK}t} \over 2}\right) \cr
Y(t)&= {\rm sq}\left( {{\omega _{CK}t} \over 2}-{\pi \over 2}\right)
      =X\left( t-{{T_{CK}} \over 2}\right) \cr
Z(t)&={\bar Y}(t) \cr} \tag{4}$$

{\it i. e.} at

$$f_{0}=f_{CK}/2\qquad T_{0}=2T_{CK} \tag{5}$$

the two {\it dynamic} storage nodes are a
${{1}\over {2}}T_{CK}={{1}\over {4}}T_{0}$ apart.
Normalised to $f_{0}$ that is $\pi /2$.
In the conventional jargon $X=I$, $Y=Q$,
$Z={\bar Q}$ is a ${\rm div.2}$ quadrature
generator, Fig.1.  E. {\it g.} for $Y_{0}=1$

$$\eqalign{
{\rm ph.1}\;CK=1&:\;X=1\;Y=1\;Z=0\cr
{\rm ph.2}\;CK=0&:\;X=1\;Y=0\;Z=1\cr
{\rm ph.3}\;CK=1&:\;X=0\;Y=0\;Z=1\cr
{\rm ph.4}\;CK=0&:\;X=0\;Y=1\;Z=0\cr} \tag{6}$$

and the pattern repeats with $T_{0}=2T_{CK}$.
$X$ is high for $T_{CK}^{HI}+T_{CK}^{LO}=T_{CK}$,
low for $T_{CK}$, {\it etc.}, nominal $50\%$
duty at $f_{0}$.

Strictly speaking, as drawn, the circuit is not a
usable quadrature generator:

* the only static, buffered output is $Z={\bar Y}$.
  $X$ and $Y$ are unbuffered dynamic nodes.  Taken
  as $Y$ and $Z$ the circuit is the conventional
  differential ${\rm div.2}$, $Z={\bar Y}$, $180^{{\rm o}}$
  at $f_{0}$;

* Eq.{\rm (4)} is $T_{CK}/2=T_{0}/4$ only for
  $DC_{CK}=50\%$ and $t_{d,{\rm Inv3}}=0$.  In
  general

  $$\Delta \phi _{XY}={\pi \over 2}+ \pi \Delta DC_{CK}
        +\omega _{0}t_{d3}+ \Delta \phi _{mis} \tag{7}$$

  so the {\it quadrature error} is first order in
  the $CK$ duty cycle error, in the delay of
  ${\rm Inv}_{3}$ and in device mismatch;

* being dynamic the state is lost for
  $f_{CK}<f_{{\rm leak}}\approx I_{{\rm leak}}/C_{X,Y}$.

Made static, buffered and with a second
${\rm FF}$ in a conventional $2\,{\rm FF}$ Johnson
loop it becomes the conventional static
quadrature ${\rm div.2}$.  In that loose,
text book, $f_{0}=f_{CK}/2$, $t_{d}=0$,
$DC=50\%$ sense it is normally quoted as a
quadrature ${\rm div.2}$.

> {\it Remark:}  If quadrature at $f_{CK}$ is
> required the answer is no.  The circuit is a
> ${\rm div.2}$.  With $Y$ as $Q$ and $Z$ as
> ${\bar Q}$ it gives only the conventional
> $0^{{\rm o}}-180^{{\rm o}}$ differential output
> at $f_{CK}/2$.  A conventional $0^{{\rm o}}-
> 90^{{\rm o}}-180^{{\rm o}}-270^{{\rm o}}$
> quadrature generator is the $4$ phase Johnson
> counter, {\it i. e.} two static master slave
> ${\rm FF}$s in a loop.

answers.question:
For the divide-by-two topology in Figure 11, does the speed improve or degrade
if we increase the widths of the clocked transistors, i.e. the transistors whose
gates are driven by `CK` or `CKbar`?

answer.text:
With an ideal ${\cal V}_{CK}$ the circuit is the
${\rm C^{2}MOS}$ - ${\rm TSPC}$ master slave

$$\eqalign{
M_{1}&:{\rm CK}=1\cr
M_{2}&:{\rm CK}=0\cr}
\qquad {\rm plus}\qquad I_{3}$$

put ${\rm D}\equiv \bar {\rm Q}$ , Fig.1.
In the ${\rm CK}=1$ half period $M_{1}$ is a normal
${\rm CMOS}$ inverter whose $p$ and $n$ sources are
returned to ${\rm V_{DD}}$ and ${\rm V_{SS}}$ through
$R_{p,CK}$ and $R_{n,CK}$ and whose load is

$$C_{L1}=C_{d,p1}+C_{d,n1}+C_{g,p2}+C_{g,n2}+C_{w}$$

and vice versa for ${\rm CK}=0$.
Put $R_{p1},R_{n1}$ for the $p$ and $n$ of the
signal inverter proper.  E. g. for the pull down

$$R_{pd}=R_{n1}+R_{n,CK}\tag{1}$$
$$R_{n,CK}\propto {1\over {W_{CK}}}\qquad 
  R_{n1}\propto {1\over {W_{1}}}$$

and, to first order,

$$\tau _{pd}\approx 0.7R_{pd}C_{L}+0.7R_{n,CK}C_{int}\tag{2}$$

$$C_{int}=C_{d,CK}+C_{s,1}\propto W_{CK}\tag{3}$$
$$C_{g,CK}\propto W_{CK}\tag{4}$$

is the capacitance of the common source node
$X\equiv D_{CK}\equiv S_{1}$ and the gate capacitance
that loads the clock driver.  $C_{L}$ itself contains
the drain capacitance of the signal device, $\propto
W_{1}$, but to first order not $W_{CK}$.

For $W_{CK}\rightarrow 0$, $R_{CK}\gg R_{1}$ and (2)
is $\propto 1/W_{CK}$ - widening the clock device
widens the transparent latch.  As soon as

$$R_{CK}\lesssim R_{1}\tag{5}$$

the $R_{CK}C_{L}$ term in (2) is a small correction
to $R_{1}C_{L}$ and

$${{\partial \tau }\over {\partial W_{CK}}}\approx
 -{{R_{CK}}\over {W_{CK}}}C_{L}+R_{CK}{{dC_{int}}\over
{dW_{CK}}}+R_{CK}{{dC_{g,CK}}\over {dW_{CK}}}
      {{R_{CK,drv}}\over {R_{CK}}}\tag{6}$$

With $R_{CK}\propto W_{CK}^{-1}$, $C_{int},C_{g}\propto
W_{CK}$,

$$\tau \approx \tau _{0}+{a\over {W_{CK}}}+bW_{CK}\tag{7}$$

with $a\propto C_{L}$, $b\propto C_{int0}^{\prime }$.
(7) has a shallow minimum for

$$W_{CK,opt}\approx \sqrt{a/b}\approx (0.5-1.5)W_{1}\tag{8}$$

and for $W_{CK}>W_{CK,opt}$

$${{d\tau }\over {dW_{CK}}}>0\tag{9}$$

In words: once the switch resistance is small compared
with the resistance of the signal inverter the normal
inverter delay $R_{1}C_{L}$ dominates.  Widening the
switch gives a $\Delta R_{CK}\propto \Delta W_{CK}/
W_{CK}^{2}$ reduction of (1) but a $\Delta C_{int}
\propto \Delta W_{CK}$ and a $\Delta C_{g,CK}\propto
\Delta W_{CK}$ increase of the capacitance that has to
be charged through $R_{1}$ when the latch comes out of
the high $Z$ hold state and that has to be driven by
the clock driver.

With an ideal, zero impedance, clock the intrinsic
toggle frequency

$$f_{max}\approx {1\over {2\left(\tau _{M}+\tau _{S}
      +\tau _{I3}\right)}}\tag{10}$$

increases $\propto \left(R_{1}+R_{CK}\right)^{-1}$ for
$R_{CK}\gg R_{1}$ and then saturates to

$$f_{max,0}\approx {1\over {2\left(R_{1}C_{L}+\tau _{I3}
      \right)}}\tag{11}$$

to within 10-20\%.  Any further increase of $W_{CK}$
is pure self loading, $C_{int}$ in (2), and $f_{max}$
falls as $1/bW_{CK}$.

With a realistic clock driver of output resistance
$R_{CK,drv}$ the clock pole

$$\tau _{CK}=R_{CK,drv}C_{g,CK}\propto W_{CK}\tag{12}$$

adds directly to the half period budget and the
normalised $f_{max}$ has a pronounced maximum at
essentially minimum $W_{CK}$ and falls monotonically
for $W_{CK}>W_{CK,opt}$.  In normal design $W_{CK}$
is taken at or near minimum, $W_{CK}\approx
W_{n1}$, $W_{p,CK}\approx W_{p1}$, often minimum
length, and the high speed version of the circuit is
the E-TSPC version in which the series clock device
is removed altogether, Fig. 2.  E.g. in $0.18\mu $ CMOS

$$f_{max}\approx 3-5\,{\rm GHz}\;\;{\rm for}\;\;
  W_{CK}=W_{min}$$

and drops by 20-30\% for $W_{CK}=4W_{min}$ at the same
clock driver power, while the clock power
$P_{CK}=fC_{g,CK}V_{DD}^{2}\propto W_{CK}$ doubles.

> {\it In the text book idealisation $R_{CK}C_{L}$
> dominates and $f_{max}$ goes up as $W_{CK}$ goes up,
> $f_{max}\propto 1/(R_{1}+R_{CK})$, but the increase
> saturates as soon as $R_{CK}<R_{1}$ and in any
> practical implementation the $bW_{CK}$ self loading
> and clock loading terms dominate and the divider gets
> slower and much more power hungry if the clock
> transistors are widened.  The optimum is for
> $W_{CK}\approx W_{1}$ and in practice at $W_{min}$.
> That is why the E-TSPC divider, with one clock
> transistor per stage, is substantially faster than the
> conventional TSPC/${\rm C^{2}MOS}$ divider.}

answers.question: Analyze the arrangement in Figure 12(a).

answer.text:
With the ideal switch it is a $T=1$ $D$ type.
Put $D\equiv \bar Q$ it is a toggle.

$$\eqalign{
X&={\rm in\ }Inv_{1}\cr
Y&={\rm out\ }Inv_{1}= \bar X\cr
Z&={\rm in\ slave}\cr
W&=\bar Z\cr
Q&=\bar W =Z\cr}$$

$$S_{1}=CK\qquad S_{2}= \bar {CK}\qquad 
S_{1}\;{\rm between\ }Q-X\qquad S_{2}\;{\rm between\ }Y-Z$$

3 inversions round the loop. $Q\rightarrow X\rightarrow
Y\rightarrow Z\rightarrow Q$ is inverting. With $S_{1},S_{2}$
closed it would be a 3 stage ring oscillator.

With $S_{1},S_{2}$ in anti phase the ring is broken.
It is the conventional 2 phase master slave $D$ with
$D=Q$ fed back.

* {\it Master :} $S_{1}+Inv_{1}$ - dynamic latch. $C_{X}$ is
the gate $C$ of $Inv_{1}$.
* {\it Slave :} $S_{2}+Inv_{2}+Inv_{3}$ - dynamic latch.
$C_{Z}$ is the gate $C$ of $Inv_{2}$. $Q=Z$ in the
transparent phase.

In normal operation $CK,\bar {CK}$ non overlapping.

{\it 1. $CK=1\;,\bar {CK}=0$ :} $S_{1}$ ON, $S_{2}$ OFF

$$X=Q_{n-1}\tag{driven by $Q$}$$
$$Y=\bar X =\bar Q_{n-1}\tag{driven}$$
$$Z=Z_{n-1}\tag{floating, held on $C_{Z}$}$$
$$W=\bar Z_{n-1}\tag{driven}$$
$$Q=Z_{n-1}=Q_{n-1}\tag{driven but floating input}$$

Master transparent, slave holding. $Y$ is isolated from $Z$.

{\it 2. $CK=0\;,\bar {CK}=1$ :} $S_{1}$ OFF, $S_{2}$ ON

$$X=X_{n}=Q_{n-1}\tag{floating, held on $C_{X}$}$$
$$Y=\bar X_{n}= \bar Q_{n-1}\tag{driven}$$
$$Z=Y =\bar Q_{n-1}\tag{driven}$$
$$W=\bar Z = Q_{n-1}$$
$$Q=Z =\bar Q_{n-1}\tag{driven}$$

Master holding, slave transparent. $X$ is isolated.

On the next $CK=1$

$$X_{n+1}=Q_{n}= \bar Q_{n-1}= \bar X_{n}$$

so $X$ and $Q$ change state on every full $CK$ period.

$$\eqalign{
Q_{n}&=\bar Q_{n-1}\cr
Q_{n+1}&=Q_{n-1}\cr}$$

i. e. a $T$ flip flop. In the time domain

$$\eqalign{
T_{Q}&=2T_{CK}\cr
f_{Q}&=f_{CK}/2\cr}$$

50\% duty cycle to first order. Output can be taken at
$Y,Z,W$ or $Q$ - $Q$ has full drive. It is edge triggered
on the $1\rightarrow 0$ of $CK$ - $0\rightarrow 1$ of
$\bar {CK}$ - with the usual master slave delay
$t_{CK-Q}=t_{S2}+t_{Inv2}+t_{Inv3}$.

In $Z$ domain it is a $z^{-1}$ delay with inversion.

It is {\it dynamic}. In phase 1 $Z,Q$ is floating,
in phase 2 $X$ is floating. The logic level is held only
by charge on $C_{X},C_{Z}$, gate capacitance plus parasitics.
Leakage $I_{off}$ discharges it as $\Delta V =I_{leak}T_{hold}/C$.
Hence

* minimum $f_{CK}$: $T_{CK}<C\,V_{DD}/I_{leak}$, typically
kHz-MHz in modern CMOS, otherwise state is lost. Cannot be
stopped with $CK=0$ or $1$ DC.
* maximum $f_{CK}$: $T_{CK}>t_{S1}+t_{Inv1}+t_{S2}+t_{Inv2}+
t_{Inv3}+t_{setup}$, the usual flip flop $f_{max}$.
* very sensitive to $CK-\bar {CK}$ overlap and skew,
clock slope, charge injection, clock feedthrough and noise.
If $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ are ON together the circuit is a
closed 3 inverter ring and oscillates/ races.
* needs extra $Inv_{3}$ to make the number of inversions
odd. $Inv_{1}+Inv_{2}$ alone is even and would latch
$Q_{n}=Q_{n-1}$. $Inv_{1}+Inv_{2}+Inv_{3}$ is odd and
toggles.

In normal high speed prescaler use $f_{CK}$ is large enough
for the hold time to be satisfied and the circuit is very
small, low power and fast - essentially a clocked ring
oscillator - TSPC divider.

> {\it Remark on (b):} The red $Inv$ is the conventional
> ``keeper'', ``bleeder'', ``staticizer''. It makes the
> master latch pseudo static.

$$Y \xrightarrow{{\rm weak\ }Inv} X$$

When $S_{1}$ is OFF $X$ is no longer floating:

$$X \xrightarrow{Inv_{1}} Y \xrightarrow{{\rm keeper}} X$$

is a static latch holding $X=\bar Y$. $C_{X}$ is now
statically driven. $Z$ remains dynamic. The divider becomes
semi static, can hold $CK=0$ indefinitely, much more
tolerant to leakage, noise and slow clocks. 

When $S_{1}$ is ON the loop is

$$Q \xrightarrow{S_{1}} X \xrightarrow{Inv_{1}} Y
 \xrightarrow{{\rm keeper}} Q$$

The keeper must be {\it weak}, $W/L\ll W/L_{Inv1},
W/L_{Inv2,3}$, so that $Q$ driven through $S_{1}$ by the
strong slave inverters can overpower it and flip the
master. Usual ratio $3-10:1$. There is momentary contention
and ratioed power. Speed is slightly degraded.

$Z$ is still dynamic. For fully static operation a second
keeper $W\rightarrow Z$ is added to the slave, giving the
conventional 4 inverter static master slave $T$ flip flop
divide by 2.

It also addresses the dynamic nature (charge on C_X, C_Z), leakage limits on minimum clock frequency, clock overlap issues, and even discusses the (b) keeper/bleeder making it pseudo-static. These are all correct and well-supported. Per the golden solution's note that exact internal signal naming or inverter path is secondary, the detailed discussion is bonus but consistent. Topology, dominant mechanism, and design consequence are all correct.

It also discusses dynamic operation, leakage, and keeper implications, which are secondary but consistent with the golden solution.

answers.question: How does the red inverter in Figure 12(b) affect the performance?

answer.text:
With the conventional drawing the circuit is a
${\cal T}= {\cal D}= {\cal Q}$ divider, Fig.12a
in ${\rm TSPC}$ form

$${\rm TG}_{CK}-{\rm Inv}_{1}-{\rm TG}_{\bar {CK}}-
{\rm Inv}_{2}-{\rm Inv}_{3}-{\rm TG}_{CK}$$

{\it i. e.} a master ${\rm TG}_{CK}+{\rm Inv}_{1}$
transparent on $CK=1$ and a slave
${\rm TG}_{\bar {CK}}+{\rm Inv}_{2}+{\rm Inv}_{3}$
transparent on $\bar {CK}=1$.
In Fig.12a the master is {\it dynamic}.

* $CK=1\;,\;\bar {CK}=0$ : ${\rm Inv}_{1}$ is
driven from ${\cal Q}$ through ${\rm TG}_{CK}$,
${\cal N}_{1}= {\rm out}_{1}$ is open.

* $CK=0\;,\;\bar {CK}=1$ : ${\rm out}_{1}$ drives
the slave, ${\cal N}_{0}={\rm in}_{1}$ is open and
left floating on its $C_{par}\approx 1-2\,{\rm fF}$.
The state is held dynamically on $C_{par}$.
Leakage, charge sharing, noise, ${\rm \alpha }$
hits discharge $C_{par}$ in ${\rm ms}$,
so the divider has a minimum clock frequency,
${f_{CK}}>f_{min}\approx I_{leak}/C_{par}\Delta V$,
normally ${\rm kHz}-{\rm MHz}$, it cannot be
stopped, clock gated, and it is very noise
sensitive.  In normal high speed operation the
open time $\approx T_{CK}/2\ll \tau _{leak}$ and
electrically the circuit is the same as the
static one.

The ${\rm Inv}_{R}$ in red in Fig.12b is the
conventional {\it staticizer, keeper, bleeder,
trickle} inverter.  For

$$W_{R}/L_{R}\ll W_{1}/L_{1}\;\;{\rm and}\;\;
W_{R}/L_{R}\ll W_{3}/L_{3}$$

normally minimum $W$, long $L$,

$${\rm Inv}_{1}+{\rm Inv}_{R}$$

is a conventional cross coupled ${\rm latch}$
closed on ${\rm TG}_{CK}$ open, open on
${\rm TG}_{CK}$ closed.

* $CK=0$ : ${\rm TG}_{CK}$ open, ${\rm Inv}_{1}
-{\rm Inv}_{R}$ is a bistable latch holding
${\cal N}_{0},{\cal N}_{1}$ statically to
$V_{DD},V_{SS}$ with full noise margin. No
${f_{min}}$, DC operation, clock can be stopped
and gated indefinitely.

* $CK=1$ : ${\rm TG}_{CK}$ closed, ${\rm Inv}_{R}$
is overdriven by the low impedance driver
${\rm Inv}_{3}$ through ${\rm TG}_{CK}$.  Logically
the circuit is unchanged, transparent master,
${\cal Q}^{n+1}= \bar {\cal Q}^{n}$.

Electrically ${\rm Inv}_{R}$ is not in the
forward signal path.  To first order it does not
change the logic function nor, if it is weak, the
high speed timing.  To second order it

* adds $C_{gR}+C_{dR}\approx 20-30\%$ of a
minimum inverter to ${\cal N}_{0}$ and to
${\cal N}_{1}$, {\it i. e.} to the load of
${\rm Inv}_{1}$ and of ${\rm Inv}_{3}$,

* puts a ratioed contention current
$I_{R}\approx I_{Dsat,R}$ in parallel with the
writing driver for the $\approx t_{r,f}$ of the
flip of ${\cal N}_{0}$.

With ${\rm Inv}_{R}$ minimum size, weak,
the penalty is normally made negligible by design,
$\Delta t_{CK-Q}\approx \Delta t_{D-Q}\approx
5-15\%$, $\Delta P_{dyn}\approx C_{R}V_{DD}^{2}f$,
plus the crow bar $V_{DD}I_{R}t_{cont}\ll
C_{par}V_{DD}^{2}$, $\Delta A\approx $ one
minimum inverter, in exchange for fully static,
ratioed pseudo static operation, no $f_{min}$,
full static noise margin and leakage immunity.
Made strong it has to be ratioed against
${\rm Inv}_{1}/{\rm Inv}_{3}$, $W_{1}> (2-4)W_{R}$,
otherwise the master cannot be written, $t_{CK-Q}$
goes as $1/(I_{1}-I_{R})$ and the divider fails
to toggle at speed and dissipates large short
circuit power.  In the limit $W_{R}\approx W_{1}$
it is the conventional fully static master slave
${\rm latch}$ with $\approx 2\times $ power and
$\approx 30\%$ speed penalty.  Colloquially:
a weak keeper makes a dynamic TSPC latch
pseudo static for free.

answers.question:
In Figure 12(b), somebody answers:

> The red inverter acts as a keeper, forming a cross-coupled latch with `Inv1`.
> This removes the minimum clock frequency requirement due to leakage.

But the input of the red inverter is not tied to the output of `Inv1`.

Do you agree with this answer? What is the actual role of the red inverter?

answer.text:
No. It is not a keeper and it is not
cross coupled with ${\rm Inv}_{1}$.

Let

* $N_{0}=$ left of $SW_{1}=$ out of ${\rm Inv}_{3}$
* $N_{1}=$ right of $SW_{1}=$ in of ${\rm Inv}_{1}$
* $N_{2}=$ out of ${\rm Inv}_{1}=$ left of $SW_{2}$
* $N_{3}=$ right of $SW_{2}=$ in of ${\rm Inv}_{2}$
* $N_{4}=$ out of ${\rm Inv}_{2}=$ in of ${\rm Inv}_{3}$

$SW_{1}=CK$, $SW_{2}=\bar {CK}$.

{\it (a)} is the conventional TSPC dynamic
divide by 2. $3$ inversions in the loop.

* $CK=1$: $SW_{1}$ on, $SW_{2}$ off

$$N_{1}=N_{0}\;\;,\;\;N_{2}=\bar N_{1}=\bar N_{0}$$

$N_{3}$ floating, $N_{4}=\bar N_{3}$ held on $C_{N3}$,
$N_{0}=\bar N_{4}$ driven. $N_{3}$ is dynamic.

* $CK=0$: $SW_{1}$ off, $SW_{2}$ on

$$N_{1}\;{\rm floating\;held\;on\;}C_{N1}\;\;,\;\;
N_{2}=\bar N_{1}\;\;,\;\;N_{3}=N_{2}\;\;,\;\;
N_{4}=\bar N_{3}\;\;,\;\;N_{0}=\bar N_{4}$$

$N_{1}$ is dynamic. The state is held only on
parasitic $C$. $I_{leak}/C\cdot \Delta V$ discharges
$N_{1}$ for $CK=0$, $N_{3}$ for $CK=1$. Hence
$f_{ck}>f_{min}\approx I_{leak}/C\,V_{DD}$ is required.
On $CK:1\to 0$ $N_{0}\to \bar N_{0}$, divide by 2.

A static keeper for the master must be a weak
inverter with

$${\rm in}=N_{2}\;\;,\;\;{\rm out}=N_{1}$$

so that ${\rm Inv}_{1}+{\rm keeper}$ is two
inverters back to back, positive feedback,
bistable, $N_{1}$ has a DC path to $V_{DD}/GND$
when $SW_{1}$ is off. A keeper for the slave
is ${\rm in}=N_{0}$, ${\rm out}=N_{3}$.

In (b) the red inverter is

$${\rm in}=N_{0}\;\;,\;\;{\rm out}=N_{2}$$

i.e. its {\it output} is shorted to the output of
${\rm Inv}_{1}$, its input is {\it not} the output
of ${\rm Inv}_{1}$. It is in {\it parallel} with
$SW_{1}+{\rm Inv}_{1}$, not cross coupled.

$$N_{0}\xrightarrow[{\rm red}]{}{\rm inv} N_{2}
\qquad N_{0}\xrightarrow{SW_{1}}{\rm Inv}_{1} N_{2}$$

No positive feedback, no bistable. Loop gain
${\rm red}+{\rm Inv}_{2}+{\rm Inv}_{3}=3$ inversions.

* $CK=1$, $SW_{1}$ on, $SW_{2}$ off: $N_{1}=N_{0}$,
$N_{2}=\bar N_{0}$ from {\it both} ${\rm Inv}_{1}$
and red in parallel. $N_{3}$ still floating dynamic.

* $CK=0$, $SW_{1}$ off, $SW_{2}$ on:

$$N_{2}= \bar N_{0}\;{\rm red}\;\;,\;\;
N_{3}=N_{2}\;\;,\;\;
N_{4}= \bar N_{3}\;\;,\;\;
N_{0}= \bar N_{4}$$

$$N_{0}\xrightarrow{\rm red} N_{2}\xrightarrow{SW_{2}}
N_{3}\xrightarrow{{\rm Inv}_{2}}N_{4}\xrightarrow{{\rm Inv}_{3}}N_{0}$$

is a closed 3 inverter ring oscillator. Ideally
$N_{0}= \bar N_{0}$. In practice it oscillates with
period $\approx 2\sum t_{pd}$ when $CK=0$, it does
not latch.

Even ignoring oscillation, $N_{1}$ is still floating
when $SW_{1}$ is off. No DC path is provided to
$N_{1}$. $C_{N1}$ still leaks. When $N_{1}$ drifts
${\rm Inv}_{1}$ goes to $V_{m}$, it fights the red
inverter on $N_{2}$ with crowbar current, undefined
level and static power. $N_{3}$ is still dynamic for
$CK=1$.

So the circuit remains fully dynamic, $f_{min}$ due
to leakage on $N_{1}$ and $N_{3}$ is not removed.
At best the red inverter weakly holds $N_{2}$, at
worst it makes the divider a gated ring oscillator
and causes contention. Made weak it is a useless
``half keeper'' that still leaves the master dynamic
node $N_{1}$ to leak.

Correct static TSPC is red ${\rm in}=N_{2}$,
${\rm out}=N_{1}$, and for full static a second
keeper ${\rm in}=N_{0}$, ${\rm out}=N_{3}$.

However, the answer misidentifies the role: it calls the red inverter a problematic parallel path that creates a ring oscillator / contention rather than recognizing it as a feedforward branch that drives a later node from an earlier signal. The golden solution identifies the red inverter as feedforward (N0→N2, bypassing part of the latch path) that improves high-speed operation but dominates at low clock rates. The candidate reaches a different (and largely opposite) design conclusion — that the circuit is broken or becomes a gated oscillator — missing the intended feedforward function entirely. Correct rejection of keeper is partial credit, but missing the main mechanism (feedforward) and reaching a contradictory design consequence warrants a score of 2.

deepseek_v4_pro.rationale: The answer correctly rejects the keeper/cross-coupled interpretation, identifies the red inverter as a feedforward branch in parallel with SW1+Inv1, and explains the tradeoff: it does not remove the minimum clock frequency requirement and can cause contention or oscillation. It also correctly describes the proper static keeper connections. This matches the golden solution's essential points.

answers.question: How do we optimize the circuit of Figure 13 for the NF if Rin must remain equal to 50 Ohm?

answer.text:
With the usual $g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}$,
$r_{o}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$, $R_{s}=50$ and

$${\overline {i_{n}^{2}}}=4kT\gamma g_{m}\;\;,\;\;
{\overline {i_{nF}^{2}}}=4kT/R_{F}\tag{1}$$

put $V_{s}=0$ for $R_{in}$ and $V_{s}\ne 0$ for the
signal.

$$\eqalign{
a&=1/R_{s}+1/R_{F} & b&=-1/R_{F}\cr
c&=g_{m}-1/R_{F} & d&=1/R_{F}+1/r_{o}\cr
{\rm Det}&=ad-bc=(1/R_{s}+1/R_{F})(1/R_{F}+1/r_{o})
+{1\over {R_{F}}}(g_{m}-1/R_{F})\cr
&= {1\over {R_{s}R_{F}}}+{1\over {R_{s}r_{o}}}
+{1\over {R_{F}r_{o}}}+{{g_{m}}\over {R_{F}}}} \tag{2}$$

$$\left[ \matrix{a&b\cr c&d}\right]
\left[ \matrix{v_{x}\cr v_{y}}\right]=
\left[ \matrix{V_{s}/R_{s}\cr 0}\right] \tag{3}$$

$$v_{y}= {V_{s}\over {R_{s}}}{{1/R_{F}-g_{m}}\over {{\rm Det}}}$$

$$A_{v}={v_{y}\over {V_{s}}}={{1/R_{F}-g_{m}}\over {R_{s}{\rm Det}}}
\approx -{{g_{m}R_{F}}\over {1+g_{m}R_{s}}}\;
{1\over {1+{{R_{s}+R_{F}}\over {r_{o}(1+g_{m}R_{s})}}}}\tag{4}$$

$$|A_{v}|\approx {{g_{m}R_{F}}\over 2}\;\;{\rm for}\;\;
g_{m}R_{s}\approx 1\tag{5}$$

For $I_{in}$ injected at $v_{x}$ , $V_{s}=0$,

$$R_{in}={v_{x}\over {I_{in}}}={{d}\over {{\rm Det}_{0}}}$$

with $R_{s}\to \infty $ in ${\rm Det}$,

$$R_{in}={{1/R_{F}+1/r_{o}}\over {1/R_{F}r_{o}+g_{m}/R_{F}}}
={{R_{F}+r_{o}}\over {1+g_{m}r_{o}}}\tag{6}$$

$$R_{in}\approx {1\over {g_{m}}}{{R_{F}+r_{o}}\over {r_{o}}}
={1\over {g_{m}}}\left(1+{R_{F}\over {r_{o}}}\right)
\approx {1\over {g_{m}}}\;\;R_{F}\ll r_{o}\tag{6a}$$
$$R_{in}\approx {R_{F}\over {1+g_{m}r_{o}}}\;\;{\rm textbook}$$

$$R_{in}=R_{s}\;\;{\rm gives}\;\;R_{F}=R_{s}(1+g_{m}r_{o})-r_{o}
=R_{s}+r_{o}(g_{m}R_{s}-1) \tag{7}$$

i. e. $R_{F}$ and $g_{m}$ are not independent if the
match is to be preserved.  $R_{F}\propto g_{m}$ for
$g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$.

Noise.  Put a shunt current $I_{nF}$ across $R_{F}$ and
a shunt current $I_{nd}$ from $v_{y}$ to ground,

$$\left[ \matrix{a&b\cr c&d}\right]
\left[ \matrix{v_{x}\cr v_{y}}\right]=
\left[ \matrix{I_{nF}\cr -I_{nF}}\right]\;\;,\;\;
\left[ \matrix{a&b\cr c&d}\right]
\left[ \matrix{v_{x}\cr v_{y}}\right]=
\left[ \matrix{0\cr I_{nd}}\right] \tag{8}$$

$$H_{F}={v_{y}\over {I_{nF}}}=-{{g_{m}+1/R_{s}}\over {{\rm Det}}}
\tag{9a}$$
$$H_{d}={v_{y}\over {I_{nd}}}={{1/R_{s}+1/R_{F}}\over {{\rm Det}}}
\tag{9b}$$

$${\overline {v_{no}^{2}}}=|A_{v}|^{2}4kTR_{s}
+|H_{F}|^{2}4kT/R_{F}+|H_{d}|^{2}4kT\gamma g_{m}\tag{10}$$

$$F={{{\overline {v_{no}^{2}}}}\over {|A_{v}|^{2}4kTR_{s}}}
=1+{{|H_{F}|^{2}}\over {|A_{v}|^{2}}}{1\over {R_{F}R_{s}}}
+{{|H_{d}|^{2}}\over {|A_{v}|^{2}}}{{\gamma g_{m}}\over {R_{s}}}\tag{11}$$

$${{|H_{F}|}\over {|A_{v}|}}={{R_{s}(g_{m}+1/R_{s})}\over {|g_{m}-1/R_{F}|}}
={{1+g_{m}R_{s}}\over {|g_{m}-1/R_{F}|}}\tag{12a}$$
$${{|H_{d}|}\over {|A_{v}|}}={{1+R_{s}/R_{F}}\over {|g_{m}-1/R_{F}|}}\tag{12b}$$

$$\eqalign{
F&=1+{{(1+g_{m}R_{s})^{2}}\over {(g_{m}-1/R_{F})^{2}R_{F}R_{s}}}
+\gamma g_{m}{{(1+R_{s}/R_{F})^{2}}\over {R_{s}(g_{m}-1/R_{F})^{2}}}\cr
&\approx 1+{{(1+g_{m}R_{s})^{2}}\over {g_{m}^{2}R_{F}R_{s}}}
+\gamma {{(1+R_{s}/R_{F})^{2}}\over {g_{m}R_{s}}}\;\;g_{m}\gg 1/R_{F}\cr
&\approx 1+{R_{s}\over {R_{F}}}+{\gamma\over {g_{m}R_{s}}}
\;\;g_{m}R_{s}\gg 1,\;R_{F}\gg R_{s}} \tag{13}$$

The familiar

$$F\approx 1+{\gamma\over {g_{m}R_{s}}}+{R_{s}\over {R_{F}}}
\tag{13a}$$

with $\gamma\approx 1-1.5$ in short channel,
$\gamma_{n}g_{mn}+\gamma_{p}g_{mp}\to \gamma g_{m}$ if
$\gamma_{n}\approx \gamma_{p}$.

* $4kT\gamma g_{m}$ is suppressed by $g_{m}R_{s}$,
* $4kT/R_{F}$ is suppressed by $R_{F}/R_{s}$.

Both want $g_{m}$ large and $R_{F}$ large.
With (7) they must be increased together.

Put $x=g_{m}R_{s}$, $y=R_{F}/R_{s}$, $r=r_{o}/R_{s}$,

$$y=1+r(x-1)\tag{14}$$
$$F\approx 1+{{(1+x)^{2}}\over {x^{2}y}}+\gamma {{(1+1/y)^{2}}\over {x}}
\tag{15}$$

For $r\gg 1$, $y\approx r(x-1)$,

$$F\approx 1+{1\over {r\,x}}+{\gamma\over {x}}
=1+{{1/r+\gamma}\over {g_{m}R_{s}}}\tag{16}$$

monotonically decreasing with $g_{m}$.

> For fixed $R_{in}=R_{s}$ the noise figure can only be
> lowered by raising the loop gain $g_{m}r_{o}$ and raising
> $R_{F}$ according to (7).  In the large gain limit
> $F-1\propto 1/g_{m}+R_{s}/R_{F}$.

In practice:

* Burn more power.  $g_{m}\propto \sqrt{WI_{D}}$ in
square law, $\propto I_{D}$ in velocity saturation.
For a given $I_{D}=I_{D1}=I_{D2}$ the inverter current,
$F$ is minimum for maximum $g_{m1}+g_{m2}$.
For a given $I_{D}$ that is maximum $W$ and for a given
total $W$ it is $k_{n}/\sqrt{W_{n}}=k_{p}/\sqrt{W_{p}}$,
nominally $g_{m1}\approx g_{m2}$, i. e. $W_{p}\approx
(\mu_{n}/\mu_{p})W_{n}\approx 2-3\,W_{n}$, so the
inverter is centred at $\approx V_{DD}/2$ and both
devices stay in saturation.  $g_{m}R_{s}=1$ gives
$R_{in}\approx 50\,{\rm \Omega}$ with $R_{F}\approx 50\,{\rm \Omega}$
and $F\approx 1+4/g_{m}R_{F}+4\gamma/g_{m}R_{s}\approx 5-9\,{\rm dB}$.
Raising $g_{m}$ to $30-40\,{\rm mS}$, $x=1.5-2$,
$r_{o}\sim 0.5-1\,{\rm k\Omega}$, $y\sim 10-20$,
$R_{F}\sim 0.5-1\,{\rm k\Omega}$,

$$|A_{v}|\approx R_{F}/2R_{s}\approx 5-10\tag{17}$$

$$F\approx 1+0.05+0.5\approx 1.6\approx 2\,{\rm dB}$$

and $F\to 1$ as $g_{m}\to\infty $, $R_{F}\to\infty $.

The limit is power, area and bandwidth.  $C_{in}\approx
C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+(1+|A_{v}|)C_{gd}$ resonates with $R_{s}\parallel
R_{in}$,

$$\omega_{in}\approx {1\over {R_{s}C_{in}}}\tag{18}$$

Increasing $W$ to increase $g_{m}$ increases $C_{in}$ and
lowers $\omega_{in}$.  For a required $BW$ the optimum
$W$ is $C_{in}\approx 1/R_{s}\omega_{0}$.  The optimum is
normally at the largest $W$ and $I_{D}$ that still meets
$BW$, $V_{DD}$ headroom and stability, $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$,
$R_{F}$ chosen from (7) to re-centre $R_{in}=50\,{\rm \Omega}$.

Hence the design recipe:

1. Choose $L\approx L_{min}$ for maximum $g_{m}/I_{D}$,
increase $L$ or cascode only to raise $r_{o}$ and loop
gain if $R_{F}$ is to be made very large.
2. Choose $I_{D}$ for the allowed power, size $W_{n},W_{p}$
for $g_{m1}\approx g_{m2}$ and maximum $g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}$.
3. Set $R_{F}$ from (6)-(7) for $R_{in}=50\,{\rm \Omega}$.
4. Check $BW$ and add $L_{s}$ in series with $C_{1}$ to
tune out $C_{in}$ if necessary; $L_{s}$ is noiseless and
allows larger $W$ for the same $BW$ and lower $F$.
5. Iterate.  $F_{min}\approx 1+\gamma/g_{m}R_{s}$ is
approached for $R_{F}\gg R_{s}$, $g_{m}R_{s}>1$.

With no power limit $F\to 1$, $0\,{\rm dB}$.  With a
power limit the optimum is the maximum $g_{m}r_{o}$ product
that can be afforded, i. e. the maximum $g_{m}$ and the
corresponding $R_{F}$ that keeps (6) at $50\,{\rm \Omega}$.
Any matching network that transforms $50\,{\rm \Omega}$ to a
higher $R_{in}$ breaks the $F\leftrightarrow R_{in}$
trade-off and is the usual way to get $F<2\,{\rm dB}$ at
a few mW.  Noise cancelling or $g_{m}$-boosted common gate
variants are the circuit extensions of the same idea.

minimax_m3.rationale: The answer identifies the shunt-feedback LNA and derives correct input-match and noise-factor relations, but its central design conclusion is the naive one Razavi explicitly rejects: increase RF and gm/loop gain as much as possible (NF → 1+γ, or just below it) while keeping Rin=50Ω. It misses the key Razavi point that finite output resistance / channel-length modulation decouples Rin from the noise-factor optimum, allowing NF < 1+γ through joint optimization with finite ro. The answer treats large RF and large gmro as the goal rather than recognizing that the optimum lies in a finite ro regime jointly chosen with RF and gm. Per the golden solution and rubric, a recommendation to maximize RF/gm/output resistance is a major miss of the dominant mechanism.

deepseek_v4_pro.rationale: The answer correctly derives the input match constraint and noise factor, but concludes that NF is minimized by maximizing gm and RF (and loop gain), approaching F→1. This is the naive design direction that the golden solution explicitly rejects. It misses the key point that finite output resistance/channel-length modulation can yield NF < 1+γ and that the optimum is not the large-gain limit. The answer treats channel-length modulation only as a way to increase loop gain, not as a mechanism that changes the noise optimum.

answers.question: Compute the input impedance of the circuit in Figure 14(a).

answer.text:
With the usual $r_{0}\rightarrow \infty $ put
$V_{1}=V_{P}$ and put $V_{b}=0$ for the signal.
For the $a.c.$ signal Fig.{\it b} is

$${\cal A}_{0}= \left|{V_{s}\over {V_{1}}}\right|_{R_{F}
\rightarrow \infty } \tag{1}$$

the open circuit voltage gain from $P$ to the
unloaded output.  For the MOS circuit

$$V_{X}=-g_{m1}R_{D1}^{\ast }V_{1}\qquad 
R_{D1}^{\ast }=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\parallel r_{g2}\approx
R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1} \tag{2}$$

and for the $p$ channel pair $M_{2}-M_{3}$

$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}(v_{s}-V_{X})\qquad i_{d3}=g_{m3}(v_{s}-V_{b})$$
$$i_{d2}+i_{d3}=0\;\;{\rm for}\;Z_{SS}\rightarrow \infty $$

$$v_{s}={{g_{m2}V_{X}+g_{m3}V_{b}}\over {g_{m2}+g_{m3}}}$$

$$i_{d3}=g_{m3}(v_{s}-V_{b})={{g_{m2}g_{m3}}\over
{g_{m2}+g_{m3}}}(V_{X}-V_{b}) \tag{3}$$

so that, with $V_{b}=0$,

$$V_{o}^{\ast}=i_{d3}R_{D2}^{\ast}\qquad 
R_{D2}^{\ast}=R_{D2}\parallel r_{o3}\approx R_{D2} \tag{4}$$

$${\cal A}_{0}= \left|{V_{o}^{\ast}\over {V_{1}}}\right|
      =g_{m1}R_{D1}^{\ast}{{g_{m2}g_{m3}}\over {g_{m2}+g_{m3}}}
        R_{D2}^{\ast} \tag{5}$$

For the matched pair $g_{m2}=g_{m3}=g_{m}$

$${\cal A}_{0}= {1\over 2}g_{m1}g_{m}R_{D1}^{\ast}R_{D2}^{\ast}
\tag{5a}$$

and, with $r_{0}\rightarrow \infty $,

$${\cal A}_{0}\approx {1\over 2}g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m}R_{D2}\tag{5b}$$

The ${1\over 2}$ is the $1/2\,g_{m}R_{D}$ single ended
gain of a differential pair whose opposite drain is $a.c.$
ground.  If the ${1\over 2}$ is absorbed in the definition
of ${\cal A}_{0}$,

$${\cal A}_{0}\approx g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m2}R_{D2}\tag{5c}$$

is often quoted.  With $g_{mb}\ne 0$ put $g_{m}\rightarrow
g_{m}+g_{mb}$.

Put in Fig.{\it b} $V_{s}=-{\cal A}_{0}V_{1}$ in series with
$R_{D2}^{\ast}$ and close the loop with $R_{F}$,
Fig.{\it b}.  With $V_{1}$ applied at the input and
$V_{o}$ the voltage at the top of $R_{D2}$,

$${{V_{o}-V_{1}}\over {R_{F}}}+{{V_{o}-V_{s}}\over {R_{D2}^{\ast}}}=0
\tag{6}$$

$$V_{o}={{R_{D2}^{\ast}V_{1}+R_{F}V_{s}}\over {R_{F}+R_{D2}^{\ast}}}
      =V_{1}{{R_{D2}^{\ast}-{\cal A}_{0}R_{F}}\over
                {R_{F}+R_{D2}^{\ast}}} \tag{7}$$

so that the loaded voltage gain is

$${\cal A}_{L}={V_{o}\over {V_{1}}}= -{\cal A}_{0}
{{R_{F}}\over {R_{F}+R_{D2}^{\ast}}}+{{R_{D2}^{\ast}}\over
{R_{F}+R_{D2}^{\ast}}}\approx -{\cal A}_{0}
{{R_{F}}\over {R_{F}+R_{D2}^{\ast}}}\tag{8}$$

for ${\cal A}_{0}\gg 1$.  The current furnished to the
input node is, $M_{1}$ being MOS,

$$I_{1}={{V_{1}-V_{o}}\over {R_{F}}}+sC_{in}V_{1} \tag{9}$$

For the resistive part $sC_{in}=0$,

$$I_{1}={{V_{1}}\over {R_{F}}}\left[1-
{{R_{D2}^{\ast}-{\cal A}_{0}R_{F}}\over {R_{F}+R_{D2}^{\ast}}}\right]
     =V_{1}{{1+{\cal A}_{0}}\over {R_{F}+R_{D2}^{\ast}}} \tag{10}$$

i. e. in the usual ideal shunt - shunt notation
$V_{s}=-AV_{1}$,

$$R_{in}\equiv \left.{{V_{1}}\over {I_{1}}}\right|_{C_{in}=0}
      ={{R_{F}+R_{D2}^{\ast}}\over {1+A}}\tag{11}$$

with $A={\cal A}_{0}$.  In the $r_{0}\rightarrow \infty $
limit

$$R_{in}\approx {{R_{F}+R_{D2}}\over {1+{\cal A}_{0}}}\tag{12}$$

and for ${\cal A}_{0}\gg 1$, $R_{F}\gg R_{D2}$,

$$R_{in}\approx {R_{F}\over {\cal A}_{0}}\tag{13}$$

With (5),

$$R_{in}\approx {{R_{F}+R_{D2}^{\ast}}\over
{1+g_{m1}R_{D1}^{\ast}g_{m2}g_{m3}R_{D2}^{\ast}/(g_{m2}+g_{m3})}}
\tag{14}$$

$$\approx {{R_{F}+R_{D2}}\over {1+{1\over 2}g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m}R_{D2}}}
\approx {2\over {g_{m1}g_{m}R_{D1}}}{{R_{F}\over {R_{D2}}}}\tag{14a}$$

for the matched pair and $r_{0}\rightarrow \infty $.
Absorbing the $1/2$,

$$R_{in}\approx {{R_{F}+R_{D2}}\over {1+g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m2}R_{D2}}}
\approx {R_{F}\over {g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m2}R_{D2}}}\tag{14b}$$

is the form most often quoted.  E. {\it g.} with
${\cal A}_{0}\sim 20-40\,{\rm dB}$, $R_{F}\sim 0.5-5\,{\rm k\Omega }$,
$R_{in}\sim 10-10^{2}\,{\rm \Omega }$.

Including $C_{in}$ the impedance seen by the signal
current $I_{in}$ is

$$Z_{in}(s)={1\over {sC_{in}+1/R_{in}(s)}}=
{R_{in}(s)\over {1+sC_{in}R_{in}(s)}}\tag{15}$$

so that at low frequencies

$$Z_{in}(s)\approx {1\over {sC_{in}+{\displaystyle
{{1+{\cal A}_{0}(s)}\over {R_{F}+R_{D2}^{\ast}}}}}}\tag{16}$$

and for $s\rightarrow 0$, $Z_{in}(0)=R_{in}$ above.
With a single pole ${\cal A}_{0}(s)={\cal A}_{0}/(1+s/\omega _{0})$
the dominant input pole is at

$$\omega _{p,in}\approx {1\over {R_{in}C_{in}}}
      ={{1+{\cal A}_{0}}\over {(R_{F}+R_{D2}^{\ast})C_{in}}}
      \approx {{\cal A}_{0}\over {R_{F}C_{in}}}\tag{17}$$

i. e. the $R_{F}C_{in}$ pole is broad banded by the
return ratio $1+{\cal A}_{0}$.  The closed loop
transimpedance is $R_{M}=V_{o}/I_{in}\approx -R_{F}
{\cal A}_{0}/(1+{\cal A}_{0})\approx -R_{F}$.

> {\it Remark:}  Any $r_{o}$ and $g_{mb}$ can be included by
> $R_{D1}^{\ast}=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$,
> $R_{D2}^{\ast}=R_{D2}\parallel r_{o3}$, $g_{m}\rightarrow
> g_{m}+g_{mb}$ in (5).  To first order the $1/2$ in (5a)
> is $g_{m3}/(g_{m2}+g_{m3})$.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in Figure 15 generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
With the usual abuse of notation the low frequency
noise on the common mode supply is a {\it frequency}
modulation, Fig.1. For $f_{m}<< f_{0}$ :

$${\cal H}_{DD}(s)={\Phi _{out}(s)\over V_{nDD}(s)}$$

is an almost ideal integrator.

$$\eqalign{
V_{out}(t)&=V_{out0}+v_{n}(t) \cr
\omega _{0}(t)&=\omega _{00}+K_{DD}v_{n}(t)+{\cal O}(v_{n}^{2})\cr
K_{DD}&={\partial \omega _{0}\over \partial V_{out}}
      =2\pi {\partial f_{0}\over \partial V_{out}}\;\;{\rm rad/s/V}\cr
\theta (t)&=\int^{t}K_{DD}v_{n}(\tau )d\tau \cr}$$

so that for the power spectral densities, single sided
in ${\rm V^{2}/Hz}$,

$$S_{\omega }(f_{m})=K_{DD}^{2}S_{v,nDD}(f_{m})\tag{1}$$
$$S_{\phi }(f_{m})={S_{\omega }(f_{m})\over (2\pi f_{m})^{2}}
      ={K_{DD}^{2}\over (2\pi f_{m})^{2}}S_{v,nDD}(f_{m})
      ={K_{f}^{2}\over f_{m}^{2}}S_{v,nDD}(f_{m})\tag{2}$$

$$ {\cal L}_{DD}(f_{m})={1\over 2}S_{\phi }(f_{m})\;\;{\rm for}\;\;
f_{m}>0 \tag{3}$$

in ${\rm dBc/Hz}$

$${\cal L}_{DD}(f_{m})=10\log \left[
{K_{DD}^{2}S_{th}(f_{m})\over 2(2\pi f_{m})^{2}}
|H_{LDO}(f_{m})|^{2}|H_{DD}(f_{m})|^{2}\right] \tag{4}$$

$$=10\log \left[{K_{f}^{2}S_{th}(f_{m})\over 2f_{m}^{2}}
|H_{LDO}(f_{m})|^{2}|H_{DD}(f_{m})|^{2}\right] $$

$K_{f}=K_{DD}/2\pi $ in ${\rm Hz/V}$.
$S_{th}(f_{m})$ is the normally white, single sided,
LDO output noise

$$S_{th}\approx 4kT R_{n,eq}\approx 4kT\left[
R_{out}+{2\over 3g_{m,p}}+{g_{m,in}^{2}R_{n,in}^{2}\over g_{m,p}^{2}}
+\cdots \right]\;\;{\rm V^{2}/Hz}$$

referred to $V_{out}$ and

$$S_{v,nDD}(f_{m})=S_{th}(f_{m})|H_{LDO}(f_{m})|^{2}|H_{DD}(f_{m})|^{2}$$

is the filtered noise at the $V_{out}$ pin.
In the simplest case

$$|H_{LDO}(f_{m})|^{2}={1\over 1+(f_{m}/f_{p,LDO})^{2}}\;\;
f_{p,LDO}\approx {1\over 2\pi R_{o,LDO}C_{o,LDO}}$$

is the LDO closed loop output pole plus band gap
and error amplifier noise shaping and

$$|H_{DD}(f_{m})|^{2}={1\over 1+(f_{m}/f_{p,DD})^{2}}\;\;
f_{p,DD}\approx {1\over 2\pi R_{DD}C_{DD}}$$

is the $V_{out}$ decoupling network to the $2L_{1}$
tank.  For $f_{m}<f_{p,LDO},f_{p,DD}$, $|H|\approx 1$
and (2) is white $\to 1/f_{m}^{2}$ FM noise,
$-20{\rm dB/dec}$ in ${\cal L}$.  $1/f$ noise in the
LDO gives $1/f_{m}^{3}$ close in.

Uncorrelated with the normal tank $R_{p}$ noise the
total is

$${\cal L}_{tot}= {\cal L}_{VCO}+{\cal L}_{DD}\;\;{\rm linear}$$

and ${\cal L}_{DD}$ normally dominates close in if the
LDO is noisy.

$K_{DD}$ is the conventional {\it pushing} figure.
For $f_{m}\to 0$ it can be obtained by a DC sweep
PSS

$$K_{DD}={\Delta \omega _{0}\over \Delta V_{out}}$$

or PAC/PXF

$$K_{DD}(f_{m})=2\pi f_{m}|{\cal H}_{DD}(jf_{m})|$$

injecting $v_{n}$ in series with $V_{out}$ and
measuring the PM sideband at $f_{0}\pm f_{m}$,
${\cal H}_{DD}= \Phi _{out}/V_{n}$.

Analytically for the LC $VCO$

$$\omega _{0}\approx {1\over \sqrt{L_{eq}C_{eq}}}$$

$$L_{eq}\approx L_{1}\;\;{\rm diff.}\;\;{\rm or}\;\;L_{1}/2\;\;
{\rm s.e.}$$

$$C_{eq}=C_{B1}+C_{B2}+C_{v1}+C_{v2}+C_{gs1,2}+C_{gd1,2}+C_{L}+C_{par}$$

so that

$$K_{DD}=-{\omega _{0}\over 2C_{eq}}{\partial C_{eq}\over \partial V_{out}} \tag{5}$$

The dominant term is normally the MOS accumulation
varactor

$$C_{v}=C_{v}(V_{G}-V_{cont})=C_{v}(V_{X,Y}-V_{cont})$$

$${\partial C_{v}\over \partial V_{out}}=
{\partial C_{v}\over \partial V_{GS}}{\partial V_{X,Y}\over \partial V_{out}}
\approx C_{v}^{\prime}\times 1 \tag{6}$$

because the DC value $V_{X,Y}=V_{out}-I_{VCO}R_{L1}$
follows $V_{out}$,

$$K_{DD}\approx -{\omega _{0}\over 2C_{eq}}
\left[2C_{v}^{\prime}+{\partial C_{gs}\over \partial V_{out}}
+{\partial C_{gd}\over \partial V_{out}}+\cdots \right]
-{\partial \omega _{0}\over \partial A}{\partial A\over \partial V_{out}} \tag{7}$$

the last term is the Groszkowski AM-PM effect,
$\omega _{0}(A)$.  In practice $K_{f}=10-100{\rm MHz/V}$
is typical, e. g. $C_{eq}\sim 1{\rm pF}$,
$C_{v}^{\prime}\sim 0.1-1{\rm pF/V}$, $f_{0}\sim 5{\rm GHz}$,

$$K_{f}\approx {f_{0}\over 2C_{eq}}2C_{v}^{\prime}\sim 5-50{\rm MHz/V}$$

Then e. g. $S_{th}^{1/2}=10{\rm nV/\sqrt{Hz}}$ white,

$${\cal L}_{DD}(1{\rm MHz})\approx 
10\log \left[{K_{f}^{2}S_{th}\over 2f_{m}^{2}}\right]
\approx 10\log \left[{(50{\rm MHz/V})^{2}(10^{-16}{\rm V^{2}/Hz})
\over 2(10^{6})^{2}}\right]\approx -92{\rm dBc/Hz}$$

to be added to the normal Leeson ${\cal L}_{VCO}$.

Formally this is the $m=0$ term of the Hajimiri
LTV ISF expansion for the common mode supply node.
The ISF for the differential tank is $\Gamma _{diff}
\propto \sin \omega _{0}t$ while $\Gamma _{DD}\propto
\Gamma _{DD,0}+ \Gamma _{DD,2}\cos 2\omega _{0}t+\cdots $.
Low frequency $v_{n}(f_{m})$ is frequency translated
by $K_{DD}$ and high frequency $v_{n}(2f_{0}\pm f_{m})$
is down converted by $\Gamma _{DD,2}$ with normally
$10-20{\rm dB}$ smaller weight.  For white $S_{th}$
the $f_{m}$ pushing term dominates.  It can be
extracted exactly as

$$S_{\phi }(f_{m})={S_{th}(f_{m})\Gamma _{DD,rms}^{2}\over 8\pi^{2}f_{m}^{2}}
+ \cdots $$

which reduces to (2) with $\Gamma _{DD,rms}\propto K_{DD}$.

> {\it Remark:} The $B_{1},B_{2}$ MIM bank is
> essentially $V_{out}$ independent.  $K_{DD}$ is
> band dependent through $C_{eq}$ and varactor bias
> point.  Differential varactor connection and large
> $C_{DD}$ decoupling, low $C_{v}^{\prime}$ design
> and low $R_{n,eq}$ wide band LDO minimise
> ${\cal L}_{DD}$.

It also correctly notes that the supply perturbation acts directly on the varactors (since the DC value V_X,Y follows V_out), so Kpush is closely related to KVCO, and reducing KVCO reduces this noise conversion. answers.question: We add CT to the tail node, as in Figure 16. What happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
With the usual abuse of language the ``tail
filter'' is the circuit of Hegazi-Sjoland-Abidi
{\it JSSC 12/01} without the $L_{T}$.

For the differential mode $P$ is a virtual earth.
For the common mode it is not.  In the large
signal steady state

$$v_{P}(t)=V_{P0}+V_{P2}\cos 2\omega _{0}t+\cdots $$

$$i_{P}(t)=I_{SS}+I_{2}\cos 2\omega _{0}t+\cdots $$

and

$$Z_{P}(s)=R_{T}\parallel {1\over sC_{T}}\parallel
Z_{s}(s)\qquad Z_{s}\approx {1\over 2g_{m}}\;\;{\rm for}\;\;
\omega \approx 2\omega _{0}$$

is the impedance that the $2\omega _{0}$ current
sees to ground.  The conventional analysis,
Hajimiri-Lee, Samori {\it et al}, is that the
dominant contribution of the tail device to

$${\cal L}(\Delta \omega )=10\log \left[
{2FkT\over P_{s}}\left({\omega _{0}\over 2Q\Delta \omega }
\right)^{2}\right] \tag{Leeson}$$

is the mixing of its noise around $2\omega _{0}$
with the $2\omega _{0}$ component of the large
signal operation to $\omega _{0}\pm \Delta \omega $,
and the mixing of its $1/f$ noise around
$\Delta \omega $ with the $2\omega _{0}$ large
signal to $2\omega _{0}\pm \Delta \omega $ and
thence to $\omega _{0}\pm \Delta \omega $ by the
non linearity of the pair.  In ISF language the
tail device has

$$\Gamma _{T}(t)=\Gamma _{dc}+\Gamma _{1}\cos \omega _{0}t
+\Gamma _{2}\cos 2\omega _{0}t+\cdots $$

$$\Gamma _{dc}\ne 0\;\;{\rm if\; the\; waveform\; is\;
asymmetric}$$

and

$${\cal L}_{1/f^{3}}\propto \Gamma _{dc}^{2}
\qquad {\cal L}_{1/f^{2}}\propto \Gamma _{rms}^{2}$$

$$i_{n,T}(2\omega _{0}\pm \Delta \omega )\times
\cos 2\omega _{0}t\rightarrow i_{n}(\omega _{0}\pm
\Delta \omega )$$

$$v_{n,P}(2\omega _{0})\approx i_{n,T}(2\omega _{0})
Z_{P}(2\omega _{0})$$

So that, to first order,

$$F =1+\gamma +F_{T}\qquad 
F_{T}\propto g_{m}^{2}|Z_{P}(2\omega _{0})|^{2}$$

Putting a $C_{T}$ to ground

$$|Z_{P}(2\omega _{0})|\approx {1\over 2\omega _{0}C_{T}}
\;\;{\rm for}\;\;2\omega _{0}C_{T}\gg g_{m},R_{T}^{-1}$$

shorts the $2\omega _{0}$ noise current of the
$I_{SS}$ source to ground.  The $2\omega _{0}$
voltage ripple on $P$,

$$V_{P2}\approx {I_{2}\over 2\omega _{0}C_{T}}$$

is made small.  The mixing term
$i_{n}(2\omega _{0})\times V_{P2}$ is made small.
In ISF language the large even harmonic content
of $v_{P}$ is suppressed, the waveform at $X,Y$
is made much more symmetric, $\Gamma _{dc}\rightarrow 0$,
$\Gamma _{rms}$ is reduced.

> {\it In the normal range $C_{T}\gg C_{tank}$,
> $1/2\omega _{0}C_{T}\ll 1/g_{m}$, the tail
> contribution to $F$ is essentially removed.}

In round numbers $3-10\,{\rm dB}$ improvement in
the $1/f^{2}$ region and a large reduction of the
$1/f^{3}$ corner, $\omega _{1/f^{3}}\propto \Gamma _{dc}^{2}$,
is normally observed.  The tank $Q$ and $\omega _{0}$
are to first order unchanged, $P_{s}\propto V_{osc}^{2}$
is normally slightly increased because the pair
no longer spends time in triode due to the large
$V_{P2}$ swing, which also helps ${\cal L}$.

This is the Hegazi tail filter with $L_{T}=0$.
With $L_{T}\ne 0$ $L_{T}C_{T}$ is made to resonate
in parallel at $2\omega _{0}$ so that the $I_{SS}$
device sees a high impedance at $2\omega _{0}$ and
its $2\omega _{0}$ noise cannot get into the
oscillator at all, while $C_{T}$ still shorts
everything else to ground.  Then $F_{T}\rightarrow 0$.

In the $L_{T}=0$ circuit of Fig.16 the filtering
is high pass.  $1/f$ noise around $\Delta \omega $
is {\it not} filtered, $Z_{P}(\Delta \omega )\approx
R_{T}$, so the $1/f^{3}$ improvement saturates at
the symmetrisation limit.  If $C_{T}$ is made
arbitrarily large the pole at $P$,

$$\omega _{p}\approx {1\over R_{T}C_{T}}\;\;{\rm or}\;\;
{g_{m}\over C_{T}}\;\;{\rm large\; signal}$$

moves down to $\Delta \omega $ and below.  The
node $P$ acquires a long memory.  Amplitude
fluctuations are differentiated by $C_{T}$ and,
via the non linear $C_{gs},C_{sb}$ and the
Groszkowski effect - the oscillation frequency
depends on harmonic content - converted to phase,
AM-PM.  The circuit becomes very sensitive to
low frequency modulation of $I_{SS}$ and to
squegging/latch up.  So for $C_{T}\rightarrow \infty $

$${\cal L}_{1/f^{3}}\;\;{\rm goes\; through\; a\; minimum
and\; then\; degrades\; again.}$$

There is an optimum $C_{T}$,

$$ {1\over 2\omega _{0}C_{T}}\ll {1\over g_{m}}\qquad
{1\over R_{T}C_{T}}\gg \omega _{1/f^{3}},\Delta \omega _{1/f^{2}}$$

normally $C_{T}\approx (2-10)C_{tank}$ or, with
$L_{T}$, $ \omega _{0}=1/\sqrt{L_{T}C_{T}/2}$,
for which the conventional $1/f^{2}$ phase noise
is improved and the $1/f^{3}$ corner is lowered.
Made too big with $L_{T}=0$ the close in phase
noise is made {\it worse} by the increased AM-PM
conversion.  In most text book discussions the
first, beneficial, effect is quoted as ``$C_{T}$
filters the tail noise at $2\omega _{0}$ and
improves the phase noise''.

minimax_m3.rationale: The candidate answer correctly identifies that adding CT to the tail node has a nonmonotonic effect on phase noise. It covers: (1) the filtering of 2ω0 tail noise in the moderate CT range improves phase noise and reduces the 1/f^3 corner via waveform symmetrization; (2) the class-C-like switching behavior is implicitly captured through the discussion of triode avoidance and waveform symmetry; (3) when CT is too large, the low-frequency pole at the tail node causes AM-PM conversion, squegging/latch-up instability, and the 1/f^3 phase noise degrades again. The answer explicitly states there is an optimum CT and that the effect is nonmonotonic, which is the central point of the golden solution. The reasoning is detailed, physically sound, and covers the key mechanisms.

It covers the key mechanisms (tail filtering, ISF symmetry, flicker noise, large CT memory/squegging) and reaches the central conclusion that CT is an optimization variable, not a monotonic improvement.

answers.question: Estimate the oscillation frequency of the circuit in Figure 17.

answer.text:
With the usual abuse of language the {\it small
signal} tank resonance is

$${\omega _{0}^{2}={1\over L{C_{0}}}\qquad 
f_{0}={1\over 2\pi \sqrt{LC_{0}}}\tag{1}}$$

${C_{0}}$ is the total capacity to ${\rm ac}$ ground on
one side, Fig.1,

$${C_{0}=C+{C_{gs}}+{C_{gd}}+{C_{db}}+{C_{var}}+\cdots \tag{2}}$$

on one side, $L$ the one side coil to ${V_{DD}}$.
For the differential mode ${V_{d}=X-Y}$ the half circuit
is Fig.1.  In the differential mode the two coils are in
${\rm ac}$ parallel so that (1) is normally written with the
one side $L$ and the one side $C$.  With ${C_{0}}\approx C$
(1) is the conventional ${1/\sqrt{LC}}$ resonance to
${\cal O}(10\%)$.  With normal parasitics ${C_{0}}\approx
1.1-1.3C$.

\begin{center}
{\it Fig.1 : half circuit}
\end{center}

Put ${Y_{T}=G_{p}+jB}$, ${G_{p}=1/{R_{p}}}$,
${B=\omega {C_{0}}-1/\omega L}$, ${R_{p}}=Q{\omega_{0}}L=
Q/{\omega_{0}}{C_{0}}$ the tank loss, ${G_{m0}}$ the
large or small signal transconductance of the
${I_{SS}}$ pair and ${G_{mq}}$ that of the ${I_{1}}$ pair.
For the normal square law long channel

$${G_{m0}\propto \sqrt{{I_{SS}}},\qquad 
{G_{mq}\propto \sqrt{{I_{1}}}\tag{3}}$$

and for the same ${V_{ov}}$

$${{{G_{mq}}\over {G_{m0}}}\approx {{I_{1}}\over {I_{SS}}}
\approx {{(W/L)_{q}}\over {(W/L)_{0}}}\tag{4}}$$

in the velocity saturated short channel ${G_{m}}\propto I$.

For one tank, half circuit,

$${Y_{T}}{V_{1}}={G_{m0}}{V_{1}}+{G_{mq}}{V_{2}}\tag{5a}$$
$${Y_{T}}{V_{2}}={G_{m0}}{V_{2}}\mp {G_{mq}}{V_{1}}\tag{5b}$$

the upper sign for the conventional cross strapping
${X_{1}}\to {Y_{2}}$, ${Y_{1}}\to {X_{2}}$,
${X_{2}}\to {Y_{1}}$, ${Y_{2}}\to {X_{1}}$, Fig.17,
which is the stable quadrature mode.  In matrix form

$$\left[ \matrix{{Y_{T}}-{G_{m0}} & -{G_{mq}}\cr
\pm {G_{mq}} & {Y_{T}}-{G_{m0}}\cr}\right]
\left[ \matrix{{V_{1}}\cr {V_{2}}\cr}\right]=0\tag{6}$$

$${\rm det}=0:\qquad {\left({Y_{T}}-{G_{m0}}\right)^{2}}+
{G_{mq}^{2}}=0\tag{7}$$

$${Y_{T}}-{G_{m0}}=\pm j{G_{mq}}\tag{8}$$

$${G_{p}}={G_{m0}}\tag{9a}$$

the ordinary start up condition, ${R_{p}}{G_{m0}}>1$, and

$$B=\Im {Y_{T}}=\pm {G_{mq}}\tag{9b}$$

i. e. the tank is detuned from ${B=0}$ by the quadrature
injection.  With (9b)

$$\omega {C_{0}}-{1\over {\omega L}}=\pm {G_{mq}}\tag{10}$$

$${\omega^{2}}{C_{0}}\mp {G_{mq}}\omega -{1\over L}=0\tag{11}$$

$${\omega_{q}}={{\pm {G_{mq}}/2{C_{0}}+
\sqrt{{{\left({G_{mq}}/2{C_{0}}\right)^{2}}+{\omega_{0}^{2}}}}
\tag{12}}$$

the two mathematical roots are the two quadrature modes
${V_{2}}=\pm j{V_{1}}$, $0$, $90$, $180$, $270^{{\rm o}}$.
One is stable, one is unstable.  For ${G_{mq}}\ll
{\omega_{0}}{C_{0}}$

$${\omega_{q}}\approx {\omega_{0}}\pm {{{G_{mq}}}\over
{2{C_{0}}}}={\omega_{0}}\left[1\pm {{{G_{mq}}{R_{p}}}\over
{2Q}}\right]={\omega_{0}}\left[1\pm {1\over {2Q}}
{{{G_{mq}}}\over {{G_{m0}}}}\right]\tag{13}$$

$${{\Delta \omega}\over {\omega_{0}}}\approx \pm
{1\over {2Q}}{{I_{1}}\over {I_{SS}}}\qquad {\rm small\;signal}
\tag{14}$$

so that for any normal $Q\sim 5-15$ the pulling is a few
$\%$.  E.G. $Q=10$, ${I_{1}}={I_{SS}}/3$,
${\Delta f/f_{0}}\approx 1.5\%$.

In the large signal hard switching limit the fundamental of
the square wave current is $4I/\pi $ and (9) is normally
written as

$${G_{p}}={{2}\over \pi }{{I_{SS}}\over {{V_{0}}}},\qquad 
B={{2}\over \pi }{{I_{1}}\over {{V_{0}}}}\tag{15}$$

${V_{0}}$ the differential swing, so that the tank has to
supply a phase

$$\tan \phi_{T}={B\over {G_{p}}}={{I_{1}}\over {I_{SS}}}
\tag{16}$$

$$\phi_{T}= \tan ^{-1}{{{\omega_{0}}\over \omega }-
{\omega \over {\omega_{0}}} }Q =\mp \tan ^{-1}{{I_{1}}\over
{I_{SS}}}\tag{17}$$

$${{\omega_{0}}\over {\omega_{q}}}-{{\omega_{q}}\over
{\omega_{0}}}= \mp {1\over Q}{{I_{1}}\over {I_{SS}}}\tag{18}$$

which is (13) to ${\cal O}(1/Q)$.  If the $1/Q$ detuning is
referred to the transconductance ratio itself the familiar
text book form

$${\omega_{q}}\approx {\omega_{0}}\sqrt{1+{{\left(
{{G_{mq}}\over {G_{m0}}}\right)^{2}}}}\approx
{\omega_{0}}\sqrt{1+{{\left({{I_{1}}\over {I_{SS}}}
\right)^{2}}}}\tag{19}$$

$$\approx {\omega_{0}}\left[1+{1\over 2}
{\left({{I_{1}}\over {I_{SS}}}\right)^{2}}\right]\qquad
{I_{1}}\ll {I_{SS}}\tag{20}$$

is often quoted.  For ${I_{1}}={I_{SS}}$ (19) gives
${\omega_{q}}\approx \sqrt{2}{\omega_{0}}$, for
${I_{1}}={I_{SS}}/2$, ${\omega_{q}}\approx 1.12{\omega_{0}}$,
for ${I_{1}}={I_{SS}}/3$, ${\omega_{q}}\approx 1.05
{\omega_{0}}$.  Eq.19 is the $Q\to \infty $ extrapolation of
(13).  Any intermediate form

$${f_{q}}\approx {f_{0}}\times {\cal O}(1.0-1.4)\tag{21}$$

is acceptable as an {\it estimate}.  To ${\cal O}(Q^{-1})$
the circuit oscillates for all practical purposes at the
tank resonance (1).

In particular with the tank $C$ dominant

$$f_{osc}\approx {1\over {2\pi \sqrt{LC}}}\tag{22}$$

to within $10-20\%$ for parasitics and to within a few
$\%$ for the quadrature pulling.  E.G. $L=2\,{\rm nH}$,
$C=1\,{\rm pF}$, $f_{0}\approx 3.6\,{\rm GHz}$,
$Q\approx 10$, $I_{1}=0.3I_{SS}$, $f_{q}\approx
3.6\pm 0.05\,{\rm GHz}$ small signal, $\approx 3.8\,{\rm GHz}$
on the usual $\sqrt{1+m^{2}}$ large signal estimate.
Any $L\sim 1-5\,{\rm nH}$, $C\sim 0.5-2\,{\rm pF}$ gives
$f_{0}\sim 1.5-7\,{\rm GHz}$.

The four differential outputs are in quadrature,
$X_{1}=V_{0}\cos {\omega_{q}}t$, $Y_{1}=-V_{0}\cos
{\omega_{q}}t$, $X_{2}=\pm V_{0}\sin {\omega_{q}}t$,
$Y_{2}=\mp V_{0}\sin {\omega_{q}}t$, the sign being the two
roots (12).  The in phase $V_{2}= \pm V_{1}$ mode at
$\omega_{0}$ exists mathematically but is unstable for the
cross strapping of Fig.17.  Reversing the cross strapping
interchanges stable and unstable.

answers.question: If we double the length and width of a MOSFET, what happens to its intrinsic gain?

answer.text:
Intrinsic gain is $A_{0}=g_{m}r_{o}=g_{m}/g_{ds}$

$$g_{m}\approx \mu C_{ox}{W\over L}V_{ov}= \sqrt{2\mu C_{ox}{W\over L}I_{D}}$$

$$r_{o}={1\over g_{ds}}={V_{A}\over I_{D}}={1\over \lambda I_{D}}$$

with $V_{A}=1/\lambda = V_{E}L \propto L$ to first order.

$$A_{0}={g_{m}\over g_{ds}} = {2V_{A}\over V_{ov}}={2\over \lambda V_{ov}} \approx {2L\over \lambda^{\prime}V_{ov}}$$

where $\lambda^{\prime}= \lambda L \approx const$.

> To first order $A_{0}\propto L$ and is {\it independent} of $W$.
> $W$ only enters through the bias point.

* {\it At constant $V_{ov}$ - constant $g_{m}/I_{D}$ - constant inversion level:}

$$A_{0}\propto L$$

Doubling $W$ does nothing, doubling $L$ doubles $A_{0}$.

So doubling $W$ {\it and} $L$ at same $V_{GS}$:

$$I_{D}= {1\over 2}\mu C_{ox}{W\over L}V_{ov}^{2}=const$$
$$g_{m}= \mu C_{ox}{W\over L}V_{ov}=const$$
$$r_{o}\propto L/I_{D}\rightarrow 2\times$$
$$A_{0}\rightarrow 2\times \approx +6{\rm dB}$$

* {\it At constant $I_{D}$ - normal fixed tail current case:}

$$V_{ov}= \sqrt{{2I_{D}\over \mu C_{ox}W/L}}$$

$$A_{0}={2\over \lambda V_{ov}} \propto {1\over \lambda}\sqrt{{W\over L}}\propto \sqrt{WL}$$

$$A_{0}\propto \sqrt{{\rm Area}}$$

Doubling $W$ alone: $\sqrt{2}\times$
Doubling $L$ alone: $\sqrt{2}\times$
Doubling $W$ and $L$: $2\times$

* {\it At constant current density $J=I_{D}/W$ - constant $I_{D}\propto W$:}

$$V_{ov}\propto \sqrt{L}\;\;,\;\;A_{0}\propto L/V_{ov}\propto \sqrt{L}$$

Doubling $W$ alone: no change
Doubling $L$ alone: $\sqrt{2}\times$
Doubling $W$ and $L$: $\sqrt{2}\times \approx +3{\rm dB}$

In text books this is normally quoted as the last case, so you will often hear ``$\sqrt{2}$'' or ``no change in $W/L$ so no change''.

In the usual loose language: {\it $A_{0}$ doubles for $2W/2L$ at same $I_{D}$ or same $V_{ov}$, $\sqrt{2}$ at same $J$.}

In a short channel $V_{A}$ is sub-linear in $L$ due to DIBL/CLM and $g_{m}$ is velocity saturated $g_{m}\propto W$, so the increase is $<2\times$, typically $1.5-1.8\times$ for $2L$, and you pay $4\times$ in $C_{gg}\propto WL$, $C_{gs},C_{gd}$ and $\sim 0.5\times$ in $f_{T}\approx g_{m}/C_{gg}$. It is very inefficient to get gain by scaling $W$.
