answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 17.

answer.text:
This is the $n$ channel common gate stage
with $p$ channel current source load. $V_{b1},V_{b2}$
a.c. ground.

$$M_{1}:p{\rm MOS}\;\;S=V_{DD}\;{\rm a.c.}\;0\;\;G=0\;\;
D=V_{o}\;\;r_{o1}=1/g_{ds1}=1/\lambda _{p}I_{D}$$
$$M_{2}:n{\rm MOS}\;\;G=V_{b1}\;{\rm a.c.}\;0\;\;
S=V_{i}\;\;D=V_{o}\;\;r_{o2}=1/g_{ds2}=1/\lambda _{n}I_{D}$$

The arrow on $M_{2}$ is drawn on the source.
In a $n$ well process that means the $n$ MOS is in
its own $p$ well with $B=S$ so that $V_{BS2}=0$ and
$g_{mb2}=0$ in first order.  With $B=GND$ keep
$g_{mb2}\ne 0$.  $M_{1}$ has $B=S=V_{DD}$.

Put $g_{m}=g_{m2}$, $g_{mb}=g_{mb2}$, $g_{ds}=g_{ds2}$,
$R_{L}=r_{o1}=1/g_{ds1}$ for the small signal
circuit, Fig.1. $V_{b1}=V_{b2}=0$ a.c.

> {\it Remark:} For $g_{mb}=0$ put $g_{m}+g_{mb}\rightarrow g_{m}$.

In saturation

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{D}={1\over 2}\mu _{p}C_{ox}
\left({W\over L}\right)_{1}\left(V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{Tp}|\right)^{2}
\left(1+\lambda _{p}V_{SD1}\right)$$
$$={1\over 2}\mu _{n}C_{ox}
\left({W\over L}\right)_{2}\left(V_{b1}-V_{i}-V_{Tn}\right)^{2}
\left(1+\lambda _{n}V_{DS2}\right)$$

$$V_{DS2}=V_{o}-V_{i}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{Tn}=V_{b1}-V_{i}-V_{Tn}$$
$$V_{SD1}=V_{DD}-V_{o}\ge V_{SG1}-|V_{Tp}|=V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{Tp}|$$

so that with $V_{i}=V_{iDC}$

$$V_{oDC}\approx V_{DD}-|V_{ov1}|\;\;{\rm to}\;\;V_{b1}-V_{Tn}$$

is the available swing.  $M_{1}$ is normally
saturated and presents only $g_{ds1}$ to a.c.,
$g_{m1}v_{sg1}=0$.

Small signal KCL, $v_{gs2}= -v_{s}$, $v_{bs2}= -v_{s}$
if $B=GND$, $0$ if $B=S$, $v_{ds2}=v_{d}-v_{s}$,
$v_{s}=v_{i}$, $v_{d}=v_{o}$:

$$i_{d2}=g_{m}v_{gs2}+g_{mb}v_{bs2}+g_{ds}v_{ds2}
      =-(g_{m}+g_{mb})v_{i}+g_{ds}(v_{o}-v_{i})\tag{1}$$
for $B=GND$, $g_{mb}=0$ for $B=S$.

At the output node $v_{o}/R_{L}+i_{d2}=0$,
$R_{L}=r_{o1}$, $i_{d2}$ entering the drain:

$${v_{o}\over R_{L}}-(g_{m}+g_{mb})v_{i}+g_{ds}(v_{o}-v_{i})=0 \tag{2}$$

$${v_{o}\over v_{i}}={g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}\over g_{ds}+G_{L}}
      ={g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}\over g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} \tag{3}$$

$$A_{v0}\approx {g_{m}+g_{mb}\over g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}
      =(g_{m}+g_{mb})\,r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}>0 \tag{4}$$

non inverting.  For $B=S$, $g_{mb}=0$,

$$A_{v0}\approx g_{m}r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\tag{4a}$$

the normal $CG$ voltage gain, the same as a
common source stage but $+$.  With
$g_{m}r_{o}\sim 20-50$, $A_{v0}\sim 10-25\,{\rm dB}$
for $r_{o1}\approx r_{o2}$.

In general with a source resistance $R_{sig}$ in
series with $v_{sig}$, $v_{s}=v_{i}$,

$${v_{sig}-v_{s}\over R_{sig}}=-i_{d2}\tag{5}$$

with (2),

$${v_{o}\over v_{sig}}=
{(g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds})R_{L}\over 1+g_{ds}R_{L}+R_{sig}(g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds})}
\tag{6}$$

$$={ (g_{m}+g_{mb})R_{L}\parallel r_{o2}\over 
1+R_{sig}(g_{m}+g_{mb}){R_{L}\over R_{L}+r_{o2}} }$$

For $R_{sig}=0$ (3). For $R_{sig}\gg 1/g_{m}$,
$A_{v}\rightarrow R_{L}/R_{sig}$, the circuit is a
current buffer, $i_{o}\approx i_{i}$.

Input resistance at the source, $R_{in}=v_{i}/i_{i}$,
$i_{i}$ entering the source $=-i_{d2}$:

$$i_{i}=-i_{d2}=(g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds})v_{i}-g_{ds}v_{o}\tag{7}$$

with (3)

$$i_{i}=(g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds})v_{i}
      -g_{ds}v_{i}{g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}\over g_{ds}+G_{L}}$$

$$R_{in}={v_{i}\over i_{i}}={g_{ds}+G_{L}\over G_{L}(g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds})}
      ={1+g_{ds}R_{L}\over g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}} \tag{8}$$

$$R_{in}\approx {1\over g_{m}+g_{mb}}{1+g_{ds2}r_{o1}}$$

For $R_{L}\ll r_{o2}$, $g_{ds}R_{L}\ll 1$,

$$R_{in}\approx {1\over g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}}\approx {1\over g_{m}+g_{mb}}\tag{8a}$$

$\approx 1/g_{m}$ for $B=S$, the well known low
impedance of the $CG$ stage, $\sim 100-500\,{\rm \Omega}$,
usable for $50\,{\rm \Omega}$ matching.  For the
active load $R_{L}=r_{o1}\approx r_{o2}$,

$$R_{in}\approx {2\over g_{m}+g_{mb}}\tag{8b}$$

twice the usual value.

Output resistance.  With $R_{sig}$ driving the source,
turn off $v_{sig}$, apply $v_{x}$ at the drain,
measure $i_{x}$.

$$R_{out}=R_{L}\parallel R_{oCG}\tag{9}$$

$$R_{oCG}=r_{o2}+ \left[1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})r_{o2}\right]R_{sig}
      \approx r_{o2}\;\;R_{sig}=0\tag{10}$$
$$\approx (g_{m}+g_{mb})r_{o2}R_{sig}\;\;R_{sig}\gg 1/g_{m}$$

So with ideal voltage drive

$$R_{out}\approx r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\tag{11}$$

high, $\sim 10-100\,{\rm k\Omega}$.  With
$R_{sig}\ne 0$ the $CG$ device cascodes and
$R_{out}\approx r_{o1}\parallel g_{m}r_{o2}R_{sig}$
can be very large.

Frequency and noise: No Miller multiplication.
Dominant pole

$$\omega_{p o}\approx {1\over (r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})C_{L}}\tag{12}$$
$$C_{L}=C_{db1}+C_{db2}+C_{gd2}+C_{gd1}+C_{ext}$$

Input pole

$$\omega_{p i}\approx {1\over (R_{sig}\parallel R_{in})C_{in}}\tag{13}$$
$$C_{in}\approx C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{ext}$$

$\omega_{pi}$ is at very high frequency because
$R_{in}$ is small, so the $CG$ stage is wide band,
used as wide band $50\,{\rm \Omega}$ input, as
current buffer and as the cascode device.

Short circuit current gain $i_{o}/i_{i}\approx -1$
to $+1$ depending on sign convention, i.e. current
follower.

Input referred thermal noise, $B=S$,

$$\overline{v_{n,in}^{2}}\approx 4kT\gamma
\left({1\over g_{m}}+{g_{m1}\over g_{m}^{2}}\right)\Delta f
+{K_{f}\over C_{ox}WLf}\Delta f \tag{14}$$

dominated by $M_{2}$.

In short: common gate, gate a.c. ground, input on
low impedance source, output on high impedance drain,
$A_{v}>0$, $A_{i}\approx 1$, $R_{in}\approx 1/g_{m}$,
$R_{out}\approx r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$, wide band,
current buffer / impedance transformer / cascode /
LNA input stage. Any $g_{m}\rightarrow g_{m}+g_{mb}$
if the body is to GND.

answers.question: How many poles does the circuit of Figure 18 have?

answer.text:
With the ${\cal O}\left( {{r_{o}}^{-1}}\right)$
neglected the small signal circuit is a two node circuit,
Fig.1, so that with the conventional
${\cal O}\left( {g_{m}r_{o}}\right) >>1$ notation

$${\rm det}\left[ {\bf Y}(s)\right] =0\tag{*}$$

is quadratic in $s$.
In the conventional ``grounded capacitor'' language there
is one capacitor to ground at the ${\cal G}_{1}$ node,

$$C_{{\cal G}}\approx C_{GS}\tag{1}$$

one {\it floating\/} capacitor between the ${\cal G}_{1}$
node and the ${\cal D}_{1}\equiv {\cal D}_{2}$ node,

$$C_{F}=C_{GD}\tag{2}$$

and one capacitor to {\it a\/}c ground at the
${\cal D}_{1}\equiv {\cal D}_{2}$ node

$$C_{{\cal D}}=C_{DB}+C_{DB2}+C_{GD2}\tag{3}$$

so that, with $R_{S}\ne 0$, $(*)$ is normally written in
the Miller form as a two pole, one zero, low pass.
Put $R_{o}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$ and $C_{L}=C_{{\cal D}}$.
To ${\cal O}\left( R_{o}^{-1}\right)$

$${\bf Y}(s)=\left[ \matrix{
{{1}\over {R_{S}}}+s\left( C_{GS}+C_{GD}\right) &-sC_{GD}\cr
g_{m1}-sC_{GD}&{{1}\over {R_{o}}}+s\left( C_{L}+C_{GD}\right)\cr}\right] \tag{4}$$

so that, with $V_{o}\equiv V_{{\cal D}_{1}}$,

$${{V_{o}}\over {V_{i}}}(s)=-{{g_{m1}-sC_{GD}}\over {{\rm det}{\bf Y}(s)}}
{{1}\over {R_{S}}}\tag{5}$$

$${\rm det}{\bf Y}(s)={{1}\over {R_{S}R_{o}}}
+s\left[ {{C_{L}+C_{GD}}\over {R_{S}}}+{{C_{GS}+C_{GD}}\over {R_{o}}}
+g_{m1}C_{GD}\right] +s^{2}\left[ C_{GS}C_{L}+C_{GD}\left(
C_{GS}+C_{L}\right)\right] \tag{6}$$

i. e. in the conventional pole zero form

$${{V_{o}}\over {V_{i}}}(s)=-{{g_{m1}R_{o}}\over {1+sR_{S}
\left[ C_{GS}+C_{GD}\left( 1+g_{m1}R_{o}\right)\right] }}
{{1-sC_{GD}/g_{m1}}\over {1+sR_{o}\left[ C_{L}+
C_{GD}{{1+sR_{S}C_{GS}}\over {1+sR_{S}\left[ C_{GS}+
C_{GD}\left( 1+g_{m1}R_{o}\right)\right] }}\right] }}+{\cal O}
\left( R_{o}^{-1}\right) \tag{7}$$

so that for

$$g_{m1}R_{o}>>1\qquad {\rm and}\qquad 
R_{S}\left[ C_{GS}+C_{GD}\left( 1+g_{m1}R_{o}\right)\right] >>
R_{o}C_{L}\tag{8}$$

in the usual dominant pole Miller approximation

$${{V_{o}}\over {V_{i}}}(s)\approx -{{g_{m1}R_{o}}\over 
\left[ 1+s/s_{p{\cal G}}\right]\left[ 1+s/s_{p{\cal D}}\right]}
\left[ 1-s/s_{z}\right] \tag{9}$$

with, to leading order in $g_{m1}R_{o}$,

$$\eqalign{
s_{z}&=+{{g_{m1}}\over {C_{GD}}}>0\cr
s_{p{\cal G}}&\approx -{{1}\over {R_{S}\left[ C_{GS}+
C_{GD}\left( 1+g_{m1}R_{o}\right)\right]}}\cr
s_{p{\cal D}}&\approx -{{1}\over {R_{o}\left[ C_{L}+
C_{GD}{{C_{GS}}\over {C_{GS}+C_{GD}\left( 1+g_{m1}R_{o}\right)}}
\right]}}\approx -{{1}\over {R_{o}C_{L}}}\cr}\tag{10}$$

the familiar Miller multiplied input pole and the output
pole at the common drain node.  $s_{z}$ is the normal
right half plane feed forward zero through $C_{GD}$.
In the $R_{S}\rightarrow 0$ limit $s_{p{\cal G}}\rightarrow
-\infty $ and $s_{z}\rightarrow +\infty $ and (9) goes
over to the conventional single pole

$${{V_{o}}\over {V_{i}}}(s)\approx -{{g_{m1}R_{o}}\over 
1+sR_{o}\left( C_{L}+C_{GD}\right)}\tag{11}$$

at the output node.

Loosely speaking the $s_{z}$ is often counted as a
``pole'' so that the circuit is often referred to as a
three pole circuit, one pole at the ${\cal G}_{1}$ node,
one pole at the ${\cal D}_{1}\equiv {\cal D}_{2}$ node and
one Miller pole.  Counting every physical capacitor to
{\it a\/}c ground there are five physical capacitors,
$C_{GS}$, $C_{GD}$, $C_{DB}$, $C_{GD2}$, $C_{DB2}$, collapsing
to the three groups (1)--(3) above, i. e. to the second
order denominator (6).  With $C_{GS2}$ and $C_{SB}$ put back
in the count is seven physical capacitors, four groups.

> {\it Remark:\/}  In many text books (1)--(3) are counted
> as three distinct poles, so that with the zero (9) is
> quoted as a three pole, one zero, system.  Strictly
> speaking the denominator is second order, i. e. two
> finite poles.

+{g_{1}+G_{m2}+g_{2}\over G_{m2}+g_{2}}
\left[g_{m2}v_{in}+v_{out}\left(g_{2}+G_{D}\right)\right]
=g_{2}v_{out}$$

$${A_{v}={v_{out}\over v_{in}}=
-{g_{m1}\left(G_{m2}+g_{2}\right)+g_{m2}g_{1}\over 
g_{1}g_{2}+G_{D}\left(g_{1}+G_{m2}+g_{2}\right)}}\tag{6}$$

$${A_{v}=-R_{D}{g_{m1}\left(G_{m2}+g_{2}\right)+g_{m2}g_{1}\over 
1+R_{D}\left(g_{1}+g_{2}+G_{m2}\right)/r_{o1}r_{o2}g_{1}g_{2}}
{R_{D}+r_{o1}+r_{o2}+G_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}} }$$

$${A_{v}=-R_{D}{g_{m1}G_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}+g_{m1}r_{o1}+g_{m2}r_{o2}
\over R_{D}+r_{o1}+r_{o2}+G_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}} }\tag{7}$$

Put $v_{in}=0$ and drive the output with $v_{x}$,
$i_{x}=g_{2}v_{x}+G_{m2}v_{x}+g_{1}v_{x}$ through the
divider $r_{o1},r_{o2}$,

$${R_{o}\equiv {v_{x}\over i_{x}}\Bigl|_{v_{in}=0}
={g_{1}+G_{m2}+g_{2}\over g_{1}g_{2}}
=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+G_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}}\tag{8}$$

the familiar cascode resistance.  With $g_{mb2}=0$

$$R_{o}\approx r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}\approx 
g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}\;\;{\rm for}\;g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$$

Then (6) can be written as

$$A_{v}=-G_{m,{\rm eff}}\,R_{D}\parallel R_{o}\tag{9}$$

with

$${G_{m,{\rm eff}}={g_{m1}\left(G_{m2}+g_{2}\right)+g_{m2}g_{1}
\over g_{1}+G_{m2}+g_{2}}}\tag{10}$$

$$G_{m,{\rm eff}}\xrightarrow[g_{1},g_{2}\ll G_{m2}]{}g_{m1}$$

so that in the {\it formal} small signal sense, with both
devices taken as saturated,

$${A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}\,R_{D}\parallel 
\left[r_{o1}+r_{o2}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}\right]}\tag{11}$$

and for $R_{D}\ll R_{o}$

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}R_{D}$$

i. e. the same $g_{m}$ as ${\rm M}_{1}$ alone but with an
output impedance multiplied by $g_{m}r_{o}$.

This is the ``self cascode'' or ``composite cascode''.
Formally it is a $CS$ stage whose active device has been
replaced by the series composite.

In large signal the formal $g_{m1}$ result is not
realisable with $V_{G1}=V_{G2}=V_{in}$ and a common
$p$--substrate.  Let

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{D}\tag{12}$$

For $\lambda =0$, $\gamma =0$, $W_{1}=W_{2}=W$,
$L_{1}=L_{2}=L$, $k=\mu C_{ox}W/L$, $V_{ov}=V_{in}-V_{TH}$,

$$I_{D1}=k\left[V_{ov}V_{x}-V_{x}^{2}/2\right]\;\;{\rm triode}$$
$$I_{D2}={1\over 2}k\left(V_{ov}-V_{x}\right)^{2}\;\;{\rm sat}$$

$I_{D1}=I_{D2}$ gives

$$2V_{x}^{2}-4V_{ov}V_{x}+V_{ov}^{2}=0$$

$${V_{x}=V_{ov}\left(1-{1\over \sqrt{2}}\right)\approx 0.29V_{ov}}\tag{13}$$

$${V_{ov2}=V_{ov}-V_{x}=V_{ov}/\sqrt{2}}\tag{14}$$

So for $V_{out}>V_{ov}$ the composite is saturated with

* ${\rm M}_{2}$ saturated
* ${\rm M}_{1}$ in the triode region

$$g_{m1}=kV_{x}\approx 0.29kV_{ov}\tag{15}$$
$$g_{1}=k\left(V_{ov}-V_{x}\right)=kV_{ov}/\sqrt{2}=g_{m2}\tag{16}$$
$$g_{m2}=kV_{ov2}=kV_{ov}/\sqrt{2}\tag{17}$$
$$g_{2}= \lambda I_{D}\ll g_{1}\tag{18}$$

Putting (15)-(18) in (8)-(10)

$$R_{o}={g_{1}+G_{m2}+g_{2}\over g_{1}g_{2}}
\approx {2g_{m2}+g_{mb2}\over g_{m2}g_{2}}
\approx \left(2+{g_{mb2}\over g_{m2}}\right)r_{o2}\tag{19}$$

$$G_{m,{\rm eff}}={g_{m1}G_{m2}+g_{m2}g_{1}\over g_{1}+G_{m2}}
\approx {g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})+g_{m2}^{2}\over 2g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}\tag{20}$$

For $g_{mb2}=0$

$${G_{m,{\rm eff}}\approx {g_{m1}+g_{m2}\over 2}={kV_{ov}\over 2}}\tag{21}$$

$${R_{o}\approx 2r_{o2}}\tag{22}$$

$${A_{v}\approx -G_{m,{\rm eff}}\,R_{D}\parallel R_{o}
\approx -{kV_{ov}\over 2}R_{D}\;\;R_{D}\ll R_{o}}\tag{23}$$

More generally for $W_{1},L_{1}\ne W_{2},L_{2}$ in
saturation

$$I_{D}={1\over 2}\mu C_{ox}{W_{\rm eff}\over L_{\rm eff}}
\left(V_{in}-V_{TH}\right)^{2}\left(1+\lambda_{\rm eff}V_{out}\right)$$

with

$${{1\over (W/L)_{\rm eff}}={1\over (W/L)_{1}}+{1\over (W/L)_{2}}
\qquad {W_{\rm eff}\over L_{\rm eff}}={1\over L_{1}/W_{1}+L_{2}/W_{2}} }\tag{24}$$

For $W_{1}=W_{2}=W$

$${(W/L)_{\rm eff}= {W\over L_{1}+L_{2}} }\tag{25}$$

i. e. the series connection emulates a single device of
length $L_{1}+L_{2}$.  Its

* transconductance is that of the long device,
$G_{m,{\rm eff}}\approx \mu C_{ox}(W/L)_{\rm eff}V_{ov}
= G_{m1}L_{1}/(L_{1}+L_{2})$,
about $1/2\,g_{m1}$ for $L_{1}=L_{2}$,
* output resistance is that of the long device,
$R_{o}\approx r_{o1}L_{\rm eff}/L_{1}\approx 2r_{o}$ for
$L_{1}=L_{2}$,
* intrinsic gain $G_{m,{\rm eff}}R_{o}\approx g_{m}r_{o}$
is unchanged.

With the $p$--substrate grounded $V_{TH2}=V_{TH0}+
\gamma\left(\sqrt{2\phi_{F}+V_{x}}-\sqrt{2\phi_{F}}\right)
>V_{TH1}$, $G_{m2}=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$, $R_{o}$ is increased
by $1+g_{mb2}/g_{m2}$ and $G_{m,{\rm eff}}$ is slightly
reduced.  Tying the $n$--well of ${\rm M}_{2}$ to its
source, if available, removes $g_{mb2}$ and makes (11)
exact in the formal sense.

In words: the circuit is a common source amplifier with
resistive load $R_{D}$ whose driver is a composite
transistor ${\rm M}_{1}+{\rm M}_{2}$ in series with common
gate.  Small signal it looks like a cascode with
$R_{o}=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}$ and
$G_{m}=G_{m,{\rm eff}}$.  Large signal it behaves as a
single long channel device $W/(L_{1}+L_{2})$, i. e. $1/2$
the $k$, $1/2$ the $g_{m}$, $2\times$ the $r_{o}$ for
$L_{1}=L_{2}$, same $g_{m}r_{o}$, same $V_{DS,sat}\approx
V_{ov}$, but with much reduced $\lambda$, DIBL and
narrow channel effects.  It is widely used as a
high impedance current mirror / active load and as a
``long $L$ without long $L$'' in short channel
technologies.  The price is $\approx C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}$
input capacitance, a pole at the intermediate node
$\omega_{x}\approx (g_{1}+G_{m2})/C_{x}$ and, with body
effect, a somewhat larger $V_{TH,{\rm eff}}$.

For $R_{D}\ll R_{o}$ the familiar

$$A_{v}\approx -G_{m,{\rm eff}}R_{D}$$

is recovered, nominally $-g_{m1}R_{D}$ if the triode
nature of ${\rm M}_{1}$ is ignored, more accurately
$-(g_{m1}+g_{m2})R_{D}/2 = -(kV_{ov}/2)R_{D}$ for the
physical bias with $L_{1}=L_{2}$, i. e. one half the gain
of a $W/L_{1}$ device alone, but with twice the available
output swing before $\lambda$ becomes important.  Any
intermediate $L_{\rm eff}$ can be synthesized by choice of
$L_{1},L_{2}$ via (24).

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 20.

answer.text:
With ${\rm M}_{b}\equiv V_{b}={\rm cst}$ for
the signal the circuit is the $n$ channel
source coupled pair with a resistive load on one side
only.  Put

$${\rm M}_{1}:g_{m1},g_{mb1},r_{o1}=1/g_{o1}\qquad 
  {\rm M}_{2}:g_{m2},g_{mb2},r_{o2}=1/g_{o2}\qquad 
  I_{1}:r_{oT}$$

and for the signal $V_{DD}=0$, $V_{b}=0$.
Let

$$v_{x}=v_{s1}=v_{s2}\qquad v_{o}=v_{d2}$$

$$v_{gs1}=v_{i}-v_{x}\;\;v_{bs1}=-v_{x}\;\;v_{ds1}=-v_{x}$$
$$v_{gs2}=-v_{x}\;\;v_{bs2}=-v_{x}\;\;v_{ds2}=v_{o}-v_{x}$$

$$\eqalign{
i_{d1}&=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{mb1}v_{bs1}+g_{o1}v_{ds1}
      =g_{m1}v_{i}-(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{o1})v_{x}\cr
i_{d2}&=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{mb2}v_{bs2}+g_{o2}v_{ds2}
      =-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2})v_{x}+g_{o2}v_{o}\tag{1}}$$

KCL at $x$ and at the output, Fig.1,

$$i_{d1}+i_{d2}=v_{x}/r_{oT}\approx 0\tag{2a}$$
$$i_{d2}+v_{o}/R_{D}=0\tag{2b}$$

for $r_{oT}\to \infty $.  In general put $g_{oT}=1/r_{oT}$
in (2a).  From (1)(2b)

$$-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2})v_{x}+g_{o2}v_{o}=-v_{o}/R_{D}$$

$$(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2})v_{x}=(g_{o2}+G_{D})v_{o}\tag{3}$$

$$G_{D}=1/R_{D}$$

$$v_{x}=v_{o}{\,G_{D}+g_{o2}\,\over g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2}}\tag{4}$$

and from (1)(2a)(2b) $i_{d1}=-i_{d2}=v_{o}/R_{D}$,

$${v_{o}\over R_{D}}=g_{m1}v_{i}-(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{o1})v_{x}\tag{5}$$

With (4)

$$g_{m1}v_{i}=v_{o}\left[{1\over R_{D}}+
(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{o1}){G_{D}+g_{o2}\over 
g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2}}\right] \tag{6}$$

i. e. the conventional non inverting gain

$$A_{v}={v_{o}\over v_{i}}=
{g_{m1}\over G_{D}+ (g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{o1})
{G_{D}+g_{o2}\over g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2}} } \tag{7}$$

$$A_{v}=g_{m1}R_{D}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2}\over 
g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{o1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2}
+g_{o2}R_{D}(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{o1})}\tag{7a}$$

Neglecting $g_{o}R_{D}\ll 1$,

$$A_{v}\approx {g_{m1}R_{D}\over 
1+{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}\over g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}}
= R_{D}{g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})\over 
g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}} \tag{8}$$

If the body effect is neglected $g_{mb}=0$,

$$A_{v}\approx {g_{m1}g_{m2}\over g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_{D}
{1\over 1+g_{o2}R_{D}{g_{m1}+g_{o1}\over g_{m1}+g_{m2}}}
\approx {g_{m1}g_{m2}\over g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_{D}\tag{9}$$

For the normally matched bias $I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{1}/2$,
$g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_{m}$, $g_{mb1}=g_{mb2}$,

$$A_{v}\approx {g_{m}R_{D}\over 2}{1\over 1+R_{D}/2r_{o}}
\approx {1\over 2}g_{m}R_{D}\qquad r_{o}\gg R_{D} \tag{10}$$

apart from the sign it is one half the normal
differential pair gain.  With differential input
$v_{id}=v_{in}-v_{b}$,

$$A_{d}={v_{o}\over v_{id}}=+{1\over 2}g_{m}R_{D}\;\;{\rm s.e.},
\qquad g_{m}R_{D}\;\;{\rm diff.}$$

The sign is $+$: ${\rm M}_{1}$ is a common drain,
$A_{v1}<1$, ${\rm M}_{2}$ is a common gate, $A_{v2}>0$.
Indeed (7) can be written as $A_{v}=A_{v1}A_{v2}$ with

$$R_{in2}={R_{D}+r_{o2}\over 1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}}
\approx {1\over g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}\tag{11}$$

the impedance looking into the source of the CG stage
loaded with $R_{D}$,

$$A_{v1}={v_{x}\over v_{i}}=
{g_{m1}\over g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{o1}+R_{in2}^{-1}}\tag{12}$$

$$A_{v2}={v_{o}\over v_{x}}=(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2})
\,R_{D}\parallel r_{o2}\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})R_{D}\tag{13}$$

so that $A_{v}=A_{v1}A_{v2}$ gives (7).  For
$g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$, $A_{v1}\approx (g_{m1}/(g_{m1}+g_{m2}))<1$.

* Input impedance: gate of ${\rm M}_{1}$,

$$Z_{in}=1/sC_{gs1}\to \infty \;\;{\rm at\;low\;frequency}$$

* Output impedance: $v_{i}=0$, look into $d_{2}$ with
$R_{S}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{oT}\parallel 1/(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{o1})$
in the source,

$$R_{o2}=r_{o2}+ \left[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right]R_{S}\tag{14}$$

$$Z_{out}=R_{D}\parallel R_{o2}\tag{15}$$

$$R_{S}\approx {1\over g_{m1}+g_{mb1}}\parallel r_{oT}$$

For $r_{oT}\to\infty $ and $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$,

$$R_{o2}\approx r_{o2}\left[1+{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}\over 
g_{m1}+g_{mb1}}\right]\approx 2r_{o}\;\;{\rm matched}$$

$$Z_{out}\approx R_{D}\parallel 2r_{o}\approx R_{D}\tag{16}$$

With $g_{mb}=0$, $R_{o2}\approx r_{o2}+g_{m2}r_{o2}/g_{m1}$.

In the usual $R_{D}\ll r_{o}$, $Z_{out}\approx R_{D}$.

The low impedance $\sim 1/g_{m}$ at the $x$ node pushes
the pole at $x$,

$$\omega_{px}\approx {g_{m1}+g_{m2}\over C_{x}},\qquad 
  C_{x}=C_{gs1}+C_{sb1}+C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{oT}$$

to high frequency.  The dominant pole is at the output

$$\omega_{po}\approx {1\over Z_{out}C_{L}},\qquad 
  C_{L}=C_{db2}+C_{gd2}+C_{D}$$

so the CD-CG cascade is wide band, no Miller multiplication
of $C_{gd1}$ because $d_{1}$ is at AC ground.  This is the
normal source coupled differential pair used as the input
stage of an op-amp, as a wide band $+g_{m}R_{D}/2$ gain
stage, level shifter, etc.

Large signal, square law in saturation,

$$I_{D1}={k_{n}\over 2}(V_{GS1}-V_{T})^{2},\;
  I_{D2}={k_{n}\over 2}(V_{GS2}-V_{T})^{2},\;
  I_{D1}+I_{D2}=I_{1}$$

$$V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_{D}$$

For $V_{id}=V_{in}-V_{b}\gg 0$, $I_{D1}\to I_{1}$, $I_{D2}\to 0$,
$V_{out}\to V_{DD}$; for $V_{id}\ll 0$, $I_{D1}\to 0$,
$I_{D2}\to I_{1}$, $V_{out}\to V_{DD}-I_{1}R_{D}$.
Linear operation for

$$|V_{id}|\lesssim \sqrt{2I_{1}/k_{n}}\;,\qquad 
  k_{n}=k_{n}'W/L$$

with $g_{m}=\sqrt{k_{n}I_{1}}$ at balance.

With finite $r_{oT}$ the common mode gain is

$$A_{cm}\approx -{R_{D}\over 2r_{oT}}{g_{m1}\over g_{m1}+g_{m2}}
\approx -{R_{D}\over 4r_{oT}}$$

so that ${\rm CMRR}=|A_{d}/A_{cm}|\approx g_{m}r_{oT}$.

DC bias: at balance $V_{in}=V_{b}$, $I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{1}/2$,
$V_{x}=V_{in}-V_{GS1}$, $V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{1}R_{D}/2$.
Saturation requires

$$V_{DS1}=V_{DD}-V_{x}\ge V_{GS1}-V_{T},\qquad 
  V_{DS2}=V_{out}-V_{x}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{T}$$

and $V_{x}\ge V_{DSAT,T}+V_{SS}$ for the tail source to stay
in saturation.  Any $R_{D}$ can be replaced by a $p$MOS
current source load for $A_{v}\approx g_{m}r_{o}/2$.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in Figure 21 can be inductive.

answer.text:
With ${\rm Vin}=0$ for $Z_{o}$ the gate is
returned to ground through $R_{S}$.

$$\eqalign{
M_{2}:&V_{b}=ac\;0\cr
&Z_{o2}\approx r_{o2}\parallel 1/sC_{o2}\approx r_{o2}\cr
M_{1}:&{\rm C.D.}}$$

Put $V_{x}$ on the source and measure $I_{x}$,
Fig.1.  Neglect $C_{sb},C_{db}$ for the idea.

$$\eqalign{
g:&\;{V_{g}\over R_{S}}+(V_{g}-V_{x})sC_{gs}+V_{g}sC_{gd}=0\tag{1}\cr
s:&\;I_{x}+g_{m}V_{gs}+g_{mb}V_{bs}+g_{o}V_{ds}
      +(V_{g}-V_{x})sC_{gs}=0\tag{2}}$$

$V_{gs}=V_{g}-V_{x}$ , $V_{bs}=-V_{x}$ for $p$ sub,
$V_{ds}=-V_{x}$, $g_{o}=g_{o1}+g_{o2}$,
$g_{m}^{\prime}=g_{m}+g_{mb}$.

From (1)

$$V_{g}\left[{1\over R_{S}}+s(C_{gs}+C_{gd})\right]=V_{x}sC_{gs}$$

$$V_{g}=V_{x}{sC_{gs}R_{S}\over 1+sR_{S}(C_{gs}+C_{gd})}\tag{3}$$

i. e. the source is coupled to the gate through
$C_{gs}$ but the gate can only move with the
$R_{S}C_{g}$ time constant.  For $s\to 0$ $V_{g}\to 0$,
for $s\to \infty $ $V_{g}\to V_{x}C_{gs}/(C_{gs}+C_{gd})$.

Put (3) in (2) with the sign that $g_{m}V_{gs}$
flows {\it into} the source node,

$$I_{x}=V_{x}\left(g_{m}^{\prime}+g_{o}+sC_{gs}\right)
      +V_{g}\left(-g_{m}-sC_{gs}\right) $$

$$Z_{o}^{-1}={I_{x}\over V_{x}}=g_{m}^{\prime}+g_{o}+sC_{gs}
      -\left(g_{m}+sC_{gs}\right){sC_{gs}R_{S}\over 
      1+sR_{S}(C_{gs}+C_{gd})}\tag{4}$$

$$Z_{o}={1+sR_{S}(C_{gs}+C_{gd})\over 
      g_{m}^{\prime}+g_{o}+s\left[C_{gs}+R_{S}g_{o}C_{gs}
      +R_{S}g_{m}^{\prime}C_{gd}\right]+s^{2}R_{S}C_{gs}C_{gd}}\tag{5}$$

in parallel with $r_{o2}$.  For $g_{o}\approx 0$,
$C_{gd}\ll C_{gs}$ the familiar form

$$Z_{o1}\approx {1+sC_{gs}R_{S}\over g_{m}^{\prime}+sC_{gs}}
      ={1\over g_{m}^{\prime}}{1+s/\omega _{z}\over 1+s/\omega _{p}}
      \parallel r_{o}\tag{6}$$

$$\omega _{z}={1\over R_{S}C_{gs}}\qquad 
  \omega _{p}={g_{m}^{\prime}\over C_{gs}}\approx \omega _{T}$$

$$Z_{o1}={1+sC_{gs}R_{S}\over g_{m}^{\prime}+sC_{gs}}
      =R_{S}+{1/g_{m}^{\prime}-R_{S}\over 1+sC_{gs}/g_{m}^{\prime}}\tag{7}$$

i. e. a pole - zero doublet.  For $R_{S}=0$

$$Z_{o1}={1\over g_{m}^{\prime}+sC_{gs}}={1\over g_{m}^{\prime}}\parallel
  {1\over sC_{gs}}$$

capacitive.  For $R_{S}\ne 0$ the zero can be at a
{\it lower} frequency than the pole.

If

$$R_{S}>{1\over g_{m}^{\prime}}\qquad \omega _{z}<\omega _{p}\tag{8}$$

$|Z_{o}|$ {\it rises} with frequency between
$\omega _{z}$ and $\omega _{p}$ and

$${\rm arg}\,Z_{o}= {\rm arg}\,(1+j\omega /\omega _{z})
                -{\rm arg}\,(1+j\omega /\omega _{p})>0$$

positive, inductive, phase.  Indeed for
$|s|C_{gs}/g_{m}^{\prime}\ll 1$

$${1\over 1+sC_{gs}/g_{m}^{\prime}}\approx 1-sC_{gs}/g_{m}^{\prime}$$

from (7)

$$Z_{o1}\approx {1\over g_{m}^{\prime}}
      +s{C_{gs}\over g_{m}^{\prime}}\left(R_{S}-{1\over g_{m}^{\prime}}\right)
      =R_{o}+sL_{eq}\tag{9}$$

$$R_{o}\approx {1\over g_{m}^{\prime}}\parallel r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$$

$$L_{eq}\approx {R_{S}C_{gs}\over g_{m}^{\prime}}-{C_{gs}\over g_{m}^{\prime 2}}
      ={C_{gs}\over g_{m}^{\prime 2}}\left(g_{m}^{\prime}R_{S}-1\right) \tag{10}$$

with $C_{gd}$ kept

$$L_{eq}\approx {R_{S}(C_{gs}+C_{gd})(g_{m}^{\prime}+g_{o})
      -C_{gs}-R_{S}g_{m}^{\prime}C_{gd}\over (g_{m}^{\prime}+g_{o})^{2}}
      \approx {C_{gs}(g_{m}^{\prime}R_{S}-1)\over g_{m}^{\prime 2}}$$

$>0$ for (8).  More exactly from (5)

$$Z_{o}(j\omega)=R(\omega)+jX(\omega)\;\;,\;\;X>0\;\;
  {\rm for}\;\omega _{z}<\omega <\omega _{p}$$

up to $\omega \sim \omega _{p}$ where $C_{gs}$ shorts
$g$ to $s$ and $Z_{o}\to R_{S}\parallel 1/j\omega C_{gd}$,
capacitive again.  In the mid band the circuit looks
like $R_{o}$ in series with $L_{eq}$, or a lossy
parallel $R_{p}\parallel L_{p}$.

Physically $C_{gs}$ feeds the output variation back to
the gate.  At $dc$ $C_{gs}$ is open, $V_{g}=0$,
$Z_{o}=1/g_{m}^{\prime}$.  On a fast positive
$\Delta V_{o}$, $C_{gs}$ pulls $V_{g}$ up but $R_{S}$
prevents $V_{g}$ from following instantaneously.
$V_{g}$ lags $V_{o}$, $V_{gs}=V_{g}-V_{o}<0$,
the $g_{m}V_{gs}$ current that would normally hold
$V_{o}$ down is reduced with a delay $\sim R_{S}C_{gs}$.
Current lags voltage - inductive.  The $R_{S}C_{gs}$
differentiator plus the $g_{m}$ voltage to current
conversion is a gyrator, $Z\propto sC_{gs}R_{S}/g_{m}$.

With a capacitive load $C_{L}$ it resonates as
$s^{2}L_{eq}C_{L}+sR_{o}C_{L}+1=0$, the well known
peaking / ringing and possible oscillation of a
source follower driving $C_{L}$ when the previous
stage has finite $R_{S}$.  Normally $R_{S}$ is the
output resistance of the driving stage.  The effect
is often used as an active inductor for shunt
peaking.  With $R_{S}<1/g_{m}^{\prime}$ $L_{eq}<0$,
capacitive.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 22.

answer.text:
With ${\rm M}_{1}$ in the ${\rm CS}$ connection
and ${\rm M}_{2}$ in the ${\rm CS}$ connection the other way
round the circuit is a 2 stage loop with an even number of
inversions.

$$\eqalign{
A_{1}&={\rm M}_{1}{\rm \;on\;}R_{D1}\cr
A_{2}&={\rm M}_{2}{\rm \;on\;}r_{o2}}$$

Put $r_{o1}=1/g_{ds1}\;,\;r_{o2}=1/g_{ds2}$,
$g_{m1},g_{m2}$ in saturation, $V_{BS}=0$.
Put $C_{X}$ on $X$ and $C_{o}$ on the output for the
dynamics.  For $s=0$

{\it Small signal} Fig.1

$$\eqalign{
v_{o}&=-g_{m1}v_{x}R_{o1}^{\prime } \tag{1}\cr
i_{in}&=g_{ds2}v_{x}+g_{m2}v_{o} \tag{2}}$$

$$R_{o1}^{\prime}=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\qquad 
g_{ds2}=1/r_{o2}$$

(1) is KCL at $v_{o}$ , $g_{m1}v_{x}+g_{ds1}v_{o}+
v_{o}/R_{D1}=0$ , (2) is KCL at $X$ , the gate of
${\rm M}_{1}$ draws no current.

> {\it Remark:}  With $r_{o}\to \infty $ the customary
> square law $I_{D}=k(V_{GS}-V_{T})^{2}/2$ gives
> $I_{in}=I_{D2}$ and $V_{o}=V_{DD}-R_{D1}I_{D1}$ so that
> formally
> $$V_{o}=V_{T}+\sqrt{2I_{in}/k}\tag{3}$$
> $$V_{x}=V_{T}+\sqrt{2(V_{DD}-V_{o})/kR_{D1}}\tag{4}$$
> i. e. a (mathematical) d. c. solution always exists.
> It is small signal unstable for $r_{o}\to \infty $.
> $r_{o}$ must be retained.

From (1)(2)

$$i_{in}=v_{x}\left[g_{ds2}-g_{m2}g_{m1}R_{o1}^{\prime}\right] \tag{5}$$

$$v_{o}=-g_{m1}R_{o1}^{\prime}v_{x} \tag{6}$$

so that with the usual return ratio

$$T_{0}=g_{m1}R_{o1}^{\prime}g_{m2}r_{o2}>0 \tag{7}$$

is the {\it d. c. loop gain}.  $T_{0}>0$ is regenerative.
In $s$

$$T(s)={T_{0}\over \left(1+sR_{o1}^{\prime}C_{o}\right)
\left(1+sr_{o2}C_{X}\right)} \tag{8}$$

$$A_{1}(s)=-{g_{m1}R_{o1}^{\prime}\over 1+sR_{o1}^{\prime}C_{o}}
\qquad A_{2}(s)=-{g_{m2}r_{o2}\over 1+sr_{o2}C_{X}} \tag{9}$$

$$T(s)=A_{1}(s)A_{2}(s) \tag{10}$$

i. e. two inversions.  Breaking the loop at $X$,
$Z_{X0}=r_{o2}$, $Z_{o0}=R_{o1}^{\prime}$,

$$T_{0}=g_{m1}g_{m2}Z_{X0}Z_{o0} \tag{11}$$

is the conventional shunt-shunt loop gain.  The
feedback $y$ - parameter is $y_{f}=g_{m2}$,
$V_{o}\to I_{f}=g_{m2}V_{o}$ shunted at $X$.

From (5)(6) the closed loop transresistance

$$R_{M}(s)={v_{o}\over i_{in}}(s)=
-{g_{m1}R_{o1}^{\prime}r_{o2}\over 
\left(1+sR_{o1}^{\prime}C_{o}\right)\left(1+sr_{o2}C_{X}\right)
-T_{0}} \tag{12}$$

$${R_{M0}\over 1-T_{0}}\;\;{\rm with}\;\;
R_{M0}=-g_{m1}R_{o1}^{\prime}r_{o2} \tag{13}$$

is the open loop $i_{in}\to v_{o}$ transresistance,
$v_{x0}=i_{in}r_{o2}$, $v_{o0}=A_{1}v_{x0}$.
I. e. Blackman

$$R_{M}={R_{M0}\over 1-T(s)} \tag{14}$$

Explicitly at $s=0$

$$R_{M0}^{cl}={v_{o}\over i_{in}}\Bigl|_{0}=
-{g_{m1}R_{o1}^{\prime}\over g_{ds2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{o1}^{\prime}}
={g_{m1}R_{o1}^{\prime}\over g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{o1}^{\prime}-g_{ds2}} \tag{15}$$

$$R_{M0}^{cl}={1\over g_{m2}}{T_{0}\over T_{0}-1}
=-{1\over g_{m2}}{T_{0}\over 1-T_{0}} \tag{16}$$

For $|1-T_{0}|\ll 1$

$$\left|R_{M}^{cl}\right|\approx 
{g_{m1}R_{o1}^{\prime}r_{o2}\over |1-T_{0}|}\gg R_{M0} \tag{17}$$

is the regenerative gain enhancement.  In the
ideal $r_{o2}\to \infty $ limit, $T_{0}\to \infty $,

$$R_{M}^{cl}\to {1\over g_{m2}} \tag{18}$$

with the sign reversed with respect to the open loop
inverting $R_{M0}$.  The sign reversal is the signature
of $T_{0}>1$.

By Blackman the driving point impedances are divided by
$1-T$,

$$Z_{X}(s)={Z_{X0}(s)\over 1-T(s)}\qquad 
Z_{o}(s)={Z_{o0}(s)\over 1-T(s)} \tag{19}$$

i. e.

$$Z_{in}(s)={v_{x}\over i_{in}}=
{r_{o2}\over \left(1+sr_{o2}C_{X}\right)\left(1+sR_{o1}^{\prime}
C_{o}\right)-T_{0}}\left(1+sR_{o1}^{\prime}C_{o}\right) \tag{20}$$

$$Z_{in0}={1\over g_{ds2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{o1}^{\prime}}
={r_{o2}\over 1-T_{0}} \tag{21}$$

$$Z_{out}(s)={R_{o1}^{\prime}\over 
\left(1+sr_{o2}C_{X}\right)\left(1+sR_{o1}^{\prime}C_{o}\right)
-T_{0}}\left(1+sr_{o2}C_{X}\right) \tag{22}$$

$$Z_{out0}={R_{o1}^{\prime}\over 1-T_{0}}
={1\over G_{o1}-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}\tag{23}$$

$$G_{o1}=1/R_{o1}^{\prime}=1/R_{D1}+g_{ds1}$$

For $T_{0}<1$ the closed loop input and output
resistances are {\it reduced} by $|1-T_{0}|$,
$|Z_{in}|\ll r_{o2}$, $|Z_{out}|\ll R_{o1}^{\prime}$,
the usual shunt-shunt low $Z_{in}$, low $Z_{out}$
property, here obtained regeneratively.  For

$$T_{0}>1\tag{24}$$

$$g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}R_{o1}^{\prime}>1\tag{25}$$

$Z_{in0}<0$ and $Z_{out0}<0$.  The circuit presents a
negative resistance at both ports.  With $r_{o}\to\infty$
$T_{0}\to\infty$ and

$$Z_{in0}\approx -{1\over g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}\qquad
Z_{out0}\approx -{1\over g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}\to 0 \tag{26}$$

The characteristic equation $1-T(s)=0$,

$$\left(1+sR_{o1}^{\prime}C_{o}\right)\left(1+sr_{o2}C_{X}\right)
-T_{0}=0 \tag{27}$$

$$s^{2}R_{o1}^{\prime}r_{o2}C_{o}C_{X}
+s\left(R_{o1}^{\prime}C_{o}+r_{o2}C_{X}\right)+1-T_{0}=0 \tag{28}$$

$$s_{p1,2}={-\left(R_{o1}^{\prime}C_{o}+r_{o2}C_{X}\right)
\pm\sqrt{\left(R_{o1}^{\prime}C_{o}-r_{o2}C_{X}\right)^{2}
+4R_{o1}^{\prime}r_{o2}C_{o}C_{X}T_{0}}\over
2R_{o1}^{\prime}r_{o2}C_{o}C_{X}} \tag{29}$$

If $T_{0}>1$ the constant term $1-T_{0}<0$ and one root
is in the right half plane.  The d. c. operating point
(3)(4) is unstable.  The circuit latches.  With
$T_{0}>1$ there are three d. c. solutions, two stable
and one unstable, i. e. hysteresis.  It is the
NMOS version of the cross coupled latch / Schmitt
trigger / thyristor.  With $T_{0}<1$ both poles are in
the LHP and the circuit is stable, but with large
sensitivity

$$S_{T_{0}}^{R_{M}}={1\over 1-T_{0}} \tag{30}$$

so that $R_{M}$ is very process and bias sensitive as
$T_{0}\to 1^{-}$.

In normal linear design the circuit is kept with

$$T_{0}=g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}\left(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\right)<1
\tag{31}$$

for stability, giving an inverting transresistance

$$R_{M}\approx -{g_{m1}R_{o1}^{\prime}r_{o2}\over 1-T_{0}}
\approx -g_{m1}R_{o1}^{\prime}r_{o2}\;\;{\rm for}\;T_{0}\ll 1
\tag{32}$$

enhanced by $1/(1-T_{0})$ as $T_{0}\to 1$.  The
enhancement is obtained at the price of low, and for
$T_{0}>1$ negative, $Z_{in}$ and $Z_{out}$ and of
potential latch-up.  With $T_{0}>1$ the small signal
negative resistance can be used to cancel loss, $Q$
enhancement, active inductor, oscillator, or, large
signal, as a current comparator / latch with hysteresis

$$I_{H}\approx { \Delta V_{o} \over |R_{M}|}\propto 
|1-T_{0}| \tag{33}$$

For $r_{o}\to\infty$ the linear small signal model is
meaningless, $T_{0}\to\infty$, the circuit is
unconditionally latch unstable.  Channel length
modulation, i. e. finite $r_{o}$, must be included to
get a finite $T_{0}$ and a stable linear amplifier
region.  Including $g_{mb}$ replace $g_{m}\to g_{m}+g_{mb}$
if the bulk is not tied to the source.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 23.

answer.text:
With $V_{b}$ ac ground the small signal
circuit is

$$\eqalign{
M_{1}&:CG\;\;S\equiv A\;\;D\equiv X\cr
M_{2}&:CS\;\;G\equiv X\;\;D\equiv o\cr
R_{F}&:o\leftrightarrow A}$$

$V_{DD}$ ac ground.  Put

$$R_{1}=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\qquad 
  R_{2}=R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}\qquad 
  A_{1}=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{o1}\approx g_{m1}$$

$$g_{o1}=r_{o1}^{-1}\;\;,\;\;g_{o2}=r_{o2}^{-1}$$

$$I_{d1}=g_{m1}V_{gs1}+g_{o1}V_{ds1}
      =-g_{m1}V_{A}+g_{o1}(V_{X}-V_{A}) \tag{1}$$
$$I_{d2}=g_{m2}V_{X}+g_{o2}V_{o} \tag{2}$$

apart from $g_{mb}$.

$$ \eqalign{
X:&\;{V_{X}\over R_{D1}}+I_{d1}=0 \tag{3}\cr
A:&\;I_{in}+I_{d1}+{V_{o}-V_{A}\over R_{F}}=0 \tag{4}\cr
o:&\;{V_{o}\over R_{D2}}+I_{d2}+{V_{o}-V_{A}\over R_{F}}=0 \tag{5}}$$

(3) is

$$V_{X}\left({1\over R_{D1}}+g_{o1}\right)=V_{A}(g_{m1}+g_{o1})$$

$$V_{X}=V_{A}{A_{1}\over g_{o1}+R_{D1}^{-1}}
     =V_{A}A_{1}R_{1}\tag{6}$$

$$R_{1}^{-1}=g_{o1}+R_{D1}^{-1}\qquad 
  R_{2}^{-1}=g_{o2}+R_{D2}^{-1}$$

Put (6) in (4)(5).  With $A_{1}=g_{m1}+g_{o1}$

$$\eqalign{
I_{in}-V_{A}\left(A_{1}+{1\over R_{F}}\right)+g_{o1}V_{X}
        +{V_{o}\over R_{F}}&=0\cr
V_{o}\left({1\over R_{2}}+{1\over R_{F}}\right)
        +g_{m2}V_{X}-{V_{A}\over R_{F}}&=0}$$

and with (6) $g_{o1}V_{X}=g_{o1}A_{1}R_{1}V_{A}$,

$$-A_{1}+g_{o1}A_{1}R_{1}=-A_{1}{R_{1}\over R_{D1}}$$

so that

$$\eqalign{
I_{in}-V_{A}\left({A_{1}R_{1}\over R_{D1}}+{1\over R_{F}}\right)
        +{V_{o}\over R_{F}}&=0 \tag{4a}\cr
V_{A}\left(g_{m2}A_{1}R_{1}-{1\over R_{F}}\right)
        +V_{o}\left({1\over R_{2}}+{1\over R_{F}}\right)&=0 \tag{5a}}$$

Hence

$$V_{A}=-V_{o}{R_{2}^{-1}+R_{F}^{-1}\over g_{m2}A_{1}R_{1}-R_{F}^{-1}} \tag{7}$$

and from (4a)

$$I_{in}=V_{A}\left({A_{1}R_{1}\over R_{D1}}+{1\over R_{F}}\right)
        -{V_{o}\over R_{F}} \tag{8}$$

i. e. the exact closed loop transimpedance

$${V_{o}\over I_{in}}=
-{\,g_{m2}A_{1}R_{1}-R_{F}^{-1}\,\over 
\left(R_{2}^{-1}+R_{F}^{-1}\right)
\left({A_{1}R_{1}\over R_{D1}}+R_{F}^{-1}\right)
+{g_{m2}A_{1}R_{1}-R_{F}^{-1}\over R_{F}} } \tag{9}$$

$${V_{o}\over I_{in}}=
-{R_{D1}R_{2}\left(g_{m2}A_{1}R_{1}R_{F}-1\right)\over 
A_{1}R_{1}\left(R_{F}+R_{2}+g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{2}\right)+R_{D1}} \tag{9a}$$

For $r_{o}\to \infty ,\;R_{1}\to R_{D1},\;R_{2}\to R_{D2},
\;A_{1}\to g_{m1}$,

$${V_{o}\over I_{in}}\approx
-{R_{D2}\left(g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{F}-1\right)\over 
g_{m1}\left(R_{F}+R_{D2}+g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}\right)+1} \tag{10}$$

$$\approx -{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}R_{F}\over 
g_{m1}R_{F}+g_{m1}R_{D2}+g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}} \tag{10a}$$

for $g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{F}\gg 1$.

This is a shunt-shunt, voltage-current, transimpedance
feedback amplifier.  $R_{F}$ senses $V_{o}$ and feeds a
current

$$i_{RF}={V_{o}-V_{A}\over R_{F}}\approx {V_{o}\over R_{F}}$$

back to the low impedance input node $A$.  The forward
path $A\to X\to o$ is non inverting $CG$,
$A_{CG}\approx g_{m1}R_{1}$, followed by inverting $CS$,
$A_{CS}\approx -g_{m2}R_{2}$, so the loop is negative.

In $Y$ parameter language the feedback network is the
single resistor $R_{F}$,

$${\bf Y}_{F}= {1\over R_{F}}
\begin{pmatrix} 1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}\qquad 
\beta \equiv {i_{f}\over v_{o}}={1\over R_{F}}$$

with the usual sign $v_{o}=R_{M0}(i_{in}+\beta v_{o})$.
Loading the forward amplifier with $R_{F}$ to ground at
input and at output,

$$R_{M0}\equiv \left.{V_{o}\over I_{in}}\right|_{Y_{12}=Y_{21}=0}
      =-{A_{1}R_{1}g_{m2}\over 
\left({A_{1}R_{1}\over R_{D1}}+{1\over R_{F}}\right)
\left({1\over R_{2}}+{1\over R_{F}}\right)} \tag{11}$$

$$R_{M0}\xrightarrow[R_{F}\to\infty]{}-g_{m2}R_{1}R_{2}
      \approx -g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m2}R_{D2}{1\over g_{m1}}$$

i. e. $I_{in}R_{D1}$ at $X$ times $-g_{m2}R_{2}$.
With $r_{o}\to\infty$

$$R_{M0}\approx -{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{F}^{2}R_{D2}\over 
(g_{m1}R_{F}+1)(R_{F}+R_{D2})} \tag{11a}$$

The return ratio, loop gain, is

$$T=-\beta R_{M0}= -{R_{M0}\over R_{F}}$$

$$|T|={A_{1}R_{1}g_{m2}R_{F}\over 
\left({A_{1}R_{1}R_{F}\over R_{D1}}+1\right)
\left(1+{R_{F}\over R_{2}}\right)} \tag{12}$$

$$|T|\approx {g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}R_{F}\over 
(g_{m1}R_{F}+1)(R_{F}+R_{D2})}
      ={g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}\over R_{F}+R_{D2}}\,
        {g_{m1}R_{F}\over g_{m1}R_{F}+1} \tag{12a}$$

For the usual $g_{m1}R_{F}\gg 1$

$$|T|\approx {g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}\over R_{F}+R_{D2}}
      \approx \cases{g_{m2}R_{D1}&$R_{D2}\gg R_{F}$\cr
                     g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}/R_{F}&$R_{F}\gg R_{D2}$} \tag{13}$$

and in closed loop

$$R_{M}\equiv {V_{o}\over I_{in}}={R_{M0}\over 1+T}
      = -R_{F}{T\over 1+T}+{\cal O}(T^{-1}) \tag{14}$$

so that for $|T|\gg 1$

$$R_{M}\approx -R_{F}{1\over 1+T^{-1}}\approx -R_{F}
\left(1-{1\over T}\right) \tag{15}$$

the familiar ideal transimpedance $-R_{F}$.  The input
node becomes a virtual ground, $i_{RF}\approx -I_{in}$.

Input resistance: from (7)(8)

$$R_{in}\equiv {V_{A}\over I_{in}}
      ={R_{F}+R_{2}\over 
        {A_{1}R_{1}\over R_{D1}}\left(R_{F}+R_{2}+g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{2}\right)+1}
        \,R_{D1} \tag{16}$$

$$R_{in}\approx {R_{F}+R_{D2}\over 
        g_{m1}\left(R_{F}+R_{D2}+g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}\right)+1}
        \xrightarrow[|T|\gg1]{} {R_{in0}\over 1+T} \tag{16a}$$

with $R_{in0}\approx 1/(g_{m1}+R_{F}^{-1})\approx 1/g_{m1}$
the open loop $CG$ input resistance loaded by $R_{F}$.
Normally

$$R_{in}\approx {R_{F}+R_{D2}\over g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}
      \approx {R_{F}\over g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}\ll {1\over g_{m1}} \tag{17}$$

Output resistance: put $I_{in}=0$, apply $V_{t}$ at $o$,
$I_{t}=V_{t}/R_{D2}+g_{o2}V_{t}+g_{m2}V_{X}+(V_{t}-V_{A})/R_{F}$,
with (6) and $V_{A}=V_{t}/(A_{1}R_{1}R_{F}/R_{D1}+1)$,

$$R_{out}\equiv {V_{t}\over I_{t}}
      ={R_{2}\left(A_{1}R_{1}R_{F}+R_{D1}\right)\over 
        A_{1}R_{1}\left(R_{F}+R_{2}+g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{2}\right)+R_{D1}} \tag{18}$$

$$R_{out}\approx R_{D2}{g_{m1}R_{F}+1\over 
        g_{m1}\left(R_{F}+R_{D2}+g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}\right)+1}
        \xrightarrow[|T|\gg1]{} {R_{2}\parallel R_{F}\over 1+T}
        \approx {R_{D2}\over 1+T} \tag{18a}$$

$$\approx {R_{F}R_{D2}\over R_{F}+R_{D2}+g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}
      \approx \cases{R_{F}/g_{m2}R_{D1}&$R_{D2}\gg R_{F}$\cr
                     R_{D2}/T&$R_{F}\gg R_{D2}$}$$

Both terminal impedances are lowered by $1+T$, as
expected for shunt-shunt feedback.

With $g_{mb1}\ne 0$ replace $g_{m1}\to g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$ in
$A_{1}$.

In the frequency domain $R_{1}\to Z_{1}=R_{1}\parallel
1/sC_{X}$, $R_{2}\to Z_{2}=R_{2}\parallel 1/sC_{o}$,
$C_{X}=C_{gs2}+C_{db1}+C_{gd1}$, $C_{o}=C_{db2}+C_{gd2}+C_{L}$,
so $T(s)$ is two pole,

$$T(s)\approx -{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{1}R_{2}\over 
(1+sR_{1}C_{X})(1+sR_{2}C_{o})}\,{R_{F}^{-1}\over 
g_{m1}+R_{F}^{-1}+sC_{A}}$$

and the closed loop transimpedance shows the usual
bandwidth extension $\approx (1+T_{0})$ with peaking if
the two poles are close.  Normally $p_{o}=1/R_{2}C_{o}$
is dominant, $p_{X}=1/R_{1}C_{X}$ non dominant; adequate
phase margin requires $g_{m2}R_{1}>C_{o}/C_{X}$ or
compensation.  This is the classic regulated cascode
TIA.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 24.

answer.text:
With ${\rm M}_{1}$ in the ${\rm C.G.}$ and
${\rm M}_{2}$ in the ${\rm C.S.}$ the circuit is the
shunt-shunt, $V-I$, prototype

$${\rm sample}\;V_{o}\;\;{\rm mix}\;I_{i}\qquad 
\beta =I_{f}/V_{o}$$

with the ${\rm PMOS}$ as the ${\rm VCCS}$ feedback
element.  Put $V_{b}=0$ for $ac$, $V_{DD}=0$ for $ac$,
$r_{o1}=1/g_{ds1}$, $r_{o2}=1/g_{ds2}$, $r_{oI}=1/g_{oI}$,
$r_{oB}=1/g_{oB}$ for the two $dc$ current sources.
Neglect $C_{gs},C_{gd}$ for the low frequency
analysis.  Body effect is $g_{m}\rightarrow g_{m}+g_{mb}$.

$$\eqalign{
V_{GS1}&=V_{b}-V_{x}\cr
V_{SG2}&=V_{DD}-V_{o}\cr
V_{DS1}&=V_{o}-V_{x}\cr
V_{SD2}&=V_{DD}-V_{x}}$$

$$I_{D1}=I_{1}\tag{1}$$

so that in $dc$

$$V_{x}=V_{b}-V_{GS1}(I_{1})\qquad 
V_{o}=V_{DD}-V_{SG2}(I_{1}+I_{B}-I_{in})$$

and for $ac$ with the usual $g_{m}v_{gs}+g_{ds}v_{ds}$
model, Fig.1,

* ${\rm M}_{1}$ : $g_{m1}v_{gs1}$ $D\rightarrow S$,
$v_{gs1}=-v_{x}$, $r_{o1}$ $D-S$
* ${\rm M}_{2}$ : $g_{m2}v_{sg2}$ $S\rightarrow D$,
$v_{sg2}=-v_{o}$, $r_{o2}$ $S-D$

$$\eqalign{
{\rm KCL}_{x}:&-(I_{in})+{{v_{x}-v_{o}}\over {r_{o1}}}
+{{v_{x}}\over {r_{o2}}}+{{v_{x}}\over {r_{oB}}}
-g_{m1}v_{gs1}-g_{m2}v_{sg2}=0\cr
{\rm KCL}_{o}:&{{v_{o}-v_{x}}\over {r_{o1}}}+{{v_{o}}\over {r_{oI}}}

$$\eqalign{
I_{in}&=v_{x}\left({1\over {r_{o1}}}+{1\over {r_{o2}}}

$$A_{v0}={{v_{o}}\over {v_{x}}}\Bigl|_{g_{m2}=0}

and with the normal $r_{oI},r_{o2}\gg r_{o1}$,

$$R_{M}\approx {1\over {g_{m2}+{1\over {r_{oI}}}+{1\over
{r_{o2}(1+g_{m1}r_{o1})}}}}\tag{7a}$$

In the ideal $r_{o}\rightarrow \infty $ limit

\approx {1\over {g_{m2}}}\tag{8}$$

The sign is non inverting for the reference direction in
Fig.24, $R_{M}=-1/\beta $ with $\beta =-g_{m2}$ for the
usual $I_{f}=-g_{m2}V_{o}$ convention.  The ${\rm PMOS}$
is a feedback resistor $R_{F}=1/g_{m2}$.  Replacing
${\rm M}_{2}$ by $R_{F}$ gives the classic resistive
shunt-shunt ${\rm TIA}$ $R_{M}=-R_{F}$.

The forward transimpedance with the feedback $g_{m2}$
killed but with its loading $r_{o2}$ retained is from
(6) with $g_{m2}=0$,

$$R_{M}^{o}={1\over {{1\over {r_{oI}}}+{{G_{2}}\over {G_{1}r_{o2}}}}}
\approx r_{oI}\parallel r_{o1}\tag{9}$$

factor is

$$\beta ={{I_{f}}\over {V_{o}}}=-g_{m2}\tag{10}$$

$$T=-\beta R_{M}^{o}=g_{m2}R_{M}^{o}
={{g_{m2}}\over {{1\over {r_{oI}}}+{{G_{2}}\over {G_{1}r_{o2}}}}}
\approx g_{m2}r_{oI}\;\;r_{o2}\gg r_{o1}\tag{11}$$

{{1\over {r_{oI}}}+{{G_{2}}\over {G_{1}r_{o2}}}}}\tag{12}$$

so that $T=-v_{r}/v_{t}$ is (11), $T\approx
g_{m2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{oI})\approx 20-50\,{\rm dB}$.
Then

$$R_{M}={{R_{M}^{o}}\over {1+T}}\approx -{1\over \beta }
={1\over {g_{m2}}}\tag{13}$$

as in (8).  The feedback is negative: $\uparrow I_{in}
\rightarrow \uparrow v_{x}\rightarrow \downarrow v_{gs1}
\rightarrow \downarrow i_{d1}\rightarrow \uparrow v_{o}
\rightarrow \downarrow v_{sg2}\rightarrow \downarrow i_{d2}
\rightarrow \downarrow v_{x}$.

Input impedance, $Z_{in}=v_{x}/I_{in}$,

$$Z_{in}={{G_{2}}\over {G_{1}}}R_{M}
={1\over {{G_{1}}\over {G_{2}}}\left(g_{m2}+{1\over {r_{oI}}}\right)
+{1\over {r_{o2}}}+{1\over {r_{oB}}}}\tag{14}$$

$$\approx {1\over {{1\over {r_{o2}}}+{{G_{1}}\over {G_{2}}}
\left(g_{m2}+{1\over {r_{oI}}}\right)}}\tag{14a}$$

For $r_{oI},r_{oB}\rightarrow \infty $

$$Z_{in}\approx {1\over {g_{m2}(1+g_{m1}r_{o1})+1/r_{o2}}}
\approx {1\over {g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1}}}\tag{15}$$

i. e. the ${\rm C.G.}$ input resistance
$1/G_{1}\approx 1/g_{m1}$ divided by $1+T$,

$$Z_{in}={{Z_{in}^{o}}\over {1+T}},\qquad 
Z_{in}^{o}\approx {1\over {G_{1}}}\parallel r_{o2}\tag{16}$$

a virtual ground, $10-10^{2}\,\Omega $ typical, ideal
$0$ for $T\rightarrow \infty $.

Output impedance, $I_{in}=0$, $v_{test}=v_{o}$,
$i_{test}$ into $V_{o}$,

$$i_{test}={{v_{o}-v_{x}}\over {r_{o1}}}+{{v_{o}}\over {r_{oI}}}
+g_{m1}v_{gs1}\tag{17}$$

with $v_{x}=-v_{o}(g_{m2}-1/r_{o1})/A$ from (4a) with
$I_{in}=0$,

$$Z_{out}={{v_{o}}\over {i_{test}}}
={1\over {{1\over {r_{oI}}}+{{g_{m2}G_{1}+1/r_{o1}r_{o2}}\over {A}}}}
\tag{18}$$

$$\approx {1\over {{1\over {r_{oI}}}+g_{m2}{{G_{1}}\over {A}}}}
\approx {1\over {g_{m2}+1/r_{oI}}}\approx {1\over {g_{m2}}}
\;\;r_{o2}\gg r_{o1}\tag{18a}$$

i. e.

$$Z_{out}={{Z_{out}^{o}}\over {1+T}},\qquad 
Z_{out}^{o}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{oI}\tag{19}$$

also lowered by $1+T$ from the high ${\rm C.G.}$ output
resistance to $\sim 1/g_{m2}$, $0.5-2\,{\rm k\Omega }$
typical.  With $g_{mb}$,

$$g_{m1}\rightarrow g_{m1}+g_{mb1},\qquad 
g_{m2}\rightarrow g_{m2}+g_{mb2}\;{\rm if\;body\;not\;to\;source}.$$

output node

$$\omega _{p o}\approx {1\over {Z_{out}^{o}C_{o}}}
\approx {1\over {(r_{o1}\parallel r_{oI})C_{o}}}$$

closed loop $\omega _{p o,cl}\approx (1+T)\omega _{p o}
\approx g_{m2}/C_{o}$, non dominant pole at the low
impedance input node

$$\omega _{p i}\approx {1\over {Z_{in}C_{i}}}
\approx {{g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1}}\over {C_{i}}}\gg \omega _{p o}$$

so the loop is normally well compensated with
$>60^{\circ}$ phase margin.  $C_{o}$ is the total
capacitance at $V_{o}$, $C_{i}$ at $V_{x}$.  Peaking
occurs if $C_{o}$ is made small so that
$\omega _{p o,cl}\approx \omega _{p i}$.

In short the circuit is a low $Z_{in}$, low $Z_{out}$
transimpedance amplifier, the active feedback version of
the $R_{F}$ shunt-shunt ${\rm TIA}$, often called the
flipped voltage follower / super ${\rm C.G.}$ / regulated
cascode ${\rm TIA}$, with ideal

$$R_{M}\approx 1/g_{m2},\qquad Z_{in}\approx 0,\qquad 
Z_{out}\approx 1/g_{m2},\qquad T\approx g_{m2}r_{oI}\gg 1$$

and more exactly (7), (14), (18).  It provides a
virtual ground for current input, e. g. photodiode or
current DAC, and a voltage output capable of driving a
moderate load, with bandwidth $\approx g_{m2}/C_{o}$.

answers.question: Does the circuit in Figure 5 fail to oscillate if the three capacitors become arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
With the usual idealisation the three pole loop is

$${\cal L}(s)=\left[-{A_{0}\over {1+sT}}\right]^{3}\qquad 
T=R_{0}C_{L}\tag{*}$$

for the small signal model of the inverter in the
vicinity of the $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_{M}$ metastable point,
$A_{0}=g_{m}R_{0}$ the conventional small signal
``gain'' of the inverter.  At $s=j\omega $

$$\eqalign{
|{\cal L}| &=\left[{A_{0}\over {\sqrt{1+\omega ^{2}T^{2}}}}\right]^{3}\cr
{\rm arg}{\cal L}&=3\left[\pi -\tan ^{-1}\omega T\right] \tag{**}}$$

${\rm arg}{\cal L}=2\pi $ for

$$3\tan ^{-1}\omega_{0}T=\pi \tag{***}$$

i. {\it e.}

$$\omega_{0}T={\rm tg}{\pi \over 3}=\sqrt{3}\tag{****}$$

$${\omega_{0}={{\sqrt{3}}\over {R_{0}C_{L}}}}\tag{*****}$$

and, at that frequency,

$$|{\cal L}(j\omega_{0})|=\left[{A_{0}\over 2}\right]^{3}\tag{******}$$

{\it i. e.} $C_{L}$ drops out of the Barkhausen
magnitude condition.  In terms of the poles of the
closed loop the characteristic is

$$(1+sT)^{3}+A_{0}^{3}=0\tag{*******}$$

$$(1+sT)=-A_{0}e^{j2k\pi /3}\qquad k=0,1,2\tag{********}$$

$$s_{k}={{-1-A_{0}e^{j2k\pi /3}}\over T}\tag{*********}$$

$$s_{1,2}={{-1+{1\over 2}A_{0}\mp j{{\sqrt{3}}\over 2}A_{0}}\over
{R_{0}C_{L}}}\tag{**********}$$

$${\rm Re}s_{1,2}>0\iff A_{0}>2\approx 6{\rm dB}\tag{***********}$$

independently of $T=R_{0}C_{L}$.
If the small signal gain of the logic inverter in the
linear region exceeds $2$ the $V_{1}=V_{2}=V_{3}=V_{M}$
DC solution is unstable and the conventional
exponential start up

$$\delta V\propto \exp \left[{{A_{0}-2}\over {2R_{0}C_{L}}}t\right]
\cos \omega_{0}t\tag{************}$$

must occur for {\it any\/} finite $C_{L}$.
Making $C_{L}$ large just makes the oscillation
arbitrarily low frequency, $f_{0}\propto 1/C_{L}\to 0$,
and arbitrarily slow to start, $\tau_{s}\propto
C_{L}\to \infty $.

In particular for the ideal logic inverter,
$A_{0}\to \infty $, the circuit is unstable for every
finite $C_{L}$.

In the singular limit $C_{L}\equiv \infty $ the three
nodes are a. c. ground, ${\cal L}\equiv 0$, and
trivially there is no loop transmission left.  For any
normal bench observation time $\tau_{{\rm obs}}\ll
\tau_{s}\propto C_{L}$ the circuit {\it appears\/} to
have latched on the metastable $V_{M}$ point and to
have ``failed to oscillate''.  In that colloquial
sense the circuit ``fails'' with $f_{0}\to 0$.

> {\it Remark:\/}  With $A_{0}<2$ the metastable point
> is stable and the circuit does latch.  Any stray
> positive feedback, power supply impedance, etc. will
> normally make $A_{0}>2$ in the ordinary CMOS
> inverter, so the textbook ring does oscillate.

answers.question: What happens to the phase noise if the three capacitors in Figure 5 are doubled?

answer.text:
With the normal long channel square law
shorthand the three pole ring is the text book
illustration of the Hajimiri Lee

$${\cal L}\propto {{{\overline {i_{n}^{2}}}\over {\Delta f}}
{{{\mit\Gamma}_{rms}^{2}}\over {q_{max}^{2}}}}{1\over {\Delta
\omega ^{2}}}\tag{*}$$

for white noise and

$${\cal L}\propto {{{\overline {i_{n}^{2}}}\over {\Delta f}}
{{c_{0}^{2}}\over {q_{max}^{2}}}}{1\over {\Delta \omega ^{3}}}$$

for the $1/f$ noise.  $q_{max}=C_{L}V_{DD}$ is the
maximum charge swing on the tank and ${\mit\Gamma}_{rms}$,
$c_{0}$ are the rms and the d. c. value of the
impulse sensitivity function.  For the normal
wave form ${\mit\Gamma}_{rms},c_{0}$ are
${\cal O}(1)$ and independent of the normalisation
$\omega _{0}t$.  I. e. to first order

$${\cal L}_{{\rm white}}\propto {1\over {q_{max}^{2}}}
\propto {1\over {C_{L}^{2}}}\qquad 
  {\cal L}_{1/f}\propto {1\over {q_{max}^{2}}}\propto
  {1\over {C_{L}^{2}}}\tag{**}$$

at {\it a given absolute} ${\mit\Delta \omega }$.
In Leeson's language

$${\cal L}\propto {kT\over P}{V_{DD}\over V_{char}}
\left({\omega _{0}\over {\Delta \omega }}\right)^{2}\tag{***}$$

with

$$\omega _{0}\approx {1\over {2NR_{0}C_{L}}}\approx
{{I_{0}}\over {NC_{L}V_{DD}}}\tag{****}$$

and

$$P = NC_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f_{0}\tag{*****}$$

so that, at {\it a given absolute} ${\mit\Delta \omega }$,

$${\cal L}\propto {1\over P}\omega _{0}^{2}\propto
{1\over {C_{L}f_{0}}}f_{0}^{2}\propto {f_{0}\over {C_{L}}}
\propto {1\over {C_{L}^{2}}}\tag{******}$$

for the $1/f^{2}$ region and $\propto 1/C_{L}^{3}$ for
the $1/f^{3}$ region if the $\omega _{0}$ of the
up conversion is kept in evidence.  In the familiar
$kT/C$ shorthand $(**)$ is normally quoted as

$${\cal L}\propto {{kT}\over C}{\left({{\omega _{0}}\over
{\Delta \omega }}\right)^{2}}\tag{*******}$$

i. e. a factor $2$ in power, $3\,{\rm dB}$ in
${\cal L}$, per factor $2$ in $C_{L}$.

With $(****)$ doubling $C_{L}$ halves $\omega _{0}$.
At a {\it fixed absolute} ${\mit\Delta \omega }$
$(**)$--$(******)$ is a factor $4$ in power

$${\cal L}{\rm \;goes\;down\;by\;6\,dB\;in\;power\;
3\,dB\;in\;voltage\atop {\rm nominally\;3\,dB\;in\;the\;
kT/C\;language}} \tag{1}$$

for the $1/f^{2}$ {\it i. e.} white noise region,
$9$--$12\,{\rm dB}$ for the $1/f^{3}$ region, Fig.1.
At a {\it fixed fractional} offset
${\mit\Delta \omega }/\omega _{0}$ the
$\omega _{0}^{2}$ in $(***)$ cancels and, to the
order of $(*)$,

$${\cal L}\left({{\Delta \omega }\over {\omega _{0}}}\right)
 ={\rm const.}\tag{2}$$

I. e. the conventional figure of merit

$${\rm FOM}= {\cal L}-20\log {{\omega _{0}}\over {\Delta \omega }}
+10\log {P\over {1\,{\rm mW}}}\tag{3}$$

is, to first order, $C_{L}$ independent.  In
particular the often quoted $kT/C$ $3\,{\rm dB}$
is normally quoted for the re tuned oscillator,
$C_{L}\rightarrow 2C_{L}$, $I_{0}\rightarrow 2I_{0}$,
$\omega _{0}={\rm const.}$, $P\rightarrow 2P$,

$${\cal L}_{\omega _{0}={\rm const.}}\propto {1\over {C_{L}}}
\propto {1\over P}\tag{4}$$

so that ${\rm FOM}={\rm const.}$

In the time domain the white noise period jitter

$$\sigma _{T}^{2}=2N\sigma _{d}^{2}\tag{5}$$

with

$$\sigma _{d}^{2}={{\overline {v_{n}^{2}}}\over {SR^{2}}}
\approx {{kT/C}\over {(I_{0}/C)^{2}}}\propto C\tag{6}$$

goes {\it up} by a factor $2$, $3\,{\rm dB}$,
$\sqrt{2}$ in rms value, on doubling $C_{L}$,
whereas the phase jitter

$$\sigma _{\phi }^{2}= \left(2\pi {{ \sigma _{T}}\over {T_{0}}}
\right)^{2}\propto {{\sigma _{T}^{2}}\over {T_{0}^{2}}}
\propto {1\over C}\tag{7}$$

with $T_{0}=1/f_{0}\propto C$, goes down by a factor
$2$, $3\,{\rm dB}$, $1/\sqrt{2}$ in rms value, as it
must from $(1)$--$(2)$.

> {\it Remark:}  With the $1/f^{2}$ ${\cal L}$ normally
> quoted as ${\cal L}\propto (f_{0}/{\mit\Delta f})^{2}
> (kT/C)/V_{DD}^{2}$ the $3\,{\rm dB}$ in $(1)$ is often
> quoted as the $kT/C$ $3\,{\rm dB}$ and the extra
> $3\,{\rm dB}$ due to $f_{0}\rightarrow f_{0}/2$ is
> exhibited explicitly.  E. g. Abidi, JSSC 41 12 (2006).

This matches the golden solution's central result. The answer also correctly derives the L ∝ 1/C_L² scaling at fixed absolute offset from multiple perspectives (Hajimiri-Lee, Leeson, kT/C, time-domain jitter). answers.question: Does the circuit in Figure 6 fail to oscillate if CL becomes arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
With the usual ideal relay model the circuit is
still astable.  Put

$$R_{o}C_{0}=\tau _{0}\qquad R_{o}C_{L}=\tau _{L}\qquad 
A=g_{m}R_{o}$$

for one inverter

$$A_{v}(s)=-\,{\frac{A}{1+s\tau }}$$

so that, breaking the loop,

$${\cal L}(s)=-\,{\frac{A^{3}}{(1+s\tau _{L})(1+s\tau _{0})^{2}}}\tag{1}$$

$${\cal L}(j\omega )=|{\cal L}|e^{j\varphi }\qquad 
\varphi =\pi -\tan ^{-1}\omega \tau _{L}-2\tan ^{-1}\omega \tau _{0}$$

$$\varphi =0\;{\rm mod}\;2\pi \iff 
\tan ^{-1}\omega _{0}\tau _{L}+2\tan ^{-1}\omega _{0}\tau _{0}=\pi \tag{2}$$

$0<\omega _{0}<\infty $ is the unique solution of (2).
For $\tau _{L}\gg \tau _{0}$

$$\tan ^{-1}\omega _{0}\tau _{L}\approx {\frac{\pi }2}\tag{3}$$

so that from (2)

$$2\tan ^{-1}\omega _{0}\tau _{0}\approx {\frac{\pi }2}\qquad 
\omega _{0}\approx {\frac{1}{\tau _{0}}}\tag{4}$$

and from (1)

$$|{\cal L}(j\omega _{0})|=
{\frac{A^{3}}{\sqrt{1+\omega _{0}^{2}\tau _{L}^{2}}\,
\left(1+\omega _{0}^{2}\tau _{0}^{2}\right)}}
\approx {\frac{A^{3}}{2\omega _{0}\tau _{L}}}
\approx {\frac{A^{3}}{2}}{\frac{\tau _{0}}{\tau _{L}}}
={\frac{A^{3}}{2}}{\frac{C_{0}}{C_{L}}}\tag{5}$$

The closed loop poles are the roots of $1-{\cal L}(s)=0$,

$$1+{\frac{A^{3}}{(1+s\tau _{L})(1+s\tau _{0})^{2}}}=0\tag{6}$$

$$(1+s\tau _{L})(1+s\tau _{0})^{2}+A^{3}=0$$

$$s^{3}\tau _{0}^{2}\tau _{L}+s^{2}\left(\tau _{0}^{2}+2\tau _{0}\tau _{L}
\right)+s\left(2\tau _{0}+\tau _{L}\right)+1+A^{3}=0\tag{7}$$

$$s^{3}+s^{2}\left({\frac{2}{\tau _{0}}}+{\frac{1}{\tau _{L}}}\right)
+s\left({\frac{1}{\tau _{0}^{2}}}+{\frac{2}{\tau _{0}\tau _{L}}}\right)
+{\frac{1+A^{3}}{\tau _{0}^{2}\tau _{L}}}=0\tag{8}$$

Routh for $s^{3}+a_{2}s^{2}+a_{1}s+a_{0}=0$ is $a_{2}a_{1}>a_{0}$
for LHP.  From (8)

$$a_{2}a_{1}-a_{0}={\frac{1}{\tau _{0}^{2}\tau _{L}}}
\left[{\frac{2\tau _{L}}{\tau _{0}}}+4+{\frac{2\tau _{0}}{\tau _{L}}}-A^{3}
\right] \tag{9}$$

so that the linear circuit is {\it unstable}, i. e. the
${\rm Barkhausen}$ ${\rm mod}\,|{\cal L}|=1$, $\varphi =0$,
condition is satisfied, iff

$$A^{3}>2{\frac{\tau _{L}}{\tau _{0}}}+4+2{\frac{\tau _{0}}{\tau _{L}}}
\approx 2{\frac{C_{L}}{C_{0}}}\tag{10}$$

i. e. iff

$$C_{L}<C_{L{\rm crit}}\approx {\frac{A^{3}-4}{2}}C_{0}
\approx {\frac12}\left(g_{m}R_{o}\right)^{3}C_{0}\tag{11}$$

normally a few $10^{2}$--$10^{3}C_{0}$.
For

$$|{\cal L}(j\omega _{0})|<1\tag{12}$$

the three pole loop is dominant pole compensated, the
$V_{DD}/2$ metastable point becomes locally stable and the
{\it small signal, sinusoidal, Barkhausen} oscillation will
not start from noise.  In the mathematical limit

$$C_{L}\to \infty \qquad \tau _{L}\to \infty \tag{13}$$

$$A_{v1}(j\omega )\to 0\qquad \omega \ne 0\tag{14}$$

the $B$ node is an a. c. ground, the small signal loop is
broken, $|{\cal L}|\to 0$, and (6) is $1=0$.

In the large signal, ideal relay, $A\to \infty $,
sense the circuit has no d. c. stable point,
$B=f\!\left(f\!\left(f(B)\right)\right)$ has the unique
solution $B=V_{TH}$, and it remains astable.  With
$R_{o}$ the large signal charging resistance the $B$
node charges as

$$V_{B}(t)=V_{DD}\left(1-e^{-t/R_{o}C_{L}}\right)\tag{15}$$

for $A=0$ and discharges as $V_{B}(t)=V_{DD}e^{-t/R_{o}C_{L}}$
for $A=V_{DD}$.  The two fast inverters act as a
${\rm buffer}$ $A={\cal B}(B(t-\tau _{d}))$,
$\tau _{d}\approx 2R_{o}C_{0}$, so that the circuit
becomes the conventional $R_{o}C_{L}$ relaxation
oscillator.  Apart from the small signal start up
problem it will still exhibit a stable limit cycle,
now highly non sinusoidal, saw tooth on $B$, square on
$C$ and $A$, of period

$$T\approx 2\left[t_{p2}+t_{p3}+R_{o}C_{L}
\ln {\frac{V_{DD}-V_{OL}}{V_{DD}-V_{TH}}}\right]
\approx T_{0}+kR_{o}C_{L}\tag{16}$$

so that $f_{0}\propto 1/C_{L}\to 0$ but $f_{0}\ne 0$.
In most text books this is phrased as {\it the
oscillation does not fail, it just gets slower and
becomes a relaxation oscillation}.  Pedantically the
linear, sinusoidal, Barkhausen ring oscillation does
fail for $C_{L}>C_{L{\rm crit}}$ given by (11) and for
$C_{L}\to \infty $ the small signal loop gain is
identically zero.

> {\it Remark:}  With the usual $g_{m}R_{o}\sim 10$,
> $C_{L{\rm crit}}\sim 5\times 10^{2}C_{0}$.  For all
> normal values of $C_{L}$ the circuit is normally
> quoted as {\it not failing to oscillate, the period
> simply increases as $T\approx 2N\bar t_{p}+R_{o}C_{L}$}.

answers.question: If we double the widths of the NMOS and PMOS devices in Figure 7, what happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
With the normal long channel square law
shorthand the circuit is the conventional $N=3$ CMOS
ring.  Put

$${{I}_{D}}\propto W\qquad {{g}_{m}}\propto W\qquad 
{{C}_{G}}\propto W\qquad {{C}_{D}}\propto W\tag{*}$$

so that, for ${\rm  {C}}_{w}=0$,

$${{\tau }_{D}}\approx {{C}_{L}}{{V}_{DD}}/{{I}_{D}}\propto
W/W={\rm const.}\qquad {{\omega }_{0}}=1/2N{{\tau }_{D}}=
{\rm const.}\tag{1}$$

$${{P}_{DC}}\approx N{{C}_{L}}V_{DD}^{2}{{f}_{0}}\propto W\tag{2}$$

is doubled.  In Hajimiri's notation

$${\cal L}\left( \Delta \omega \right)\approx 
{{1}\over {8{{\pi }^{2}}}}{{\Gamma _{rms}^{2}}\over {\Delta {{\omega }^{2}}}}
{{{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}}\over {\Delta f}}\over {q_{{\rm max}}^{2}}}\tag{3}$$

$${{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}}\over {\Delta f}}=4kT\gamma {{g}_{m}}\propto W\tag{4}$$

$${{q}_{{\rm max}}}={{C}_{L}}{{V}_{DD}}\propto W\tag{5}$$

${{\Gamma }_{rms}}\approx 0.5-1$ for the ring is $W$
independent.  Hence for the white, ${{f}^{-2}}$, part

$${\cal L}\propto {{{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}}}\over {q_{{\rm max}}^{2}}}
{{\omega _{0}^{2}}\over {\Delta {{\omega }^{2}}}}\propto
{{{{g}_{m}}}\over {C_{L}^{2}}}{{\omega _{0}^{2}}\over {\Delta {{\omega }^{2}}}}
\propto {1\over W}{{\omega _{0}^{2}}\over {\Delta {{\omega }^{2}}}}\tag{6}$$

c. f. the Leeson form

$${\cal L}\approx {{2FkT}\over {{{P}_{s}}}}{{\left( {{\omega }_{0}}
\over {2Q\Delta \omega }\right)}^{2}}\propto {1\over {{{P}_{DC}}}}
{{\omega _{0}^{2}}\over {\Delta {{\omega }^{2}}}}\tag{7}$$

For the ${{f}^{-3}}$ part

$${{\overline{v_{1/f}^{2}}}\over {\Delta f}}={{K}\over {{{W}_{{}}}{{L}_{{}}}
{{C}_{ox}}f}}\propto {1\over W}\tag{8}$$

so that, with $\left( * \right)$,

$${{\cal L}_{1/{{f}^{3}}}}\propto {{1}\over W}
{{\omega _{0}^{2}}\over {\Delta {{\omega }^{3}}}}\tag{9}$$

as well.  I. e. for ${{C}_{w}}=0$ and the same
${{V}_{DD}}$ the {\it absolute\/} single side band
noise power normally quoted as ${\cal L}\,[{\rm dBc/H_{z}}]$
goes as $1/W$.  Doubling $W$ halves the SSB
noise power,

$${{{\cal L}_{2W}}\over {{{\cal L}_{W}}}}\approx {1\over 2}\tag{10}$$

about $10\log 1/2\approx -3\,{\rm dB}$ in power,
$20\log 1/\sqrt{2}\approx -3\,{\rm dB}$ normally quoted as
$-6\,{\rm dB}$ in voltage, $-3\,{\rm dB}$ on the
${{f}^{-2}}$ skirt and, counting ${\bar v}_{1/f}^{2}$
alone, $-6\,{\rm dB}$ in voltage, $-3\,{\rm dB}$ in power,
on the ${{f}^{-3}}$ skirt.  E. {\it g\/}. with $kT/{{C}_{L}}$
noise

$$\sigma _{t}^{2}\approx {{kT/{{C}_{L}}}\over {{{\left( {{I}_{D}}/{{C}_{L}}
\right)}^{2}}}}={{kT{{C}_{L}}}\over {I_{D}^{2}}}\propto {1\over W}\tag{11}$$

$$\sigma _{T}^{2}\approx 2N\sigma _{t}^{2}\propto {1\over W}\tag{12}$$

$${\cal L}\approx {{\omega _{0}^{2}\sigma _{T}^{2}}\over {2T\Delta {{\omega }^{2}}}}
\propto {1\over W}\tag{13}$$

The factor $1/2$ is just the factor $2$ increase in
${{P}_{DC}}$, Eq.\,2.  Normalised to the DC power,
or to the charge swing, the conventional
oscillator figure of merit,

$${\rm FOM}={\cal L}\left( \Delta \omega \right)-20\log
\left( {{\omega }_{0}}\over {\Delta \omega }\right)
+10\log \left( {{{P}_{DC}}}\over {1{\rm mW}}\right)
\qquad {\rm dBc/H_{z}}\tag{14}$$

$${\rm FOM}\propto {{{\cal L}{{P}_{DC}}}\over {\omega _{0}^{2}}}
={\rm const.}\tag{15}$$

is $W$ independent to first order.  In that
normalised sense it is customary to say loosely that
the phase noise {\it does not change\/} with $W$.
If the power, or the frequency, is kept constant by
re biasing there is no change at all to ${\cal O}(W)$.

With a $W$ independent wiring capacitance ${{C}_{w}}$

$${{C}_{L}}={{C}_{dev}}+{{C}_{w}}\qquad {{C}_{dev}}\propto W\tag{16}$$

Eq.\,1 becomes ${{\omega }_{0}}\propto {{I}_{D}}/{{C}_{L}}
\propto W/({{C}_{dev}}+{{C}_{w}})$ and

$${\cal L}\propto {{{{g}_{m}}}\over {C_{L}^{2}}}\omega _{0}^{2}
\propto {W\over {{{\left( {{C}_{dev}}+{{C}_{w}} \right)}^{2}}}}
{{{{W}^{2}}}\over {{{\left( {{C}_{dev}}+{{C}_{w}} \right)}^{2}}}}\tag{17}$$

so the $3\,{\rm dB}$ improvement is reduced to

$$\Delta {\cal L}\approx 10\log \left[ {{{{{C}_{dev}}+{{C}_{w}}}
\over {2{{C}_{dev}}+{{C}_{w}}}}\right] <3\,{\rm dB}\tag{18}$$

and for ${{C}_{w}}\gg {{C}_{dev}}$, ${{\omega }_{0}}\propto W$,
${{P}_{DC}}\propto W$, ${\cal L}\propto \omega _{0}^{2}/{{P}_{DC}}
\propto W$, the phase noise can even get worse with $W$.
Any short channel increase of $\gamma $ with $W$ also
erodes the $3\,{\rm dB}$.

> {\it Remark:\/}  For the ideal device dominated ring the
> textbook shorthand is {\it the {\rm (FOM)} phase noise is
> $W$ independent\/}.  Unnormalised to power the SSB
> phase noise power is $\propto 1/W$, i. e. a factor $2$,
> $3\,{\rm dB}$ in ${\cal L}[{\rm dBc/H_{z}}]$, $6\,{\rm dB}$
> in ${\cal L}[{\rm V/\sqrt{H_{z}}}]$, lower for $2W$ at the
> same ${{V}_{DD}}$, just the $3\,{\rm dB}$ increase in
> ${{P}_{DC}}$.  On the ${{f}^{-3}}$ skirt the flicker
> ${\rm PSD}\propto 1/W$ gives nominally the same $1/W$
> law, $3\,{\rm dB}$ in power, $6\,{\rm dB}$ in voltage if
> the $1/W$ of the flicker ${\rm PSD}$ is counted
> separately.

The central result and reasoning align with the golden solution.

The core conclusion and reasoning are correct.

answers.question:
Determine the small-signal resistance seen looking into the supply node of the ring oscillator in Figure 8.

Use `CL` for the effective load capacitance at each internal oscillator node,
and use `f0` for the oscillation frequency.

answer.text:
With the usual switched ${\rm C}$ idealisation the
oscillator is a ${\rm C}$ which is dumped from $V_{DD}$ to
$0$ once per period, Fig.1, so that, on the average,

$${\rm d}Q_{D}=C_{L}{\rm d}V_{DD}\tag{*}$$

per transition.  For the conventional
${\rm C}V^{2}f$ estimate, for one ${\rm C}_{L}$,

$$P_{1}=C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f_{0}\qquad 
I_{1}={{P_{1}}\over {V_{DD}}}=C_{L}V_{DD}f_{0}\tag{1}$$

once per period $T_{0}=1/f_{0}$ the ${\rm C}_{L}$ is charged
to $V_{DD}$ through the $p$ device, ${\rm d}Q=C_{L}V_{DD}$,
and discharged to earth through the $n$ device with no
${\rm d}Q_{D}$.  For the $N=3$ loop

$$P_{N}=NC_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f_{0}\qquad 
I_{N}=NC_{L}V_{DD}f_{0}\tag{2}$$

so that, on the average, i. e. for $|s|\ll 2\pi f_{0}$,
the circuit looks from the $V_{DD}$ terminal like a
linear resistor to earth

$$R_{X}^{({\rm av})}\equiv {{V_{DD}}\over {I_{N}}}
      \approx {1\over {NC_{L}f_{0}}}\tag{3}$$

i. e. per stage

$$R_{1}^{({\rm av})}\approx {1\over {C_{L}f_{0}}}\tag{4}$$

and for the $N=3$ circuit of Fig. 8

$$R_{X}^{({\rm av})}\approx {1\over {3C_{L}f_{0}}}\tag{5}$$

in parallel with $\approx NC_{L}$.  $I_{N}$ in (2) is
normally quoted as the large signal or average
current.  For the incremental or small signal resistance
$r_{x}=dV_{DD}/dI_{N}$,

$$g_{x}={{dI_{N}}\over {dV_{DD}}}=NC_{L}f_{0}
      +NC_{L}V_{DD}{{df_{0}}\over {dV_{DD}}}\tag{6}$$

so that, to first order in the $V_{DD}$ sensitivity of
$f_{0}$, $f_{0}\propto V_{DD}$,

$$r_{x}\equiv g_{x}^{-1}\approx {1\over {2NC_{L}f_{0}}}\tag{7}$$

i. e. per stage

$$r_{1}\approx {1\over {2C_{L}f_{0}}}\tag{8}$$

and for $N=3$

$$r_{x}\approx {1\over {6C_{L}f_{0}}}\tag{9}$$

apart from the sign.  In the conventional linear,
metastable, small signal analysis the sign is negative,
$|r_{x}|$ in (7)--(9) is the magnitude of the negative
resistance which must be cancelled by the positive
$R_{X}^{({\rm av})}$ in order to sustain the oscillation.
With the sign exhibited

$$R_{X}\approx -R_{X}^{({\rm av})}\approx -{1\over {NC_{L}f_{0}}}
      \;\;,\;\;r_{x}\approx -{1\over {2NC_{L}f_{0}}}\tag{10}$$

so that, nominally,

$$|R_{X}|\sim {1\over {C_{L}f_{0}}}\;\;{\rm per\;stage}
\tag{11}$$

$$|r_{x}|\sim {1\over {2C_{L}f_{0}}}\;\;{\rm per\;stage}
\tag{12}$$

i. e. for the three stage loop normally quoted as

$$|R_{X}^{({\rm av})}|\approx {1\over {3C_{L}f_{0}}}\;\;,
\;\;|r_{x}|\approx {1\over {6C_{L}f_{0}}}\tag{13}$$

in parallel with $3C_{L}$.  Any factor $2$--$3$ is the
same physics.  E. {\rm g.} with $f_{0}$ taken as a
parameter, $r_{x}=R_{X}^{({\rm av})}$, (5) is often quoted
simply as $R_{X}\approx 1/C_{L}f_{0}$ per stage,
$R_{X}\approx 1/3C_{L}f_{0}$ for the loop, the
$1/2$ in (7)--(9) being exhibited explicitly only when the
$f_{0}(V_{DD})$ sensitivity is retained.  Up to that
conventional factor of two the circuit is a switched
capacitor resistor

$$R_{SC}={1\over {C_{SC}f_{SC}}}\tag{14}$$

with $C_{SC}=C_{L}$ and $f_{SC}=f_{0}$ per stage,
$C_{SC}=NC_{L}$ for the $N$ stage loop.  In compact form

$$|Z_{X}(s)|\approx {1\over {sC_{X}}}\;||\;R_{X}\qquad 
C_{X}\approx NC_{L}\tag{15}$$

with $R_{X}$ given by (3), (7).  For $N=3$ this is
normally abbreviated to $R_{X}\approx 1/2C_{L}f_{0}$ per
stage, $R_{X}\approx 1/6C_{L}f_{0}$ for the loop,
negative in the linear small signal sense, positive in the
large signal averaged sense.

> {\it Remark:}  With $g_{m}$ exhibited the linear
> metastable small signal impedance at the $V_{DD}$ node is,
> from $I_{x}=\sum I_{Dp}$,
> $$Z_{x}(s)={{A+B}\over {3C\,(g_{mn}+g_{dsn}+sC_{L})}}\tag{16}$$
> $$A=g_{mp}-g_{mn}\;\;,\;\;B=g_{dsp}-g_{dsn}-sC_{L}\;\;,\;\;
> C=g_{mp}+g_{dsp}\tag{17}$$
> i. e.
> $$Z_{x}(s)={{g_{mp}-g_{mn}+g_{dsp}-g_{dsn}-sC_{L}}
> \over {3(g_{mp}+g_{dsp})(g_{mn}+g_{dsn}+sC_{L})}}\tag{18}$$
> so that at $s\to 0$
> $$R_{x}(0)={{g_{mp}-g_{mn}+g_{dsp}-g_{dsn}}
> \over {3(g_{mp}+g_{dsp})(g_{mn}+g_{dsn})}}<0\tag{19}$$
> for $g_{mn}>g_{mp}$, the usual condition for oscillation.
> Putting $|g_{m}|\approx 2\pi f_{0}C_{L}$ this is
> $|R_{x}|\sim 1/g_{m}\sim 1/2\pi f_{0}C_{L}$, i. e. (11)
> to within $2\pi $.

answers.question:
For the ring oscillator in Figure 8, consider the small-signal resistance `RX`
seen looking into the supply node.

Use `CL` for the effective load capacitance at each internal oscillator node,
`f0` for the oscillation frequency, and `TD` for the delay of one inverter stage.

From the dynamic charging and discharging of the three load capacitances, one
can write

```text
RX ~= 1 / (3 f0 CL)
```

Somebody then argues that, because the circuit is oscillating, the path from
`VDD` to ground through the transistors is off for much of the cycle, so the
average resistance should be much higher than the MOS on-resistance or inverse
transconductance scale.

Do you agree with this argument?

answer.text:
With the usual abuse of language $R_{X}$ is
the {\it low frequency} incremental resistance.
Put $\Delta V_{DD}$ on the common $V_{DD}$ node,
$f_{p}\ll f_{0}$.

$${\rm d}Q =C_{L}{\rm d}V_{DD}\tag{1}$$

per charge.  In one $T_{0}=1/f_{0}$ every $C_{L}$
is charged once to $V_{DD}$ and discharged to
$0$ through the $n$ device.  The charge taken
from the supply in $T_{0}$ is

$$Q_{0}=3C_{L}V_{DD}\tag{2}$$

if the $RC$ charging is complete, $R_{on}C_{L}\ll
T_{0}$, so that

$$I_{0}=Q_{0}f_{0}=3f_{0}C_{L}V_{DD}\tag{3}$$

is the {\it large signal} average current.
For ${\rm d}V_{DD}$ at $f_{p}\ll f_{0}$ the
oscillator can follow and

$${\rm d}Q_{0}=3C_{L}{\rm d}V_{DD}\tag{4}$$

$${\rm d}I_{0}=3f_{0}C_{L}{\rm d}V_{DD}+3C_{L}V_{DD}{\rm d}f_{0}\tag{5}$$

To first order for the incremental $R$ at
essentially constant $f_{0}$, {\it i. e.} for
${\rm d}f_{0}$ second order in the usual
switched capacitor approximation,

$$R_{X}^{-1}={\rm d}I_{0}/{\rm d}V_{DD}\approx 3f_{0}C_{L}\tag{6}$$

$$R_{X}\approx \frac{1}{3f_{0}C_{L}}\tag{7}$$

in the sense of

$$R_{X}= \left\langle \frac{{\rm d}v}{{\rm d}i}
\right\rangle_{T_{0},\,f_{p}\ll f_{0}} \tag{8}$$

the $T_{0}$ average of the periodically time
varying small signal impedance.  It is the
switched capacitor resistor $1/fC$ with
$f=3f_{0}$ charging events per second.  It is
{\it not} the d.c. $V_{DD}$ to $GND$ short
through $p$ in series with $n$.

$$V_{DD}\to p\to C_{L}\to GND\tag{9}$$

not $V_{DD}\to p\to n\to GND$.  The latter,
the crow bar current during the $\sim T_{D}$
transition, is indeed $0$ most of the cycle
and its $T_{0}$ average conductance is small.
The former carries no d.c. current when the
$p$ is on but $C_{L}$ is already charged.
Current flows only in $\sim R_{on}C_{L}$
pulses.  Time average of $R$ is not $1/$
time average of $G$.

Indeed (7) {\it is} $O(R_{on})\sim O(1/g_{m})$.
Formally $f_{0}$ is not independent of
$R_{on},g_{m}$.

For the ring

$$f_{0}= \frac{1}{2NT_{D}}=\frac{1}{6T_{D}}\tag{10}$$

and to $O(1)$

$$T_{D}\approx 0.7R_{on}C_{L}\approx
\frac{C_{L}V_{DD}}{I_{D}}\approx \frac{C_{L}}{g_{m}}\tag{11}$$

so that

$$R_{X}\approx \frac{1}{3C_{L}}\,6T_{D}
\approx 2T_{D}/C_{L}\approx 1.4R_{on}\approx
\frac{2}{g_{m}}\tag{12}$$

up to the $0.7$ and the shape factor.
In words: $1/f_{0}C_{L}\sim R_{on}$.
If $R_{on}\to 0$, $T_{D}\to 0$, $f_{0}\to\infty$
and $R_{X}\to 0$.  If you make the switch
more resistive the oscillator slows down so
that $f_{0}C_{L}$ goes down in proportion.

Averaging $R(t)$: $R=\infty$ when $p$ is off,
$R=R_{on}$ when $p$ is on, would give
$\langle R\rangle =\infty$.  Averaging $G(t)$:
$G=0$ when off, $G=g_{m}$ when on, duty
cycle $\sim 1/2$ for the $p$ being on,
$\sim T_{D}/T_{0}\sim 1/6$ for actually
conducting charging current with peak
$V_{DD}/R_{on}$, gives $\langle G\rangle
\sim g_{m}$ and $\langle I\rangle =V_{DD}
\langle G_{eff}\rangle =V_{DD}f_{0}C_{L}$.

So for $f_{p}\ll f_{0}$ the supply looks like
$\sim k/g_{m}$ to ground, $k\sim 1-2$, not
$\gg 1/g_{m}$.  Put differently the supply
current is a train of $\sim V_{DD}/R_{on}$
pulses of width $\sim R_{on}C_{L}$ and
repetition rate $3f_{0}$, average
$3f_{0}C_{L}V_{DD}$.

For $f_{p}\sim f_{0}$ the $T_{0}$ averaged
description fails and $Z_{X}(jf_{p})$ is the
Floquet impedance, in general complex and
can exhibit negative resistance at
$f_{p}\approx f_{0}$, but its low frequency
limit is (7) $\sim R_{on}$.  With the
oscillation stopped, latched, $R_{X}$ is
indeed the leakage $R_{off}\gg R_{on}$.

The reasoning explicitly addresses the dynamic charging mechanism, the distinction between DC path and dynamic switching path, and the averaging argument. answers.question: In the circuit of Figure 9, what happens to the initial voltage gain as the width of M7 increases?

answer.text:
With the usual definition the {\it useful} gain is the
integrated gain at the end of the linear phase, Fig. 12.33
in Razavi.  Put $C_{X}=C_{Y}=C_{L}$ and, for
${\rm CK}=0$, $V_{X}=V_{Y}=V_{P}=V_{Q}=V_{DD}$.
For ${\rm CK}=1$ ${\cal S}_{1}-{\cal S}_{4}$ are off,
${\cal M}_{7}$ is on and, with

$$I_{T}=I_{D7}\propto W_{7}\tag{1}$$

$${\cal M}_{1}-{\cal M}_{2}\;\;{\rm in\; saturation\;\;},
\qquad I_{D1,2}=I_{T}/2\pm \Delta I\tag{2}$$
$$\Delta I =g_{m1,2}\Delta V_{in}\tag{3}$$

$${\cal M}_{3}-{\cal M}_{4}\;\;V_{DS}=V_{GS}\;\;{\rm saturated},
\qquad {\cal M}_{5}-{\cal M}_{6}\;\;{\rm off}\tag{4}$$

so that, to first order, ${\cal M}_{3}-{\cal M}_{4}$ cascode
${\cal M}_{1}-{\cal M}_{2}$ onto $C_{L}$,

$${{dV_{X}}\over {dt}}=-{{I_{D1}}\over {C_{L}}}\qquad
{{dV_{Y}}\over {dt}}=-{{I_{D2}}\over {C_{L}}}\tag{5}$$

and, differentially,

$${{d\Delta V_{XY}}\over {dt}}={{g_{m}\Delta V_{in}}\over {C_{L}}}
\tag{6}$$

so that after a time $T_{int}$ spent in the linear
phase

$$\Delta V_{0}\equiv \Delta V_{XY}(T_{int})=
{{g_{m}T_{int}}\over {C_{L}}}\Delta V_{in}\tag{7}$$

$$A_{0}\equiv {{\Delta V_{0}}\over {\Delta V_{in}}}=
{{g_{m}T_{int}}\over {C_{L}}}\tag{8}$$

is the {\it integration} gain that is normally quoted as
the {\q initial} gain of the latch.  In the small signal
sense $T_{int}\rightarrow \infty $

$$A_{0}^{(\infty )}=g_{m1}\left( r_{o1}\parallel r_{o3}
\parallel r_{o5}\right) \propto g_{m}/I_{T}\tag{9}$$

For the normal strong inversion square law

$$g_{m1,2}= \mu _{n}C_{ox}{\left({W\over L}\right)}_{1,2}
V_{ov1,2}= \sqrt{2\mu _{n}C_{ox}{\left({W\over L}\right)}_{1,2}
I_{D1,2}}\propto \sqrt{I_{T}}\propto \sqrt{W_{7}}\tag{10}$$

$$r_{o1,3}\propto 1/I_{D1,3}\propto 1/I_{T}\propto 1/W_{7}\tag{11}$$

so that, formally,

$$A_{0}^{(\infty )}\propto {{g_{m}}\over {I_{T}}}\propto
{1\over {\sqrt{I_{T}}}}\propto {1\over {\sqrt{W_{7}}}}\tag{12}$$

normally written as

$$A_{0}^{(\infty )}\propto {1\over {V_{ov1,2}}}\tag{13}$$

If the $g_{m}r_{o}$ reduction is neglected $A_{0}^{(\infty )}
\propto g_{m}\propto \sqrt{W_{7}}$ is often quoted as {\q the
gain goes up with $W_{7}$}.

What is normally meant by the {\q initial gain} in the
Strong Arm literature is the gain at the moment the
p-channel cross coupled pair turns on, i. e. $T_{int}=T_{p}$
where $V_{X,Y}$ have fallen by $|V_{Tp}|$ from $V_{DD}$,

$$T_{p}\approx {{C_{L}|V_{Tp}|}\over {I_{T}/2}}=
{{2C_{L}|V_{Tp}|}\over {I_{T}}}\propto {1\over {W_{7}}}\tag{14}$$

so that from (8)

$$A_{0p}= {{g_{m}T_{p}}\over {C_{L}}}=
{{2|V_{Tp}|g_{m}}\over {I_{T}}}= {{2|V_{Tp}|}\over {V_{ov1,2}}}
\tag{15}$$

i. e. the conventional

$$A_{0p}\approx {{g_{m}|V_{Tp}|}\over {I_{T}/2}}$$

quoted in Razavi, {\it Design of Analog CMOS Integrated
Circuits}, 2nd ed. Chap. 12.  With (10)

$$A_{0p}\propto {1\over {\sqrt{W_{7}}}}\qquad {\rm square\;law}
\tag{16}$$

$$A_{0p}\propto {1\over {W_{7}}}\qquad {\rm velocity\;saturated}
\tag{17}$$

$$A_{0p}\approx {{|V_{Tp}|}\over {nV_{T}}}\approx {\rm const.}
\qquad {\rm weak\;inversion,\;\;}g_{m}=I_{D}/nV_{T}\tag{18}$$

In words: widening ${\cal M}_{7}$ raises $I_{T}$ and
$g_{m1,2}\propto \sqrt{W_{7}}$ but it shortens the time
available for linear integration as $1/W_{7}$ and lowers
$r_{o}\propto 1/W_{7}$.  The net, useful, pre-regeneration
voltage amplification seen differentially at $X-Y$ [or at
$P-Q$] at the onset of regeneration therefore {\it goes
down} when ${\cal M}_{7}$ is made wider, $A_{0}\propto
V_{ov1,2}^{-1}$.  In square law $A_{0}\propto W_{7}^{-1/2}$,
in velocity saturation $A_{0}\propto W_{7}^{-1}$ and in
weak inversion $A_{0}$ becomes to first order independent
of $W_{7}$.

Neglecting the $T_{p}\propto 1/I_{T}$ [or the $r_{o}\propto
1/I_{T}$] reduction the customary small signal
$g_{m}r_{o}$ gain $A_{0}^{(\infty )}\approx g_{m1}r_{o1}$
is often quoted as $A_{0}\propto g_{m}\propto \sqrt{W_{7}}$,
i. e. as increasing with $W_{7}$ until velocity
saturation/sub-threshold is reached.  The $g_{m}T_{p}/C_{L}$
gain (15) is the quantity that determines input referred
offset and noise and it decreases with $W_{7}$ as above.
Any intermediate definition gives a shallow optimum at
moderate $W_{7}$.

answers.question: In Figure 9, what happens to the initial voltage gain if we increase the capacitance at nodes P and Q?

answer.text:
With the usual long channel square law model the
{\it switching} voltage is ${\cal C}$ independent.
Put $C_{P}=C_{Q}=C_{P}$ , $C_{X}=C_{Y}=C_{X}$ and
$I_{T}=I_{M_{7}}$.  For $CK=0$

$$V_{P}=V_{Q}=V_{X}=V_{Y}=V_{DD}\qquad M_{7}{\rm \;off}$$

For $CK=1$, $S_{1}\dots S_{4}$ off, $M_{7}$ on,
$M_{3},M_{4}$ off, $M_{5},M_{6}$ off

$${{dV_{P}}\over {dt}}=-{{I_{D1}}\over {C_{P}}}\qquad
  {{dV_{Q}}\over {dt}}=-{{I_{D2}}\over {C_{P}}}\tag{1}$$

so that for the differential signal, $I_{D1}-I_{D2}=
g_{m1}\Delta V_{in}$,

$$\Delta V_{PQ}(t)={{g_{m1}\Delta V_{in}}\over {C_{P}}}t\tag{2}$$

in the conventional $g_{m}T/C$ language the
{\it small signal} gain before $M_{3},M_{4}$ switch is

$$A_{0}(s)={{g_{m1}}\over {g_{ds1}+g_{ds3}+sC_{P}}}\approx
{{g_{m1}}\over {sC_{P}}}\tag{3}$$

i. e. for a given $T$ it goes as $1/C_{P}$, $1/(C_{P}+
C_{X})$ after $M_{3},M_{4}$ are on, the $-3{\rm dB}$
frequency at $P,Q$ goes as $1/C_{P}$.

The switching time itself is $C_{P}$ proportional.
$M_{3}$ {\it resp.} $M_{4}$ switch when

$$V_{P,Q}=V_{DD}-V_{Tn}\tag{4}$$

i. e.

$$T_{0}={{C_{P}V_{Tn}}\over {I_{T}/2}}\tag{5}$$

so that at the switching point, from (2),

$$\Delta V_{0}\equiv \Delta V_{PQ}(T_{0})
      ={{g_{m1}T_{0}}\over {C_{P}}}\Delta V_{in}
      ={{2g_{m1}V_{Tn}}\over {I_{T}}}\Delta V_{in}\tag{6}$$

$C_{P}$ cancels.  After $T_{0}$ $X$ is tied to $P$
through $M_{3}$ and $Y$ to $Q$ through $M_{4}$ and,
common mode, the tail current discharges $C_{P}+C_{X}$,

$${{dV_{Xcm}}\over {dt}}={{dV_{Pcm}}\over {dt}}
      =-{{I_{T}/2}\over {C_{P}+C_{X}}}\tag{7}$$

$M_{5},M_{6}$ switch when $V_{X,Y}=V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|$,

$$T_{1}={{(C_{P}+C_{X})|V_{Tp}|}\over {I_{T}/2}}\tag{8}$$

During $T_{1}$ the circuit is a $g_{m3}$ latch on
$C_{P}+C_{X}$,

$$\tau _{r}={{C_{P}+C_{X}}\over {g_{m3}}}\tag{9}$$

so that, to first order,

$$\Delta V_{X}(T_{0}+T_{1})=
 \Delta V_{0}{\rm e}^{T_{1}/\tau _{r}}
 +\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{0}+T_{1}}{{g_{m1}\Delta V_{in}}\over
 {C_{P}+C_{X}}}e^{(T_{0}+T_{1}-t)/\tau _{r}}dt \tag{10}$$

and, with (5)(8)(9),

$$\eqalign{
A_{v0}&\equiv {{\Delta V_{X}(T_{0})}\over {\Delta V_{in}}}
      ={{2g_{m1}V_{Tn}}\over {I_{T}}}\cr
A_{v1}&\equiv {{\Delta V_{X}(T_{0}+T_{1})}\over {\Delta V_{in}}}
      \approx A_{v0}{\rm e}^{2g_{m3}|V_{Tp}|/I_{T}}
       +{{2g_{m1}|V_{Tp}|}\over {I_{T}}}{\rm e}^{2g_{m3}|V_{Tp}|/I_{T}}
       \cr}\tag{11}$$

i. e. to first order, long channel, square law, $C_{P}$
and $C_{X}$ cancel both in $T_{0}/C_{P}$ and in
$T_{1}/\tau _{r}$.  In the conventional shorthand

$$A_{v}\approx {{g_{m1}T_{0}}\over {C_{P}}}
        \approx {{g_{m1}V_{T}}\over {I_{T}}}\tag{12}$$

is nominally ${\cal C}$ independent.

If the finite $r_{o}=1/g_{ds}$ and/or a fixed
evaluation window $T$ is kept the textbook form (2)
is normally quoted as

$$A_{v}(T)\approx {{g_{m1}T}\over {C_{P}}}\propto {1\over {C_{P}}}
\qquad T_{0}<T<T_{0}+T_{1}\tag{13}$$

and, after $M_{3},M_{4}$ are on,

$$A_{v}(T)\approx {{g_{m1}T}\over {C_{P}+C_{X}}}\propto
{1\over {C_{P}+C_{X}}}\tag{14}$$

so that for all practical purposes the {\it usable}
voltage that the $g_{m1}$ stage can build up before the
back to back inverters $M_{3},M_{4}$--$M_{5},M_{6}$ take
over goes down when $C_{P},C_{Q}$ is increased.  In
every day language: the pole at $P,Q$,

$$\omega _{pP}\approx {{g_{ds1}+g_{ds3}}\over {C_{P}}}\tag{15}$$

moves down as $1/C_{P}$, the $-3{\rm dB}$ gain
$g_{m1}/g_{ds}$ stays the same but the gain at any
finite frequency, and the large signal integrated gain
$g_{m1}T/C_{P}$ for a given $T$, falls as $1/C_{P}$,
normally quoted simply as {\it the (initial) pre
regeneration gain falls as $1/C_{P}\;(1/(C_{P}+C_{X}))$}.

The price is paid in delay.  From (5), (8) and (9)

$$T_{0}\propto C_{P}\qquad 
  T_{1}\propto C_{P}+C_{X}\qquad 
  \tau _{r}\propto C_{P}+C_{X}\tag{16}$$

so the comparator gets slower by $\Delta T\approx
\Delta C_{P}V_{T}/I_{T}$ and, $A_{v0}$ being
nominally constant, the input referred offset and
noise of the latch,

$$V_{os,in}\approx {{V_{os,latch}}\over {A_{v0}}}\tag{17}$$

goes up as $1/A_{v0}\propto C_{P}\;(C_{P}+C_{X})$ in the
finite $r_{o}$ model.  With the ideal square law
cancellation (11) $V_{os,in}$ is to first order
${\cal C}$ independent; the second order correction is
the $1/C_{P}\;(1/(C_{P}+C_{X}))$ fall just quoted.
Any of the forms (11)--(14) is accepted as {\it the
initial gain is (to first order) ${\cal C}$ independent
and, for a fixed $T$, falls as $1/C_{P}$}.  Loosely:
it goes down, the latch gets slower.
