answers.question: If we increase the widths of M5 and M6 in Figure 9, does the speed improve or degrade?

answer.text:
With the usual dimensioning the circuit is {\it
{\rm integration} limited} and the ${\rm p}$ latch is
just a capacity on $X,Y$.

Put $C_{X}=C_{Y}=C_{0}+C_{p}W_{5}+C_{n}W_{3}$,
$g_{m5}=g_{m5}^{\prime}W_{5}$, $g_{m3}=g_{m3}^{\prime}W_{3}$.

For $CK=0$

$$X=Y=V_{DD}\qquad M_{5,6}\;\;{\rm off}$$

For $CK=1$, $M_{7}$ on, $M_{1,2}$ discharge $P,Q$
and, through $M_{3,4}$ on, $X,Y$ with

$$I_{D1,2}\approx I_{T}/2\tag{1}$$

until

$$V_{X,Y}=V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|\tag{2}$$

$M_{5,6}$ turn on and the conventional
${\rm n}-{\rm p}$ latch regenerates.  To first order

$$t_{D}=t_{0}+t_{l}\tag{3}$$

$$t_{0}\approx C_{X}|V_{Tp}|/I_{D1,2}\tag{4}$$

is the time to get to (2), the so called
amplifier - integrator time, and

$$V_{X}-V_{Y}\approx \left(V_{in1}-V_{in2}\right)
{{g_{m1,2}t_{0}}\over {C_{X}}}\tag{5}$$

is the voltage amplified at $X,Y$ at $t_{0}$ and

$$t_{l}= \tau _{l}{\rm ln}{{V_{DD}}\over {V_{X}-V_{Y}}}\tag{6}$$

$$\tau _{l}^{-1}\approx {{g_{m3}+g_{m5}}\over {C_{X}}}
+{{g_{m4}+g_{m6}}\over {C_{Y}}}\approx
2{{g_{m3}+g_{m5}}\over {C_{X}}}\tag{7}$$

is the small signal regeneration time constant of the
two cross coupled inverters $M_{3}-M_{5}$, $M_{4}-M_{6}$.

$$t_{D}\approx {{C_{X}|V_{Tp}|}\over {I_{T}/2}}+
{{C_{X}}\over {g_{m3}+g_{m5}}}{\rm ln}
{{V_{DD}C_{X}}\over {(V_{in1}-V_{in2})g_{m1,2}t_{0}}}\tag{8}$$

$$C_{X}=C_{0}+k_{p}W_{5}+k_{n}W_{3}\qquad 
g_{m5}=g_{m0p}W_{5}\tag{9}$$

so that, for $W_{5}=W_{6}$,

$${{\partial t_{0}}\over {\partial W_{5}}}=k_{p}{{|V_{Tp}|}\over
{I_{T}/2}}>0\tag{10}$$

$${{\partial \tau _{l}}\over {\partial W_{5}}}=
{{k_{p}(g_{m3}+g_{m5})-C_{X}g_{m0p}}\over
{(g_{m3}+g_{m5})^{2}}}=
{{k_{p}g_{m3}-g_{m0p}(C_{0}+k_{n}W_{3})}\over
{(g_{m3}+g_{m5})^{2}}}\tag{11}$$

I. e. $M_{5,6}$ are {\it off} during $t_{0}$ and contribute
only cold capacity $k_{p}W_{5}$ to $C_{X,Y}$.  $t_{0}$
goes {\it up} linearly with $W_{5,6}$.

During $t_{l}$ they contribute $g_{m}$ as well as $C$,
so that

$$\tau _{l}={{C_{0}+k_{p}W_{5}+k_{n}W_{3}}\over
{g_{m3}+g_{m0p}W_{5}}}\xrightarrow[W_{5}\to \infty]{}
{{k_{p}}\over {g_{m0p}}}\approx {\rm const.}\tag{12}$$

For $W_{5}$ small

$${{\partial \tau _{l}}\over {\partial W_{5}}}<0\tag{13}$$

the latch gets faster with $W_{5}$, for $W_{5}$ large
$\tau _{l}$ saturates at $k_{p}/g_{m0p}$ and

$${{\partial t_{D}}\over {\partial W_{5}}}\approx
k_{p}{{|V_{Tp}|}\over {I_{T}/2}}>0\tag{14}$$

In normal design $C_{0}+k_{n}W_{3}\gg k_{p}W_{5}$ is
already satisfied for $W_{5}$ minimum and (11) is
$\approx 0$.  E. {\rm g.} with $k_{p}\approx C_{ox}L_{p}$,
$g_{m0p}\approx \mu_{p}C_{ox}V_{ovp}/L_{p}$,

$$\tau _{l}(\infty )\approx L_{p}^{2}/\mu_{p}V_{ovp}\tag{15}$$

independent of $W_{5}$.

So to first order the small signal latching time constant
can be made a few ${\rm ps}$ faster by making $M_{5,6}$
wider if you start from $W_{5}\ll W_{3}$, but it very
quickly saturates, whereas the large signal
integration time $t_{0}\propto C_{X}$ keeps going up
linearly with $W_{5,6}$ and dominates the
$CK\rightarrow V_{out}$ delay for small $V_{id}$,
i. e. for the normal metastable operation.

In the conventional optimum $W_{5,6}$ is minimum,
$W_{5,6}\approx 0.5-1.0\,W_{3,4}$, and any appreciable
increase of $W_{5,6}$ at fixed $I_{T},W_{1-4}$ increases
$C_{X,Y}$, increases the time to turn $M_{5,6}$ on,
increases the precharge time, increases the kick back
and the offset and {\it increases}} the normal
quoted $CK$ to $Q$ propagation delay.  In the
text book jargon {\it the speed degrades}}.

If the $C_{X}$ increase is discounted, $dC_{X}=0$,
$g_{m5}\uparrow $ does make $\tau _{l}\downarrow $ and
the exponential regeneration faster.  That is the
often quoted {\it the latch gets stronger}} remark.

While the answer correctly identifies the relevant competing mechanisms (added capacitance vs. increased gm) and even shows that the latch time constant decreases with W5 for small W5, it frames the dominant conclusion as speed degradation, missing the central result that speed improves initially.

answers.question: In the circuit of Figure 10, does the speed improve or degrade if we increase the widths of the clocked transistors?

answer.text:
With the ideal clock the circuit is the conventional
${\rm C^{2}MOS}$ ${\rm TFF}\equiv \div 2$ of Fig.1

$${\rm Inv}_{1}:V_{DD}-M_{p}-M_{pck}-M_{nck}-M_{1}-GND\;\;X$$
$${\rm Inv}_{2}:V_{DD}-M_{p}-M_{pck}-M_{nck}-M_{1}-GND\;\;Y\tag
{1}$$

$$Y\stackrel{{\rm Inv}_{3}}{\longrightarrow }Z\stackrel{{\rm
Inv}_{1}}{\longrightarrow }X\stackrel{{\rm Inv}_{2}}{\longrightarrow }Y$$

${\rm Inv}_{1}$ is on for $CK=1$, ${\rm Inv}_{2}$ is on for
$CK=0$ and vice versa.  In the evaluate half period the
dynamic node, $X$ or $Y$, has to be (dis)charged through the
series combination

$$R_{eq}=R_{D}+R_{ck}\qquad R_{ck}\propto 1/W_{ck}\tag{2}$$

to the capacitance of the dynamic node

$$C_{eq}=C_{0}+C_{ck}\qquad 
C_{0}=C_{db,ck}+C_{g,{\rm next}}+C_{w}\tag{3}$$
$$C_{ck}=C_{g,ck}+C_{db,ck}+C_{sb,ck}\propto W_{ck}$$

plus the capacitance of the internal series node

$$C_{i}=C_{db,D}+C_{sb,ck}\propto W_{ck}\tag{4}$$

so that, to Elmore,

$$\tau _{p}\approx R_{D}(C_{i}+C_{eq})+R_{ck}C_{eq}\tag{5}$$
$$\tau _{n}\approx R_{D}(C_{i}+C_{eq})+R_{ck}C_{eq}$$

for the $p$ and the $n$ side.  E. {\it g.} for the pull
up of $X$

$$\tau _{X}\approx R_{Mp}(C_{A1}+C_{X})+R_{Mpck}C_{X}\tag{6}$$

$$C_{X}=C_{db,Mpck}+C_{db,Mnck}+C_{g,Mp}+C_{g,M1}+C_{w}$$
$$C_{A1}=C_{db,Mp}+C_{sb,Mpck}$$

and the same for $Y$.  Putting (2)-(3) in (5)

$$\tau (W_{ck})=\left(R_{D}+{R_{ck}^{\prime}\over W_{ck}}\right)
\left(C_{0}+C_{ck}^{\prime}W_{ck}\right)
 =R_{D}C_{0}+R_{D}C_{ck}^{\prime}W_{ck}
+{R_{ck}^{\prime}C_{0}\over W_{ck}}+R_{ck}^{\prime}C_{ck}^{\prime}
\tag{7}$$

$${{d\tau}\over {dW_{ck}}}=R_{D}C_{ck}^{\prime}
-{{R_{ck}^{\prime}C_{0}}\over {W_{ck}^{2}}}=0$$

$$W_{ck,opt}= \sqrt{{{R_{ck}^{\prime}C_{0}}\over
{R_{D}C_{ck}^{\prime}}}}\tag{8}$$

i. {\it e.} $\tau (W_{ck})$ has a shallow minimum.
For $W_{ck}<W_{ck,opt}$

$${{d\tau}\over {dW_{ck}}}<0\tag{9}$$

the reduction of the series resistance wins and the
small signal $3\,{\rm dB}$ bandwidth goes up as
$\approx 1/R_{ck}$.  For

$$W_{ck}>W_{ck,opt}\qquad {{d\tau}\over {dW_{ck}}}>0\tag{10}$$

the self loading $C_{ck}^{\prime}W_{ck}$ and the
capacitance of the internal series node $C_{i}$ win and
$\tau $ goes up again.  With the normal choice
$R_{D}\approx R_{ck}$ and $C_{0}$ dominated by the
gate capacitance of the next inverter and the wiring,
(8) is

$$W_{ck,opt}\approx 1-2\,W_{min}\tag{11}$$

so that for all practical purposes the divider is
fastest with minimum, or at most $1.5-2\times $ minimum,
clock devices.  Neglecting the diffusion capacitance,
$C_{ck}^{\prime}=0$, (7) is monotone decreasing,
$\tau \propto R_{D}+R_{ck}^{\prime}/W_{ck}$, the usual
text book ``the wider the faster''.

Including the parasitics the large signal toggle
frequency

$$f_{max}\approx {1\over {\tau _{X}+\tau _{Y}+\tau _{{\rm Inv}3}}}
\tag{12}$$

goes through the maximum (8) and then falls as
$\propto 1/W_{ck}$.  In the normal design window the
series resistance is already dominated by the data
devices $M_{1},M_{p}$, $R_{D}$, so that making
$R_{ck}\rightarrow 0$ buys very little in $R_{eq}$
while $C_{eq}=C_{0}+C_{ck}^{\prime}W_{ck}$ grows
linearly with $W_{ck}$.

In addition

* $C_{g,ck}\propto W_{ck}$ loads the clock driver.
With a realistic clock driver of output resistance
$R_{ckdrv}$ an extra term $R_{ckdrv}C_{g,ck}\propto
W_{ck}$ has to be added to (7) which moves
$W_{ck,opt}$ to even smaller $W_{ck}$ and makes
$f_{max}$ fall even faster with $W_{ck}$.

* $C_{i}\propto W_{ck}$ aggravates charge sharing
between the internal series node $A_{1},A_{2},B_{1},
B_{2}$ and the dynamic node $X,Y$ when the transmission
gate turns on.  The well known ${\rm C^{2}MOS}$ droop

$$\Delta V_{X}= {{C_{i}}\over {C_{i}+C_{X}}}(V_{i}-V_{X})\tag{13}$$

grows with $W_{ck}$ and eventually makes the divider
fail.  The clock feedthrough

$$\Delta V_{X}\approx {{C_{ov,ck}}\over {C_{X}}}V_{CK}\tag{14}$$

also grows $\propto W_{ck}$.

So that, apart from the very shallow theoretical
improvement for $W_{ck}<W_{ck,opt}$, any substantial
widening of the $CK,\overline{CK}$ devices increases
the $RC$ product at $X$ and $Y$, increases the load on
$CK$, increases charge sharing and clock feedthrough
and makes the useful toggle rate of the $\div 2$
go down, while the clock power $P_{ck}=fC_{g,ck}V_{DD}^{2}
\propto W_{ck}$ goes up.  In text book language
``the speed degrades'' if the $CK$ FETs are made wide.
The optimum is essentially the minimum size device.
A $2-3\times $ minimum device is often quoted as the
practical optimum; beyond that the divider gets
slower.  With $C_{db}=C_{ov}=0$ and an ideal $CK$
source the circuit gets faster as $1/W_{ck}$.

> {\it Remark:}  With $C_{ck}^{\prime}=0$ and
> $R_{ckdrv}=0$ the Elmore delay (7) is
> $\tau = (R_{D}+R_{ck}^{\prime}/W_{ck})C_{0}$ and is
> monotone decreasing with $W_{ck}$.  That is the
> ``speed improves'' answer often quoted in elementary
> treatments.

answers.question: Does the structure in Figure 10 provide quadrature outputs?

answer.text:
With the usual ${\rm ``}C_{p}{\rm ''}\ne 0$ idealisation
the circuit is the conventional dynamic master slave
${\cal D}= \bar {\cal Q}$ ${\rm div.2}$.

Put

$${\cal M}:~~Z\rightarrow X\qquad 
{\cal S}:~~X\rightarrow Y\qquad Z=\bar Y\tag{*}$$

$${\cal M}~~{\rm on~for}~~CK=1\qquad 
{\cal S}~~{\rm on~for}~~CK=0\tag{**}$$

so that, with $C_{X}$ and $C_{Y}$ holding the charge,

$$\eqalign{
CK=1:&\;X=\bar Z\;\;{\rm driven},\;Y=Z_{0}\;\;{\rm held},\;
Z=\bar Y\;\;{\rm held}\cr
CK=0:&\;X=X_{0}\;\;{\rm held},\;Y=\bar X\;\;{\rm driven},\;
Z=\bar Y=X_{0}\;\;{\rm driven}\cr} \tag{***}$$

In particular $Y\equiv \bar Z$ at every instant and, from
$(***)$,

$$\eqalign{
X &=\bar Z\;\;{\rm on}\;CK=1\cr
X &= Z\;\;{\rm on}\;CK=0\cr
Y &=\bar Z\;\;{\rm always}\cr} \tag{****}$$

so that on every $1\rightarrow 0$ transition of $CK$ the
slave is made transparent and

$$Y_{n+1}= \bar X_{n}\qquad Z_{n+1}= \bar Y_{n+1}=X_{n}\tag{1}$$

and on every $0\rightarrow 1$ transition of $CK$ the master
is made transparent and

$$X_{n+1}= \bar Z_{n}\tag{2}$$

Hence, with $Z_{0}$ the state at $t=0^{-}$,

$$\eqalign{
0<t<T/2\;\;CK=1:&\;Z=Z_{0},\;X=\bar Z_{0},\;Y=\bar Z_{0}\cr
T/2<t<T\;\;CK=0:&\;Z=\bar Z_{0},\;X=\bar Z_{0},\;Y=Z_{0}\cr
T<t<3T/2\;\;CK=1:&\;Z=\bar Z_{0},\;X=Z_{0},\;Y=Z_{0}\cr
3T/2<t<2T\;\;CK=0:&\;Z=Z_{0},\;X=Z_{0},\;Y=\bar Z_{0}\cr} \tag{3}$$

{\it etc.}  $T$ is the $CK$ period.  E. {\it g.} for
$Z_{0}=0$

$$\eqalign{
Z&:\;0\;{\rm for}\;0<t<T/2,\;1\;{\rm for}\;T/2<t<3T/2,\;
0\;{\rm for}\;3T/2<t<5T/2\ldots\cr
X&:\;1\;{\rm for}\;0<t<T,\;0\;{\rm for}\;T<t<2T\ldots\cr
Y&:\;1\;{\rm for}\;0<t<T/2,\;0\;{\rm for}\;T/2<t<3T/2,\;
1\;{\rm for}\;3T/2<t<5T/2\ldots =\bar Z\cr} \tag{4}$$

{\it cf.} Fig.1.  In words

* the loop divides by two,

$$f_{X}=f_{Y}=f_{Z}=f_{CK}/2\tag{5}$$

with nominal $50\%$ duty cycle;

* the {\it master} $X$ is clocked on the $0\to 1$ edge of
$CK$ and the {\it slave} $Y$, and therefore the static
output $Z=\bar Y$, is clocked on the $1\to 0$ edge of $CK$.

To first order in $t_{d}({\rm Inv}_{3})/T_{CK}$ the two
${\rm div.2}$ phases are a quarter of the ${\rm div.2}$
period apart,

$$\left| \angle (X,Y)\right| =\left| \angle (X,Z)\right|
 = {1\over 4}T_{{\rm div.2}}={1\over 2}T_{CK}=90^{{\rm o}}
+O\!\left({{t_{d3}}\over {T_{CK}}}\right)
+O\!\left({{\Delta D_{CK}}\over {T_{CK}}}\right) \tag{6}$$

{\it e. {\rm g.}} with the normalisation (4) $X\uparrow $ at
$t=0,2T\ldots $, $Z\uparrow $ at $t=T/2,5T/2\ldots $,
$Y\uparrow $ at $t=3T/2\ldots $, {\it etc.}  In the
text book $C_{p}\ne 0$, $t_{d3}=0$, $D_{CK}=50\%$ sense the
circuit {\it is} the conventional $I/Q$ ${\rm div.2}$,
normally quoted as $X$ {\it versus} $Y$, Fig.1, or,
what is the same to within $180^{{\rm o}}$, $X$ {\it versus}
$Z$.

> {\it Remark:}  In the strict static, rail to rail sense
> the answer is {\it no}.  From $(****)$ $Y\equiv \bar Z$,
> $180^{{\rm o}}$, the only low impedance static phase is
> $Z$.  $X$ is high $Z$ for $CK=0$ and $Y$ is high $Z$ for
> $CK=1$, Eq.$(**)$.  The $90^{{\rm o}}$ of (6) is
> normally quoted as $X=Y$ for $CK=1$ and $X=\bar Y$ for
> $CK=0$, {\it i. {\rm e.}} $X=Y$ $50\%$ of the time and
> $X\ne Y$ $50\%$ of the time, $25\%$ $11$, $25\%$ $00$,
> $25\%$ $10$, $25\%$ $01$, which is the $90^{{\rm o}}$
> square wave quadrature condition, but it is obtained on
> two dynamic nodes.  With $t_{d3}\ne 0$ the $90^{{\rm o}}$
> is

> $$\Delta \phi _{X-Z}=90^{{\rm o}}
> +2\pi {{t_{d}({\rm Inv}_{3})+t_{d}({\cal S})-t_{d}({\cal M})}
> \over {T_{{\rm div.2}}}} \tag{7}$$

> and it is corrupted by any $D_{CK}\ne 50\%$ and by
> $CK\!\leftrightarrow\!\bar CK$ overlap, during which
> both ${\cal M}$ and ${\cal S}$ are momentarily on, and,
> more importantly, the hold on $C_{X}$ and $C_{Y}$ is lost
> to leakage at low $f_{CK}$ or to charge sharing at high
> $f_{CK}$.  Made static with the usual cross coupled
> keepers on $X$ and on $Y$ the circuit becomes the
> conventional static TSPC $I/Q$ ${\rm div.2}$ with

> $$I=X\qquad Q=Y=\bar Z\qquad f_{I}=f_{Q}=f_{CK}/2\qquad
> \angle (I,Q)=90^{{\rm o}} \tag{8}$$

> to within the normal static phase error (7).

In particular the two normally accessible static pins $Y$
and $Z$ are {\it not} in quadrature, $Y=\bar Z$, Fig.1.
If by {\it quadrature outputs} you mean two simultaneously
valid static $50\%$ $I$ and $Q$ phases the circuit as drawn,
without keepers, is not a usable quadrature generator.

> {\it Fig.1:} Ideal $C_{p}$ hold waveforms, $Z_{0}=0$,
> $t_{d3}=0$.  $X$ toggles on $CK\uparrow $, $Y/Z$ on
> $CK\downarrow $, $f_{X}=f_{Y}=f_{Z}=f_{CK}/2$,
> $X$ is $T_{CK}/2=T_{{\rm div.2}}/4$ away from $Y$ and from
> $Z$.  $Y=\bar Z$.

answers.question:
For the divide-by-two topology in Figure 11, does the speed improve or degrade
if we increase the widths of the clocked transistors, i.e. the transistors whose
gates are driven by `CK` or `CKbar`?

answer.text:
With an ideal ${\cal R}_{CK}=0$ clock the circuit
is the conventional ${\rm C^{2}MOS}$ ${\rm M/S}$
${\rm D}=\bar {\rm Q}$ latch of Fig.1.

$${\rm M}:{\rm CK}=1\;\;{\rm S}:{\rm CK}=0\qquad 
  {\rm M}:{\rm CK}=0\;\;{\rm S}:{\rm CK}=1\tag{*}$$

so that in the transparent phase the signal has to go
through

$$V_{DD}-R_{pCK}-R_{p}-C_{L}\tag{1}$$
$$V_{SS}-R_{nCK}-R_{n}-C_{L}\tag{2}$$

$R_{CK}\propto 1/W_{CK}$ is the triode resistance of the
series switch, $R_{p,n}\propto 1/W_{p,n}$ the resistance of
the logic device, $C_{L}=C_{d\,p,n}+C_{g\,{\rm next}}+C_{w}$
the ordinary load at the high impedance output node and

$$C_{sw}=C_{dCK}+C_{sp,n}\propto W_{CK}+W_{p,n}\tag{3}$$

the capacitance of the internal, in the hold phase floating,
node $A\equiv S_{p}/D_{pCK}$, $B\equiv S_{n}/D_{nCK}$,
Fig.1.  In the Elmore sense

$$\tau _{M,S}=R_{CK}\left(C_{sw}+C_{L}\right)+R_{p,n}C_{L}
\tag{4}$$

and the loop that has to be closed in one $CK$ period is

$$T_{0}\approx \tau _{M}+\tau _{S}+\tau _{{\rm inv}}\tag{5}$$

$$f_{{\rm max}}\approx {1\over {2T_{0}}}\tag{6}$$

is the toggle, i. e. the divide by two, frequency.
Put $R_{CK}=R_{\square }/W_{CK}$, $C_{sw}=C_{\square }W_{CK}
+C_{0}$, $C_{L}=C_{L0}\propto W_{p,n}$,

$$\tau ={{R_{\square }}\over {W_{CK}}}
\left(C_{\square }W_{CK}+C_{0}+C_{L0}\right)+R_{p,n}C_{L0}
 =R_{\square }C_{\square }+R_{p,n}C_{L0}
+{{R_{\square }\left(C_{0}+C_{L0}\right)}\over {W_{CK}}}\tag{7}$$

so that for $R_{CK\,{\rm driver}}=0$

$${{\partial \tau }\over {\partial W_{CK}}}<0\tag{8}$$

and

$$\tau \xrightarrow[W_{CK}\to \infty ]{}R_{\square }C_{\square }
+R_{p,n}C_{L0}\tag{9}$$

the ordinary unclocked inverter delay.  I. e. with an
ideal clock you can at most asymptotically approach the
intrinsic ring made of the two logic inverters plus the
feedback inverter.  E. {\it g.} doubling $W_{CK}$ from
$W_{CK}=W_{p,n}$ cuts about $25\%$ off $R_{CK}C_{L0}$ and
less than $10\%$ off $T_{0}$.

If the capacitance that is dumped on the signal node when
the logic device goes on is lumped with $C_{L}$,

$$C_{L}^{{\rm eff}}\approx C_{L}+C_{sw}\tag{10}$$

$$\tau _{{\rm eff}}\approx \left(R_{CK}+R_{p,n}\right)
\left(C_{L}+C_{sw}\right) \tag{11}$$

$$\tau _{{\rm eff}}\propto \left({1\over {W_{CK}}}+{1\over
{W_{p,n}}}\right)\left(W_{CK}+W_{p,n}\right)
 =2+{{W_{p,n}}\over {W_{CK}}}+{{W_{CK}}\over {W_{p,n}}}\tag{12}$$

which has the well known shallow minimum

$$W_{CK}^{{\rm opt}}\approx \sqrt{{{C_{L0}}\over {C_{\square }}}}
\approx (0.5-1.0)W_{p,n}\tag{13}$$

for $W_{CK}\gg W_{CK}^{{\rm opt}}$

$$\tau _{{\rm eff}}\propto W_{CK}\tag{14}$$

goes {\it up} linearly with $W_{CK}$.

In a real circuit you have to add

* the clock load

$$C_{CK}=C_{gCK}\propto W_{CK}\tag{15}$$

$$ \tau _{CK}=R_{CK\,{\rm driver}}C_{CK}\propto W_{CK}\tag{16}$$

so that the finite rise/fall time of $CK$ spends more and
more time with both latches half on with crow bar current,
and

* the charge sharing of the floating node $A,B$ on to
$C_{L}$ when the latch goes transparent.  The charge that
has to be restored is $\propto C_{sw}\propto W_{CK}$ through
$R_{CK}\propto 1/W_{CK}$, i. e. $R_{CK}C_{sw}={\rm const}$,
but the disturbance on $C_{L}$ is $\propto C_{sw}/C_{L}$.

Normally the divider is already sized at about the minimum
(13), $W_{CK}\approx W_{n}\approx {1\over 2}W_{p}$, so that
any substantial increase of $W_{CK}$ increases $C_{sw}$,
$C_{CK}$, clock feed through, dynamic power

$$P_{d}\approx f\left(C_{L}+C_{sw}+C_{CK}\right)V_{DD}^{2}
\propto W_{CK}\tag{17}$$

and, for a normally driven clock, the total

$$T_{0}^{{\rm tot}}=T_{0}+\tau _{CK}\tag{18}$$

so that $f_{{\rm max}}$ goes through a shallow maximum at
(13) and then falls $\propto 1/W_{CK}$.

In text book shorthand the result is quoted as {\it no
improvement and, for any normal, finite impedance clock
driver, a degradation of the attainable toggle frequency
once $W_{CK}\gtrsim W_{p,n}$}.  With the usual ideal clock
abstraction the statement is {\it the frequency improves
monotonically but saturates very rapidly to the intrinsic
$R_{p,n}C_{L0}$ limit, so that for all practical purposes
making $W_{CK}$ big is useless and, with $C_{CK}$ included,
harmful}.  E. {\it g.} Spectre with ideal $CK$:

> $W_{CK}=W_{n}\;f_{{\rm max}}=f_{0}$,
> $W_{CK}=2W_{n}\;f_{{\rm max}}\approx 1.05f_{0}$,
> $W_{CK}=4W_{n}\;f_{{\rm max}}\approx 1.07f_{0}$ ideal,
> $f_{{\rm max}}\approx 0.9f_{0}$ with $R_{CK\,{\rm driver}}=
> 50\,{\rm \Omega }$ loaded clock.

That is normally abbreviated to {\it the divider gets
slower if you make the clock devices wide}.

answers.question: Analyze the arrangement in Figure 12(a).

answer.text:
This is the $C^{2}MOS$ dynamic $D$ in
toggle connection, Fig.a, and pseudo static
Fig.b. $3$ inversions $= {\rm odd}$.

$$\eqalign{
A&={\rm in\;of\;}Inv_{1}\cr
B&={\rm out\;of\;}Inv_{1}= \bar A\cr
E&={\rm in\;of\;slave}\cr
C&=\bar E\cr
D&=\bar C =E\cr}$$

so that with the outer connection

$$D = E = B = \bar A \tag{1}$$

$$A = D\;{\rm when\;}S_{CK}{\rm \;closed}$$

$$E = B\;{\rm when\;}S_{\bar {CK}}{\rm \;closed}$$

It is a master slave $DFF$ with $D=\bar Q$.

* $L_{M}: S_{CK}+Inv_{1}+C_{A}$ - dynamic latch
* $L_{S}: S_{\bar {CK}}+Inv_{2}+Inv_{3}+C_{E}$ - dynamic
latch, non inverting $E\to D$.

With ideal complementary non overlapping clocks

* $CK=1,\;\bar {CK}=0$: $S_{CK}$ ON, $S_{\bar {CK}}$ OFF

$$A=D_{n}\;\;,\;\;B_{n+1}= \bar A =\bar D_{n}$$
$L_{S}$ isolated. $E=C_{E}$ holds $E_{n}=D_{n}$,
$C_{n}=\bar D_{n}$, $D_{n}$ holds on $C_{L}$ of
$Inv_{3}$. $L_{S}$ is in hold, $L_{M}$ transparent.

* $CK=0,\;\bar {CK}=1$: $S_{CK}$ OFF, $S_{\bar {CK}}$ ON

$$E = B_{n+1}\;\;,\;\;C =\bar B_{n+1}\;\;,\;\;
D_{n+1}= \bar C = B_{n+1}= \bar D_{n}$$
$C_{A}$ holds $A_{n+1}=D_{n}$ on gate capacitance of
$Inv_{1}$. $L_{M}$ in hold, $L_{S}$ transparent.

On every $CK=1\to 0$ or $0\to 1$ transition the
information is transferred $M\to S$. In one full
$CK$ period

$$D_{n+1}= \bar D_{n}\qquad B_{n+1}= \bar B_{n}$$

$$Q_{n+1}= \bar Q_{n}$$

i. e. $T-FF$. Edge triggered - falling edge if
$CK$ is reference - toggle. 

$$f_{Q}=f_{CK}/2$$

$Q$ can be taken as $D$ or $B=\bar D$. $50\%$ duty
cycle irrespective of $CK$ duty cycle. Cascading
$n$ stages $:2^{n}$. Usual high speed $:2$ prescaler
in $PLL$ synthesizer. No static current, $CV^{2}f$
only, $3$ inverters $+2$ switches, very fast. The
$2$ inverters in the slave are the buffer that makes
the total number of inversions in the loop $1+2=3$
odd so that (1) is an inversion for toggle. With
$1+1=2$ the feedback would be $D=A$ and no division.

In Fig.a both storage nodes $A$ and $E$ are
floating in hold phase. State is held only on
parasitic capacitance

$$C_{A}=C_{g1}+C_{d,SW}+C_{w}\qquad 
  C_{E}=C_{g2}+C_{d,SW}+C_{w}$$

for $T_{hold}=T_{CK}/2$. Correct operation requires

$$T_{CK}/2 \ll \tau_{leak}=C_{A,E}\Delta V/I_{leak}$$

$$f_{CK} \gg I_{leak}/C\Delta V$$

Minimum frequency, temperature dependent, a few
$kHz$ to $MHz$ in modern CMOS, fails for $DC$ or
gated clock. Slow $CK$ slope, clock feedthrough
$C_{gd}$ of switch, charge injection, charge sharing,
capacitive coupling and supply noise on the high
$Z$ node corrupt $\Delta V$ and destroy noise margin.
If $NMOS$ only switch $V_{H}=V_{DD}-V_{T}$ degraded
high, static current in $Inv_{1,2}$.

Both switches must never be ON together. With
$CK$ and $\bar {CK}$ ON the loop is closed with
$3$ inverters: a $3$ stage ring oscillator. Any
overlap $>t_{p}$ makes it oscillate and lose
division. So non overlapping clocks with

$$t_{non-overlap} >0\;\;{\rm but}\;\;t_{non-overlap}\ll
\tau_{leak}$$

are required. Generation of non overlap at $GHz$
is itself a limit. Single phase $TSPC$ with clocked
inverters is normally used.

> Dynamic divider: high speed, low area, low
> power, but ratioed by leakage, needs continuous
> clock, sensitive to clock skew, slope and noise.

Fig.b is the conventional fix: weak keeper.

$Inv_{k}$ in red with $Inv_{1}$ makes a cross
coupled latch

$$A \rightleftharpoons B$$

When $S_{CK}$ OFF the master is now static: $A$
is always driven, either by $D$ through $S_{CK}$
when $CK=1$ or by $Inv_{k}$ when $CK=0$. Leakage
on $C_{A}$ is compensated, $f_{min}$ for the master
goes to $DC$, clock can be stopped with $CK=0$,
noise immunity greatly improved, clock slope
requirement relaxed for the master.

$Inv_{k}$ must be weak, ratioed, so that the
driver $Inv_{3}$ can overpower it on write:

$$(W/L)_{k}\ll (W/L)_{3}\;\;,\;\;(W/L)_{k}\ll (W/L)_{1}$$

normally long $L$, minimum $W$, skewed inverter.
Contention current flows only during the
transparent half period transition, small power
and delay penalty. If too strong write failure,
if too weak no keeper action.

The slave $E$ is still dynamic in Fig.b. It holds
only for $T_{CK}/2$ while $CK=1$. For high $f_{CK}$
this is acceptable. For fully static, $DC$ operation
with clock stopped in either phase a second keeper
on $E-D$, i. e. a weak inverter $D\to E$, is added.
Then the whole $:2$ is static $C^{2}MOS$ master
slave $TFF$. In many libraries Fig.b is called
pseudo static or modified dynamic divider and is
sufficient as prescaler where the clock never stops
for long.

answers.question: How does the red inverter in Figure 12(b) affect the performance?

answer.text:
With ${\rm Inv}_{1}$ the circuit is {\it dynamic}.
{\it e. g.} for $CK=0$ the ${\rm Inv}_{1}$ input is
floating. In normal operation

$${\rm Inv}_{3}\to CK\to {\rm Inv}_{1}\to \bar {CK}\to
{\rm Inv}_{2}\to {\rm Inv}_{3}$$

is the signal path. The ${\rm Inv}_{1}$ input
capacitance is the dynamic storage node. It leaks
away in ${\cal O}({\rm ms})$ and the latch has a
$f_{{\rm min}}$ and is very noise sensitive.

The red ${\rm Inv}$ is the conventional weak
cross coupled {\it keeper, bleeder, staticiser,
jam latch, half keeper} which makes the master
pseudo static

$${\rm Inv}_{1}\rightleftharpoons {\rm Inv}_{R}$$

is a normal ${\rm latch}$ for $CK=0$, $\bar {CK}=0$.
For $CK=1$ the latch is over written by the
low impedance ${\rm Inv}_{3}$ through the $CK$
${\rm TG}$.

Logically no change. Electrically:

* the storage node is now always driven, $f_{{\rm min}}
\rightarrow 0$, DC operation, no refresh, much larger
noise margin, no leakage failure, no charge sharing
failure

* price: the input capacitance of ${\rm Inv}_{R}$ on
the ${\rm Inv}_{1}$ output, the output capacitance of
${\rm Inv}_{R}$ on the ${\rm Inv}_{1}$ input and,
during a $0\rightarrow 1$, $1\rightarrow 0$ transition
of the master, a ratioed fight

$${\rm Inv}_{3}\;{\rm versus}\;{\rm Inv}_{R}$$

for the ${\rm Inv}_{1}$ input node.

If ${\rm Inv}_{R}$ is made weak, $W_{R}\approx
{1\over 5}-{1\over 10}W_{1,3}$, $L_{R}>L_{{\rm min}}$,
high $V_{T}$, {\it etc.} the fight current is
${\cal O}(10\%)$ of the normal switching current and
the extra $C_{g}+C_{d}$ is ${\cal O}({\rm fF})$.
Normally quoted as {\it no} penalty:

$$\Delta t_{CK-Q}\approx \Delta t_{su}\approx
5-15\%\;\;,\;\;\Delta P_{dyn}\approx 5-10\%\;\;
\Delta P_{sc}>0$$

during the write contention plus the normal
$CV^{2}f$ of the keeper, ${\cal O}(10\%)$ area,
for the very large advantage of a fully static,
$f_{{\rm min}}=0$, pseudo static operation.
Made strong it ratioes the latch, the write
time, $t_{su}$, $t_{CK-Q}$ goes up very fast
and for $W_{R}\sim W_{3}$ the latch will not
write at all.

answers.question:
In Figure 12(b), somebody answers:

> The red inverter acts as a keeper, forming a cross-coupled latch with `Inv1`.
> This removes the minimum clock frequency requirement due to leakage.

But the input of the red inverter is not tied to the output of `Inv1`.

Do you agree with this answer? What is the actual role of the red inverter?

answer.text:
With the conventional notation

```
N0 = \bar {CK}{\rm -left}= {\rm Inv}_{3}{\rm -out}
     =CK{\rm -left}
N1 = CK{\rm -right}= {\rm Inv}_{1}{\rm -in}
N2 = {\rm Inv}_{1}{\rm -out}= \bar {CK}{\rm -left}
N3 = \bar {CK}{\rm -right}= {\rm Inv}_{2}{\rm -in}
```

Fig.12a is the conventional 3 ${\rm Inv}$ dynamic
${\cal T}$ - divider

```
N1\stackrel{{\rm Inv}_{1}}{\longrightarrow}N2
      \stackrel{\bar {CK}}{\longrightarrow}N3
      \stackrel{{\rm Inv}_{2}}{\longrightarrow}
      \stackrel{{\rm Inv}_{3}}{\longrightarrow}N0
      \stackrel{CK}{\longrightarrow}N1
```

* $CK=1,\bar {CK}=0$ : $N0$ is strapped to $N1$,
$N2$ is cut from $N3$. $N3$ is floating, so
${\rm Inv}_{2,3}$ are floating, so $N0\equiv N1$ is
floating. The master is dynamic.

* $CK=0,\bar {CK}=1$ : $N1$ is cut from $N0$, $N2$ is
strapped to $N3$. $N1$ is floating. The master is
dynamic.

In both phases there is a high $Z$ node at the
input of ${\rm Inv}_{1}$. It is held only by
capacitance. Leakage $\to $ minimum $f_{ck}$,
maximum $t_{CK=0}$ and $t_{CK=1}$.

A conventional {\it keeper}, {\it bleeder},
{\it trickle} ${\rm Inv}$ to make the master
static is a {\it weak} ${\rm Inv}$ with

```
in = N2  out = N1
```

so that

```
N1 -> Inv1 -> N2 -> keeper -> N1
```

is a normal cross coupled, 2 ${\rm Inv}$, even,
bistable latch closed when $CK=0$ and over
powerable when $CK=1$ if the keeper is weak,
$W/L_{k}\ll W/L_{1}$. With a second keeper
$N0\to N3$ the whole divider becomes fully static.

What is drawn in red in Fig.12b is {\it not} that.
With the conventional drawing the red ${\rm Inv}$
is

```
in = N0  out = N2
```

{\it i. e.} input is the slave output, output is
the master output. It is {\it not}
$N2\to N1$. So it can not be cross coupled with
${\rm Inv}_{1}$.

* $CK=1$ : $N0\equiv N1$ is floating because
$N3$ is floating. The red ${\rm Inv}$ has a
floating input. It holds nothing. $N1$ is still
dynamic.

* $CK=0$ : $N1$ is floating and is cut from $N0$
by the open $CK$ switch. The red ${\rm Inv}$
drives $N2$ from $N0$ but $N1$ is completely
disconnected from it. $N1$ is still dynamic.

So the critical dynamic node, $N1$, is never
closed by the red ${\rm Inv}$. In the hold phase
of the master, $CK=0$, the keeper is on the wrong
side of the open switch. In the transparent phase
of the master, $CK=1$, the keeper has a floating
input. In no phase does

```
Inv1 + red Inv + CK
```

make a closed bistable latch in the hold phase.

What the red ${\rm Inv}$ does close is

$$N2\stackrel{\bar {CK}}{\to}N3
      \stackrel{{\rm Inv}_{2}}{\to}
      \stackrel{{\rm Inv}_{3}}{\to}N0
      \stackrel{{\rm red}}{\to}N2\tag{*}$$

when $\bar {CK}=1$. That is ${\rm Inv}_{2}+
{\rm Inv}_{3}+{\rm red}=3$ inversions, odd, not
bistable. When $\bar {CK}=0$ it is
$N0\equiv N1\to {\rm Inv}_{1}\to N2\to {\rm red}
\to N0$, 2 inversions, but closed only when
$CK=1$, {\it i. e.} in the transparent phase where
no holding is required.

In other words as drawn the red ${\rm Inv}$ is a
misplaced weak feed back. At best it is a
half keeper for the {\it slave} $N2/N3/N0$ loop,
leaving the master $N1$ fully dynamic. Normally
it is just a contention load:

* $CK=0$ : ${\rm Inv}_{1}$ and the red ${\rm Inv}$
both drive $N2$ to opposite values for half the
states. If the red ${\rm Inv}$ is made weak the
divider will still write, but with ratioed,
static crow bar current.

* $CK=1$ : ${\rm Inv}_{3}$ and the red ${\rm Inv}$
both drive $N0$.

It adds capacitance, it adds contention, it does
not close a cross coupled pair around ${\rm Inv}_{1}$
in the hold phase. The circuit remains dynamic,
pseudo static at best, half static. Leakage on
$N1$ will still destroy the state for
$t_{CK=0}>t_{leak}$ and leakage on $N0\equiv N1$
will destroy the state for $t_{CK=1}>t_{leak}$.
The $f_{ck,min}$ imposed by junction and subthreshold
leakage on the floating $N1$ node is essentially
unchanged. To make it fully static you need
$N2\to N1$ and $N0\to N3$ weak keepers. As drawn
the red ${\rm Inv}$ is ineffective as an
${\rm Inv}_{1}$ keeper. In the literature it is
often called an ineffective bleeder/trickle
keeper - active in the wrong phase.

answers.question: How do we optimize the circuit of Figure 13 for the NF if Rin must remain equal to 50 Ohm?

answer.text:
With the usual $g_{m}r_{o}>>1$

$${\cal L}(s)=g_{m}r_{o}\;\;,\;\;g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}
\;\;,\;\;r_{o}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\tag{1}$$

$$A_{v}={v_{y}\over {v_{x}}}={{1-g_{m}R_{F}}\over {1+R_{F}/r_{o}}}
\approx -g_{m}R_{F}\tag{2}$$

$${{v_{y}}\over {v_{s}}}={{G_{F}-g_{m}}\over {D}}G_{s}\;\;,\;\;
{{v_{x}}\over {v_{s}}}={{G_{o}+G_{F}}\over {D}}G_{s}\tag{3}$$

$$D=G_{s}G_{o}+G_{F}\left(G_{s}+G_{o}+g_{m}\right) \tag{4}$$

$$G_{s}=1/R_{s}\;\;G_{F}=1/R_{F}\;\;G_{o}=1/r_{o}$$

$$R_{in}={v_{x}\over {(v_{s}-v_{x})/R_{s}}}={{G_{o}+G_{F}}
\over {G_{F}\left(G_{o}+g_{m}\right)}}={{r_{o}+R_{F}}\over
{1+g_{m}r_{o}}}\tag{5}$$

$$R_{in}\approx {1\over {g_{m}}}{1+R_{F}/r_{o}}\approx {1\over {g_{m}}}
\qquad r_{o}>>R_{F} \tag{6}$$

so that for the conventional $r_{o}\sim 0.5-2{\rm k}$
wide band matching

$$g_{m}R_{s}\approx 1\tag{7}$$

$$g_{m1}+g_{m2}\approx 20\,{\rm mA/V}\;\;{\rm for}\;\;R_{s}=50\Omega $$

$$R_{F}=R_{in}\left(1+g_{m}r_{o}\right)-r_{o}
      =R_{s}+{{r_{o}R_{s}}\over {R_{s}}}\left(g_{m}R_{s}-1\right)
      \approx R_{s}\left(1+g_{m}r_{o}\right) \tag{8}$$

is the {\it matching} condition.  One equation for the two
unknowns $g_{m},R_{F}$.  Put a current noise
$4kT\gamma g_{mi}$ in parallel with $g_{mi}$,
$4kTG_{F}$ in parallel with $R_{F}$ and $4kTR_{s}$ in
series with the source.  With (3)

$$v_{y}={{(G_{F}-g_{m})G_{s}v_{s}+(G_{s}+g_{m})I_{F}
-(G_{s}+G_{F})I_{d}}\over {D}} \tag{9}$$

$$S_{v_{s}}=4kTR_{s}\;\;S_{F}=4kTG_{F}\;\;S_{d}=4kT\gamma g_{m}
\;\;,\;\;g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}\tag{10}$$

$$\eqalign{
S_{y}&=|H_{s}|^{2}S_{v_{s}}+|H_{F}|^{2}S_{F}+|H_{d}|^{2}S_{d}\cr
H_{s}&={{(G_{F}-g_{m})G_{s}}\over {D}}\cr
H_{F}&={{G_{s}+g_{m}}\over {D}}\cr
H_{d}&=-{{G_{s}+G_{F}}\over {D}}\cr} \tag{11}$$

$$F={{S_{y}}\over {|H_{s}|^{2}S_{v_{s}}}}
 =1+{{|H_{F}|^{2}S_{F}+|H_{d}|^{2}S_{d}}\over {|H_{s}|^{2}S_{v_{s}}}}
 \tag{12}$$

$$F=1+{{G_{F}(G_{s}+g_{m})^{2}+\gamma g_{m}(G_{s}+G_{F})^{2}}
\over {G_{s}(g_{m}-G_{F})^{2}}} \tag{13}$$

For $g_{m}>>G_{F},G_{o}$

$$F\approx 1+{{G_{F}}\over {G_{s}}}{\left(1+{{G_{s}}\over {g_{m}}}\right)^{2}
\over {\left(1-G_{F}/g_{m}\right)^{2}}}
+\gamma {{g_{m}}\over {G_{s}}}{\left(1+G_{F}/G_{s}\right)^{2}
\over {\left(g_{m}/G_{s}-G_{F}/G_{s}\right)^{2}}} \tag{14}$$

and with the matching (7), $G_{s}=g_{m}$,

$$F\approx 1+\gamma +4{{R_{s}}\over {R_{F}}}+{\cal O}\left({{R_{s}}\over
{R_{F}}}\right)^{2}+{\cal O}\left({{R_{F}}\over {r_{o}}}\right) \tag{15}$$

more generally

$$F\approx 1+{{\gamma}\over {g_{m}R_{s}}}+{{R_{s}}\over {R_{F}}}
\left(1+{{1}\over {g_{m}R_{s}}}\right)^{2}\tag{16}$$

apart from the $r_{o}$ correction.
The $R_{F}$ noise is $\propto R_{F}^{-1}$, the MOS noise
$\propto \left(g_{m}R_{s}\right)^{-1}$.

* For $r_{o}\rightarrow \infty $ $R_{in}=1/g_{m}$ is
independent of $R_{F}$.  $g_{m}$ is fixed by (7) and (16)
is monotone decreasing in $R_{F}$,

$${{\partial F}\over {\partial R_{F}}}<0\tag{17}$$

$$F_{min}\rightarrow 1+{{\gamma_{n}g_{m1}+\gamma_{p}g_{m2}}
\over {R_{s}(g_{m1}+g_{m2})^{2}}}\approx 1+\gamma \tag{18}$$

for $g_{m1}\approx g_{m2}$, $\gamma _{n}\approx \gamma _{p}
=\gamma $, i. e. $\sim 3\,{\rm dB}$ for long channel
$\gamma =1$, $4-5\,{\rm dB}$ for short channel
$\gamma =1.5-2$, for $R_{F}\rightarrow \infty $.
In practice $R_{F}$ is made as large as the gain

$$|A_{v,cl}|=\left|{{v_{y}}\over {v_{s}}}\right|
\approx {{R_{F}}\over {2R_{s}}}\tag{19}$$

and the band width allow.  $R_{F}=300-1000\Omega $ makes
$R_{s}/R_{F}=0.05-0.15$ negligible and

$$F\approx 1+\gamma +{\cal O}(R_{s}/R_{F})\tag{20}$$

is the conventional optimum.  $C_{1}$ is an a.c. short.

* For finite $r_{o}$ (5) couples $g_{m}$ and $R_{F}$.
With $ \epsilon =R_{s}/r_{o}=G_{o}/G_{s}<<1$,
$t=R_{s}/R_{F}=G_{F}/G_{s}$,

$$g_{m}=G_{s}\left[1-\epsilon +{\epsilon\over {t}}\right]\tag{21}$$

$$F=1+{{t\left(1+A\right)^{2}+\gamma A\left(1+t\right)^{2}}
\over {\left(A-t\right)^{2}}}\;\;,\;\;A=1-\epsilon +{\epsilon\over {t}}
\tag{22}$$

$F(t)$ is monotone decreasing for $0<t<1$.
$t\rightarrow 0$, $R_{F}\rightarrow \infty $,

$$F\rightarrow 1+\left(1+{\gamma\over {\epsilon}}\right)t
\rightarrow 1\tag{23}$$

$$g_{m}\rightarrow {{\epsilon}\over {t}}G_{s}={{r_{o}^{-1}R_{s}^{-1}}
\over {R_{F}^{-1}}}= {{R_{F}}\over {r_{o}R_{s}}}\rightarrow \infty \tag{24}$$

I. e. with finite $r_{o}$ the matching condition can be
kept with arbitrarily large $g_{m}$ and $R_{F}$ and

$$F\approx 1+{{G_{F}}\over {G_{s}}}+{{\gamma G_{s}}\over {g_{m}}}
\rightarrow 1\tag{25}$$

for $g_{m},R_{F}\rightarrow \infty $.

In other words the circuit has one degree of freedom
left after imposing $R_{in}=R_{s}$.  $F$ is improved by
increasing $R_{F}$ and, if $r_{o}$ is finite, increasing
$g_{m}$ with it so that (5) stays $50\Omega $.
Physically the $4kT/R_{F}$ current noise and the
$4kT\gamma g_{m}$ drain noise are divided by the
(loop) gain $\propto g_{m}R_{F}$ when referred to the
input.

Hence, for a given technology:

* use minimum $L$ for maximum $g_{m}/I_{D}$ and $f_{T}$,
* make $g_{m1}+g_{m2}$ satisfy (5), nominally $20\,{\rm mS}$,
  $W_{p}\approx (\mu _{n}/\mu _{p})W_{n}$ so that
  $g_{m1}\approx g_{m2}$ and the self biased inverter
  sits at $V_{DD}/2$ for maximum $r_{o}$ and swing,
  $\gamma _{n}g_{m1}\approx \gamma _{p}g_{m2}$ for minimum
  (18),
* make $R_{F}$ as large as possible satisfying (8).
  $R_{F}\uparrow $ $\Rightarrow $ $F\downarrow $,
  $|A_{v}|\uparrow $.

The limit is power dissipation, $I_{D}\propto g_{m}$,
and band width.  $C_{in}=C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+(1+|A_{v}|)C_{gd}$
with $R_{s}$ gives the input pole

$$f_{in}={1\over {2\pi R_{s}C_{in}}}\tag{26}$$

and $r_{o}\parallel R_{F}$ with $C_{L}+C_{gd}(1+|A_{v}|^{-1})$
gives the output pole.  Increasing $W\propto g_{m}$ increases
$C_{in}$ and $C_{L}$ and kills the band width.
For a prescribed $BW$ the optimum is the largest $W$,
largest $I_{D}$ and largest $R_{F}$ that still keeps
$f_{in},f_{out}>BW$ and $R_{in}=50\Omega $ to the required
$S_{11}<-10\,{\rm dB}$.  In a $0.13\mu $ CMOS process this is
typically $R_{F}\approx 400-800\Omega $, $g_{m}\approx
20-40\,{\rm mS}$, $I_{D}\approx 5-15\,{\rm mA}$,
$|A_{v}|\approx 6-12\,{\rm dB}$, $F\approx 2-3\,{\rm dB}$,
and $F\rightarrow 1.5\,{\rm dB}$ can be approached by
burning more current and using $R_{F}\sim 1-2\,{\rm k}$ at
the expense of $C_{in}$.

Any further improvement needs to decouple $R_{in}$ from
$F$, e. g. inductive series peaking, $g_{m}$-boosted
common gate or noise cancelling.  In simulation sweep
$W_{n},W_{p},R_{F}$ with (5) $=50\Omega $ and minimise (13).

minimax_m3.rationale: The answer identifies the shunt-feedback LNA, derives Rin and NF expressions, and recognizes finite ro couples gm and RF. However, the central design conclusion directly contradicts Razavi's key point: the answer repeatedly recommends making RF as large as possible and driving F toward 1+gamma (eqs. 17-20), explicitly stating 'make RF as large as possible satisfying (8)' and 'F→1.5 dB can be approached by burning more current and using RF~1-2k'. This is precisely the naive large-RF/infinite-ro direction that the golden solution says Razavi rejects. While there is a brief mention of finite ro lowering F below 1+gamma (eq. 25), it is presented as a limiting case with gm, RF→∞ rather than as a finite optimum achievable with reasonable sizing. The main design conclusion is wrong (opposite of Razavi's), so per rubric this is mostly incorrect despite correct background analysis.

deepseek_v4_pro.rationale: The answer derives the shunt-feedback input match and noise factor, but its optimization conclusion is the naive direction: make RF and gm as large as possible, approaching NF=1+gamma or even NF→1 with finite ro. It misses Razavi's key point that channel-length modulation and feedback jointly allow NF<1+gamma with finite output resistance, and that the optimum is not simply the large-RF/infinite-ro limit. The final recommendation to maximize RF and gm while maintaining Rin=50Ω contradicts the golden solution's central result.

answers.question: Compute the input impedance of the circuit in Figure 14(a).

answer.text:
With the usual $r_{o}\rightarrow \infty $ the forward
path can be Theveninised as in Fig.b

$${\cal A}_{0}= \left. {V_{o}\over V_{1}}\right|_{R_{F}\rightarrow
\infty }<0\qquad R_{o}=R_{D2}$$

Put a test $V_{1}$ at $P$ and put $I_{in}=0$.

$$\eqalign{
V_{x}&=-A\,V_{1}\cr
{{V_{o}-V_{1}}\over {R_{F}}}+{{V_{o}-V_{x}}\over {R_{D2}}}&=0\tag{1}\cr
I_{x}&={{V_{1}-V_{o}}\over {R_{F}}}\tag{2}}$$

for the ideal shunt feedback amplifier $Z_{i}^{o}=\infty $.
From (1)

$$V_{o}\left({1\over {R_{F}}}+{1\over {R_{D2}}}\right)
      =V_{1}{1\over {R_{F}}}+V_{x}{1\over {R_{D2}}}$$

$$V_{o}=V_{1}{{R_{D2}-AR_{F}}\over {R_{D2}+R_{F}}}\tag{3}$$

$$1-{V_{o}\over V_{1}}={{R_{F}(1+A)}\over {R_{D2}+R_{F}}}$$

and from (2)

$$R_{in}\equiv {V_{1}\over I_{x}}={R_{F}\over {1-V_{o}/V_{1}}}$$

$$\;R_{in}={R_{F}+R_{D2}\over 1+A}\;\tag{4}$$

$$A=|{\cal A}_{0}|>0\qquad {\cal A}_{0}=-A$$

For $A\gg 1$ and $R_{F}\gg R_{D2}$

$$R_{in}\approx {R_{F}\over A}\approx {R_{D2}+R_{F}\over A}\tag{5}$$

i. e. the shunt at the input is divided by the return
difference $1+A$.  In the conventional $Y$ feedback
notation $A$ is the loop gain.  With $R_{F}$ removed the
circuit is loaded only by $R_{D2}$ so that (4) is exact
for the model of Fig.b including the $R_{F}$ loading.
For $R_{F}\gg R_{D2}$ the loading can be neglected.

For Fig.a, with $r_{o}=\infty $,

$${\cal A}_{0}={{V_{o}}\over {V_{P}}}\Bigl|_{R_{F}\to \infty }
 =-g_{m1}R_{D1}{{g_{m2}g_{m3}}\over {g_{m2}+g_{m3}}}R_{D2}\tag{6}$$

For the PMOS pair $M_{2}-M_{3}$ with $V_{b}=ac\;0$

$$\eqalign{
i_{d2}&=g_{m2}(V_{S}-V_{X})\cr
i_{d3}&=g_{m3}V_{S}\cr
i_{d2}+i_{d3}&=0\;(R_{SS}\to \infty )\cr
V_{S}&={{g_{m2}}\over {g_{m2}+g_{m3}}}V_{X}\cr
i_{d3}&={{g_{m2}g_{m3}}\over {g_{m2}+g_{m3}}}V_{X}}$$

and $V_{X}=-g_{m1}R_{D1}V_{P}$.  Hence

$$|{\cal A}_{0}|=A=g_{m1}R_{D1}{{g_{m2}g_{m3}}\over
{g_{m2}+g_{m3}}}R_{D2}\tag{7}$$

For the normally matched pair $g_{m2}=g_{m3}=g_{m}$

$$\;A\approx {1\over 2}g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m}R_{D2}\;\tag{8}$$

so that from (4)

$$\;R_{in}\approx {{R_{F}+R_{D2}}\over
{1+g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m2}g_{m3}R_{D2}/(g_{m2}+g_{m3})}}
      \xrightarrow[g_{m2}=g_{m3}]{}{{R_{F}+R_{D2}}\over
{1+{1\over 2}g_{m1}g_{m}R_{D1}R_{D2}}}\; \tag{9}$$

$$\approx {R_{F}\over 1+A}\approx {2R_{F}\over g_{m1}g_{m}R_{D1}R_{D2}}
\qquad A\gg 1,\;R_{F}\gg R_{D2}$$

With finite $r_{o}$,

$$R_{D1}\to R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\qquad 
  R_{D2}\to R_{D2}\parallel r_{o3}\parallel r_{o2}\approx R_{D2}\parallel r_{o3}$$

and $g_{m}\to g_{m}+g_{mb}$ where appropriate.  To first
order the $g_{mb}$ of the matched PMOS pair cancels and
(8)-(9) remain with the $R_{D}\parallel r_{o}$ substitution,
e. g.

$$A\approx {1\over 2}g_{m1}(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1})
      g_{m}(R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o3})\tag{10}$$

In parallel with the extrinsic $C_{in}$ the impedance
seen by the source $I_{in}$ is

$$Z_{in}(s)=R_{in}\parallel {1\over sC_{in}}
        ={R_{in}\over 1+sC_{in}R_{in}}\tag{11}$$

so that at low frequencies $Z_{in}\approx R_{in}$ given by
(4),(9) and the dominant input pole is

$$\omega _{p,in}\approx {1\over R_{in}C_{in}}
      \approx {{1+A}\over {(R_{F}+R_{D2})C_{in}}}\approx
        {{A}\over {R_{F}C_{in}}}\tag{12}$$

i. e. divided by the loop gain.  Neglecting $R_{D2}$ in
(4) the familiar $R_{in}\approx R_{F}/(1+A)$,
$Z_{T}=V_{o}/I_{in}\approx -R_{F}A/(1+A)\approx -R_{F}$ for
$A\gg 1$ is recovered.  Any parasitic $C_{X}$ at $X$ and
$C_{o}$ at the output add the usual two non dominant poles
$\omega _{pX}\approx 1/R_{D1}C_{X}$,
$\omega _{po}\approx 1/R_{D2}C_{o}$ divided by the loop
gain in the closed loop response.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in Figure 15 generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
With the usual abuse of language the low frequency
noise on $V_{out}$ is {\it frequency} modulated on the
carrier. For $f_{m}<< f_{0}$ the oscillator can be
considered a quasi static $VCO$ with

$$\omega _{0}=\omega _{0}(V_{out},V_{cont})$$

$$d\omega _{0}=K_{VCO}dV_{cont}+K_{VDD}dV_{out}+...$$

$$K_{VDD}={\partial \omega _{0}\over {\partial V_{out}}}
\approx -{\omega _{0}\over {2C_{T}}}{\partial C_{T}\over
{\partial V_{out}}}\;\;{\rm r/s/V}$$

$$K_{VDD,Hz}={1\over {2\pi }}K_{VDD}\;\;{\rm Hz/V}$$

$$C_{T}=C_{B1}+C_{B2}+C_{var}(V_{X}-V_{cont})+C_{p}(V_{X})$$

is the tank capacitance at $X$ or $Y$.
E. {\rm g.} for the MOS varactor

$$C_{var}\approx {C_{0}\over {\sqrt{1+(V_{X}-V_{cont})/\Phi _{B}}}}$$

$${\partial C_{T}\over {\partial V_{out}}}\approx
{\partial C_{var}\over {\partial V_{X}}}{\partial V_{X}\over
{\partial V_{out}}}+{\partial C_{p}\over {\partial V_{X}}}
{\partial V_{X}\over {\partial V_{out}}}$$

and ${\partial V_{X}/ \partial V_{out}}\approx 1$ at
low $f_{m}$, $L_{1}$ is a short, plus the AM-PM
conversion through the $V_{out}$ dependence of the
steady state amplitude

$$A_{0}\approx {2\over {\pi }}I_{VCO}R_{p}\;\;{\rm current
limited}\tag*{$A_{0}\approx V_{out}-V_{DS,sat}\;\;{\rm voltage
limited}$}$$

and the Groszkowskii shift

$${\delta \omega \over {\omega _{0}}}\propto {1\over {Q}}
{\rm Im}\left[{I_{1}\over {I_{1,0}}}\right]$$

In practice $K_{VDD}$ is obtained from a $PSS$
${\rm sweep}$

$$K_{VDD}={\Delta f_{0}\over {\Delta V_{out}}}\Bigl|_{V_{cont}}$$

typically $10-100\,{\rm MHz/V}$ for a $n$MOS
cross coupled $LC$ with MOS varactor. It is
$f_{m}$ dependent through the impedance seen
looking into $V_{out}$

$$Z_{DD}(jf_{m})=R_{o,LDO}\parallel {1\over {jf_{m}C_{DD}}}
\parallel jf_{m}L_{1}+...$$

so that with $v_{n,LDO}(t)$ the {\it output referred}
LDO noise, ${\cal E}[v_{n}^{2}]=S_{th}(f)df$,
${\rm V^{2}/Hz}$ one sided, white for thermal noise,

$$V_{out}=V_{out0}+v_{n}(t)*h_{LDO}(t)$$

$$S_{v,DD}(f)=S_{th}(f)|H_{LDO}(jf)|^{2}|H_{DD}(jf)|^{2}$$

$$H_{LDO}(jf)\approx {1\over {1+jf/f_{p,LDO}}}$$

is the closed loop LDO transfer, $f_{p,LDO}=1/2\pi
R_{o,LDO}C_{o,LDO}$, $H_{DD}$ the supply decoupling.
For $f_{m}$ well inside the LDO loop $H_{LDO}\approx 1$.

For $f_{m}<<f_{0}$ the supply noise is quasi static
FM:

$$\omega _{inst}(t)=\omega _{0}+K_{VDD}v_{n,DD}(t)$$

$$\phi _{n}(t)=\int^{t}K_{VDD}v_{n,DD}(\tau )d\tau $$

in the frequency domain

$$S_{\omega }(f_{m})=K_{VDD}^{2}S_{v,DD}(f_{m})\;\;
{\rm (r/s)^{2}/Hz}$$

$$S_{f}(f_{m})=K_{VDD,Hz}^{2}S_{v,DD}(f_{m})\;\;{\rm Hz^{2}/Hz}$$

$$S_{\phi }(f_{m})={S_{\omega }(f_{m})\over {(2\pi f_{m})^{2}}}
={K_{VDD}^{2}S_{v,DD}(f_{m})\over {(2\pi f_{m})^{2}}}
={K_{VDD,Hz}^{2}S_{v,DD}(f_{m})\over {f_{m}^{2}}}\;\;
{\rm rad^{2}/Hz\;double\;sideband}$$

Single side band ${\cal L}$ normally quoted as
${\rm dBc/Hz}$,

$${\cal L}_{DD}(f_{m})={1\over {2}}S_{\phi }(f_{m})$$

$${\cal L}_{DD}(\Delta f)=10\log \left[
{K_{VDD}^{2}S_{th}(\Delta f)|H_{LDO}|^{2}|H_{DD}|^{2}
\over {2(2\pi \Delta f)^{2}}}\right] \tag*{{\rm r/s/V}}$$

$$=10\log \left[
{K_{VDD,Hz}^{2}S_{th}(\Delta f)|H_{LDO}|^{2}|H_{DD}|^{2}
\over {2\Delta f^{2}}}\right] \tag*{{\rm Hz/V}}$$

For white $S_{th}=S_{0}={\rm const.}$

$${\cal L}_{DD}\propto {1\over {\Delta f^{2}}}\;\; -20{\rm dB/dec}$$

to be added power wise to the intrinsic $VCO$
${\cal L}_{VCO}$,

$$S_{\phi ,tot}=S_{\phi ,VCO}+S_{\phi ,DD}$$

In Hajimiri language $S_{\phi ,DD}=
\Gamma _{dc,DD}^{2}S_{v,DD}/2\Delta f^{2}q_{max}^{2}$
with $\Gamma _{dc,DD}$ the dc value of the ISF for a
common mode supply injection, $\Gamma _{dc,DD}\propto
K_{VDD}$.

In a simulator: $PSS+PAC$ inject a small $ac$ source
in series with $V_{out}$, measure $PM$ sideband
$H_{PM}(jf_{m})= \phi _{n}/v_{n}$ and

$${\cal L}_{DD}=10\log \left[{S_{th}|H_{PM}|^{2}\over {2}}\right]$$

which for $f_{m}<<f_{0}$ reduces to $|H_{PM}|\approx
K_{VDD}/2\pi f_{m}$. High frequency $S_{th}$ around
$f_{0}\pm f_{m}$ and $2f_{0}\pm f_{m}$ is normally
filtered by $C_{DD}$ and contributes only through
mixing with the second harmonic, ${\cal O}(1/Q)$.

E. {\rm g.} $S_{th}^{1/2}=10\,{\rm nV/\sqrt{Hz}}$,
$K_{VDD,Hz}=50\,{\rm MHz/V}$, $|H|=1$,

$${\cal L}_{DD}(1\,{\rm MHz})\approx
10\log \left[{(5\times 10^{7})^{2}\times 10^{-16}\over
{2\times 10^{12}}}\right]\approx -86\,{\rm dBc/Hz}$$

white, $-20\,{\rm dB/dec}$ until the LDO pole
$f_{p,LDO}$ where it rolls off as $1/f_{m}^{4}$.

Any low pass filtering on $V_{out}$, $C_{DD}\gg
1/2\pi R_{o,LDO}f_{m}$, and minimisation of
$K_{VDD}$ - differential varactor biasing, separate
quiet varactor supply, low $K_{VCO}$ design - reduces
the conversion. Formally it is the supply pushing
figure of merit.

minimax_m3.rationale: The candidate answer correctly identifies supply pushing (K_VDD) as the mechanism, converts LDO thermal noise S_th to frequency deviation through K_push, and applies FM-to-PM conversion yielding a 1/Delta f^2 dependence with the standard -20 dB/dec rolloff. It also notes the design insight that reducing K_VDD reduces this noise conversion. The answer is more detailed than the golden solution, covering LDO transfer function, decoupling, Hajimiri ISF formalism, and simulation methodology, but these are all consistent with and go beyond the essential answer. The proportionality and trend are correct, and the final conclusion aligns with the golden solution's central result.

It also notes the design insight that K_VDD is related to varactor sensitivity and reducing it lowers noise conversion. Minor extra details (AM-PM, ISF, simulation methods) are secondary and do not contradict the golden solution.

answers.question: We add CT to the tail node, as in Figure 16. What happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
With the usual abuse of language the circuit is the
{\it Hegazi} {\it et al.} tail filtered circuit,
{\tt JSSC 12/01}.  For the {\it differential} mode

$${\cal P}\equiv {\rm ac\; ground}$$

so that to first order $C_{T}$ does nothing.  For the
common mode, Fig.16b, $L_{1}\parallel L_{2}=L/2$ to
${\rm ac}$ ground, $M_{1}\parallel M_{2}$ and

$$Z_{P}(s)=r_{o}\parallel {1\over sC_{T}}\parallel
{1\over g_{m1}+g_{m2}+sC_{P}} \tag{1}$$

is the impedance seen at the common source node.
In the normal cross coupled oscillator

$$v_{P}(t)=V_{P0}+V_{P2}\cos 2\omega _{0}t+\cdots \tag{2}$$

is a full wave rectified sine at $2\omega _{0}$.
The tail device noise $i_{n,SS}$ produces

$$v_{nP}=i_{n,SS}Z_{P}(s) \tag{3}$$

and is commutated by the $M_{1}-M_{2}$ current
switch to the drains.  In Hajimiri language the
impulse sensitivity function of the tail is

$$\Gamma _{P}(t)=\Gamma _{P0}+\Gamma _{P2}\cos 2\omega _{0}t
+\cdots \tag{4}$$

$\Gamma _{P0}\ne 0$ only while the two sides are
simultaneously on, i. e. during the zero crossing of
$v_{X}-v_{Y}$.  The effective ISF for the tail is

$$\Gamma _{{\rm eff},P}= \Gamma _{P}(t)\,
\alpha (t)\qquad \alpha =g_{m}Z_{P} \tag{5}$$

so that, e. g. for white tail noise

$${\cal L}(\Delta \omega )\propto 
{{i_{n,SS}^{2}\over \Delta f}\,
\Gamma _{{\rm eff},P,rms}^{2}\over \Delta \omega ^{2}} \tag{6}$$

and for $1/f$ tail noise

$${\cal L}_{1/f^{3}}(\Delta \omega )\propto 
{{i_{n,SS,1/f}^{2}\over \Delta f}\,
\Gamma _{{\rm eff},P,0}^{2}\over \Delta \omega ^{3}} \tag{7}$$

where $\Gamma _{{\rm eff},P,0}$ is the $0$th Fourier
coefficient of (5).  Normally

$$|Z_{P}(2\omega _{0})|\approx {1\over g_{m}}\;\;{\rm to}\;\;
r_{o}\tag{8}$$

so that $\alpha (2\omega _{0})\approx 1$ and the
$2\omega _{0}$ tail noise is mixed with the
$2\omega _{0}$ component of $\Gamma _{P}$ to
$\Delta \omega $ and the low frequency $1/f$ tail
noise is mixed with the $2\omega _{0}$ component of
$\Gamma _{P}$ to $2\omega _{0}\pm \Delta \omega $
and then to $\omega _{0}\pm \Delta \omega $.

Putting $C_{T}$ from ${\cal P}$ to ground,

$$Z_{P}(s)\rightarrow Z_{P}(s)\parallel {1\over sC_{T}} \tag{9}$$

so that at $2\omega _{0}$

$$|Z_{P}(2\omega _{0})|\approx {1\over 2\omega _{0}C_{T}}
\qquad 2\omega _{0}C_{T}\gg g_{m} \tag{10}$$

and

$$\alpha (2\omega _{0})\approx {1\over 2\omega _{0}C_{T}r_{o}}
\ll 1 \tag{11}$$

is shorted to ground.  In the limit $C_{T}\to \infty $
${\cal P}$ is ${\rm ac}$ ground at $2\omega _{0}$
and at all the even harmonics.  The $2\omega _{0}$
current of the differential pair circulates in
$M_{1}-M_{2}-C_{T}$ and does not go through
$I_{SS}$.  Formally $\Gamma _{{\rm eff},P}\to 0$.

In particular the $0$th coefficient $\Gamma _{{\rm eff},0}$
which controls the $1/f\to 1/f^{3}$ up conversion can be
made nominally zero by making the differential waveform
symmetric.  With $Z_{P}(2\omega _{0})=0$ the Groszkowski
frequency shift

$${\Delta \omega \over \omega _{0}}\propto 
{{1\over Q}{\rm Im}\{Z_{P}(2\omega _{0})\}\over {\rm Re}\{Z_{tank}\}}$$

vanishes, the rise and fall times become symmetric and
$\Gamma _{0}\to 0$.  This is normally quoted as a
$5-10\,{\rm dB}$ reduction of the $1/f^{3}$ phase noise
corner and $2-4\,{\rm dB}$ reduction of the $1/f^{2}$
{\it thermal} phase noise due to $I_{SS}$,

$${\cal L}_{SS}\propto \left|{Z_{P}(2\omega _{0})
\over Z_{P}(2\omega _{0})+1/g_{m}}\right|^{2}
\approx {1\over \left(2\omega _{0}C_{T}/g_{m}\right)^{2}}\tag{12}$$

for $2\omega _{0}C_{T}\gg g_{m}$.  The $kT/C_{T}$
noise is common mode and to first order does not appear
differentially.  $C_{T}$ is normally chosen so that

$$2\omega _{0}C_{T}\gg g_{m}\tag{13}$$

i. e. $C_{T}\gg C_{P,par}$ and

$$\omega _{p}={g_{m}\over C_{T}}\ll \omega _{0}\tag{14}$$

so that it is an ${\rm ac}$ ground at $2\omega _{0}$
but still open at $\Delta \omega $ in the $1/f$ band.
It does {\it not} filter the $1/f$ noise itself; it
filters the {\it conversion gain} at $2\omega _{0}$.

In its more sophisticated form a small inductor
$L_{T}$ is put in series with $I_{SS}$ so that

$$\omega _{CM}={1\over \sqrt{L_{T}C_{T}}}=2\omega _{0}\tag{15}$$

with $L_{T}$ the $L_{1}\parallel L_{2}$ common mode
inductance if no explicit $L_{T}$ is used.  Then
$Z_{P}(2\omega _{0})\to \infty $ and the differential
pair does not load the tank at $2\omega _{0}$, the
tank $Q$ at $2\omega _{0}$ is preserved and the
symmetry is optimum.  That is the conventional
``tail filtering'' optimum.

> {\it Remark:}  If (13) is not satisfied $C_{T}$
> resonates with $L_{1}\parallel L_{2}$ and with
> $C_{P}$ at
> $$\omega _{CM}\approx {1\over \sqrt{(L/2)C_{T}}}$$
> close to $\omega _{0}$ or $2\omega _{0}$.  $|Z_{P}|$
> then peaks, $\alpha \to >1$, the common mode loop
> can even oscillate, the waveform becomes very
> asymmetric, the Groszkowski shift becomes large and
> the AM-PM conversion through the $C_{gs}-C_{gd}$
> non linearity makes the close in phase noise {\it
> larger} than without $C_{T}$ and can produce
> squegging.  With $C_{T}$ very large the low
> frequency pole (14) gives the bias a long memory and
> any AM-PM will convert amplitude relaxation into
> phase noise.  In practice $C_{T}$ must be $\gg
> C_{P,par}$ but not so large that $\omega _{p}$ falls
> in the PLL band.  With optimum $C_{T}$, or $L_{T}C_{T}$
> tuned to $2\omega _{0}$, the Hegazi experiment shows
> $\sim 8\,{\rm dB}$ improvement at $1\,{\rm MHz}$
> offset and more than $10\,{\rm dB}$ lowering of the
> $1/f^{3}$ corner.  With non optimum $C_{T}$ the
> phase noise can be degraded by the same amount.

answers.question: Estimate the oscillation frequency of the circuit in Figure 17.

answer.text:
With the usual abuse of language the {\it tank}
resonance

$${\omega _{T}^{2}={1\over {L{C_{T}}}} \qquad 
f_{T}={1\over {2\pi \sqrt{L{C_{T}}}}}\tag{1}}$$

is quoted.  ${C_{T}}$ is the total shunt $C$ on the
$X_{1}\equiv -Y_{1}$ $\left( X_{2}\equiv -Y_{2}\right) $ node,

$${C_{T}}=C+{C_{{\rm par}}}\tag{2}$$

$C$ the normally explicit tank $C$ and

$${C_{{\rm par}}}\approx \sum {{C_{gs}}+{C_{gd}}+{C_{db}}+{C_{L}}}$$

of the four devices that hang on the node plus the
self capacitance of the coil.  For a normal design the
explicit $C\gg {C_{{\rm par}}}$ and (1) is normally
written simply as ${\omega _{0}}=1/\sqrt{LC}$.

Put

$${V_{1}}={X_{1}}-{Y_{1}}\qquad {V_{2}}={X_{2}}-{Y_{2}} \tag{3}$$

and let ${G_{m0}}={g_{m}}({I_{SS}}/2)$ be the small signal
${g_{m}}$ of one side of the ordinary ${\rm X}$ coupled
pair and ${G_{m1}}={g_{m}}({I_{1}}/2)$ the ${g_{m}}$ of one
side of the coupling pair.  For the differential signal
the ordinary pair puts

$${I_{0}}=-{G_{m0}}{V_{1}}\tag{4}$$

in parallel with the tank and the coupling pair puts

$${I_{c}}=\pm {G_{m1}}{V_{2}}\tag{5}$$

in parallel with the tank, the sign depending on whether
the gates are taken straight, ${X_{2}}\to {X_{1}}$,
${Y_{2}}\to {Y_{1}}$, or crossed, ${X_{2}}\to {Y_{1}}$,
${Y_{2}}\to {X_{1}}$.  With

$${Y_{T}}(\omega )={1\over {{R_{p}}}}+j\left( \omega {C_{T}}-
{1\over {\omega L}}\right) ={1\over {Z_{T}(\omega )}} \tag{6}$$

${R_{p}}$ the parallel loss of the coil and of the
devices, KCL on the two tanks is, in phasor notation,

$$\eqalign{
\left[{Y_{T}}-{G_{m0}}\right]{V_{1}}\pm {G_{m1}}{V_{2}}&=0\cr
\mp {G_{m1}}{V_{1}}+\left[{Y_{T}}-{G_{m0}}\right]{V_{2}}&=0\cr}
\tag{7}$$

the upper sign for straight coupling, the lower sign for
crossed coupling.  In compact form

$$\left[{Y_{T}}-{G_{m0}}\right]=\mp j{G_{m1}}\tag{8}$$

for the conventional quadrature connection, one side
straight, one side crossed, and

$$\left[{Y_{T}}-{G_{m0}}\right]=\mp {G_{m1}}\tag{9}$$

for the completely symmetric, as drawn, connection.
(8) is the $90^{{\rm o}}$ coupled case, (9) the
$0^{{\rm o}}-180^{{\rm o}}$ coupled case.  From (6)-(8)

$${1\over {{R_{p}}}}={G_{m0}}\tag{10}$$

is the usual start up condition, ${G_{m0}}{R_{p}}>1$, and

$$\omega {C_{T}}-{1\over {\omega L}}=\pm {G_{m1}}\tag{11}$$

is the frequency condition for the quadrature mode.
I. e. the two mathematical oscillation modes are

$${\omega _{{\rm osc}}}^{2}L{C_{T}}\mp {G_{m1}}L{\omega _{{\rm osc}}}-1=0\tag{12}$$

$${\omega _{{\rm osc}}}={{\pm {G_{m1}}L+\sqrt{{G_{m1}}^{2}{L^{2}}+
4L{C_{T}}}}\over {2L{C_{T}}}}\tag{13}$$

For ${G_{m1}}\to 0$

$${\omega _{{\rm osc}}}\to {\omega _{T}}={1\over {\sqrt{L{C_{T}}}}}\tag{14}$$

and for ${G_{m1}}L{\omega _{T}}\ll 1$, i. e. weak coupling,

$${\omega _{{\rm osc}}}\approx {\omega _{T}}\pm {{{G_{m1}}}
\over {2{C_{T}}}}={\omega _{T}}\left[1\pm {{{G_{m1}}}\over
{2{G_{m0}}}}{1\over Q}\right]\tag{15}$$

where

$$Q={R_{p}}{\omega _{T}}{C_{T}}={{R_{p}}\over {{\omega _{T}}L}}\tag{16}$$

is the loaded $Q$ of the tank.  With a square law
${G_{m}}\propto \sqrt{WI}$,

$${{{G_{m1}}}\over {{G_{m0}}}}=\sqrt{{{W_{1}}{I_{1}}\over
{{W_{0}}{I_{SS}}}}}\tag{17}$$

so that, e. g. for ${W_{1}}={W_{0}}$,

$${\omega _{{\rm osc}}}\approx {\omega _{T}}\pm
{\omega _{T}}{1\over {2Q}}\sqrt{{I_{1}}\over {I_{SS}}}\tag{18}$$

and, to ${\cal O}({G_{m1}}/{G_{m0}})$,

$${\omega _{{\rm osc}}}\approx {\omega _{T}}
\sqrt{1\pm {{{G_{m1}}}\over {{G_{m0}}}}}\approx
{\omega _{T}}\sqrt{1\pm \sqrt{{I_{1}}\over {I_{SS}}}}\tag{19}$$

is often quoted.  For the usual $Q\approx 5-10$ and
${I_{1}}\approx (1/4-1/3){I_{SS}}$ this is a $2-5\%$
correction to (1).  To within that correction the
normal text book estimate

$$f_{{\rm osc}}\approx {f_{T}}={1\over {2\pi \sqrt{L{C_{T}}}}}
\approx {1\over {2\pi \sqrt{LC}}}\tag{20}$$

is quoted as the oscillation frequency.  The $+$ sign in
(11)-(13) is the $0^{{\rm o}}$ quadrature mode,
${V_{2}}=j{V_{1}}$, i. e.

$${X_{1}}={V_{0}}\cos {\omega _{{\rm osc}}}t\qquad
{Y_{1}}=-{V_{0}}\cos {\omega _{{\rm osc}}}t\tag{21}$$
$${X_{2}}={V_{0}}\sin {\omega _{{\rm osc}}}t\qquad
{Y_{2}}=-{V_{0}}\sin {\omega _{{\rm osc}}}t\tag{22}$$

the $-$ sign the opposite quadrature mode,
${V_{2}}=-j{V_{1}}$.  Which one is stable depends on the
non linearities.

For the completely symmetric connection as literally drawn
in Fig. 17 Eq. 8 is replaced by Eq. 9, i. e.

$${1\over {{R_{p}}}}={G_{m0}}\pm {G_{m1}}\qquad 
\omega {C_{T}}-{1\over {\omega L}}=0\tag{23}$$

so that to first order the frequency stays at the tank
resonance (1), (14), (20).  The two mathematical solutions
are the in phase mode ${V_{1}}={V_{2}}$,
${G_{m0}}+{G_{m1}}={R_{p}}^{-1}$, and the anti phase mode
${V_{1}}=-{V_{2}}$, ${G_{m0}}-{G_{m1}}={R_{p}}^{-1}$.
Crossing one and only one of the two couplings changes
(9) into (8) and gives the quadrature $90^{{\rm o}}$
operation (11)-(15) with the familiar
${\omega _{{\rm osc}}}={\omega _{T}}\pm {G_{m1}}/2{C_{T}}$
pulling.  In either case the hand estimate (20), (1) is
normally adequate, the pulling (15) being a small
fraction of ${\omega _{T}}$ for weak coupling,
${G_{m1}}\ll {G_{m0}}$, ${I_{1}}\ll {I_{SS}}$.

> {\it Remark:}  With ${C_{T}}\approx C$ Eq. 20 is often
> written simply as ${\omega _{{\rm osc}}}\approx
> 1/\sqrt{LC}$.  Any explicit factor $2$ that appears in
> some texts, e. g. ${\omega _{{\rm osc}}}\approx
> 1/\sqrt{2LC}$ or $\sqrt{2}/\sqrt{LC}$, is just the
> $L\parallel L=L/2$ or $C\parallel C=2C$ counting of the
> two tanks when they are lumped together.

minimax_m3.rationale: The answer correctly identifies the tank resonance ω₀ = 1/√(LC_T) as the starting point, derives the coupling-induced frequency shift Δω ≈ ±G_m1/(2C_T) = ω_T · (G_m1/G_m0)/(2Q) (eq. 15), and relates the coupling coefficient to √(I_1/I_SS) for large-signal operation (eqs. 17-18), matching the golden solution's Δω = αω₀/(2Q) with α ≈ gmc/gm1 or I1/ISS. The edge-of-oscillation warning is also present (eq. 10). Sign ambiguity and small notation differences are explicitly allowed as secondary.

It correctly identifies the tank term and the coupling-shift term, includes the edge-of-oscillation warning, and handles the sign as dependent on coupling orientation. The derivation is detailed and consistent with the golden solution.

answers.question: If we double the length and width of a MOSFET, what happens to its intrinsic gain?

answer.text:
With channel length modulation the
{\it low frequency} small signal voltage gain of
the common source is

$$A_{0}=g_{m}r_{o}=g_{m}/g_{ds}\approx {2V_{A}\over V_{ov}}
\approx {2\over \lambda V_{ov}} \approx \sqrt{{W\over L}{2\mu C_{ox}\over \lambda^{2}I_{D}}}$$

$$V_{A}=1/\lambda \propto L\qquad 
g_{ds}= \lambda I_{D}\propto I_{D}/L$$

$$g_{m}= {2I_{D}\over V_{ov}}=
\mu C_{ox}{W\over L}V_{ov}= \sqrt{2\mu C_{ox}{W\over L}I_{D}}$$

in strong inversion long channel, 

$$g_{m}r_{o}\propto {L\over V_{ov}}\propto \sqrt{{WL\over I_{D}}}$$

in weak inversion $g_{m}=I_{D}/nV_{T}$ so

$$g_{m}r_{o}=V_{A}/nV_{T}\propto L$$

independent of $W,I_{D}$.

So to first order $W/L={\rm const}$ is {\it not}
constant $A_{0}$.

* {\it At constant $V_{ov}\;\;{\rm or}\;\;g_{m}/I_{D}$ or constant $I_{D}$:}

$$I_{D}\propto {W\over L}V_{ov}^{2}={\rm const}$$

$$g_{m}\propto {W\over L}V_{ov}={\rm const}$$

$$r_{o}=1/\lambda I_{D}\propto L$$

> $$A_{0}\propto L\propto \sqrt{WL}$$

Doubling $W$ and $L$ together, $W/L\to W/L$,
$I_{D},V_{ov},g_{m}=$ const, $V_{A}$ and $r_{o}\to 2r_{o}$

> $$A_{0}\to 2A_{0}\;\;{\rm about +6dB}$$

in weak inversion exactly $2\times$, in strong
inversion long channel exactly $2\times$.

Formally $A_{0}\propto \sqrt{WL}$ at constant $I_{D}$,
so $2W\times 2L \to \sqrt{4}A_{0}=2A_{0}$.

In particular doubling $L$ alone doubles $A_{0}$,
doubling $W$ alone at constant $I_{D}$ goes as
$\sqrt{W}$.

If you re-bias to constant current {\it density}
$J=I_{D}/W$ or constant $I_{D}/W$ normally used to
keep $f_{T}$ and $V_{ov}$ constant, $I_{D}\propto W$,

$$A_{0}\propto \sqrt{{L\over J}}\propto \sqrt{L}$$

at constant $J$, so $2L\to \sqrt{2}A_{0}\approx +3{\rm dB}$.
With $2W$ and $2L$ and $I_{D}\to 2I_{D}$:

$$A_{0}\to \sqrt{2}A_{0}$$

at constant $J$.

> {\it Remark:} In velocity saturation $g_{m}\approx
W C_{ox}v_{sat}\propto W$ independent of $L$, so
> $$A_{0}\propto {WL\over I_{D}}$$
> at constant $I_{D}$ $2W\times 2L\to 4A_{0}$, at
> constant $J$ or constant $V_{ov}$, $I_{D}\propto W$,
> $A_{0}\propto L\to 2A_{0}$.

In a modern short channel the $\lambda\propto 1/L$
law is degraded by DIBL, $V_{A}$ is sub-linear in $L$,
so you get typically $1.3-1.8\times$ for $2L$ in
practice, $\sim 1.5-2.5\times$ for $2W\times 2L$ at
constant $I_{D}$.

Neglecting $\lambda$ altogether $r_{o}\to \infty$ and
$A_{0}\to \infty$ is often quoted as ``no change''.

You pay for it in area $\propto WL\to 4\times$,
gate capacitance $C_{gg}\approx WLC_{ox}\to 4\times$,
so at constant $g_{m}$

$$f_{T}=g_{m}/2\pi C_{gg}\propto 1/WL\to f_{T}/4$$

and self loaded $g_{m}/C_{gg}$ bandwidth.

The final conclusion matches the golden solution: intrinsic gain approximately doubles. The answer also correctly notes the dependence on bias conditions, matching the golden solution's caveat. The extensive additional analysis (weak inversion, velocity saturation, constant current density) goes beyond the question but is correct and does not contradict the essential answer.

answers.question: Student A says the transconductance of a MOSFET goes up as the overdrive voltage increases. Student B says it goes down. Who is correct?

answer.text:
With a qualification the square law in
strong inversion saturation is

$${\rm with}\;\;V_{ov}=V_{GS}-V_{T}$$

$$I_{D}={\tfrac{1}{2}}\mu C_{ox}{W\over L}V_{ov}^{2}\tag{1}$$

$$g_{m}\equiv {\partial I_{D}\over \partial V_{GS}}
      =\mu C_{ox}{W\over L}V_{ov}
      =\sqrt{2\mu C_{ox}{W\over L}I_{D}}={2I_{D}\over V_{ov}} \tag{2}$$

so that $g_{m}/I_{D}=2/V_{ov}$ {\it decreases}} with
$V_{ov}$.

* {\it For the device,} i. e. for given $W/L$,
Eq.2 is $g_{m}\propto V_{ov}$.  If you just turn up
$V_{GS}$ on that device $I_{D}\propto V_{ov}^{2}$ and
$g_{m}\propto V_{ov}$ goes {\it up}} linearly with $V_{ov}$
until velocity saturation sets in and

$$g_{m}\rightarrow WC_{ox}v_{sat}={\rm const.}$$

In weak inversion $g_{m}=I_{D}/nV_{T}$ is independent of
$V_{ov}$ to first order. In that conventional
device physics sense {\bf A} is right.

* {\it For the circuit,} i. e. for given bias current
$I_{D}=$ const. fixed by power dissipation, noise etc.,
Eq.2 is normally written in the third form,
$g_{m}=2I_{D}/V_{ov}\propto 1/V_{ov}$.  To increase
$V_{ov}$ at constant $I_{D}$ you have to {\it shrink}
the device, $W/L\propto 1/V_{ov}^{2}$, and the
available $g_{m}$ goes {\it down}} as $1/V_{ov}$.
In that very common analog design language {\bf B}
is what is meant by ``$g_{m}$ goes down with overdrive'',
more properly $g_{m}/I_{D}$ goes down with overdrive.

> {\it Remark:} In most text books the second form is
> quoted as ``$g_{m}$ is inversely proportional to
> $V_{ov}$'' with $I_{D}=$ const. understood.

With $I_{D}$ understood constant B is the intended
answer. Without that qualification A is the literal
device answer.

minimax_m3.rationale: The candidate answer correctly derives all three forms of gm, explicitly identifies that Student A is correct for fixed W/L and Student B is correct for fixed ID, and notes the velocity saturation limit. This fully matches the golden solution's central conclusion that both statements can be true depending on what is held fixed, with the usual interpretation being fixed device size.

deepseek_v4_pro.rationale: The answer correctly explains that both students can be right depending on whether W/L or ID is held fixed, matches the golden solution's central result, and includes the standard fixed-device interpretation. It also adds valid secondary details (velocity saturation, weak inversion, gm/ID) without contradicting the essential answer.

answers.question: Is the small-signal model of a PMOS device identical to that of an NMOS device?

answer.text:
In AC sense yes, topologically and
analytically identical.

The linearization does not know if the
carrier is $e^{-}$ or $h^{+}$. With

$$I_{D,n}= \frac12 k_{n}(V_{GS}-V_{Tn})^{2}(1+\lambda_{n}V_{DS})$$
$$I_{D,p}= \frac12 k_{p}(V_{SG}-|V_{Tp}|)^{2}(1+\lambda_{p}V_{SD})$$

$$k = \mu C_{ox}W/L$$

linearization about the $Q$ point:

$$g_{m}= \left.\frac{\partial I_{D}}{\partial V_{GS}}\right|_{Q}
      =\left.\frac{\partial I_{D}}{\partial V_{SG}}\right|_{Q}
      =\sqrt{2kI_{D}} = \frac{2I_{D}}{V_{ov}}$$

$$g_{mb}= \left.\frac{\partial I_{D}}{\partial V_{BS}}\right|_{Q}
       =\chi g_{m}$$

$$g_{ds}=r_{o}^{-1}= \left.\frac{\partial I_{D}}{\partial V_{DS}}\right|_{Q}
       =\left.\frac{\partial I_{D}}{\partial V_{SD}}\right|_{Q}
       \approx \lambda I_{D}$$

$$i_{d}= g_{m}v_{gs}+g_{mb}v_{bs}+g_{ds}v_{ds}\;\;{\rm NMOS}$$
$$i_{d}= g_{m}v_{sg}+g_{mb}v_{sb}+g_{ds}v_{sd}\;\;{\rm PMOS}$$

for $i_{d}$ defined in the direction of DC bias
current, $D\to S$ for NMOS, $S\to D$ for PMOS.

If you keep the conventional reference polarities
with all terminal currents {\it entering} the device
and $v_{gs},v_{ds}$ positive at the gate/drain
with respect to source, then formally

$$i_{d,p}= -g_{m}v_{gs}-g_{mb}v_{bs}-g_{ds}v_{ds}$$

i.e. the same network with $g_{m}\to -g_{m}$.

Normally we remove the minus sign by defining
for PMOS $v_{sg}=-v_{gs}>0$, $v_{sd}=-v_{ds}>0$
and $i_{sd}=-i_{ds}>0$ flowing from source to drain.

With that convention the low frequency hybrid-$\pi$
and $T$ and high frequency model $C_{gs},C_{gd},
C_{gb},C_{sb},C_{db}$ are indistinguishable:

```
NMOS:                     PMOS with vsg,vsd:

  G o----                  G o----
       |                       |
      vgs                     vsg
       |                       |
  S o--+--o D             S o--+--o D
       |  |                    |  |
      ro gm*vgs              ro gm*vsg
       |  |  S->D is up        |  |
  S o--+--o D             S o--+--o D
       |                       |
      vbs/gmb*vbs             vsb/gmb*vsb
       |                       |
  B o--                       B o--
```

Turn the PMOS upside down, $S$ on top at AC ground
$V_{DD}$, $D$ at bottom, and it looks exactly like
an NMOS $S$ on bottom at AC ground $GND$.

In particular for $B$ tied to $S$, AC ground, the
familiar simplified model is identical:

$$i_{d}=g_{m}v_{gs}+g_{ds}v_{ds}$$

with $v_{gs}\to v_{sg}$ for PMOS.

The only difference is DC: $V_{SG}>|V_{Tp}|$,
$V_{SD}>V_{SG}-|V_{Tp}|$ for saturation, current
flows out of the source, and for the same $W/L$

answer.text:
With the conventional enhancement notation the
3 terminal symbol is the ${\rm body}={\rm source}$
symbol so that the arrow is on the source.
In the conventional ${\rm N}{\rm MOS}$ notation the
upper terminal is the source, the lower terminal the
drain.  In the small signal sense put $v_{g}=v_{d}=0$
and look into the source.  E. {\it g.} for the
${\rm N}{\rm MOS}$

$${\rm N}{\rm MOS}: \qquad V_{GS}=V_{G}-V_{S}=-V_{S}\tag
*$$

so that with $V_{G}=0$ the device is cut off for
$V_{S}>0$ and for $V_{S}<0$

$$I_{X}=-I_{D}=-{1\over 2}\mu _{n}C_{ox}{W\over L}
\left( V_{GS}-V_{T}\right)^{2}\left( 1+\lambda V_{DS}
\right) \tag{**}$$

is the normal active current with the source and the
drain interchanged.  In the small signal sense

$$v_{x}= -v_{gs}\qquad i_{x}=-i_{d}=-
\left( g_{m}v_{gs}+g_{mb}v_{bs}+g_{ds}v_{ds}\right) $$

with $v_{g}=0$, $v_{d}=0$, $v_{s}=v_{x}$, $v_{b}=0$,

$$i_{x}= \left( g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}\right)v_{x}$$

$${{v_{x}}\over {i_{x}}}= {1\over {g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}}}
\approx {1\over {g_{m}}}\;{\rm  \ll }\;r_{0}\tag{***}$$

i. {\it e.} the familiar diode connected common gate
with the drain at a.c. ground.  In the conventional
drain output notation the upper terminal is the drain,
the lower the ${\rm grounded}$ source and

$$V_{GS}=0\tag{\dagger}$$

so that for the conventional enhancement device the
device is cut off,

$$I_{X}=I_{D}=0\qquad {\rm to\; }O\left( \lambda \right) $$

and, if you want to call cut off a current source, a
$0$ current current source whose small signal
impedance is $r_{0}$ but whose large signal current is
zero.  Normally the circuit is said {\it not} to be a
current source.  If you force a ${\rm d.c.}$ current
$I_{X}$ into the source, {\it cf.} $(*)$--$(**)$, the
device will go to the edge of saturation,
$V_{DS}=V_{GS}$, and $(***)$ is normally referred to as
a {\it very bad} current source, a diode connected
load of impedance $1/g_{m}$ to ground.  With
$r_{0}\rightarrow \infty $ it is not a current source
at all in the $r_{0}$ sense.

In the ${\rm PMOS}$ notation the same remark with
$S\leftrightarrow D$, $V_{SG}=-V_{GS}$, {\it etc.}
For $V_{SG}=0$ the ${\rm PMOS}$ is cut off; with
current forced into the ${\rm PMOS}$ source the source
will rise to $V_{SG}>|V_{T}|$ and the device will
saturate with $V_{SD}=V_{SG}$, {\it i. e.} on the edge
of saturation, and present the low impedance $(***)$ at
the source.  It is sometimes loosely called a
${\rm PMOS}$ diode connected current source of current
given by $(**)$ with $\mu _{p},|V_{T}|$ but of
parallel impedance $1/(g_{m}+g_{mb})||r_{0}\approx
1/g_{m}$.

> {\it Remark:} For a depletion device $V_{T}<0$,
> ${\rm N}{\rm MOS}$, $V_{T}>0$, ${\rm PMOS}$, $(**)$
> with $V_{GS}=0$ does give the normal
> $I_{DSS}=({1}/{2})\mu C_{ox}(W/L)V_{T}^{2}$ current
> source at high impedance $r_{0}$ looking into the
> drain, $V_{G}=V_{S}=0$.

v_{sb}&=v_{s}-v_{b}\cr

i_{sd}=-v_{s}/R_{S}\tag{2a}$$

i_{sd}=v_{out}/R_{D}\tag{2b}$$

so that in small signal

apart from $r_{o}$ which is already in (1).  More

+{{g_{mb}R_{S}}\over {R_{D}}}+{{R_{S}+R_{D}}\over {R_{D}r_{o}}}\right]
=-g_{m}v_{in}$$

$$\;A_{v}\equiv {{v_{out}}\over {v_{in}}}=
-{{g_{m}R_{D}}\over {1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})R_{S}+{{R_{S}+R_{D}}\over {r_{o}}}}\; \tag{5}$$

For $r_{o}\gg R_{S},R_{D}$

$$G_{m,eff}={{g_{m}}\over {1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})R_{S}}}\tag{8}$$

is the degenerated transconductance.  For
$g_{m}R_{S}\gg 1$

$$A_{v}\rightarrow -{{R_{D}}\over {R_{S}}}\;{1\over {1+g_{mb}/g_{m}}}$$

independent of $g_{m}$, linearised by series feedback.

$$A_{v0}=-g_{m}\left(R_{D}\parallel r_{o}\right)\approx -g_{m}R_{D}$$

the normal $CS$ gain, inverting.

With test source $v_{x}$ at $d$, $v_{g}=0$,

$${{v_{s}}\over {R_{S}}}+{{v_{s}-v_{x}}\over {r_{o}}}+g_{m}v_{s}

Enhancement $NMOS$, $V_{T}=V_{T0}>0$.

$$I_{D}= \frac{k_{n}}{2}\left(V_{GS}-V_{T}\right)^{2}
\left(1+\lambda V_{DS}\right)\;\;{\rm sat.}$$

$$V_{DS}\ge V_{GS}-V_{T}=V_{ov}$$

So once on the device stays in saturation until

$$0\le V_{out}\le V_{DD}-V_{ov}$$

```
      |
  +---+
  |  M1  g_m v_gs + g_mb v_bs + g_ds v_ds
v_in G---+
         S---+--- v_out
             |   |
             R_S C_L
             |   |
            gnd gnd
```

$$v_{gs}=v_{in}-v_{out}$$
$$v_{bs}= \begin{cases}0 & {\rm body\;to\;source}\\ -v_{out} & {\rm body\;to\;gnd}\end{cases}$$
$$v_{ds}= -v_{out}$$

KCL at output node:

$$g_{m}v_{gs}+g_{mb}v_{bs}+g_{ds}v_{ds}= \frac{v_{out}}{R_{S}}$$

$$g_{m}(v_{in}-v_{out})-g_{mb}v_{out}-g_{ds}v_{out}=v_{out}/R_{S}$$

for body to $GND$. For body to source put $g_{mb}=0$.

$$\;A_{v}\equiv \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
\frac{g_{m}}{g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}+R_{S}^{-1}}\;$$

With $r_{o}=1/g_{ds}$:

$$A_{v}= \frac{g_{m}(r_{o}\parallel R_{S})}
{1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})(r_{o}\parallel R_{S})}$$

No body effect:

$$\;A_{v0}= \frac{g_{m}}{g_{m}+g_{ds}+R_{S}^{-1}}
= \frac{g_{m}(r_{o}\parallel R_{S})}{1+g_{m}(r_{o}\parallel R_{S})}
= \frac{1}{1+1/g_{m}(r_{o}\parallel R_{S})}<1\;$$

$$A_{v0}\approx \frac{g_{m}R_{S}}{1+g_{m}R_{S}}\;\;{\rm if}\;r_{o}\gg R_{S}$$

$$A_{v0}\approx \frac{g_{m}r_{o}}{1+g_{m}r_{o}}
=1-\frac{1}{g_{m}r_{o}}\;\;{\rm if}\;R_{S}\gg r_{o}$$

Typical $g_{m}R_{S}\gg 1$, $g_{m}r_{o}=20-100$ so

$$A_{v0}\approx 0.9-0.99$$

With body effect $g_{mb}=\chi g_{m}$:

$$A_{v}\approx \frac{g_{m}}{g_{m}+g_{mb}}=\frac{1}{1+\chi}
\approx 0.7-0.9$$

for $R_{S}\parallel r_{o}\to \infty$. Always $<1$, $>0$,
non inverting, $100\%$ series voltage feedback.
Loop gain $T=(g_{m}+g_{mb})(r_{o}\parallel R_{S})$,
$A_{v}=T/(1+T)$.

Current and power gain $\gg 1$: $A_{i}\approx g_{m}R_{S}$.

### 3. Terminal impedances

Gate draws no $DC$ current:

$$\;R_{in}= \infty \;\;{\rm low\;freq.}\;$$

$$C_{in}\approx C_{gd}+C_{gs}/(1+g_{m}R_{S})$$
Miller reduced, very high $Z_{in}$ - ideal to drive
without loading previous stage.

Output impedance: $v_{in}=0$, apply $v_{x}$ at source,
measure $i_{x}$.

$$i_{x}= \frac{v_{x}}{R_{S}}+g_{m}v_{gs}+g_{mb}v_{bs}+g_{ds}v_{ds}$$

$$v_{gs}=-v_{x}\;\;,\;\;v_{bs}=-v_{x}\;(0)\;\;,\;\;v_{ds}=-v_{x}$$

$$\;R_{out}= \frac{v_{x}}{i_{x}}=
\frac{1}{g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}}\parallel R_{S}
\approx \frac{1}{g_{m}+g_{mb}}\parallel R_{S}\;$$

No body effect: $R_{out}\approx 1/g_{m}\parallel R_{S}\parallel r_{o}$.

Typically $1/g_{m}= 50-500\,\Omega$, so low $Z_{out}$,
good voltage source, can drive $R_{L}$, $C_{L}$.

With active current source load $R_{S}\to r_{o2}$:

$$A_{v}= \frac{g_{m}}{g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}\;\;,\;\;
R_{out}= \frac{1}{g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}$$

### 4. Remarks

* Follows $v_{in}$ with $DC$ shift $V_{GS}$, hence source follower.
* No voltage gain but impedance transformation.
* High linearity due to $100\%$ feedback, low distortion,
  wide band. Dominant pole at output
  $\omega_{p}\approx 1/R_{out}C_{L}$, can drive capacitive load.
* Used as buffer, level shifter, output stage of op-amp,
  to isolate high impedance node from low impedance load.
* To increase gain to $\approx 1$ need $g_{m}(r_{o}\parallel R_{S})\gg 1$
  and eliminate body effect by body to source or PMOS in n-well.
* Replacing $R_{S}$ by current source gives higher $R_{S}$,
  higher gain, better $PSRR$ and linearity, but same $R_{out}\approx 1/g_{m}$.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 6.

answer.text:
This is the $G_{g}$ or $CG$ stage.
$V_{DD}$ is $a.c.$ ground through the
supply decoupling.

$$v_{g}=0\;\;a.c.\;\;v_{s}=v_{in}\;\;v_{d}=v_{out}$$

$$v_{gs}=v_{g}-v_{s}=-v_{in}\;\;a.c.$$

In the figure the bulk is strapped to the
source, $V_{BS}=0$, $g_{mb}=0$ on the
symbol as drawn. If the bulk is to $GND$
put $g_{m}\rightarrow g_{m}+g_{mb}$ in what
follows.

### 1. D.C.

$$V_{GS}=V_{DD}-V_{IN}$$
$$V_{DS}=V_{D}-V_{S}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{D}-V_{IN}$$

In saturation, $\lambda =0$:

$$I_{D}={\frac12}k_{n}\left(V_{GS}-V_{T}\right)^{2}
={\frac12}\mu _{n}C_{ox}{\frac{W}{L}}\left(V_{DD}-V_{IN}-V_{T}\right)^{2}$$

$$V_{OUT}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{D}
=V_{DD}-{\frac12}k_{n}R_{D}\left(V_{DD}-V_{IN}-V_{T}\right)^{2}$$

parabolic $V_{OUT}(V_{IN})$, non inverting.

Saturation:

$$V_{DS}\ge V_{GS}-V_{T}$$

$$V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{D}-V_{IN}\ge V_{DD}-V_{IN}-V_{T}$$

$$I_{D}R_{D}\le V_{T}\tag{*}$$

i. e. with $V_{G}=V_{DD}$ the allowable
drop on $R_{D}$ for saturation is $\le V_{T}$.
In practice $V_{G}$ is biased at
$V_{B}<V_{DD}$ to get headroom. $(*)$ becomes
$I_{D}R_{D}\le V_{B}-V_{IN}-V_{T}+V_{DS,sat}$.
With bulk to $GND$, $V_{T}=V_{T0}+\gamma
\left(\sqrt{2\phi _{F}+V_{SB}}-\sqrt{2\phi _{F}}\right)$.

Small signal about the bias point $I_{D}$:

$$g_{m}=k_{n}\left(V_{GS}-V_{T}\right)=\sqrt{2k_{n}I_{D}}$$
$$r_{o}=1/g_{ds}=1/\lambda I_{D}$$

### 2. $a.c.$ model $r_{o}<\infty $

```
          g
          o
          |  +--R_D--+-- V_DD ac gnd
          |  |       |
          D--o vout  |
          |         _|_
         / \  g_m v_gs + g_ds v_ds
        /   \
        S----o vin
          |
         _|_ v_bs=0 if bulk=S
```

$$i_{d}=g_{m}v_{gs}+g_{mb}v_{bs}+g_{ds}v_{ds}$$

$$v_{gs}=-v_{in}\;\;,\;\;v_{bs}=0\;\;{\rm bulk}=S$$
$$v_{ds}=v_{out}-v_{in}$$

$$i_{d}=-g_{m}v_{in}+g_{ds}\left(v_{out}-v_{in}\right)$$

$$v_{out}=-i_{d}R_{D}\;\;a.c.$$

$$v_{out}=R_{D}g_{m}v_{in}-R_{D}g_{ds}v_{out}+R_{D}g_{ds}v_{in}$$

$$\left(1+g_{ds}R_{D}\right)v_{out}=R_{D}\left(g_{m}+g_{ds}\right)v_{in}$$

> $$A_{v}\equiv {\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}}=
> {\frac{R_{D}\left(g_{m}+g_{ds}\right)}{1+g_{ds}R_{D}}}
> =g_{m}R_{D}{\frac{1+g_{ds}/g_{m}}{1+R_{D}/r_{o}}}$$

For $r_{o}\gg R_{D}$:

> $$A_{v}\approx +g_{m}R_{D}\approx g_{m}\left(R_{D}\parallel r_{o}\right)>0$$

non inverting. With bulk to $GND$:

$$A_{v}\approx +\left(g_{m}+g_{mb}\right)\left(R_{D}\parallel r_{o}\right)$$

Current gain $i_{d}/i_{in}\approx -1$, the stage
is a current buffer, voltage gain is obtained
on $R_{D}$. Power gain $\approx g_{m}R_{D}$.

Input resistance at the source:

$$i_{in}=-i_{d}=-g_{m}v_{gs}-g_{ds}v_{ds}$$

$$R_{in}={\frac{v_{in}}{i_{in}}}=
{\frac{1+g_{ds}R_{D}}{g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}\left(1+g_{ds}R_{D}\right)}}
\approx {\frac{R_{D}+r_{o}}{1+\left(g_{m}+g_{mb}\right)r_{o}}}$$

> $$R_{in}\approx {\frac{1}{g_{m}+g_{mb}}}\parallel r_{o}\approx {\frac{1}{g_{m}}}\;\;{\rm for}\;r_{o}\gg R_{D},\;g_{mb}=0$$

Low, $\sim 10^{1}-10^{2}{\rm \Omega}$ to $1{\rm k\Omega}$,
can be made $50{\rm \Omega}$ for RF matching.

Output resistance, with source resistance $R_{sig}$
driving the source, $R_{sig}=0$ for ideal $V_{in}$:

$$R_{out}=R_{D}\parallel R_{o\,d}$$

$$R_{o\,d}=r_{o}+\left[1+\left(g_{m}+g_{mb}\right)r_{o}\right]R_{sig}$$

> $$R_{out}\approx R_{D}\parallel r_{o}\approx R_{D}\;\;{\rm for}\;R_{sig}=0$$

High. With $R_{sig}\ne 0$, $R_{o\,d}\approx
\left(g_{m}+g_{mb}\right)r_{o}R_{sig}\gg r_{o}$.

Remarks:

* No Miller multiplication of $C_{gd}$. Input pole
$\omega_{p\,in}\approx \left(g_{m}+g_{mb}\right)/C_{in}$,
output pole $\omega_{p\,out}\approx 1/R_{D}C_{out}$.
Wide band, used as RF LNA input, as current buffer
and as the upper device of a cascode.

* For large $R_{D}$ the $V_{G}=V_{DD}$ bias of the
figure violates $(*)$ and drives $M_{1}$ into triode.
Normal $CG$ bias is $V_{G}=V_{B}$ with $V_{B}$ a
$DC$ bias $\approx V_{IN}+V_{GS}$ generated by a
divider/current source, $AC$ bypassed to $GND$.
