All essential points of the golden solution are covered, and the additional analysis is consistent with the longer-effective-channel mechanism.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 20.

answer.text:
With ${\rm M}_{1}-{\rm M}_{2}-I_{1}$ put
${\rm M}_{1}$ ${\rm C}{\rm D}$ to ${\rm ac}$ ground this is
the long tailed pair taken single ended on the ${\rm M}_{2}$
side or, what is the same, a ${\rm C}{\rm D}$ driving a
${\rm C}{\rm G}$ stage.

$$I_{D1}+I_{D2}=I_{1}\tag{1}$$

For $V_{I}=V_{b}$ in the normal saturated
design

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{1}/2\qquad 
g_{m}= \sqrt{2\mu C_{ox}W/LI_{D}}\qquad 
r_{o}=1/\lambda I_{D}\tag{2}$$

$$V_{S}=V_{I}-V_{GS1}=V_{b}-V_{GS2}\tag{3}$$

$${\rm M}_{1}:V_{DS1}=V_{DD}-V_{S}\ge V_{GS1}-V_{T}\;\;
{\rm i.e.}\;\;V_{I}\le V_{DD}+V_{T}$$
$${\rm M}_{2}:V_{DS2}=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_{D}-V_{S}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{T}
\;\;{\rm i.e.}\;\;V_{D2}\ge V_{b}-V_{T}\tag{4}$$
$$V_{S}\ge V_{DS,sat}(I_{1})$$

so that with $V_{ov}=V_{GS}-V_{T}$

$$V_{GS}+V_{DS,sat}(I_{1})<V_{I}<V_{DD}+V_{T}\tag{5}$$
$$V_{b}-V_{T}<V_{o}=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_{D}<V_{DD}\tag{6}$$

and for $|\,V_{I}-V_{b}\,|\ll V_{ov}$

$$I_{D1,2}={I_{1}\over 2}\pm {1\over 2}
\sqrt{2\mu C_{ox}W/LI_{1}}\,(V_{I}-V_{b})
\tag{7}$$

i. e. the conventional $\tanh $ large signal
characteristic, linear for

$$|\,V_{I}-V_{b}\,|\lesssim \sqrt{2}V_{ov}\tag{8}$$

and $P_{DC}=V_{DD}I_{1}$.

Put $V_{b}=0$ for ${\rm ac}$ and $R_{T}=r_{oI_{1}}$ the
${\rm ac}$ impedance of $I_{1}$ to ground, $R_{T}\to \infty $
for the ideal source.  With the usual $g_{m},g_{mb},r_{o}$
model, Fig.1,

$$\eqalign{
I_{ds1}&=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{mb1}v_{bs1}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1}\cr
&=g_{m1}(v_{i}-v_{x})-g_{mb1}v_{x}-g_{ds1}v_{x}\cr
I_{ds2}&=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{mb2}v_{bs2}+g_{ds2}v_{ds2}\cr
&=-g_{m2}v_{x}-g_{mb2}v_{x}+g_{ds2}(v_{o}-v_{x})\cr}
\tag{9}$$

where $v_{x}$ is the common source node and
$g_{ds}=r_{o}^{-1}$, $v_{bs}=-v_{x}$ for $n$ well to
ground.  Put $g_{mbi}=g_{mi}+g_{mbi}$ for brevity,
$g_{ds}=0$ for hand calculation.

$${\rm KCL}_{x}: I_{ds1}+I_{ds2}=v_{x}/R_{T}\tag{10}$$
$${\rm KCL}_{o}: I_{ds2}+v_{o}/R_{D}=0\tag{11}$$
the $R_{D}$ current being $(V_{DD}-v_{o})/R_{D}$.

From (11)

$$-v_{x}(g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})+g_{ds2}v_{o}+v_{o}/R_{D}=0\tag{12}$$

$$v_{x}=v_{o}{{g_{ds2}+R_{D}^{-1}}\over{g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}}
\tag{13}$$

and from (10) with $R_{T}\to \infty $

$$g_{m1}v_{i}-v_{x}(g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})
+g_{ds2}v_{o}=0\tag{14}$$

Hence, for $R_{T}\to \infty $,

$$A_{v}\equiv {v_{o}\over v_{i}}=
{{g_{m1}(g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})}
\over{(g_{ds2}+R_{D}^{-1})(g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})
/(g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})-g_{ds2}}}\tag{15}$$

i. e.

$$A_{v}=g_{m1}{{g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}\over{
{{g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}}\over{r_{o2}}}+{{g_{mb1}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}
\over{R_{D}}}}}\tag{16}$$

$$A_{v}=g_{m1}(g_{mb2}r_{o2}+1)R_{D}
\Big/\Big[(g_{mb1}r_{o2}+r_{o2}/r_{o1})R_{D}/r_{o2}
+(g_{mb1}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2})r_{o2}\Big]\tag{17}$$

In particular with $g_{mb}=0$,

$$A_{v}=g_{m1}(g_{m2}r_{o2}+1)R_{D}
\Big/\Big[1+r_{o2}/r_{o1}+g_{m1}(R_{D}+r_{o2})
+g_{m2}r_{o2}+R_{D}/r_{o1}\Big]\tag{18}$$

For $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$, $r_{o}\gg R_{D}$,

$$A_{v}\approx {{g_{m1}g_{mb2}}\over{g_{mb1}+g_{mb2}}}R_{D}
\tag{19}$$

and with $g_{mb}=0$

$$A_{v}\approx {{g_{m1}g_{m2}}\over{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}}R_{D}
\tag{20}$$

For the matched pair $g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_{m}$,
$g_{mb1}=g_{mb2}=g_{mb}$,

$$A_{v}\approx +\,{g_{m}\over 2}R_{D}\;\;{\rm to}\;\;
{{g_{m}r_{o}\over 1+g_{m}r_{o}}}\,R_{D}\tag{21}$$

more exactly $A_{v}=+g_{m}(R_{D}\parallel r_{o})/2$,
the $+$ sign denoting the non inverting side.
The inverting side, $v_{o1}$ at the drain of
${\rm M}_{1}$ if a $R_{D}$ were put there, is
$A_{v}=-g_{m}R_{D}/2$.  The differential voltage
gain $A_{d}=g_{m}R_{D}$ differential, $g_{m}R_{D}/2$
single ended, as for any long tailed pair.
With $r_{o}$ kept,

$$A_{v}=+g_{m}(R_{D}\parallel r_{o})/2\times
{1\over{1+(R_{D}+r_{o})/g_{m}r_{o}^{2}}}\approx
+g_{m}(R_{D}\parallel r_{o})/2\tag{22}$$

The factor $g_{m1}/(g_{m1}+g_{m2})$ is the voltage
division of the ${\rm C}{\rm D}$ stage loaded by the
${\rm C}{\rm G}$ input resistance $1/g_{mb2}$,

$$A_{v}= \underbrace{{g_{mb1}\over{g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}}
{1/g_{mb2}\parallel r_{o1}\over{1/g_{mb1}\parallel r_{o1}
+1/g_{mb2}\parallel r_{o1}}}}_{A_{CD}<1}
\;\underbrace{g_{mb2}R_{D}}_{A_{CG}}\tag{23}$$

so that the Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$ is
$\approx 1$.

* Input impedance: $R_{i}=1/sC_{g}\to \infty $ at
low frequency, $C_{i}\approx C_{gs1}+C_{gb1}$.

* Output impedance: with $v_{i}=0$ the resistance
seen looking into the source of ${\rm M}_{1}$ is

$$R_{s1}= {1\over{g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}}}\parallel R_{T}\tag{24}$$

$\approx 1/g_{mb1}$ for $R_{T}\to \infty $.
The resistance seen looking into the drain of the
${\rm C}{\rm G}$ device with source resistance $R_{s}$
is $r_{o2}+(1+g_{mb2}r_{o2})R_{s}$.  Hence

$$R_{o}=R_{D}\parallel \Big[r_{o2}+(1+g_{mb2}r_{o2})
\big(R_{s1}\parallel R_{T}\big)\Big]\tag{25}$$

$$R_{o}\approx R_{D}\parallel
\left[r_{o2}+{{1+g_{mb2}r_{o2}}\over{g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}}}\right]
\tag{26}$$

For $R_{T}\to \infty $, $g_{mb}r_{o}\gg 1$,

$$R_{o}\approx R_{D}\parallel r_{o2}\left(1+
{{g_{mb2}}\over{g_{mb1}}}\right)\tag{27}$$

and for the matched, $g_{mb}=0$ case

$$R_{o}\approx R_{D}\parallel 2r_{o}\tag{28}$$

normally $R_{o}\approx R_{D}$ because $R_{D}\ll r_{o}$.

With finite $R_{T}$ the common mode gain is

$$A_{cm}={{v_{o}}\over{v_{cm}}}\approx
-{{R_{D}}\over{2R_{T}}}{1\over{1+1/2g_{mb}R_{T}}}\approx
-{{R_{D}}\over{2R_{T}}}\tag{29}$$

so that

$${\rm CMRR}=|A_{d}/A_{cm}|\approx g_{mb}R_{T}\tag{30}$$

The circuit is wide band: the pole at the common
source node is

$$\omega_{px}\approx {{g_{mb1}+g_{mb2}}\over{C_{x}}}\tag{31}$$

$C_{x}=C_{gs1}+C_{sb1}+C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{T}$,
at very high frequency, the dominant pole is

$$\omega_{po}\approx {1\over{R_{o}C_{L}}}\tag{32}$$

at the output node.  This is the usual advantage of
the ${\rm C}{\rm D}-{\rm C}{\rm G}$ / differential
pair over the simple common source stage.

minimax_m3.rationale: The candidate misidentifies the circuit as a differential pair (long-tailed pair) rather than the golden solution's source follower driving a common-gate stage. While the candidate does mention 'a CD driving a CG stage' in passing, the entire analysis is built around a differential pair framework with tail current source, common-mode analysis, CMRR, and differential gain. The topology recognition is fundamentally wrong: the input is applied to M1's gate and M1's source drives M2's source (source follower + common-gate), not a differential pair. The dominant mechanism, signal path, and circuit detail asked by the task are missed.

deepseek_v4_pro.rationale: The answer correctly identifies the circuit as a source follower (CD) driving a common-gate (CG) stage, which is the essential topology required by the golden solution. It provides a thorough small-signal analysis, including gain, input/output impedance, and bandwidth, with correct device roles and dominant mechanisms. The analysis is consistent with the golden solution's central result, and any additional details (e.g., differential pair interpretation, common-mode behavior) are secondary but not contradictory.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in Figure 21 can be inductive.

answer.text:
With ${\rm M}_{2}$ $V_{b}=ac~0$ it is
$r_{o2}\parallel C_{o2}$ to ground. Put it in parallel
afterwards. For ${\rm M}_{1}$

$${\rm D}=ac~0\qquad {\rm G}=R_{S}~{\rm to}~ac~0\qquad 
{\rm S}=V_{x}$$

$$C_{gs}\equiv C_{1}\;\;C_{gd}\equiv C_{2}\;\;g_{m}\equiv g_{m1}
\;\;g_{mb}=0~{\rm body~to~source}$$

$$V_{gs}=V_{g}-V_{x}\qquad V_{ds}=-V_{x}$$

$${\rm G:}\;\;{V_{g}\over R_{S}}+sC_{2}V_{g}+sC_{1}(V_{g}-V_{x})=0\tag{1}$$

$${\rm S:}\;\;I_{x}= {\rm current~leaving~S~to~G~and~to~D}$$

$$I_{x}=sC_{1}(V_{x}-V_{g})-I_{d}\tag{2}$$
$$I_{d}=g_{m}V_{gs}+g_{ds}V_{ds}=g_{m}(V_{g}-V_{x})-g_{ds}V_{x}$$

so that with the sign $I_{d}:{\rm D}\to {\rm S}$

$$I_{x}=sC_{1}(V_{x}-V_{g})-g_{m}(V_{g}-V_{x})+g_{ds}V_{x}$$
$$I_{x}=V_{x}(g_{m}+g_{ds}+sC_{1})-V_{g}(g_{m}+sC_{1})\tag{3}$$

From (1)

$$V_{g}\left[{1\over R_{S}}+s(C_{1}+C_{2})\right]=sC_{1}V_{x}$$

$$V_{g}=V_{x}{sC_{1}R_{S}\over 1+sR_{S}(C_{1}+C_{2})}\tag{4}$$

$$Z_{1}\equiv {V_{x}\over I_{x}}=
{1+sR_{S}(C_{1}+C_{2})\over 
(g_{m}+g_{ds}+sC_{1})[1+sR_{S}(C_{1}+C_{2})]-sC_{1}R_{S}(g_{m}+sC_{1})}$$

$$Z_{1}={1+sR_{S}(C_{1}+C_{2})\over 
g_{m}+g_{ds}+s\left[C_{1}+g_{m}R_{S}C_{2}+g_{ds}R_{S}(C_{1}+C_{2})\right]
+s^{2}R_{S}C_{1}C_{2}}\tag{5}$$

$g_{ds}\to 0$ for illustration

$$Z_{1}\approx {1+sR_{S}(C_{1}+C_{2})\over g_{m}+s(C_{1}+g_{m}R_{S}C_{2})
+s^{2}R_{S}C_{1}C_{2}}\tag{6}$$

and for $C_{2}\ll C_{1}$ the usual text book form

$$Z_{1}\approx {1+sC_{1}R_{S}\over g_{m}+sC_{1}}
={1\over g_{m}}{1+sC_{1}R_{S}\over 1+sC_{1}/g_{m}}\tag{7}$$

i. e. a zero at

$$\omega _{z}={1\over R_{S}(C_{1}+C_{2})}\tag{8}$$

and a pole at

$$\omega _{p}\approx {g_{m}\over C_{1}}\;\;{\rm for}\;R_{S}C_{2}\ll C_{1}/g_{m}
\tag{9}$$

more generally $\omega _{p}\approx g_{m}/C_{1}$ to
$g_{m}R_{S}C_{2}$.

For $R_{S}=0$

$$Z_{1}={1\over g_{m}+sC_{1}}={1/g_{m}\over 1+sC_{1}/g_{m}}\tag{10}$$

capacitive, ${\rm Im}Z_{1}<0$, low pass $1/g_{m}\parallel 1/sC_{1}$.

For $R_{S}\ne 0$ put $s=j\omega $ in (6)

$$Z_{1}(j\omega )={1+j\omega a\over b-\omega^{2}d+j\omega c}$$

$$a=R_{S}(C_{1}+C_{2}),\;b=g_{m},\;c=C_{1}+g_{m}R_{S}C_{2},\;
d=R_{S}C_{1}C_{2}$$

$$Z_{1}={(1+j\omega a)(b-\omega^{2}d-j\omega c)\over 
(b-\omega^{2}d)^{2}+\omega^{2}c^{2}}$$

$${\rm Im}Z_{1}={\omega \left[ab-c-\omega^{2}ad\right]\over 
(b-\omega^{2}d)^{2}+\omega^{2}c^{2}}\tag{11}$$

$$ab-c =g_{m}R_{S}(C_{1}+C_{2})-(C_{1}+g_{m}R_{S}C_{2})
=C_{1}(g_{m}R_{S}-1)-g_{ds}R_{S}(C_{1}+C_{2})\tag{12}$$

Neglecting $g_{ds}$,

$${\rm Im}Z_{1}\approx \omega C_{1}(g_{m}R_{S}-1)-\omega^{3}R_{S}^{2}
C_{1}C_{2}(C_{1}+C_{2})\over {\rm Den}\tag{13}$$

So for

$$\omega^{2}<{C_{1}(g_{m}R_{S}-1)\over R_{S}^{2}C_{1}C_{2}(C_{1}+C_{2})}
\approx {g_{m}R_{S}-1\over R_{S}^{2}C_{2}(C_{1}+C_{2})}\tag{14}$$

and in particular at low $\omega $

$${\rm Im}Z_{1}\approx \omega C_{1}(g_{m}R_{S}-1)/g_{m}^{2}\tag{15}$$

$${\rm Im}Z_{1}>0\;\;{\rm iff}\;\;g_{m}R_{S}>1\tag{16}$$

with $g_{mb}\ne 0$, $g_{m}\to g_{m}+g_{mb}$,
$g_{m}R_{S}\to (g_{m}+g_{mb})R_{S}>1$.

In that band $Z_{1}$ is $R+j\omega L$.

E. g. from (7) for $\omega \ll g_{m}/C_{1}$,

$$Z_{1}\approx {1\over g_{m}}{1+sC_{1}R_{S}\over 1+sC_{1}/g_{m}}
\approx {1\over g_{m}}+s{C_{1}(R_{S}-1/g_{m})\over g_{m}}
{1\over 1+sC_{1}/g_{m}}$$

$$\approx {1\over g_{m}}+sL_{eq}\qquad 
L_{eq}\approx {C_{1}\over g_{m}}\left(R_{S}-{1\over g_{m}}\right)
\approx {R_{S}C_{gs}\over g_{m}}\;\;{\rm for}\;g_{m}R_{S}\gg 1\tag{17}$$

i. e. a resistance $1/(g_{m}+g_{mb})\parallel r_{o1}$ in series
with an inductance $L_{eq}$ to first order, shunted at very
high frequency by $1/sC_{2}$ so that

$$Z_{out}=Z_{1}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel {1\over sC_{o2}}\approx
\left({1\over g_{m}}+sL_{eq}\right)\parallel r_{o2}\tag{18}$$

resistive at $dc$, inductive for $\omega_{z}<\omega<\omega_{p}$,
capacitive for $\omega\to\infty$.

Physically $R_{S}$ isolates the gate at high frequency.
A $+ \Delta V_{x}$ couples through $C_{gs}$ to the gate but the
gate can only follow through the $R_{S}C_{gs}$ low pass, so
$V_{g}$ lags $V_{x}$. Hence $V_{gs}=V_{g}-V_{x}$ goes negative
on a rising $V_{x}$, $g_{m}V_{gs}$ decreases, the transistor
supplies less current when the voltage is rising - current lags
voltage - the definition of an inductance. It is the
capacitor $C_{gs}$ gyrated by the $g_{m}$ stage with the
$R_{S}$ phase shift. With $R_{S}=0$ the gate is $ac$ ground,
$V_{gs}=-V_{x}$ in phase and $Z_{1}=1/(g_{m}+sC_{gs})$ is
capacitive. The zero $1/R_{S}(C_{gs}+C_{gd})$ moves below the
pole $g_{m}/C_{gs}$ when $g_{m}R_{S}>1$ and the phase of $Z_{1}$
becomes positive.

In the complete circuit $Z_{out}=Z_{1}\parallel Z_{2}$,
$Z_{2}\approx r_{o2}\parallel 1/s(C_{gd2}+C_{db2}+C_{L})$
capacitive, so the inductive $Z_{1}$ resonating with the
capacitive load $C_{L}$ gives the well known peaking and
possible oscillation of a source follower driving a capacitive
load. It is an active simulated inductor.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 22.

answer.text:
With the usual $g_{m}r_{o}>>1$ the
circuit is a $shunt-shunt$ $V-I$ loop with
two inversions.

$$M_{1}:v_{o}=-g_{m1}v_{x}R_{1}\qquad 
R_{1}=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\tag{1}$$

$$M_{2}:i_{f}=g_{m2}v_{o}+g_{o2}v_{x}\qquad 
g_{o2}=r_{o2}^{-1}\tag{2}$$

$$i_{in}=i_{f}\;\;{\rm at}\;X\tag{3}$$

is $shunt$ at the input, $shunt$ at the output.
$X\to V_{o}$ is inverting, $V_{o}\to X$ is
inverting $\to $ positive feedback.

Small signal Fig. $C_{x}$ at $X$, $C_{o}$ at
$V_{o}$.

$$\eqalign{
C_{x}\dot v_{x}&=i_{in}-g_{m2}v_{o}-g_{o2}v_{x}\cr
C_{o}\dot v_{o}&=-g_{m1}v_{x}-G_{1}v_{o}\cr}
\qquad G_{1}=g_{o1}+R_{D1}^{-1}=R_{1}^{-1}\tag{4}$$

Put $s=0$ for the d.c. small signal.

$$v_{o}=-g_{m1}R_{1}v_{x}\tag{5}$$
$$i_{in}=g_{m2}v_{o}+g_{o2}v_{x}\tag{6}$$

$$\;v_{x}= {i_{in}\over g_{o2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{1}}\;
\tag{7}$$

$$\;v_{o}= -g_{m1}R_{1}v_{x}
      ={g_{m1}R_{1}\over g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{1}-g_{o2}}i_{in}
      ={g_{m1}R_{1}r_{o2}\over T_{0}-1}i_{in}\;\tag{8}$$

$$R_{M}\equiv {v_{o}\over i_{in}}=
{g_{m1}R_{1}\over g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{1}-g_{o2}} \tag{9}$$

For $r_{o}\to \infty $

$$R_{M}\approx {1\over g_{m2}}>0\tag{10}$$

i. e. non inverting transresistance.  With
$g_{o2}\ne 0$ and $T_{0}<1$

$$R_{M}\approx -g_{m1}R_{1}r_{o2}<0\tag{11}$$

large inverting gain.  $R_{M}\to \pm \infty $
for

$$g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{1}=g_{o2}\tag{12}$$

is the small signal infinite gain point.

Return ratio.  Break the loop at $X$, $i_{in}=0$
a.c. open, inject $v_{t}$ at the gate of $M_{1}$.

$$v_{o}=-g_{m1}R_{1}v_{t}$$
$$0=g_{m2}v_{o}+g_{o2}v_{r}\;\; \to\;\;
v_{r}=-g_{m2}r_{o2}v_{o}$$

$$\;T_{0}\equiv {v_{r}\over v_{t}}=g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{1}r_{o2}\;
\tag{13}$$

$$T(s)={T_{0}\over (1+sR_{1}C_{o})(1+sr_{o2}C_{x})}\tag{14}$$

$T_{0}>0$ - positive feedback.  In Blackman
form

$$R_{M}=R_{M0}{1\over 1-T_{0}}\tag{15}$$

with $R_{M0}=-g_{m1}R_{1}r_{o2}$ the $T=0$
transresistance.

Input impedance $Z_{x}=v_{x}/i_{in}$ from (7)

$$\;Z_{in}={1\over g_{o2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{1}}
      ={r_{o2}\over 1-T_{0}}={r_{o2}\over 1-T(s)}\Bigl|_{s=0}\;
\tag{16}$$

Output impedance.  Put $i_{in}=0$, apply $v_{t}$
at $V_{o}$.

$$0=g_{m2}v_{t}+g_{o2}v_{x}\;\;v_{x}=-g_{m2}r_{o2}v_{t}$$
$$i_{t}=G_{1}v_{t}+g_{m1}v_{x}+g_{o1}v_{t}
      =G_{1}v_{t}-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}v_{t}$$

$$\;Z_{out}={v_{t}\over i_{t}}={1\over G_{1}-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}
      ={R_{1}\over 1-T_{0}}\;\tag{17}$$

i. e. Blackman $Z=Z_{0}/(1-T)$.  For $T_{0}>1$

$$Z_{in}\approx -{1\over g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{1}}<0\qquad
  Z_{out}\approx -{1\over g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}<0\tag{18}$$

negative resistance.

Poles of the closed loop from (4)

$$\det \pmatrix{g_{o2}+sC_{x}&g_{m2}\cr g_{m1}&G_{1}+sC_{o}\cr}=0$$

$$s^{2}+s\left({G_{1}\over C_{o}}+{g_{o2}\over C_{x}}\right)
   +{G_{1}g_{o2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}\over C_{x}C_{o}}=0\tag{19}$$

$${\rm Tr}<0\;\;{\rm always}\qquad 
  \Delta ={1-T_{0}\over R_{1}r_{o2}C_{x}C_{o}}\tag{20}$$

Stable iff $\Delta >0$

$$\;T_{0}=g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{1}r_{o2}<1\;\tag{21}$$

$$g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{1}<g_{o2}\tag{22}$$

Normally $g_{m}r_{o}\sim 20-100$, $g_{m}R_{D}\sim
5-20$ so $T_{0}\sim 10^{2}-10^{3}>>1$.  The
linearised d.c. point is a saddle, one pole in
the RHP, ${\rm Re}\,s>0$.  Any perturbation
grows $\propto \exp (+t/\tau )$ and the circuit
latches.  It is not a linear TIA for normal
sizing.  With $T_{0}<1$ it is a regenerative
TIA with

$$|R_{M}|\approx g_{m1}R_{1}r_{o2}/(1-T_{0})$$

enhanced by $1/(1-T_{0})$ and very sensitive to
process.

Large signal the $T_{0}=1$ point is the
hysteresis threshold.  With square law,
$k_{i}={1\over 2}\mu C_{ox}W_{i}/L_{i}$,

$$(V_{DD}-V_{o})/R_{D1}=I_{D1}(V_{x},V_{o})\tag{23}$$
$$I_{in}=I_{D2}(V_{o},V_{x})\tag{24}$$

e.g. $M_{1}$ sat., $M_{2}$ triode, high $V_{o}$
branch

$$V_{o}=V_{DD}-k_{1}R_{D1}(V_{x}-V_{TH})^{2}$$
$$I_{in}=k_{2}\left[2(V_{o}-V_{TH})V_{x}-V_{x}^{2}\right]\tag{25}$$

$$I_{in}(V_{x})=k_{2}\left[2(V_{DD}-V_{TH})V_{x}
 -V_{x}^{2}-2k_{1}R_{D1}V_{x}(V_{x}-V_{TH})^{2}\right]$$

$dI_{in}/dV_{x}=0$ gives the upper trip point

$$V_{DD}-V_{TH}-V_{x}-k_{1}R_{D1}(V_{x}-V_{TH})
 (3V_{x}-V_{TH})=0\tag{26}$$

$$3k_{1}R_{D1}V_{x}^{2}+(1-4k_{1}R_{D1}V_{TH})V_{x}
 +k_{1}R_{D1}V_{TH}^{2}-V_{DD}+V_{TH}=0$$

and $I_{TH+}=I_{in}(V_{x})$.  The low $V_{o}$
branch, $M_{1}$ triode, $M_{2}$ sat.,

$$(V_{DD}-V_{o})/R_{D1}=k_{1}\left[2(V_{x}-V_{TH})V_{o}
 -V_{o}^{2}\right]\tag{27}$$
$$I_{in}=k_{2}(V_{o}-V_{TH})^{2}\tag{28}$$

gives the lower trip point, in the ideal
square law $I_{TH-}\to 0$, in practice limited
by $V_{x}\le V_{DD}$ to

$$V_{o}^{2}-V_{o}\left[2(V_{DD}-V_{TH})+1/k_{1}R_{D1}\right]
 +V_{DD}/k_{1}R_{D1}=0\tag{29}$$

The d.c. $V_{o}(I_{in})$ is therefore S-shaped:
middle branch $dV_{o}/dI_{in}=R_{M}<0$ unstable,
outer branches stable, Fig. 1.  Sweeping $I_{in}$
up the circuit stays on the high $V_{o}\approx
V_{DD}$, $M_{1}$ off, $M_{2}$ triode,
$V_{x}\approx I_{in}/2k_{2}(V_{DD}-V_{TH})$ until
$I_{TH+}$ where it snaps to $V_{o}\approx
V_{TH}+\sqrt{I_{in}/k_{2}}$ low.  Sweeping down
it stays low until $I_{TH-}$ where it snaps
high.  For $T_{0}>>1$ the hysteresis window is
large, the circuit is a current mode Schmitt
trigger / latch.

In particular for $T_{0}>1$ the small signal
model is that of a negative resistor
$-|R_{in}|$ at $X$ and $-|R_{out}|$ at $V_{o}$
which can cancel loss and be used as an active
load or in a relaxation oscillator.  To obtain
linear amplification the loop must be
degenerated, $T_{0}<1$, e.g. source degeneration
of $M_{2}$ or $R_{S}$ in series with $M_{1}$,
or $R_{D1}$ made small, at the expense of gain.

> *Remark:* Including $g_{mb}$ replace $g_{m1}$
> by $g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$ if body not tied to source.
> Here both sources are grounded so $g_{mb}=0$ to
> first order.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 23.

answer.text:
With $V_{b}={\rm ac~gnd}$ put $g_{m1}^{\prime
}=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$ for the $CG$ device, $g_{m2}$ for the
$CS$ device

$${\rm X}\equiv D_{1}\equiv G_{2}\qquad 
A\equiv S_{1}\equiv {\rm in}\qquad O\equiv D_{2}$$

$$R_{D1}^{\prime}=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\qquad 
R_{D2}^{\prime}=R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}\qquad 
G_{D1}=1/R_{D1}^{\prime}\;\;G_{D2}=1/R_{D2}^{\prime}\;\;
G_{F}=1/R_{F}$$

$$v_{gs1}=-v_{A}\qquad v_{gs2}=v_{X}$$

The $R_{F}$ senses $v_{O}$ and returns a current to the
low impedance node $A$.  $v_{O}$ sampling is in parallel,
$i_{in}$ mixing is in parallel : shunt - shunt,
voltage - current, transimpedance feedback.  In the
ideal $A_{v}\rightarrow \infty $

$$i_{RF}=\frac{v_{A}-v_{O}}{R_{F}}\approx -\frac{v_{O}}{R_{F}}
\qquad i_{in}+i_{RF}=i_{s1}\tag{1}$$

$$R_{M}^{id}= \left.\frac{v_{O}}{i_{in}}\right|_{A_{v}\to \infty}
=-\frac{1}{\beta }=-R_{F}\qquad 
\beta =\left.\frac{i_{f}}{v_{O}}\right|_{v_{A}=0}=-\,G_{F} \tag{2}$$

shunt at the input and shunt at the output both lower the
port impedance by $1+T$.

Put $r_{o}\to \infty $ for brevity.  The exact small
signal KCL, Fig.1, is

$$\eqalign{
{\rm X:}&\;{v_{X}\over R_{D1}}+{v_{X}-v_{A}\over r_{o1}}
+g_{m1}^{\prime}v_{gs1}=0 \cr
{\rm O:}&\;{v_{O}\over R_{D2}}+{v_{O}\over r_{o2}}
+g_{m2}v_{X}+{v_{O}-v_{A}\over R_{F}}=0\cr
{\rm A:}&\;i_{in}={v_{A}-v_{O}\over R_{F}}+{v_{A}-v_{X}\over r_{o1}}
-g_{m1}^{\prime}v_{gs1} } \tag{3}$$

i. e.

$$\eqalign{
v_{X}\left(G_{D1}+g_{ds1}\right)-v_{A}\left(g_{ds1}+g_{m1}^{\prime}
\right)&=0\cr
v_{O}\left(G_{D2}+g_{ds2}+G_{F}\right)+g_{m2}v_{X}-G_{F}v_{A}&=0\cr
i_{in}&=v_{A}\left(G_{F}+g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\right)
-g_{ds1}v_{X}-G_{F}v_{O}} \tag{4}$$

so that with $G_{o2}=G_{D2}+g_{ds2}+G_{F}$

$$v_{X}=v_{A}\,{g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\over G_{D1}+g_{ds1}}
\approx g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{D1}^{\prime}v_{A} \tag{5}$$

$$v_{O}= {G_{F}-g_{m2}{g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\over G_{D1}+g_{ds1}}
\over G_{o2}}\,v_{A}\approx -\,{g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{D1}^{\prime}
g_{m2}\over G_{o2}}v_{A} \tag{6}$$

and

$$i_{in}=v_{A}\left[G_{F}+g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}
-{g_{ds1}(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1})\over G_{D1}+g_{ds1}}\right]
-G_{F}v_{O} \tag{7}$$

Hence the exact closed loop transimpedance

$$R_{M}\equiv {v_{O}\over i_{in}}=
{{G_{F}-g_{m2}{g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\over G_{D1}+g_{ds1}}\over G_{o2}}
\over 
G_{F}+g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}-{g_{ds1}(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1})
\over G_{D1}+g_{ds1}}-{G_{F}\over G_{o2}}
\left[G_{F}-g_{m2}{g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\over G_{D1}+g_{ds1}}\right]}
\tag{8}$$

i. e. after clearing denominators, $g_{ds2}=0$ for brevity,

$$R_{M}=-{\,g_{m2}(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1})-G_{F}(G_{D1}+g_{ds1})\,
\over 
G_{D2}G_{F}(G_{D1}+g_{ds1})+(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1})
\left[G_{D1}G_{o2}+G_{F}g_{m2}\right]}\tag{9}$$

For $r_{o1},r_{o2}\to \infty $

$$R_{M}=-{g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{D1}-G_{F}\over 
G_{F}G_{D2}+g_{m1}^{\prime}(G_{D2}+G_{F})+G_{F}g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{D1}}
\tag{10}$$

$$R_{M}={G_{F}-g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{D1}\over 
g_{m1}^{\prime}G_{D2}+g_{m1}^{\prime}G_{F}+G_{F}G_{D2}
+G_{F}g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{D1}} \tag{10a}$$

$$|R_{M}|\approx {g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}R_{F}
\over R_{F}+R_{D2}+g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{D2}R_{F}
+g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}R_{F}}\tag{10b}$$

In the usual $g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{F}\gg 1$,
$g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}\gg 1$ limit

$$R_{M}\approx -{1\over G_{F}}{1\over 1+{1\over T}}
\approx -R_{F}\left(1-{1\over T}\right)\tag{11}$$

the familiar $R_{M}^{id}=-R_{F}$.

The $Y$ feedback network is

$${\bf Y}_{F}= \pmatrix{G_{F}&-G_{F}\cr -G_{F}&G_{F}\cr}\tag{12}$$

so that with the conventional $Y$ loading the forward
amplifier is loaded at the input by $G_{F}$ to ground and
at the output by $G_{F}$ to ground.  With the loading

$$\eqalign{
v_{X}&=v_{A}{g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\over G_{D1}+g_{ds1}}\cr
v_{O}&=-g_{m2}v_{X}/G_{o2}\cr
i_{in}&=v_{A}\left[G_{F}+{G_{D1}(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1})\over 
G_{D1}+g_{ds1}}\right] } \tag{13}$$

so that the open loop, loaded, transimpedance is

$$R_{M}^{o}= \left.{v_{O}\over i_{in}}\right|_{Y_{12}=Y_{21}=0}
=-{g_{m2}(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1})\over 
G_{o2}\left[G_{F}(G_{D1}+g_{ds1})+G_{D1}(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1})\right]}
\tag{14}$$

$$R_{M}^{o}\xrightarrow[r_{o}\to\infty]{}-
{g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{D1}\over G_{o2}(G_{F}+g_{m1}^{\prime})}
=-{g_{m1}^{\prime}\over g_{m1}^{\prime}+G_{F}}\,
g_{m2}R_{D1}\left(R_{D2}\parallel R_{F}\right) \tag{14a}$$

$$\approx -g_{m2}R_{D1}\left(R_{D2}\parallel R_{F}\right)
\qquad g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{F}\gg 1 \tag{14b}$$

i. e. the $CG$ gain $g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{D1}^{\prime}$ times the
$CS$ gain $g_{m2}R_{D2}^{\prime}\parallel R_{F}$ divided by the
input division $1+g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{F}$.

The loop gain $T=R_{M}^{o}\beta $ with $\beta =-G_{F}$,

$$T=-R_{M}^{o}G_{F}=
{G_{F}g_{m2}(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1})\over 
G_{o2}\left[G_{F}(G_{D1}+g_{ds1})+G_{D1}(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1})\right]}
>0 \tag{15}$$

$$T\xrightarrow[r_{o}\to\infty]{}
{G_{F}g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{D1}\over 
G_{o2}(G_{F}+g_{m1}^{\prime})}
={g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{D1}g_{m2}\left(R_{D2}\parallel R_{F}\right)
\over 1+g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{F}} \tag{15a}$$

$$T\approx {g_{m2}R_{D1}\left(R_{D2}\parallel R_{F}\right)\over R_{F}}
\approx {g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}\over R_{F}(R_{D2}+R_{F})}R_{F}
\qquad g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{F}\gg 1 \tag{15b}$$

More commonly written

$$T\approx g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{D1}\,g_{m2}R_{D2}\,
{R_{F}\over R_{F}+R_{D2}}\,{1\over 1+g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{F}} \tag{15c}$$

so that $R_{M}=R_{M}^{o}/(1+T)$ reproduces (9) to within the
$G_{F}^{2}$ loading error, $R_{M}=R_{M}^{o}/(1+T)\approx -R_{F}$
for $T\gg 1$.

Input impedance.  Open loop loaded

$$R_{in}^{o}= \left.{v_{A}\over i_{in}}\right|_{o}
={1\over G_{F}+G_{D1}(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1})/(G_{D1}+g_{ds1})}
\approx {1\over g_{m1}^{\prime}+G_{F}}\approx {1\over g_{m1}^{\prime}}
\tag{16}$$

Closed loop, Blackman,

$$R_{in}=R_{in}^{o}{1\over 1+T_{sc}}\approx {R_{in}^{o}\over 1+T}
\tag{17}$$

Exactly from (7)–(8)

$$R_{in}\equiv {v_{A}\over i_{in}}=
{(G_{D1}+g_{ds1})G_{o2}\over 
G_{D2}G_{F}(G_{D1}+g_{ds1})+(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1})
\left[G_{D1}G_{o2}+G_{F}g_{m2}\right]} \tag{18}$$

$$\xrightarrow[r_{o}\to\infty]{}
{G_{o2}\over G_{F}G_{D2}+g_{m1}^{\prime}G_{o2}+G_{F}g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{D1}}
\approx {1\over g_{m1}^{\prime}(1+T)}\approx
{R_{F}\over g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{D1}g_{m2}R_{D2}}\tag{18a}$$

for $T\gg 1$, $R_{F}\gg R_{D2}$,

$$R_{in}\approx {R_{D2}+R_{F}\over g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}
\approx {R_{F}\over g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}\tag{18b}$$

i. e. the $1/g_{m1}^{\prime}$ of the $CG$ stage divided by the
extra loop gain $g_{m2}R_{D2}$.  This is the regulated cascode
low $R_{in}$ used for wide band TIAs.

Output impedance.  Open loop loaded

$$R_{out}^{o}=1/G_{o2}=R_{D2}^{\prime}\parallel R_{F}\tag{19}$$

$$R_{out}= {R_{out}^{o}\over 1+T}\tag{20}$$

Exactly, driving $O$ with $i_{in}=0$,

$$R_{out}={1\over G_{o2}+G_{F}\left[g_{m2}(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1})
-G_{F}(G_{D1}+g_{ds1})\right]/\left[G_{F}(G_{D1}+g_{ds1})
+G_{D1}(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1})\right]} \tag{21}$$

$$\xrightarrow[r_{o}\to\infty]{}
{1\over G_{o2}+G_{F}g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{D1}/(1+g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{F})}
={R_{D2}\parallel R_{F}\over 1+T}\approx
{1+g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{F}\over g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{D1}}
\approx {R_{F}\over g_{m2}R_{D1}}\tag{21a}$$

for $g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{F}\gg 1$.

In words: two stage $CG$–$CS$ voltage gain
$A_{v}=g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{D1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{D2}^{\prime}$ enclosed
in a shunt–shunt loop of $R_{F}$.  For $T\gg 1$ the circuit is a
transimpedance $v_{O}\approx -R_{F}i_{in}$ with input resistance
$\sim R_{F}/A_{v}$ and output resistance $\sim R_{D2}/A_{v1}$,
normally a few $10\,{\rm \Omega }$.  The loop has two dominant
poles $p_{X}\approx -1/R_{D1}^{\prime}C_{X}$ and
$p_{O}\approx -1/R_{D2}^{\prime}C_{O}$ and needs the usual
$R_{F}$–$C_{F}$ or $C_{X}$ compensation for $>60^{\circ}$ phase
margin.  Including $r_{o}$ replace $R_{D}$ by $R_{D}\parallel r_{o}$
and $g_{m1}$ by $g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}$ as above.  Any of the
forms (8)–(21) is acceptable for first order hand analysis;
with $r_{o}\to\infty ,\,g_{mb}=0$ they reduce to the textbook

$$T\approx {g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m2}(R_{D2}\parallel R_{F})\over 1+g_{m1}R_{F}},\;
R_{M}\approx -R_{F}{T\over 1+T},\;
R_{in}\approx {1\over g_{m1}}{1\over 1+g_{m2}R_{D2}},\;
R_{out}\approx {R_{D2}\parallel R_{F}\over 1+T}$$

and $R_{M}\to -R_{F}$ for $T\gg 1$.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 24.

answer.text:
With ${\rm M}_{1}$ put ${\rm G}$ to ${\rm ac}$
ground and ${\rm M}_{2}$ put ${\rm S}$ to ${\rm ac}$ ground

$${\rm M}_{1}:{\rm CG}\qquad {\rm M}_{2}:{\rm CS}\qquad 
V_{G1}=V_{b}={\rm ac}\;0\;\;V_{S2}=V_{DD}={\rm ac}\;0$$

$$I_{D1}=I_{1}\tag{1}$$
$$I_{D2}+I_{in}=I_{D1}+I_{B}\tag{2}$$

at the ${\rm O/P}$ node and at the ${\rm I/P}$ node.
For the signal $I_{in}=i_{in}$ put $I_{B}=g_{B}V_{x}$,
$I_{1}=g_{I}V_{out}$,

$$g_{B}=1/R_{B}\;\;g_{I}=1/R_{I}\;\;g_{ds1}=1/r_{o1}\;\;
g_{ds2}=1/r_{o2}$$

$$g_{m1}^{\prime}=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}\tag{3}$$

for the ${\rm NMOS}$ if the bulk is to ground.
For the ${\rm PMOS}$ $g_{mb2}=0$ if $n$ well to $V_{DD}$.

Small signal Fig.1.  $v_{gs1}=-v_{x}$,
$v_{sg2}=-v_{out}$,

$${\rm M}_{1}:I_{M1}=g_{m1}^{\prime}v_{gs1}+g_{ds1}(v_{out}-v_{x})
      =-g_{m1}^{\prime}v_{x}+g_{ds1}(v_{out}-v_{x})\tag{4}$$
directed ${\rm D}\to {\rm S}$, i. e. $v_{out}\to v_{x}$.

$${\rm M}_{2}:I_{M2}=g_{m2}v_{sg2}+g_{ds2}(0-v_{x})
      =-g_{m2}v_{out}-g_{ds2}v_{x}\tag{5}$$
directed ${\rm S}\to {\rm D}$, i. e. $V_{DD}\to v_{x}$.

KCL $v_{x}$ , currents leaving $v_{x}$,

$$\eqalign{
-I_{M1}-I_{M2}+g_{B}v_{x}-i_{in}=0\cr
\left[g_{m1}^{\prime}v_{x}+g_{ds1}(v_{x}-v_{out})\right]
      +\left[g_{m2}v_{out}+g_{ds2}v_{x}\right]+g_{B}v_{x}-i_{in}=0\cr
v_{x}\left(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}+g_{B}\right)
      +v_{out}\left(g_{m2}-g_{ds1}\right)=i_{in}\tag{6}}$$

KCL $v_{out}$,

$$I_{M1}+g_{I}v_{out}=0\tag{7}$$
$$-g_{m1}^{\prime}v_{x}+g_{ds1}(v_{out}-v_{x})+g_{I}v_{out}=0$$
$$v_{x}\left(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\right)-v_{out}\left(g_{ds1}+g_{I}\right)=0\tag{8}$$

$$v_{out}=v_{x}{\displaystyle{g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\over g_{ds1}+g_{I}}}\tag{9}$$

non inverting ${\rm CG}$ gain.  Put (9) in (6)

$$v_{x}=i_{in}{\displaystyle{g_{ds1}+g_{I}\over 
\left(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}+g_{B}\right)\left(g_{ds1}+g_{I}\right)
+\left(g_{m2}-g_{ds1}\right)\left(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\right)}}\tag{10}$$

$${\cal R}_{m}\equiv {v_{out}\over i_{in}}
      ={g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\over 
      \left(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\right)\left(g_{m2}+g_{I}\right)
      +\left(g_{ds2}+g_{B}\right)\left(g_{ds1}+g_{I}\right)}\tag{11}$$

$${\cal R}_{m}>0\tag{12}$$

$$Z_{in}\equiv {v_{x}\over i_{in}}
      ={g_{ds1}+g_{I}\over 
      \left(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\right)\left(g_{m2}+g_{I}\right)
      +\left(g_{ds2}+g_{B}\right)\left(g_{ds1}+g_{I}\right)}\tag{13}$$

For $Z_{out}$ put $i_{in}=0$, drive $v_{out}=v_{t}$,
measure $i_{t}$,

$$i_{t}=I_{M1}+g_{I}v_{t}
      =-g_{m1}^{\prime}v_{x}+g_{ds1}(v_{t}-v_{x})+g_{I}v_{t}\tag{14}$$
with from (6) with $i_{in}=0$

$$v_{x}=-v_{t}{\displaystyle{g_{m2}-g_{ds1}\over 
      g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}+g_{B}}}\tag{15}$$

$$Z_{out}^{-1}={i_{t}\over v_{t}}
      =g_{ds1}+g_{I}+{\displaystyle{\left(g_{m2}-g_{ds1}\right)
      \left(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\right)\over 
      g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}+g_{B}}}\tag{16}$$

In the usual $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$, $g_{m}\gg g_{ds},g_{I},g_{B}$,

$${\cal R}_{m}\approx {1\over g_{m2}+g_{I}
      +{\displaystyle{g_{ds2}+g_{B}\over g_{m1}^{\prime}r_{o1}}}}\approx
      {1\over g_{m2}}\;\;{\rm for}\;R_{I}\to \infty \tag{17}$$

$$Z_{in}\approx {g_{ds1}+g_{I}\over g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}}
      \approx {1\over g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}r_{o1}}\;\;R_{I}\to\infty
      \approx {1\over g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}R_{I}}\;\;R_{I}\;{\rm finite}\tag{18}$$

$$Z_{out}\approx {1\over g_{m2}+g_{I}}\approx {1\over g_{m2}}
      \;\;R_{I}\to\infty \tag{19}$$

i. e. shunt at the input, shunt at the output.
Voltage sampling, current mixing, shunt-shunt,
voltage-current, transimpedance feedback.

With $g_{I}=g_{B}=0$

$${\cal R}_{m0}\approx {1\over g_{m2}}\tag{20}$$
$$R_{in0}\approx {1\over g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}r_{o1}}\tag{21}$$
$$R_{out0}\approx {1\over g_{m2}}\tag{22}$$

and with $r_{o}\to\infty$ ideal

$${\cal R}_{m}\to 1/g_{m2}\qquad R_{in}\to 0\qquad R_{out}\to 0\tag{23}$$

the ideal transimpedance amplifier.

Feedback interpretation: Break at the high impedance
gate of ${\rm M}_{2}$, $v_{t}\to v_{r}$,

$$T_{0}={v_{r}\over v_{t}}
      ={g_{m2}\left(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\right)\over 
      \left(g_{ds1}+g_{I}\right)\left(g_{ds2}+g_{B}\right)
      +g_{I}\left(g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\right)}\tag{24}$$

$$T_{0}\approx g_{m2}R_{I}\;{\rm for}\;g_{m1}^{\prime}R_{B}\gg 1
      \approx g_{m1}^{\prime}g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}\;\;R_{I},R_{B}\to\infty\tag{25}$$

product of the ${\rm CG}$ gain $\approx g_{m1}^{\prime}r_{o1}$
and the ${\rm CS}$ gain $\approx g_{m2}r_{o2}$.
Indeed from (11)

$${\cal R}_{m}={{\cal R}_{m}^{o}\over 1+T_{0}}\tag{26}$$

$${\cal R}_{m}^{o}={g_{m1}^{\prime}+g_{ds1}\over 
      \left(g_{ds2}+g_{B}\right)\left(g_{ds1}+g_{I}\right)}\approx
      g_{m1}^{\prime}r_{o1}r_{o2}\tag{27}$$

is the open loop transimpedance with $g_{m2}=0$ but
with the loading $r_{o2},R_{B}$ at the input and $R_{I}$
at the output left in place, and

$$R_{in}={R_{in}^{o}\over 1+T_{0}}\qquad 
  R_{out}={R_{out}^{o}\over 1+T_{0}}\tag{28}$$

$$R_{in}^{o}\approx r_{o2}\parallel {1\over g_{m1}^{\prime}}\approx
      {1\over g_{m1}^{\prime}}\qquad 
  R_{out}^{o}\approx r_{o1}\parallel R_{I}\tag{29}$$

in the normal Blackman form.  The feedback factor is

$$\beta ={i_{f}\over v_{out}}\approx -g_{m2}\tag{30}$$

so that ideally ${\cal R}_{m}=-1/\beta =1/g_{m2}$.

The loop is negative: $i_{in}\uparrow\to v_{x}\uparrow\to
v_{out}\uparrow\to v_{sg2}\downarrow\to i_{D2}\downarrow\to
v_{x}\downarrow$.

Poles: $p_{o}\approx 1/R_{out}^{o}C_{out}$ dominant at the
high impedance output, $p_{i}\approx 1/R_{in}^{o}C_{in}$
at the input.  With feedback both are divided by
$1+T_{0}$ and pushed to high frequency, giving wide band
low $Z_{in}$ current input.  For $T_{0}\gg 1$ the closed
loop poles become complex

$$p_{1,2}\approx \omega_{0}\left[\zeta\pm\sqrt{\zeta^{2}-1}\right]
\qquad \omega_{0}\approx\sqrt{T_{0}p_{o}p_{i}}\tag{31}$$

and the circuit is stable if $p_{o}$ is dominant,
$C_{out}\gg C_{in}$, with phase margin $\approx
90^{o}-\tan^{-1}(\omega_{0}/p_{i})$.  Normally $R_{in}$
is made very small so $p_{i}$ is at very high frequency
and the amplifier is a wide band regulated cascode
transimpedance amplifier, RGC-TIA, used as optical
receiver front end, current buffer, low impedance
current mirror with active feedback.  $1/g_{m2}$ sets the
transimpedance, $g_{m1}$ sets the input pole and the
loop gain.  Headroom is $V_{DS1}+V_{SG2}$ plus $I_{B}R_{B}$.

Including $g_{mb1}$ replace $g_{m1}\to g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$
in all formulae.  Large signal swing is limited by
${\rm M}_{1}$ leaving saturation when $v_{x}>V_{b}-V_{Tn}$
and ${\rm M}_{2}$ leaving saturation when
$v_{out}<V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|-V_{ov2}$.

answers.question: Does the circuit in Figure 5 fail to oscillate if the three capacitors become arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
With the usual unilateral one pole model the
circuit is a $3$ pole phase shift oscillator.
Put $R_{0}=r_{oN}\parallel r_{oP}$ and

$${{V_{o}}\over {V_{i}}}(s)= -{{A_{0}}\over {1+sR_{0}C_{L}}}\qquad 
A_{0}=g_{m}R_{0}\tag{*}$$

for the normal operation about $V_{I}=V_{IL}$.
Unilaterally

$$L(s)=\left[-{{A_{0}}\over {1+s\tau }}\right]^{3}\qquad 
\tau =R_{0}C_{L} \tag{1}$$

so that, with $s=j\omega $,

$$\eqalign{
|{L}|&={{A_{0}^{3}}\over {\left[1+(\omega \tau )^{2}\right]^{3/2}}}\cr
{\rm arg}{L}&=3\pi -3{\rm arctg}\omega \tau \;\;{\rm mod}\;2\pi } \tag{2}$$

${\rm arg}{L}=0\,{\rm mod}\,2\pi $ for

$$3{\rm arctg}\omega_{0}\tau =\pi \tag{3}$$

i. {\rm e.}

$${\rm arctg}\omega_{0}\tau =60^{{\rm o}}\qquad 
\omega_{0}\tau =\sqrt{3}\tag{4}$$

$${\omega_{0}={{\sqrt{3}}\over {R_{0}C_{L}}}}\tag{5}$$

apart from the normalisation by $R_{0}$.
At that frequency

$$|{L}(j\omega_{0})|={{A_{0}^{3}}\over {8}}\tag{6}$$

so that the Barkhausen start up condition

$$|{L}(j\omega_{0})|\ge 1\tag{7}$$

is

$$A_{0}=g_{m}R_{0}\ge 2\tag{8}$$

$C_{L}$ independent.  In closed loop

$$(1+s\tau )^{3}+A_{0}^{3}=0\tag{9}$$

$${1+s\tau =A_{0}e^{j(\pi +2k\pi )/3}}\tag{10}$$

$$s_{k}={{\, -1+A_{0}e^{j(\pi +2k\pi )/3}\,}\over {\tau }}\tag{11}$$

e. {\rm g.} for $k=0$

$$s_{0}={{\, -1+{1\over 2}A_{0}+j{{\sqrt{3}}\over 2}A_{0}\,}\over {\tau }}
\tag{12}$$

$${\rm Re}\,s_{0}>0\;\;{\rm for}\;\;A_{0}>2\tag{13}$$

for every $0<\tau <\infty $.  The normal
CMOS inverter has $A_{0}\sim 10-30$, so the
${\rm d.c.}$ solution $V_{1}=V_{2}=V_{3}=V_{M}$,
$V_{M}:V_{o}(V_{M})=V_{M}$, is unstable and the
circuit is astable for every finite $C_{L}>0$.

In the large signal digital language

$$t_{p}\approx 0.69R_{0}C_{L}\tag{14}$$

$$f_{{\rm osc}}={1\over {2Nt_{p}}}\approx {1\over {4.1R_{0}C_{L}}}
\propto {1\over {C_{L}}}\tag{15}$$

for $N=3$.  I. {\rm e.} in the ideal model the
circuit goes on oscillating with

$$f_{{\rm osc}}\to 0\qquad {\rm as}\qquad C_{L}\to \infty \tag{16}$$

with essentially $C_{L}$ independent start up
amplitude condition (8).  Normally quoted as

$$f_{{\rm osc}}\approx {1\over {2\pi R_{0}C_{L}}}\sqrt{3}\tag{17}$$

for the sinusoidal phase shift version.

For $C_{L}\to \infty $ the period becomes
arbitrarily long and, with any parasitic second
pole $1/R_{0}C_{p}$, supply leakage, etc., the
available small signal $g_{m}R_{0}$ at
$\omega_{0}\to 0$ is eventually degraded and the
oscillation amplitude collapses to the
meta stable $V_{M}$ point.  In that practical
sense the circuit {\it looks\/} latched if you
wait a finite time.  Apart from that second order
effect the ideal $3$ pole loop does not become
stable by making $C_{L}$ large.

> {\it Remark:\/} With the often used
> $g_{m}/sC_{L}$ integrator approximation,
> $A(s)\approx -g_{m}/sC_{L}$, ${\rm arg}A\approx
> +90^{{\rm o}}$, $3{\rm arg}A\approx 270^{{\rm o}}\ne
> 0\,{\rm mod}\,360^{{\rm o}}$, the approximation
> is invalid at the oscillation frequency (4) where
> $\omega_{0}\tau =O(1)$.

answers.question: What happens to the phase noise if the three capacitors in Figure 5 are doubled?

answer.text:
With the conventional square law long channel
${\cal R}_{o}\approx {\rm const.}$ model the circuit is the
text book ${\cal N}=3$ ring

$${\rm d}t_{d}\approx 0.69{\cal R}_{o}C_{L}\qquad 
f_{0}\approx {1\over 2{\cal N}{\rm d}t_{d}}\propto {1\over 
{\cal R}_{o}C_{L}} \tag{1}$$

$${\cal P}_{D}= {\cal N}C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f_{0}\propto 
{V_{DD}^{2}\over {\cal R}_{o}}={\rm const.}\tag{2}$$

on $C_{L}$ and in the Hajimiri-Lee time variant

$${d\varphi \over dt}={\mit\Gamma}(\omega _{0}t)
{i_{n}(t)\over q_{{\rm max}}}\qquad 
q_{{\rm max}}=C_{L}V_{sw} \tag{3}$$

$${\cal S}_{\varphi }(\Delta \omega )=
{{\mit\Gamma}_{rms}^{2}\over \Delta \omega ^{2}}
{{{\cal S}_{i}}\over {q_{{\rm max}}^{2}}}\tag{4}$$

$${\cal L}(\Delta \omega )={1\over 2}{\cal S}_{\varphi }
={{\mit\Gamma}_{rms}^{2}\over 8\pi ^{2}}
{{{\cal S}_{i}}\over {q_{{\rm max}}^{2}\Delta \omega ^{2}}}
\propto {1\over {q_{{\rm max}}^{2}}}\propto {1\over {C_{L}^{2}}}
\tag{5}$$

at a fixed absolute $\Delta \omega $ for white
${\cal S}_{i}=4kT\gamma g_{m}\approx {\rm const.}$ and,
for the ${\cal R}_{o}C_{L}$ wave form, ${\mit\Gamma}_{rms}
\approx {\rm const.}$  In Leeson's form (5) is normally
written, with (1), as

$${\cal L}(\Delta \omega )\propto {kT\over {C_{L}}}
\left({{\omega _{0}}\over {\Delta \omega }}\right)^{2}
\propto {1\over {{\cal R}_{o}^{2}C_{L}^{3}}}\tag{6}$$

i. e. in the conventional $kT/C$ shorthand

$${\cal L}\propto {1\over {C_{L}}}\tag{7}$$

so that for the same ${\cal R}_{o},V_{DD},{\cal S}_{i}$

* $f_{0}\rightarrow f_{0}/2$,
* ${\cal P}_{D}\rightarrow {\cal P}_{D}$,
* the normali{\rm s}ed, Leeson, figure of merit

$${\rm FOM}= {\cal L}(\Delta \omega )
-20\log {{\omega _{0}}\over {\Delta \omega }}
+10\log {\cal P}_{D}\tag{8}$$

is to first order invariant.

At a fixed {\it absolute\/} offset $\Delta \omega $ (6)
is

$${\cal L}_{|_{\Delta \omega ={\rm const.}}}\propto
{1\over {C_{L}^{2}}}\;\;{\rm i.e.}\;\;{1\over 4}\;{\rm per\;
doubling\;of\;}C_{L}\tag{9}$$

normally quoted in the $kT/C$ shorthand as a factor $2$,
$-3\,{\rm dB}$ per doubling of $C_{L}$, i. e. $-6\,{\rm dB}$
at fixed $\Delta \omega $ when the $\omega _{0}^{2}$ in
(6) is counted in, $-9\,{\rm dB}$ if (6) is written as
$\omega _{0}^{2}/C_{L}$.  With the usual textbook
abbreviation (7) the SSB white $1/f^{2}$ phase noise power
is halved, $-3\,{\rm dB}$, the $1/f^{3}$ $1/f$ phase noise
power is reduced by the same amount, on doubling $C_{L}$.
Including the $f_{0}\rightarrow f_{0}/2$ shift this is a
factor $4$, $-6\,{\rm dB}$, at the same absolute $\Delta f$,
a factor $8$, $-9\,{\rm dB}$, in the form (6).

Referred to the new carrier, i. e. at $\Delta \omega \propto
\omega _{0}$, ${\cal L}(\Delta \omega \propto \omega _{0})
\approx {\rm const.}$, ${\rm FOM}\approx {\rm const.}$  In
absolute jitter language the threshold crossing jitter

$$\sigma _{v}^{2}={kT\over {C_{L}}}\qquad 
{\rm SR}={V_{sw}\over {{\cal R}_{o}C_{L}}}\qquad 
\sigma _{t}={\sigma _{v}\over {{\rm SR}}}\propto 
{\cal R}_{o}\sqrt{kTC_{L}}\tag{10}$$

$$\sigma _{T}^{2}={\cal N}\sigma _{t}^{2}\propto 
{\cal R}_{o}^{2}kTC_{L}\tag{11}$$

so that the period jitter variance grows $\propto C_{L}$,
${\rm rms}\propto \sqrt{C_{L}}$, $\times \sqrt{2}$ per
doubling of $C_{L}$, while

$${\cal S}_{t}={{\cal S}_{\varphi }\over {\omega _{0}^{2}}}
\propto {\cal R}_{o}\tag{12}$$

is to first order $C_{L}$ independent.  In compact form:
$f_{0}/2$, ${\cal P}_{D}\approx {\rm const.}$, ${\rm FOM}
\approx {\rm const.}$, ${\cal L}(\Delta f={\rm const.})
\approx {\cal L}_{0}-3\,{\rm dB}$ in $kT/C$ language,
${\cal L}_{0}-6\,{\rm dB}$ at fixed absolute $\Delta f$
including the $f_{0}^{2}$ factor, $\sigma _{T}\rightarrow
\sqrt{2}\sigma _{T}$.  Any of the equivalent $-3\,{\rm dB}$
$kT/C$, $-6\,{\rm dB}$ at fixed $\Delta f$, ${\rm FOM}=
{\rm const.}$ statements is accepted as {\it the phase
noise gets better by $3\,{\rm dB}$, $6\,{\rm dB}$ at fixed
offset, while the oscillator gets a factor two slower\/}. 
With normalisation to the carrier the phase noise is often
quoted as {\it unchanged\/}.

answers.question: Does the circuit in Figure 6 fail to oscillate if CL becomes arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
With the usual idealisation the 3 invertor ring is a
large signal relaxation oscillator and a large signal
limit cycle exists for every finite ${\cal C}_{L}$.
Put

$$L(s)=-{g_{m1}r_{01}\over {1+s r_{01}{\cal C}_{L}}}
{g_{m2}r_{02}\over {1+s r_{02}C_{0}}}
{g_{m3}r_{03}\over {1+s r_{03}C_{0}}}\tag{*}$$

$C_{0}$ the normal parasitic pole,
$\omega _{0}=1/r_{0}C_{0}$, $\omega _{1}=1/r_{01}{\cal C}_{L}$.
For ${\cal C}_{L}=0$, $\omega _{1}\approx \omega _{0}$,

$$1-L(s)=0\qquad L(j\omega )=1\tag{**}$$

has a pair of complex poles in the RHP for

$$A=g_{m}r_{0}>2$$

and the conventional $3\times 60^{{\rm o}}$ Barkhausen
oscillation at

$$\omega _{{\rm osc}}\approx \sqrt{3}\,\omega _{0}\qquad 
|{L(j\omega _{{\rm osc}})}|\approx {A^{3}\over 8}>1$$

starts up from noise.

Put $\omega _{1}=\varepsilon \ll \omega _{0}$.
From {\rm (*)} for $\varepsilon <\omega <\omega _{0}$

$$|{L}|\approx {A^{3}\varepsilon \over {\omega }},\qquad 
\arg L = \pi -\tan ^{-1}{\omega \over {\varepsilon }}
-2\tan ^{-1}{\omega \over {\omega _{0}}}$$

$\arg L =2\pi $ for

$$\tan ^{-1}{\omega \over {\varepsilon }}+
2\tan ^{-1}{\omega \over {\omega _{0}}}=\pi \tag{***}$$

For $\varepsilon \ll \omega _{0}$ {\rm (***)} is

$${\pi \over 2}+2\tan ^{-1}{\omega \over {\omega _{0}}}=\pi
\;\;,\;\; \omega \approx \omega _{0}$$

and at the $2\pi $ cross over

$$|{L(j\omega _{0})}|\approx {A^{3}\over {\sqrt{1+(\omega _{0}/
\varepsilon )^{2}}}}{1\over 2}\approx {A^{3}\over 2}
{\varepsilon \over {\omega _{0}}}= {A^{3}\over 2}{C_{0}\over 
{\cal C}_{L}}\rightarrow 0\tag{****}$$

for ${\cal C}_{L}\rightarrow \infty $.
In closed loop

$$(1+s/\varepsilon )(1+s/\omega _{0})^{2}+A^{3}=0$$

$${s^{3}\over {\varepsilon \omega _{0}^{2}}}+
s^{2}\left({1\over {\omega _{0}^{2}}}+{2\over {\varepsilon 
\omega _{0}}}\right)+s\left({2\over {\omega _{0}}}+{1\over 
{\varepsilon }}\right)+1+A^{3}=0$$

$$s^{3}+s^{2}(\varepsilon +2\omega _{0})+s(\omega _{0}^{2}+
2\varepsilon \omega _{0})+\varepsilon \omega _{0}^{2}(1+A^{3})=0$$

Routh gives stability, {\it i. e.} the normal
meta stable $V_{1}=V_{2}=V_{3}=V_{T}$ bias point becomes
stable, for

$$a_{2}a_{1}>a_{0}\;\;,\;\;(\varepsilon +2\omega _{0})
(\omega _{0}^{2}+2\varepsilon \omega _{0})>
\varepsilon \omega _{0}^{2}(1+A^{3})$$

$$A^{3}<2{\omega _{0}\over {\varepsilon }}+4+2{\varepsilon 
\over {\omega _{0}}}\approx 2{{\cal C}_{L}\over {C_{0}}}\tag{\dag}$$

So for

$${\cal C}_{L}>{\cal C}_{L{\rm crit}}\approx {1\over 2}A^{3}C_{0}$$

the linearised circuit is stable and will not start up
from ${\cal O}(kT/C)$ noise.  In AC terms the big
${\cal C}_{L}$ short circuits the loop, the loop is a
one pole $\approx 90^{{\rm o}}$ loop and can never make
the $180^{{\rm o}}$ excess phase with $|{L}|>1$ required
for Barkhausen.

That is the small signal story.  Large signal the
invertors are comparators.  With $r_{01}{\cal C}_{L}\gg
t_{p2}+t_{p3}$ put $t_{p}=t_{p2}+t_{p3}$ and idealise
$I_{2},I_{3}$ as $0$ delay relays, $V_{T}=V_{DD}/2$,

$$\eqalign{
X<V_{T}&\Rightarrow Y=V_{DD}\;,\;Z=0\cr
X>V_{T}&\Rightarrow Y=0\;,\;Z=V_{DD}\cr}$$

so that $Z(t)=X(t-2t_{p})$ in the relay sense and

$${\cal C}_{L}\dot X = \left[f(Z)-X\right]/r_{01}\tag{\ddag}$$

$f$ the normal $V_{TC}$, $f^{\,\prime}(V_{T})=-A$.
For $X$ outside the $\sim V_{DD}/A^{2}$ wide
$Z=f(f(X))$ transition $Z$ is saturated and {\rm (\ddag)}
is $X\to V_{DD}$ for $Z=0$ and $X\to 0$ for $Z=V_{DD}$.
$X$ ramps exponentially to the opposite rail, crosses
$V_{T}$, $2t_{p}$ later $Z$ flips and $X$ ramps back.
That is the normal relaxation limit cycle with, for
$0\to V_{DD}$ charging through $r_{p}$ and $V_{DD}\to 0$
discharging through $r_{n}$,

$$T\approx r_{p}{\cal C}_{L}\ln {V_{DD}-V_{L}\over 
V_{DD}-V_{H}}+r_{n}{\cal C}_{L}\ln {V_{H}\over V_{L}}
+2(t_{pLH}+t_{pHL})\tag{\S}$$

$V_{H,L}$ the $I_{2}$ thresholds, {\it i. e.} $f_{{\rm
osc}}\propto 1/{\cal C}_{L}\to 0$ for ${\cal C}_{L}\to
\infty $.  The $2t_{p}$ delay makes the $X$ over shoot

$$\Delta V\approx (V_{DD}-V_{T})\left[1-
\exp (-2t_{p}/r_{0}{\cal C}_{L})\right]\approx
(V_{DD}-V_{T}){2t_{p}\over r_{0}{\cal C}_{L}}\to 0\tag{\P}$$

so the large signal limit cycle shrinks to the meta
stable point $X=Y=Z=V_{T}$ as ${\cal C}_{L}\to \infty $.
For ${\cal C}_{L}>{\cal C}_{L{\rm crit}}$ the meta
stable point is small signal stable, the ${\cal O}
(\Delta V)$ limit cycle is small signal stable and can
only be reached with a finite, ${\cal O}(V_{DD})$,
kick, {\it e. g.} power up with ${\cal C}_{L}$
discharged.  With infinitesimal noise the circuit stays
put at $V_{T}$.

In ordinary language: for every finite ${\cal C}_{L}$
there is still, mathematically, a periodic solution;
its frequency goes as {\rm (\S)} to zero and its
amplitude goes as {\rm (\P)} to zero.  For all
practical, small signal, Barkhausen, self starting
purposes the circuit is normally said to {\it fail to
oscillate} for

$${\cal C}_{L}\gg A^{3}C_{0}\tag{\dag}$$

and in the strict ${\cal C}_{L}\to \infty $ AC short
limit the loop is broken.  With the usual textbook
idealisation {\it the odd ring always oscillates} the
answer is often quoted as {\it no, it still oscillates,
just with $f_{{\rm osc}}\approx [2(r_{0}{\cal C}_{L}+
2t_{p})]^{-1}$ and with an exponential saw tooth on the
loaded node.}  The caveat above is the rigorous
small signal version of that statement.

answers.question: If we double the widths of the NMOS and PMOS devices in Figure 7, what happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
With the normal long channel square law
shorthand the 3 stage current starved loop can be
written, e. g. in the Hajimiri form, as

$${\cal L}(\Delta \omega )=10\log \left[
{1\over 8\pi ^{2}\Delta f^{2}}{1\over q_{{\rm max}}^{2}}
\sum_{n}{1\over T_{0}}\int_{0}^{T_{0}}\Gamma _{n}^{2}(t)
{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}\over {\mit\Delta} f}dt\right]\tag{*}$$

$$q_{{\rm max}}=C_{T}V_{DD}\qquad 
{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}\over {\mit\Delta} f}=4kT\gamma g_{m}
+K_{f}{g_{m}^{2}\over C_{ox}WL}{1\over f}+\cdots $$

$$f_{0}\approx {1\over 2NT_{D}}\qquad 
T_{D}\approx {C_{T}V_{DD}\over I_{D}}\tag{**}$$

$C_{T}=C_{gs}+C_{gd}+C_{db}+C_{int}$ is the total
capacitance on the node and, for $C_{int}\ll C_{dev}$,

$$C_{T}\propto W\qquad I_{D}\propto W\qquad g_{m}\propto W\tag{***}$$

so that, to first order, from (**) the small signal
loop gain, the large signal swing, $\approx V_{DD}$,
the delay $T_{D}$ and the oscillation frequency

$$f_{0}\propto {I_{D}\over C_{T}}$$

and the shape of the waveform and of the
isochrone sensitivity function $\Gamma (t)$ are
unchanged.  From (*)--(***)

$${\overline{i_{n,W}^{2}}\over {\mit\Delta} f}\propto W\tag{1}$$
$$q_{{\rm max}}^{2}\propto C_{T}^{2}\propto W^{2}\tag{2}$$

so that for the white, ${\cal L}\propto 1/{\mit\Delta}
f^{2}$, part

$${\cal L}_{W}\propto {{\overline{i_{n,W}^{2}}/{\mit\Delta} f}
\over q_{{\rm max}}^{2}}\propto {1\over W}\tag{3}$$

and, with ${\overline{i_{n,1/f}^{2}}/{\mit\Delta} f}
\propto g_{m}^{2}/WL\propto W$,

$${\cal L}_{1/f}\propto {{\overline{i_{n,1/f}^{2}}/{\mit\Delta} f}
\over q_{{\rm max}}^{2}}\propto {1\over W}\tag{4}$$

in power, $\propto 1/\sqrt{W}$ in voltage.
Normalised to the input referred $1/f$ voltage,
${\overline{v_{n,1/f}^{2}}/{\mit\Delta} f}\propto 1/WL$,

$${\cal L}_{1/f}\propto {1\over W^{2}}\tag{4a}$$

is often quoted as $6\,{\rm dB}$ per octave of $W$.
In absolute ${\rm dBc/Hz}$ at the same $V_{DD}$,
$L$ and $W$ the same,

$${\cal L}{\Bigl|}_{2W}\approx {1\over 2}{\cal L}{\Bigl|}_{W}
\;\;{\rm white}\tag{5}$$

i. e. $\approx 3\,{\rm dB}$ lower power, $\approx
\sqrt{2}$ lower voltage, $\approx 6\,{\rm dB}$ lower
in the $1/{\mit\Delta} f^{3}$ $1/f$ skirt if (4a) is
used, at the expense of

$$P_{D}=NC_{T}V_{DD}^{2}f_{0}\propto W\tag{6}$$

twice the dynamic, and twice the static,
$I_{D}V_{DD}$, power dissipation.  Normalised to
power dissipation the conventional

$${\rm FoM}={\cal L}(\Delta f)-20\log {f_{0}\over \Delta f}
+10\log P_{D}\tag{7}$$

is to first order $W$ independent,

$${\rm FoM}_{2W}\approx {\rm FoM}_{W}\tag{8}$$

so that at constant $P_{D}$ there is, to first order,
no improvement.  In the form (7) the result is normally
quoted as {\it no change\/}.  With $C_{int}\ne 0$ the
absolute improvement is $<3\,{\rm dB}$, white, $<6\,{\rm
dB}$, $1/f^{3}$, and the FoM normally degrades.

> {\it Remark:\/}  With $C_{T}=C_{dev}+C_{int}$,
> $C_{dev}\propto W$, $f_{0}\propto I_{D}/C_{T}$ rises
> somewhat and (3)--(4) become ${\cal L}\propto
> C_{T}^{-2}$.  E. g. for $C_{int}\approx C_{dev}$ doubling
> $W$ gives $C_{T}\rightarrow 1.5C_{T}$,
> $f_{0}\rightarrow 1.33f_{0}$, $P_{D}\rightarrow 2P_{D}$,
> ${\cal L}_{W}\rightarrow 0.66{\cal L}_{W}$, $-1.8\,{\rm dB}$,
> ${\rm FoM}\rightarrow +1.2\,{\rm dB}$ degradation.

answers.question:
Determine the small-signal resistance seen looking into the supply node of the ring oscillator in Figure 8.

Use `CL` for the effective load capacitance at each internal oscillator node,
and use `f0` for the oscillation frequency.

answer.text:
With the usual averaging the ${\rm V}_{DD}$ current is
the charge that has to be put on to the ${\rm N}$ ${\rm
C}_{L}$'s once a period

$${\rm d}Q_{D}= {\rm N}{\rm C}_{L}{\rm d}{\rm V}_{DD}\tag{*}$$

so that, with ${\rm T}_{0}=f_{0}^{-1}$ the (large signal)
period,

$${\rm I}_{DD}={{\rm d}Q_{D}\over {\rm T}_{0}}
      ={\rm N}{\rm C}_{L}{\rm V}_{DD}f_{0}\tag{1}$$

and, for ${\rm N}=3$,

$${\rm R}_{X0}={{\rm V}_{DD}\over {\rm I}_{DD}}={1\over 
{\rm N}{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}}={1\over 3{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}}\tag{2}$$

per inverter

$${\rm R}_{X0}^{(1)}\approx {1\over {\rm C}_{L}f_{0}}\tag{2a}$$

in parallel for the ${\rm N}$ phases.
In the conventional ${\rm S-C}$ notation

$${\rm R}_{X0}^{(1)}={1\over {\rm C}_{L}f_{{\rm c}}}\qquad 
{\rm R}_{X0}={1\over {\rm N}{\rm C}_{L}f_{{\rm c}}}\tag{3}$$

with $f_{{\rm c}}=f_{0}$ the commutation frequency.
Eq.{\rm (2)} is normally quoted, to within a factor $2$,
simply as

$$\left|{\rm R}_{X}\right|\sim {1\over {\rm C}_{L}f_{0}}\tag{4}$$

The incremental resistance is

$${\rm r}_{x}^{-1}={{\rm d}{\rm I}_{DD}\over {\rm d}{\rm V}_{DD}}
      ={\rm N}{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}+{\rm N}{\rm C}_{L}{\rm V}_{DD}
        { {\rm d}f_{0}\over {\rm d}{\rm V}_{DD}} \tag{5}$$

so that, for $f_{0}={\rm const.}$,

$${\rm r}_{x}={\rm R}_{X0}={1\over {\rm N}{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}}\tag{6}$$

If the ${\rm V}_{DD}$ dependence of the oscillation
frequency is retained, e. {\rm g.} in the conventional
${\rm t}_{d}\propto {\rm C}_{L}{\rm V}_{DD}/{\rm I}_{D}$,
$f_{0}\propto {\rm V}_{DD}$ approximation,

$${\rm V}_{DD}{ {\rm d}f_{0}\over {\rm d}{\rm V}_{DD}}\approx f_{0}\tag{7}$$

$${\rm r}_{x}\approx {1\over 2{\rm N}{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}}\tag{8}$$

i. {\rm e.} for the three phase ring, large signal,

$${\rm R}_{X}\approx {1\over 3{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}}\;\;{\rm per\;ring}
\;\;{1\over {\rm C}_{L}f_{0}}\;\;{\rm per\;phase}\tag{9}$$

and, incremental,

$${\rm r}_{x}\approx {1\over 6{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}}\;\;{\rm per\;ring}
\;\;{1\over 2{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}}\;\;{\rm per\;phase}\tag{10}$$

normally quoted with the sign of the active circuit,

$${\rm r}_{x}\approx -{1\over 2{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}}\;\;{\rm per\;phase}
\qquad {\rm r}_{x}\approx -{1\over 6{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}}\;\;
{\rm for\;N}=3 \tag{11}$$

and ${\rm R}_{X}\approx -1/{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}$,
$-1/3{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}$ large signal.  Any factor $2$,
$3$, $\pi $ is normally dropped and the circuit is quoted
simply as a ${\rm S-C}$ resistor

$$\left|{\rm r}_{x}\right|\sim {1\over {\rm C}_{L}f_{0}}\tag{12}$$

per phase, $\left|{\rm r}_{x}\right|\sim 1/{\rm N}{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}$
for the ${\rm N}$ phases in parallel.

With the Barkhausen linearisation, ${\rm G}_{m}{\rm R}_{0}=2$,
$\omega _{0}{\rm R}_{0}{\rm C}_{L}=\sqrt{3}$ for ${\rm N}=3$,

$${\rm G}_{m}={2\over {\rm R}_{0}}={2\omega _{0}{\rm C}_{L}\over 
\sqrt{3}}={4\pi \over \sqrt{3}}{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}\tag{13}$$

so that, e. {\rm g.} with ${\rm g}_{mp}={\rm g}_{mn}={\rm G}_{m}/2$,

$${\rm R}_{X}(0)={{\rm G}_{m}+{\rm R}_{0}^{-1}\over 
3\left({\rm g}_{mp}+{\rm r}_{op}^{-1}\right)
\left({\rm g}_{mn}+{\rm r}_{on}^{-1}\right)}
\approx {{\rm G}_{m}\over 3{\rm g}_{mp}{\rm g}_{mn}}
\approx {2\over 3{\rm g}_{m}}\approx {1\over \pi \sqrt{3}\,
{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}}\approx 0.18{{\rm 1}\over {\rm C}_{L}f_{0}}\tag{14}$$

per ring, $\approx 0.55/{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}$ per phase,
i. {\rm e.} to within the usual factor $2\pi /\sqrt{3}$ the
same as Eq.{\rm (2)}--{\rm (4)}.  In magnitude

$$\left|{\rm Z}_{x}(j\omega _{0})\right|\approx 
{1\over {\rm g}_{m}}\approx {\sqrt{3}\over 4\pi }{1\over 
{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}}\approx 0.14{1\over {\rm C}_{L}f_{0}}\tag{15}$$

per phase, $\approx 0.05/{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}$ for the three
phases in parallel.  Dropping the $2\pi /\sqrt{3}$ this is
Eq.{\rm (4)}, ${\rm R}_{X}\sim 1/{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}$,
${\rm R}_{X}\sim 1/3{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}$ for the complete
oscillator, a factor $2$ smaller, ${\rm R}_{X}\sim
1/2{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}$, $1/6{\rm C}_{L}f_{0}$ total, for the
incremental resistance.  E. {\rm g.} ${\rm C}_{L}=50\,{\rm fF}$,
$f_{0}=1\,{\rm GHz}$, $\left|{\rm R}_{X}\right|\sim
20\,{\rm k\Omega }$ per phase, $\sim 7\,{\rm k\Omega }$
large signal, $\sim 3\,{\rm k\Omega }$ incremental for the
$3$ phase ring, $\sim 1\,{\rm k\Omega }$ in the linearised
Barkhausen approximation.

answers.question:
For the ring oscillator in Figure 8, consider the small-signal resistance `RX`
seen looking into the supply node.

Use `CL` for the effective load capacitance at each internal oscillator node,
`f0` for the oscillation frequency, and `TD` for the delay of one inverter stage.

From the dynamic charging and discharging of the three load capacitances, one
can write

```text
RX ~= 1 / (3 f0 CL)
```

Somebody then argues that, because the circuit is oscillating, the path from
`VDD` to ground through the transistors is off for much of the cycle, so the
average resistance should be much higher than the MOS on-resistance or inverse
transconductance scale.

Do you agree with this argument?

answer.text:
With the usual abuse of language $R_{X}=V_{DD}/I_{DD}$
is not $\langle R(t)\rangle $ but $V_{DD}/\langle I(t)\rangle $.
It is a switched $C$ resistor.

$${\rm Energy/cycle}= \sum C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}\tag{1}$$

$$P_{DC}=V_{DD}I_{av}=3C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f_{0}\tag{2}$$

$$I_{av}=3C_{L}V_{DD}f_{0}\tag{3}$$

$$R_{X,DC}\equiv {V_{DD}\over I_{av}}={1\over 3f_{0}C_{L}}\tag{4}$$

in the low frequency, $f\ll f_{0}$, time averaged sense.
For $f\sim f_{0}$ it is a $R\parallel C$ with
a large reactive part and, with the usual
linearisation about the limit cycle, even a
negative $R$ at $f\approx f_{0}$.  The
magnitude is (4).

For the free running ring

$$T_{0}={1\over f_{0}}\approx 2NT_{D}\tag{5}$$

$$N=3\qquad T_{0}\approx 6T_{D}\qquad f_{0}\approx {1\over 6T_{D}} \tag{6}$$

so that

$$R_{X}\approx {2T_{D}\over C_{L}} \tag{7}$$

But $T_{D}$ is itself $C_{L}$ times the
inverter driving impedance.

To order of magnitude

$$T_{D}\approx 0.69R_{on}C_{L}\approx {C_{L}\over g_{m}}
\approx {C_{L}V_{DD}\over 2I_{D}} \tag{8}$$

$R_{on}\sim 1/g_{m}\sim V_{DD}/I_{D}$ is the
large signal on resistance, small signal
$1/g_{m}$, $r_{o}$ of the inverter at the
switching point.

Hence from (7)-(8)

$$R_{X}\approx 1.4R_{on}\approx {2\over g_{m}}\approx {V_{DD}\over I_{D}} \tag{9}$$

more generally

$$R_{X}\sim {N\over g_{m}}\sim N\,R_{on}\tag{10}$$

i. e. of the order of the MOS driving
impedance, inverse $g_{m}$, $r_{o}$, $R_{on}$.

In switched $C$ language $R=1/fC$.  $R$ is
large only if $f\ll 1/R_{on}C$.  Here
$f_{0}\sim 1/R_{on}C$ by construction, so
$R_{X}\sim R_{on}$.

The time averaged small signal conductance

$$\langle G(t)\rangle ={1\over T_{0}}\int_{0}^{T_{0}}G(t)dt
\approx {1\over R_{on}}{T_{D}\over T_{0}}\sim {1\over NR_{on}} \tag{11}$$

is $1/NR_{on}$, not $0$.  The time averaged
resistance $\langle R(t)\rangle $ diverges
when the switch is off, but

$$\langle R(t)\rangle \ne {1\over \langle G(t)\rangle }
\ne {V_{DD}\over \langle I(t)\rangle } \tag{12}$$

What is averaged is the charge, the current.
When the $p$-switch is on the current is
large, $\sim V_{DD}/R_{on}$, charging $C_{L}$
with $dV/dt\sim I/C_{L}$.  The $I_{DD}$ is
essentially displacement current into $C_{L}$,
not $d.c.$ crow bar current $V_{DD}$ to $GND$.
$C_{L}$ is an $a.c.$ short to ground at
$f\sim f_{0}$.  The fact that the $d.c.$
path $V_{DD}$ to $GND$ is open most of the
time is irrelevant to the $a.c.$ impedance
seen looking into $V_{DD}$.

In small signal incremental form, $f_{0}=f_{0}(V_{DD})$,

$$I_{av}=3C_{L}V_{DD}f_{0}(V_{DD})$$

$$G_{x}={dI_{av}\over dV_{DD}}=3C_{L}f_{0}+3C_{L}V_{DD}{df_{0}\over dV_{DD}}>3C_{L}f_{0}\tag{13}$$

$$R_{x}={1\over G_{x}}<{1\over 3f_{0}C_{L}}=R_{X,DC}\tag{14}$$

because $df_{0}/dV_{DD}>0$, so incrementally
it is even smaller.

Only if the ring is slowed down artificially,
current starved, $C_{L}$ heavily padded,
$f_{0}\ll 1/R_{on}C_{L}$, does (4) become
$\gg R_{on}$.  For the normal free running
ring it is $\sim R_{on}$.  The $CV^{2}f$
power is not small.  Up to a factor $N$ the
``resistor'' seen from the supply is the
MOS $1/g_{m}$ itself.

answers.question: In the circuit of Figure 9, what happens to the initial voltage gain as the width of M7 increases?

answer.text:
With the usual abuse of language the {\it small signal}
gain before the ${\rm p}$ latch fires is the gain of the
${\rm n}$ latch

$${\cal A}_{0}\approx g_{m1,2}R_{0}\qquad 
R_{0}^{-1}=g_{o1}+g_{o3}\mp g_{m3}\tag{*}$$

and, in the dynamic sense, the integrated gain

$${\cal A}_{0,{\rm int}}={{g_{m1,2}\Delta t}\over {C_{X}}}$$

$\Delta t$ being the time the $X-Y$ capacity has to
integrate the $g_{m}v_{id}$ current before the ${\rm p}$
cross coupled pair fires.  In normal operation

* $S_{1}-S_{4}$ on, $M_{7}$ off, $P=Q=X=Y=V_{DD}$,
$M_{3}-M_{6}$ off;
* $CK\uparrow $, $S_{i}$ off, $M_{7}$ on, $P,Q$ ramp
down with

$$I_{0}=I_{D7}\approx {1\over 2}\mu _{n}C_{ox}
\left({W\over L}\right)_{7}\left( V_{DD}-V_{T}\right)^{2}
\tag{1}$$

in strong inversion, $I_{0}=I_{0}(W_{7})$,

$$C_{P}{{dV_{P}}\over {dt}}\approx -{I_{0}\over 2}\tag{2}$$

so that $M_{3,4}$ fire after

$$t_{1}=C_{P}V_{Tn}/I_{0}/2\tag{3}$$

and $X,Y$ stay at $V_{DD}$ for $0<t<t_{1}$.

For $t>t_{1}$ $M_{3,4}$ are on in saturation and

$$C_{X}{{dV_{X}}\over {dt}}\approx -{I_{0}\over 2}\tag{4}$$

so that the ${\rm p}$ pair fires when

$$|V_{X}-V_{DD}|=|V_{Tp}|$$

i. e. after

$$t_{2}-t_{1}\equiv \Delta t =C_{X}|V_{Tp}|/I_{0}/2\tag{5}$$

from the firing of the ${\rm n}$ pair.  During $\Delta t$
the signal current

$$\Delta I =g_{m1,2}v_{id}\tag{6}$$

is integrated on $C_{X}$,

$$\Delta V_{XY}= {{\Delta I\Delta t}\over {C_{X}}}
      =g_{m1,2}v_{id}{{\Delta t}\over {C_{X}}}
      ={{2g_{m1,2}|V_{Tp}|}\over {I_{0}}}v_{id}\tag{7}$$

i. e. the normally quoted {\it initial} or {\it
pre--amp} gain at the moment the CMOS latch is enabled is

$${\cal A}_{0,{\rm int}}\equiv {{\Delta V_{XY}}\over {v_{id}}}
      ={{2|V_{Tp}|g_{m1,2}}\over {I_{0}}}\tag{8}$$

apart from the conventional $g_{m}R_{0}$ form (*).

For the square law long channel MOS

$$g_{m1,2}= \sqrt{2\mu _{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}I_{D1}}\propto
\sqrt{I_{0}}\propto \sqrt{W_{7}}\tag{9}$$

$$g_{o1,3}\propto I_{0}\propto W_{7}\qquad 
R_{0}\propto 1/I_{0}\tag{10}$$

so that, formally,

$${\cal A}_{0}=g_{m1,2}R_{0}\propto {1\over {\sqrt{I_{0}}}}
\propto {1\over {\sqrt{W_{7}}}}\tag{11}$$

and from (8)--(9)

$${\cal A}_{0,{\rm int}}\propto {{g_{m1,2}}\over {I_{0}}}
\propto {1\over {\sqrt{I_{0}}}}\propto {1\over {\sqrt{W_{7}}}}
\tag{12}$$

in strong inversion,

$${\cal A}_{0,{\rm int}}\approx 
|V_{Tp}|\sqrt{{{2\mu _{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}}\over {I_{0}}}}
\propto W_{7}^{-1/2}\tag{13}$$

i. e. the $g_{m}$ increase $\propto \sqrt{W_{7}}$ is more
than compensated by the $1/W_{7}$ decrease of the
integration time, Eq.\,5, or, what is the same, by the
$1/W_{7}$ decrease of $R_{0}$.  In velocity saturation
$g_{m}\propto W_{1}$ is $I_{0}$ independent and

$${\cal A}_{0,{\rm int}}\propto 1/I_{0}\propto 1/W_{7}\tag{14}$$

while in weak inversion

$$g_{m}=I_{D}/nV_{T}\tag{15}$$

so that

$${\cal A}_{0,{\rm int}}={{2|V_{Tp}|}\over {nV_{T}}}={\rm const.}
\tag{16}$$

$W_{7}$ independent to first order.  Including the
conventional $r_{o}\propto 1/\lambda I_{D}$ the product
$g_{m}r_{o}=2/\lambda V_{ov}\propto 1/\sqrt{I_{0}}$ is
normally quoted as {\it to first order $W_{7}$
independent}.  With the usual textbook abuse of language
the $g_{m}$ in the numerator is often quoted alone,

$${\cal A}_{0}\propto g_{m1,2}\propto \sqrt{W_{7}}\;\;{\rm
naive},\tag{17}$$

so that the small signal $g_{m}R_{0}$ gain is said to
{\it increase} as $\sqrt{W_{7}}$.  The physically
relevant, dynamically integrated, gain (8) does the
opposite.  To the order most text books keep the two
effects cancel and ${\cal A}_{0}$ is quoted as
essentially $W_{7}$ independent, the second order
correction being a weak decrease with $W_{7}$, Eq.\,12,
at constant $(W/L)_{1}$, becoming $W_{7}$ independent,
Eq.\,16, in subthreshold and falling as $1/W_{7}$,
Eq.\,14, when $M_{1,2}$ are pushed into the triode by the
large $I_{0}$.

In particular for the normal strong inversion design the
useful pre--amplification before regeneration,

$${\cal A}_{0}\approx {{g_{m1,2}}\over {g_{m3}+g_{o1}+g_{o3}}}
\approx {{g_{m1,2}|V_{Tp}|}\over {I_{0}/2}},$$

degrades when $M_{7}$ is widened, the price paid for the
decrease of the latch time constant

$$\tau_{{\rm latch}}\approx {C_{X}\over {g_{m3}+g_{m5}}}
\propto {1\over {\sqrt{W_{7}}}}$$

and the increase in speed.  Any increase quoted as
${\cal A}_{0}\propto \sqrt{W_{7}}$ is the bare $g_{m}$
increase, Eq.\,17, before the $1/I_{0}$ integration time
is accounted for.  With that conventional definition
${\cal A}_{0}$ increases $\propto W_{7}^{1/2}$ in strong
inversion and is $\propto W_{7}^{0}$ in weak inversion.

answers.question: In Figure 9, what happens to the initial voltage gain if we increase the capacitance at nodes P and Q?

answer.text:
With the usual long channel square law
notation the circuit can be looked at as a
dynamic integrator

$${\rm d}V_{P,Q}/{\rm d}t=-I_{D1,2}/C_{P,Q}\qquad 
{\rm d}V_{X,Y}/{\rm d}t=-I_{D3,4}/C_{X,Y}\tag{1}$$

for $CK=0\;V_{P}=V_{Q}=V_{X}=V_{Y}=V_{DD}$,
$M_{7}$ off.  For $CK=1$, $S_{1-4}$ off,
$M_{7}$ on, $I_{T}=I_{D1}+I_{D2}$,

$$V_{P,Q}(t)=V_{DD}-I_{D1,2}t/C_{P,Q}\tag{2}$$

$$V_{X,Y}(t)=V_{DD}\;\;t<t_{1}\tag{3}$$

$M_{3}$ conducts when

$$V_{GS3}=V_{Y}-V_{P}=V_{Tn}\tag{4}$$

i. e. when $V_{P}$ has fallen by $V_{Tn}$,

$$t_{1}=C_{P}V_{Tn}/I_{CM}\qquad I_{CM}=I_{T}/2\tag{5}$$

and $M_{5}$ conducts when $V_{X,Y}$ has fallen by
$|V_{Tp}|$,

$$t_{2}=C_{X}|V_{Tp}|/I_{CM}\tag{6}$$

$t_{2}$ is $C_{P}$ independent.  During $0<t<t_{1}$

$$\Delta V_{PQ}(t)=V_{P}-V_{Q}
      =-\,{\Delta I_{D}\over C_{P}}t
      =-\,{g_{m1}\Delta V_{in}\over C_{P}}t\tag{7}$$

so that at the moment the $n$ - cross coupled pair
turns on

$$\Delta V_{PQ1}\equiv \Delta V_{PQ}(t_{1})
      =-\,{g_{m1}\Delta V_{in}\over C_{P}}t_{1}
      =-\,{g_{m1}V_{Tn}\over I_{CM}}\Delta V_{in}\tag{8}$$

$C_{P}$ drops out.  In the conventional
$I\,t/C$ language the {\it integration} gain

$$A_{0}\equiv {\Delta V_{PQ1}\over \Delta V_{in}}
      ={g_{m1}V_{Tn}\over I_{CM}}\tag{9}$$

and, if the $n$ -pair is regarded as a simple
cascode,

$$A_{X}\approx {g_{m1}t_{2}\over C_{X}}
      ={g_{m1}|V_{Tp}|\over I_{CM}}\tag{10}$$

are $C_{P}$ independent.  Keeping the small
signal positive feedback of $M_{3}-M_{4}$,
$g_{ds}\approx 0$,

$$\eqalign{
C_{P}{\rm d}\Delta V_{P}/{\rm d}t &=
      -g_{m1}\Delta V_{in}+g_{m3}(\Delta V_{P}+\Delta V_{X})\cr
C_{X}{\rm d}\Delta V_{X}/{\rm d}t &=
      \phantom{-}g_{m3}(\Delta V_{P}+\Delta V_{X})\cr}\tag{11}$$

$\Delta V_{P}=V_{P}-V_{Q}$, $\Delta V_{X}=V_{X}-V_{Y}$.
Put ${\bf v}=[\Delta V_{P}\;\Delta V_{X}]^{T}$,

$${\rm d}{\bf v}/{\rm d}t={\bf A}{\bf v}+{\bf b}\Delta V_{in},
\qquad 
{\bf A}=g_{m3}\left[{{1/C_{P}\;\;1/C_{P}}\atop{1/C_{X}\;\;1/C_{X}}}\right]
\tag{12}$$

${\bf A}$ has eigen values $0$ and

$$\lambda_{2}=g_{m3}\left({1\over C_{P}}+{1\over C_{X}}\right)
      =g_{m3}{C_{P}+C_{X}\over C_{P}C_{X}}={1\over \tau_{r}}\tag{13}$$

$\tau_{r}=C_{P}\!\parallel\! C_{X}/g_{m3}$ is the
regeneration time constant of the $n$ -pair.
With ${\bf v}(0)=[\Delta V_{PQ1}\;0]^{T}$,

$${\bf v}(t)=e^{{\bf A}t}{\bf v}(0)+\int_{0}^{t}
      e^{{\bf A}(t-\tau)}{\bf b}{\rm d}\tau \tag{14}$$

$$e^{{\bf A}t}={1\over C_{P}+C_{X}}
\left[{{C_{P}+C_{X}e^{\lambda_{2}t}\;\;C_{X}(e^{\lambda_{2}t}-1)}
\atop{C_{P}(e^{\lambda_{2}t}-1)\;\;C_{X}+C_{P}e^{\lambda_{2}t}}}\right]
\tag{15}$$

so that, in magnitude,

$$\eqalign{
|\Delta V_{X}(t)|&={C_{P}\left(e^{\lambda_{2}t}-1\right)\over 
      C_{P}+C_{X}}|\Delta V_{PQ1}|
      +{g_{m1}|\Delta V_{in}|\over C_{P}+C_{X}}
        \left[{e^{\lambda_{2}t}-1\over \lambda_{2}}-t\right]\cr
&\approx {g_{m1}|\Delta V_{in}|\over C_{P}+C_{X}}
        \left(e^{\lambda_{2}t}-1\right)
        \left(t_{1}+{1\over \lambda_{2}}\right)\qquad e^{\lambda_{2}t}\gg 1\cr
&={g_{m1}|\Delta V_{in}|\left(e^{\lambda_{2}t}-1\right)\over 
      C_{P}+C_{X}}
        C_{P}\left[{V_{Tn}\over I_{CM}}+{C_{X}\over g_{m3}(C_{P}+C_{X})}\right]
      }\tag{16}$$

At the moment the $p$ -pair turns on, $t=t_{2}$,

$$\lambda_{2}t_{2}= {g_{m3}|V_{Tp}|\over I_{CM}}
      \left(1+{C_{X}\over C_{P}}\right) \tag{17}$$

and the {\it pre regeneration} or {\it initial}
voltage gain normally quoted as

$$A_{i}\equiv {|\Delta V_{X}(t_{2})|\over |\Delta V_{in}|}
      \approx {g_{m1}V_{Tn}\over I_{CM}}
        {C_{P}\over C_{P}+C_{X}}\left(e^{\lambda_{2}t_{2}}-1\right)
        \left[1+{I_{CM}C_{X}\over g_{m3}V_{Tn}(C_{P}+C_{X})}\right] \tag{18}$$

For $C_{P}\gg C_{X}$, $\lambda_{2}\to g_{m3}/C_{X}$,
$C_{P}/(C_{P}+C_{X})\to 1$ and

$$A_{i}\to {g_{m1}V_{Tn}\over I_{CM}}
        \left(e^{g_{m3}|V_{Tp}|/I_{CM}}-1\right)=A_{0}
        \left(e^{g_{m3}|V_{Tp}|/I_{CM}}-1\right) \tag{19}$$

$C_{P}$ independent.  For finite $C_{P}$ the factor
$C_{P}/(C_{P}+C_{X})<1$ and, more important,
$\lambda_{2}=g_{m3}(1/C_{P}+1/C_{X})$ decreases when
$C_{P}$ is increased, so that $e^{\lambda_{2}t_{2}}
 =\exp \left[{g_{m3}|V_{Tp}|/I_{CM}}\,(1+C_{X}/C_{P})\right]$
decreases exponentially with $1/C_{P}$.

In words: to first order the $I\,t/C$ integration
gain $A_{0}=g_{m}V_{T}/I$ is $C_{P}$ independent
because $t_{1}\propto C_{P}$ cancels $1/C_{P}$.
Normally quoted as

$$A_{i}\propto {C_{P}\over C_{P}+C_{X}}\tag{20}$$

i. e. a very weak increase which saturates at
$A_{0}$ for $C_{P}\gg C_{X}$.  Keeping the finite
loop gain of the $n$ cross coupled pair the
transient, pre regeneration gain {\it decreases}
when $C_{P,Q}$ is made larger.  The regeneration
pole

$$\tau_{r}^{-1}=g_{m3}\left({1\over C_{P}}+{1\over C_{X}}\right)
\tag{21}$$

moves to lower frequency, the exponential build up
$\exp (t_{2}/\tau_{r})$ on $X,Y$ before the $p$ -
pair fires is smaller and the net voltage presented
to the back to back inverters at $t=t_{1}+t_{2}$ is
smaller.

Loosely phrased in many text books as {\textquotedblleft}
$A_{i}\approx g_{m1}(t_{1}+t_{2})/C_{X}\propto C_{P}$
so $A_{i}$ goes up with $C_{P}$ {\textquotedblright} the
more exact statement is: $A_{i}$ is nominally
$C_{P}$ independent and, with the $M_{3}-M_{4}$
positive feedback included, it falls as
$\propto (C_{P}+C_{X})^{-1}\exp [-C_{X}/C_{P}]$ and
saturates at (9)–(10) for $C_{P}\gg C_{X}$.

The practical consequences are:

* $t_{1}=C_{P}V_{Tn}/I_{CM}$ grows $\propto C_{P}$,
  the evaluation delay $t_{D}=t_{1}+t_{2}+\tau_{r}
  \ln (V_{DD}/\Delta V_{X}(t_{2}))$ grows,
  the comparator gets slower, roughly $\Delta t_{D}
  \approx \Delta C_{P}V_{Tn}/I_{CM}$;

* the input referred offset and noise contributed
  by the latch, $V_{os,{\rm latch}}/A_{i}$,
  $v_{n,{\rm latch}}/A_{i}$, go up as $1/A_{i}$;

* the sampled $kT/C_{P}$ noise $\sqrt{kT/C_{P}}$
  and the kick back onto $V_{in1,2}$,
  $\Delta Q\approx C_{gd} \Delta V_{P,Q}$, are
  filtered by the larger $C_{P}$.

That is why a small explicit $C_{P,Q}\sim 10$–$30\,{\rm fF}$
is often added deliberately to swamp kick back and
to filter $kT/C$ noise, trading the (at best flat,
normally slightly reduced) pre regeneration gain and
speed for lower kick back.  In the crude $I\,t/C$
picture this is described as a modest
$C_{P}/(C_{P}+C_{X})$ increase of $A_{i}$ which
quickly saturates at $g_{m}V_{T}/I$.

answers.question: If we increase the widths of M5 and M6 in Figure 9, does the speed improve or degrade?

answer.text:
With the usual sizing the circuit is {\it integration}
limited and ${\rm M}_{5}{\rm M}_{6}$ are a dead
capacitance for most of the decision time.

Put $C_{X}=C_{Y}=C_{0}+C_{5,6}$,
$C_{5,6}\propto W_{5,6}$ and

$${\rm M}_{7}{\rm \;on\; }S_{1-4}{\rm \;off\; }$$

$${\rm M}_{3}{\rm \;on\; }Y\approx V_{DD}\;\;{\rm M}_{4}
{\rm \;on\; }X\approx V_{DD}$$

$$X\approx P\;\;Y\approx Q\tag{1}$$

so that for $CK=1$

$$I_{1,2}\approx {1\over 2}\mu _{n}C_{ox}{W_{1,2}\over L}
\left(V_{GS}-V_{T}\right)^{2}$$

discharges $C_{P}+C_{X}$ and $C_{Q}+C_{Y}$,
Fig.9.  ${\rm M}_{5}{\rm M}_{6}$ are {\it off}

$$V_{SG5}=V_{DD}-X<V_{Tp}\qquad V_{SG6}=V_{DD}-Y<V_{Tp}\tag{2}$$

until

$$V_{X,Y}=V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}| \tag{3}$$

The time to get to (3), the so called integration
time, is

$$t_{0}\approx {{C_{X,Y}|V_{Tp}|}\over {I_{1,2}}}
      \approx {{C_{0}+W_{5,6}C_{ov}+W_{5,6}C_{g}}\over {I_{1,2}}}
        |V_{Tp}| \tag{4}$$

proportional to $C_{X,Y}$ and normally $\sim 30-50\%$
of the total $CK-Q$ delay.  For $t<t_{0}$ $W_{5,6}$
is pure capacitance to ground at the high impedance
nodes $X,Y$, $P,Q$ and pure gate capacitance on the
opposite side.

For $t>t_{0}$ the cross coupled pair closes the loop.
In small signal

$$C_{X}\dot v_{x}+g_{m3}v_{y}+g_{m5}v_{y}+g_{ds}v_{x}=0$$
$$C_{Y}\dot v_{y}+g_{m4}v_{x}+g_{m6}v_{x}+g_{ds}v_{y}=0$$

$$v_{o}=v_{x}-v_{y}\propto \exp t/\tau _{reg}\tag{5}$$

$$\tau _{reg}^{-1}\approx {{g_{m3}+g_{m5}-g_{ds}}\over {C_{X}}}
      \approx {{g_{m4}+g_{m6}-g_{ds}}\over {C_{Y}}} \tag{6}$$

so that with $V_{o}(t_{0})= \Delta V_{0}\approx
\left( \Delta I/I\right) |V_{Tp}|$ the normal
latch delay is

$$t_{latch}=t_{0}+\tau _{reg}\ln {V_{DD}/2\Delta V_{0}} \tag{7}$$

$$t_{latch}\approx {{C_{X}|V_{Tp}|}\over I}+
      {{C_{X}}\over {g_{mN}+g_{mP}}}\ln {V_{DD}\over 2\Delta V_{0}} \tag{8}$$

$$C_{X}=C_{0}+c_{p}W_{5,6}\qquad g_{mP}=g_{m0}W_{5,6}\tag{9}$$

Formally

$${{\partial \tau _{reg}}\over {\partial W_{5,6}}}
   \propto {{c_{p}\left(g_{mN}+g_{mP}\right)-C_{X}g_{m0}}
                {\left(g_{mN}+g_{mP}\right)^{2}}} \tag{10}$$

i. e.

$$\tau _{reg}(W_{P})={{C_{0}+c_{p}W_{P}}\over {g_{mN}+g_{m0}W_{P}}}
      ={{1+\alpha (W_{P}/W_{P0}-1)}\over {1+\beta (W_{P}/W_{P0}-1)}}
        \tau _{reg0} \tag{11}$$

$$\alpha ={{c_{p}W_{P0}}\over {C_{0}+c_{p}W_{P0}}}\qquad 
  \beta ={{g_{m0}W_{P0}}\over {g_{mN}+g_{m0}W_{P0}}} \tag{12}$$

For the usual process $g_{m}/c_{p}\approx \omega _{T}$
is about the same for $N$ and $P$ and, $g_{mN}\approx
2-3g_{mP}$ for the same $W$, $\alpha \approx \beta
\approx 0.2-0.3$.  I. e. to first order $\tau _{reg}$
is {\it unchanged} by $W_{P}$.  A very small $W_{P}$
increase from minimum $W$ will decrease $\tau _{reg}$
by

$$\Delta \tau _{reg}/\tau _{reg}\approx (\beta -\alpha )
      \Delta W_{P}/W_{P0}\tag{13}$$

a few {\%}, whereas $t_{0}$ in (4) increases
{\it linearly} with $C_{X}$,

$$\Delta t_{0}/t_{0}= \alpha \Delta W_{P}/W_{P0}>0\tag{14}$$

and dominates (7).  In addition the $CK=0$ precharge
time

$$t_{pc}\approx R_{S3,4}C_{X}\ln \cdots \tag{15}$$

goes up linearly with $C_{X}$ so that for a given
$CK$ frequency the precharge becomes incomplete and
leaves memory.

In other words for $t<t_{0}$ the ${\rm PMOS}$ latch
does no work and is just extra diffusion and gate
load on $X,Y$.  Putting $W_{5,6}$ up makes the
normally dominant $t_{0}$ larger and, at best,
leaves $\tau _{reg}$ about constant.  There is a
shallow optimum, normally for

$$W_{5,6}\approx {1\over 2}{ {\mu _{n}}\over {\mu _{p}}}W_{3,4}
\tag{16}$$

i. e. $g_{mP}\approx {1\over 2}g_{mN}$, beyond which
any increase in $W_{5,6}$ increases $C_{X,Y}$ faster
than it increases $g_{mP}$ and the $CK-Q$ delay
increases, the conventional Strong Arm being
normally already at or beyond the optimum.  With
$S_{3,4}$ kept constant the delay increases
monotonically with $W_{5,6}$.

> {\it In normal parlance: the comparator gets slower.
> A small increase from absolute minimum $W$ can make
> $\tau _{reg}$ a little smaller, but the $C_{X,Y}
> |V_{Tp}|/I$ integration time and the $R_{S}C_{X,Y}$
> precharge time increase makes the total $t_{CK-Q}$
> larger for any appreciable increase.  There is an
> optimum $W_{P}\sim 0.5-1.0\,W_{N}$; the usual design
> is already optimum and any substantial increase
> degrades speed, by $\sim 10-20\%$ for $2\times W_{P}$
> in $65\,{\rm nm}$ as an example.  If $S_{3,4}$ are
> re-sized to keep $t_{pc}$ constant the degradation
> is second order in $\Delta W_{P}$ around the optimum
> and first order beyond it.}

If the extra $C_{X,Y}$ is compensated by e. {\rm g.}
reducing $W_{3,4}$ or $S_{3,4}$ capacitance the
$g_{mP}$ increase does speed up $\tau _{reg}\propto
1/(g_{mN}+g_{mP})$ in the usual way.

answers.question: In the circuit of Figure 10, does the speed improve or degrade if we increase the widths of the clocked transistors?

answer.text:
With the usual abuse of language the circuit is the
${\rm C^{2}MOS}$ ${\rm M/S}$ put in the ${\rm T}$
connection, Fig.1, i. e. a ${\rm div.2}$.

$$\eqalign{
Z\nearrow X&{\rm on}\;CK=1\cr
X\nearrow Y&{\rm on}\;CK=0\cr
Y\nearrow Z&{\rm always}\cr}$$

$X$ and $Y$ are high impedance dynamic nodes.
Put $R_{D}$ for the data device, the outside
${\rm p}$ and the ${\rm M_{1}}$ ${\rm n}$, and $R_{C}$
for the inside clock device and $C_{X,Y}$ for the
total capacitance on the dynamic node.

For definiteness on $X$, Fig.2

$$C_{X}=C_{G}(X)+C_{D,C}+C_{w}\approx C_{0}+kW_{C}\tag{1}$$
$$R_{X}=R_{D}+R_{C}\approx R_{D}+{R_{0}\over {W_{C}}}\tag{2}$$

$C_{D,C}\propto W_{C}$ is the drain diffusion plus
overlap of the clock device whose drain {\it is}}
the output node.  $C_{G}(X)$ is the gate capacitance
of the next data devices, $R_{D}\propto 1/W_{D}$ is
fixed if you do not touch the data devices.
The internal node $D-C$ is not on $X$ so $C_{D,D}$
does not load $X$ to first order.

The time to put $X$ to ${\bar Z}$ when $CK=1$ and
to put $Y$ to ${\bar X}$ when $CK=0$ is, to first
order,

$$\tau _{X}\approx R_{X}C_{X}\qquad 
  \tau _{Y}\approx R_{Y}C_{Y}\tag{3}$$

and the loop delay which determines $f_{{\rm max}}$
for correct toggling, the so called self oscillation
frequency of the divider, is

$$\tau _{0}\approx \tau _{X}+\tau _{Y}+\tau _{I3}
      \approx \left(R_{D}+{R_{0}\over {W_{C}}}\right)
               \left(C_{0}+kW_{C}\right)+\tau _{I3} \tag{4}$$

$${\rm i.e.}\;\; \tau _{0}=R_{D}C_{0}+R_{D}kW_{C}
      +{R_{0}C_{0}\over {W_{C}}}+R_{0}k+\tau _{I3}\tag{5}$$

$${{d\tau _{0}}\over {dW_{C}}}=R_{D}k-{R_{0}C_{0}\over {W_{C}^{2}}}=0\tag{6}$$

at

$$W_{C,{\rm opt}}=\sqrt{{{R_{0}C_{0}}\over {R_{D}k}}}\tag{7}$$

which for normal $R_{D}\sim R_{0}$, $C_{0}\sim
C_{G}\sim kW_{D}$ is of the order of minimum
geometry.  For $W_{C}<W_{C,{\rm opt}}$

$${{d\tau _{0}}\over {dW_{C}}}<0\tag{8}$$

widening the clock device does reduce the
$R_{C}C_{0}$ term and the intrinsic latch delay
gets a few {\rm pc} faster.  For

$$W_{C}>W_{C,{\rm opt}}\qquad {{d\tau _{0}}\over {dW_{C}}}>0\tag{9}$$

$$\tau _{0}\approx R_{D}kW_{C}\tag{10}$$

the self loading $C_{D,C}\propto W_{C}$ charged
through the fixed $R_{D}$ dominates and the delay
goes {\it up}} linearly with $W_{C}$.

In words: the current that has to charge/discharge
$C_{X}$ [$C_{Y}$] is limited by the outside data
transistors $W_{D}$, $W_{{\rm M1}}$.  Widening the
inside clock transistors does not increase that
current appreciably, it just puts more diffusion
and overlap capacitance directly on the critical
dynamic nodes $X$ and $Y$ and, of course, more
capacitance on the $CK$ line itself, and it
increases the charge sharing capacitance of the
internal $D-C$ node,

$$ \Delta V_{X}\approx {{C_{DC}}\over {C_{DC}+C_{X}}}V_{DD}\tag{11}$$

so that when $R_{C}$ goes on $X$ [$Y$] shares its
charge with $C_{DC}$.

For any normally designed latch $W_{C,{\rm opt}}$
is essentially minimum $W$, so that in colloquial
language {\it widening the clock devices makes the
latch/divider slower and much more power hungry on
the clock}}.  The $R_{C}$ reduction is second order.
If the whole latch, $W_{D}$ and $W_{C}$ together,
is widened $\tau _{0}\propto 1/W$ in the normal
way.  With $W_{D}$ fixed the textbook shorthand is:
no improvement, normally a degradation of $f_{{\rm
max}}$.

> {\it Remark:}  If you start from $W_{C}\to 0$ the
> $R_{0}C_{0}/W_{C}$ term dominates and a small
> increase from minimum $W$ to $\sim 1.5-2\times
> {\rm min.\,}W$ will give a shallow, a few percent,
> intrinsic speed improvement before the
> $R_{D}kW_{C}$ self loading takes over.  System
> speed, including the $CK$ driver which now has to
> drive $C_{CK}\propto W_{C}$, is degraded for any
> increase.  That is why ${\rm C^{2}MOS}$ and
> ${\rm TSPC}$ latches are normally laid out with
> minimum, or at most $2\times $ minimum, clock
> devices.
