answers.question: Does the structure in Figure 10 provide quadrature outputs?

answer.text:
With the conventional zero delay abstraction the
circuit is the conventional ${\rm C^{2}MOS}$ master slave
${{:}}2$ of Fig.7.36 of Razavi.  Put ${\rm CK}= {\rm CK}_{0}
\cos \omega _{0}t$.

$${\rm L}_{1}:Z\rightarrow X\qquad 
  {\rm L}_{2}:X\rightarrow Y\qquad {\rm I}_{3}:Y\rightarrow Z$$

$${\rm L}_{1}\;\;{\rm on\;for\;say\;CK}=1\qquad 
  {\rm L}_{2}\;\;{\rm on\;for\;CK}=0\tag{*}$$

so that, apart from the propagation time $t_{p}$,

* for ${\rm CK}=0$, ${\rm L}_{1}$ is in hold, ${\rm L}_{2}$
is transparent

$$Y={\bar X}\tag{1}$$

* for ${\rm CK}=1$, ${\rm L}_{2}$ is in hold, ${\rm L}_{1}$
is transparent

$$X={\bar Z}\tag{2}$$

and

$$Z={\bar Y}\tag{3}$$

after the conventional extra inversion which is necessary in
order to make the number of inversions round the loop odd.
In the $t_{p}\rightarrow 0$ limit (1)--(3) give

$$f_{X}=f_{Y}=f_{Z}=f_{0}={{f_{{\rm CK}}}\over {2}}$$

and, Fig.1, $X$ changes on, say, the $1\rightarrow 0$
transition of ${\rm CK}$ and $Y,Z$ change on the
$0\rightarrow 1$ transition of ${\rm CK}$.  I. e. in the
$t_{p}=0$ limit

> {\it $X$ and $Y$ and $X$ and $Z={\bar Y}$ are nominally
> $T_{{\rm CK}}/2=T_{0}/4$ apart at $\omega _{0}/2$, i. e.
> nominally in quadrature at $f_{{\rm CK}}/2$.}

In the normal language $X=I$, $Y=Q$, $Z={\bar Q}$ at
$f_{{\rm CK}}/2$, Fig.1.  With $t_{p}\ne 0$ let $t_{L}$ be
the $L_{1,2}$ propagation time and $t_{I}$ the ${\rm Inv}_{3}$
propagation time.  E. {\it g.} for ${\rm CK}=0\rightarrow 1$

$$Y(t)= {\bar X}(t-t_{L})\qquad 
  Z(t)={\bar Y}(t-t_{I})={\bar Y}(t)-t_{I}{\dot Y}+ \cdots \tag{4}$$

so that, Fig.1,

* $Y$ follows $X$ by $t_{L}$,
* $Z$ follows $Y$ by $t_{I}$,
* $X$ follows $Z$ by $t_{L}$.

Hence, to first order in $t_{p}/T_{0}$,

$$ \phi _{Y}-\phi _{X}={\pi \over 2}\tag{5a}$$
$$ \phi _{Z}-\phi _{X}={\pi \over 2}+ \omega _{0}t_{I}/2
      ={\pi \over 2}+ \Delta \phi \tag{5b}$$

with

$$\Delta \phi =2\pi {{t_{I}}\over {T_{0}}}= \pi {{t_{I}}\over
{T_{{\rm CK}}}} \tag{6}$$

and a duty cycle error $\propto t_{I}/T_{0}$ on $Z$.
In particular $X$ and $Y$ are still nominally in quadrature
but $X$ and $Z$ are in quadrature only to within the
systematic error (6).  With $t_{I}\sim 20-50\,{\rm ps}$ at
${{f_{{\rm CK}}}}\sim 2-5\,{\rm GHz}$ $\Delta \phi \sim
5-15^{{\rm o}}$ at $f_{0}$.

That, plus the very large sensitivity of the single ended
${\rm C^{2}MOS}$ storage nodes $X,Y$ to supply and to
${\rm CK}\rightarrow X,Y$ feed through, rise-fall
unbalance, ${\rm CK}-{\bar{{\rm CK}}}$ skew etc., makes the
single ended loop with the extra inverter normally {\it not}}
quoted as a {\it precision\/} quadrature generator.
The conventional precision $I/Q$ ${\{:}}2$ is the
{\it differential\/} cross coupled version, Fig.7.37 in
Razavi, {\it e. g.} the differential ${\rm C^{2}MOS}$ or,
normally, the CML version, with no extra inverter, in which
the inversion is obtained by cross coupling the differential
outputs, $I\rightarrow {\bar Q}$, $Q\rightarrow I$, and
$X=I,{\bar I}$ and $Y=Q,{\bar Q}$ are exact complementary
quadrature phases at $f_{{\rm CK}}/2$ to within device
mismatch.

> {\it Remark:\/}  In the $t_{p}=0$ text book sense the
> circuit {\it is\/} normally described as a quadrature
> ${{:}}2$, $X=I$, $Y=Q$, $Z={\bar Q}$ at $f_{{\rm CK}}/2$.
> Strictly speaking the single ended implementation of
> Fig.10 is not a usable quadrature generator.

For $t_{p}=0$ the often quoted form is

* $X$ and $Y$ are $90^{{\rm o}}$ at $f_{{\rm CK}}/2$,
  $Z={\bar Y}$ is $90^{{\rm o}}+t_{I}$ from $X$.

If the $t_{I}$ error is counted the binary answer is
{\it no\/}.  Neglecting $t_{I}$ the binary answer is
{\it yes, $X=I$, $Y=Q\;(Z={\bar Q})$ at $f_{0}=f_{{\rm CK}}/2$}.

> {\it Fig.1\/} Idealised waveforms, $t_{p}=0$.  $X$ toggles
> on ${\rm CK}\downarrow $, $Y,Z$ toggle on ${\rm CK}\uparrow $,
> $f_{X}=f_{Y}=f_{Z}=f_{{\rm CK}}/2$, $X\perp Y$, $X\perp Z$
> to within $t_{I}$.

answers.question:
For the divide-by-two topology in Figure 11, does the speed improve or degrade
if we increase the widths of the clocked transistors, i.e. the transistors whose
gates are driven by `CK` or `CKbar`?

answer.text:
With the ideal clock the circuit is the
2 latch TSPC ${\rm div.}\div 2$ of Fig.15.18
Razavi.  Put $X\equiv S_{p1},Y\equiv S_{n1}$,
$X^{\prime }\equiv S_{p2},Y^{\prime }\equiv S_{n2}$,
Fig.1.

$${\rm CK}=1\;{\rm :}\;M_{p1},M_{n1}\;{\rm on}\;
      M_{p2},M_{n2}\;{\rm off}\tag {M\;transp.,S\;hold}$$
$${\rm CK}=0\;{\rm :}\;M_{p1},M_{n1}\;{\rm off}\;
      M_{p2},M_{n2}\;{\rm on}\tag {M\;hold,S\;transp.}$$

and ${\rm D}\equiv \bar Q$ through the
unclocked inverter.  In the transparent phase the
signal path is

$$V_{DD}-R_{cp}-R_{p}-C_{L}\qquad 
  C_{L}-R_{n}-R_{cn}-GND $$

$$R_{c}\propto 1/W_{c}\qquad 
  C_{L}=C_{dbp}+C_{dbn}+C_{g,next}+C_{w}+C_{c} \tag{1}$$

$C_{c}=C_{db,c}+C_{sb,inv}\propto W_{c}$ is the
capacitance on the internal nodes $X,Y,X^{\prime
},Y^{\prime }$.  When the inverter device is on
$X$ is shorted to the output through $R_{p}$,
$Y$ to the output through $R_{n}$, so that $C_{c}$
is seen at the output in the transparent phase.
E. {\rm g.} for the $1\to 0$ transition of the
slave while the slave is still opaque

$$V_{o}(0^{+})=V_{DD}{C_{o}\over C_{o}+C_{Y}}\tag{2}$$

is the charge sharing of $C_{o}$ with $C_{Y}$ and
the final $0$ has to be re-established through
$R_{n}+R_{cn}$ on $C_{o}+C_{Y}$.

Hence, to first order,

$$\tau _{p}\approx \left(R_{p}+R_{cp}\right)
      \left(C_{o}+C_{cp}\right)\tag{3a}$$
$$\tau _{n}\approx \left(R_{n}+R_{cn}\right)
      \left(C_{o}+C_{cn}\right)\tag{3b}$$

$$R_{c}=R_{c0}{W_{0}\over W_{c}}\qquad 
  C_{c}=C_{c0}{W_{c}\over W_{0}} \tag{4}$$

$$\tau =\left({R_{c0}W_{0}\over W_{c}}+R_{inv}\right)
        \left(C_{o0}+C_{c0}{W_{c}\over W_{0}}\right) \tag{5}$$

$${d\tau \over dW_{c}}=0\;{\rm at}\;
  W_{c,opt}=W_{0}\sqrt{{R_{c0}C_{o0}\over R_{inv}C_{c0}}}
  \tag{6}$$

For the normal $0.18-65\,{\rm nm}$ process
$R_{inv}C_{c0}\sim R_{c0}C_{o0}$ and (6) is of the
order of the minimum $W$.  For $W_{c}>W_{c,opt}$

$$\tau \approx R_{inv}C_{c0}{W_{c}\over W_{0}}\propto W_{c}
 \tag{7}$$

i. {\rm e.} the conventional $R_{c}$ reduction
$\propto 1/W_{c}$ is already negligible with respect
to $R_{inv}$ and you only pay the linear increase
of the diffusion capacitance on $X,Y$ and of the
gate capacitance

$$C_{g,c}=C_{ox}W_{c}L\tag{8}$$

on the ${\rm CK}$ line.

With a realistic ${\rm CK}$ driver of resistance
$R_{CK}$

$$\tau _{CK}=R_{CK}\left(C_{g,cp}+C_{g,cn}+C_{w,CK}\right)
      \propto W_{c}\tag{9}$$

so the rise/fall time of the clock, i. {\rm e.} the
time the latch is effectively transparent, is
degraded $\propto W_{c}$ and the normal
charge sharing/clock feedthrough on the high $Z$
node is increased $\propto W_{c}$.

In other words once $R_{c}\ll R_{inv}$ widening
$M_{c}$ buys you essentially nothing in drive
current and costs you $C_{db,c}$ on the signal
path and $C_{g,c}$ on the clock path.  The
maximum toggle frequency

$$f_{max}\approx {1\over 2\left(\tau _{M,tr}+
      \tau _{S,tr}+ \tau _{inv}\right)}\tag{10}$$

goes through a very shallow maximum for
$W_{c}\approx W_{min}\approx {1\over 2}-1\times
W_{inv}$ and decreases $\propto 1/W_{c}$ for
$W_{c}\gg W_{c,opt}$.  In first order widening the
${\rm CK}$ devices above minimum makes the divider
slower.  E. {\rm g.} SPICE for the $0.18\mu $
TSPC ${\rm div.}\div 2$ with $W_{p}/W_{n}=2/1\mu $,
$W_{c}=1\mu $ $f_{max}\approx 8-10\,{\rm GHz}$;
$W_{c}=4\mu $ $f_{max}$ is $15-25\%$ lower, the
clock power $\propto W_{c}$ is $4\times $ larger.

Normal design keeps $M_{c}$ at $W_{min}$, often
$W_{c}<W_{inv}$, $W_{cp}\approx W_{cn}\approx
W_{min}$.  Any increase from there is at best
second order on $R_{c}$ and first order detrimental
on $C_{L}$ and on $C_{CK}$.  With an ideal,
zero impedance clock the circuit gets at best
marginally faster for a very small increase from
$W_{min}$ and monotonically slower thereafter.
With a realistic clock driver it gets monotonically
slower.  This is normally quoted as {\it widening
the clock devices degrades the speed}.  Cf. Razavi,
{\it Design of Analog CMOS Integrated Circuits},
Chap. 15, and {\it JSSC} 31, 32.

answers.question: Analyze the arrangement in Figure 12(a).

answer.text:
With the ideal switch the circuit is the
2 phase shift register with ${\rm INV}$ in the loop.
Put

$$A={\rm in~}I_{1}\qquad B={\rm out~}I_{1}\qquad 
C={\rm in~}I_{2}\qquad E={\rm out~}I_{2}\qquad 
D={\rm out~}I_{3}$$

$$E=\bar C\qquad D=\bar E =C\qquad B=\bar A\tag{1}$$

$A$ is the gate capacity of $I_{1}$, $C$ the gate
capacity of $I_{2}$. $B,D$ are low impedance.

> {\it Remark on Fig.12b:} The conventional drawing is
> with the weak ${\rm INV}$ in anti parallel to $I_{1}$,
> $B\rightarrow A$.  In the print the ${\rm INV}$ is
> drawn reversed.  What is meant is the conventional
> keeper $I_{1}\rightleftarrows I_{w}$ on the master
> latch.  $I_{w}$ is $W/L\ll W/L_{1}$ so it can be
> over written.  With the drawing as it is $I_{w}:
> D\rightarrow B$ is the same function to first order.

{\it (a) Dynamic $T$ latch.}  $S_{1}=CK$, $S_{2}=\bar
{CK}$ complementary, normally non overlapping.

* $CK=1\;,\;\bar{CK}=0$ : $S_{1}$ ON, $S_{2}$ OFF

$$A=D\tag{2}$$
$$B=\bar A =\bar D$$
$C,E,D$ floating. $C$ is held on $C_{g2}$, $D=C$ held
on the ${\rm INV}_{3}$ output.  Master transparent,
slave in hold.

* $CK=0\;,\;\bar{CK}=1$ : $S_{1}$ OFF, $S_{2}$ ON

$$A=A_{1}{\rm \;held\;on\;}C_{g1}\tag{3}$$
$$B=\bar A_{1}$$
$$C=B=\bar A_{1}$$
$$E=\bar C =A_{1}\qquad D=C=\bar A_{1}$$

Master in hold, slave transparent.  The loop is
normally open.  If $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ were closed
together the circuit is the 3 ${\rm INV}$ ring
oscillator.

Put $D_{0}=C_{0}$ the state at the end of a
$CK=0$ phase.  Then

$$\eqalign{
CK=1: & A_{1}=D_{0}\cr
      & B_{1}=\bar D_{0}\cr
      & C_{1}=C_{0}=D_{0}\cr
      & D_{1}=C_{1}=D_{0}{\rm \;no\;change}\cr
CK=0: & A_{2}=A_{1}=D_{0}\cr
      & B_{2}=\bar D_{0}\cr
      & C_{2}=B_{2}=\bar D_{0}\cr
      & D_{2}=C_{2}=\bar D_{0}\cr} \tag{4}$$

i. e. on the $1\rightarrow 0$ transition of $CK$,
on closing of $S_{2}$,

$$D_{n+1}= \bar D_{n}\tag{5}$$

and $D$ is held for the whole $CK=1$ phase.
In $z$ domain $D(z)=z^{-1}\bar D(z)$.  After two
clock periods

$$D_{n+2}=D_{n}\tag{6}$$

The circuit is the master slave $D$ latch

* master: $S_{1}+I_{1}$
* slave: $S_{2}+I_{2}$ plus $I_{3}$ as the
${\bar Q}$ inverter

connected as $D={\bar Q}$ i. e. as a $T=1$
flip flop.  It is negative edge triggered to first
order.  With $50\%$ $CK$

$$f_{D}=f_{E}= {\tfrac12}f_{CK}\tag{7}$$

$$T_{D}=2T_{CK}$$

with $50\%$ duty cycle, Fig.1.  It is the
$\div 2$ prescaler, Johnson counter, binary
counter stage.  $n$ stages in cascade $\div 2^{n}$.
Any odd number $2k+1$ of ${\rm INV}$ in the loop
gives inversion, any even number gives a latch.
Three is the minimum for $\div 2$.

$$\eqalign{
CK & 1111000011110000\cr
A  & D_{0}D_{0}D_{0}D_{0}\bar D_{0}\bar D_{0}\cr
B  & \bar D_{0}\bar D_{0}\bar D_{0}\bar D_{0}D_{0}D_{0}\cr
C  & D_{0}D_{0}\bar D_{0}\bar D_{0}\bar D_{0}\bar D_{0}\cr
D  & D_{0}D_{0}\bar D_{0}\bar D_{0}\bar D_{0}\bar D_{0}\cr}$$

$D$ toggles on $\,CK\downarrow $.

In the ideal switch model the operation is
ratioless, fast and low power, no DC contention.

In reality $A$ is floating for $T_{CK}/2$ during
$CK=0$ and $C$ is floating for $T_{CK}/2$ during
$CK=1$.  The state is held only on gate and
parasitic capacitance $C_{g}$.

$$ \Delta V \approx I_{leak}T_{hold}/C_{g}\tag{8}$$

$I_{leak}=I_{j}+I_{subth}+I_{gate}$.  At low
$f_{CK}$, high $T$, or with clock stopped the
floating node drifts, the ${\rm INV}$ goes into
conduction, the state is lost.  Minimum clock
frequency

$$f_{min}\approx I_{leak}/C_{g}V_{DD}\tag{9}$$

typically $10^{3}-10^{5}{\rm Hz}$ in modern CMOS,
no DC operation.  Also sensitive to charge sharing
between $C_{g}$ and the switch diffusion capacity,
to clock feedthrough, to coupling noise and to
$CK/\bar{CK}$ overlap.  Overlap $S_{1}=S_{2}=ON$
shorts the 3 ${\rm INV}$ loop.  Needs non
overlapping or very fast $CK$ edges.  Power up
state random.

Maximum $f$ is $\approx \left[t_{S}+t_{I1}+t_{I2}
+t_{I3}\right]^{-1}$.

> {\it (b) Pseudo static.} The weak cross coupled
> ${\rm INV}_{w}$ in red makes the master latch
> static.  Normally $I_{w}:B\rightarrow A$,
> $I_{1}:A\rightarrow B$ is a bistable latch.
> $I_{w}$ is sized $ (W/L)_{w}\ll (W/L)_{1},
> (W/L)_{S}$ so that when $S_{1}$ is ON the low
> impedance driver $D$ can over write the keeper
> with a small contention current for $t_{cont}$.
>
> * $CK=1$: $D$ forces $A$ through $S_{1}$ against
> $I_{w}$, $B=\bar A$ follows.  $I_{w}$ reinforces
> the new state after $S_{1}$ opens.
> * $CK=0$: $S_{1}$ OFF, $A$ is held actively by
> $I_{1}\rightleftarrows I_{w}$, no longer
> dynamically.  The divider will hold indefinitely
> with $CK=0$.
>
> $C$ is still dynamic, held only during $CK=1$.
> With $CK$ stopped $=1$ the slave will still leak.
> For full static operation a second keeper on
> $C/E$ is added.  As drawn the circuit is
> ``staticized dynamic'' or pseudo static: it can
> operate to DC for $CK$ stopped LOW, it is much
> more tolerant to low $f_{CK}$, to noise and to
> soft errors, at the price of contention power,
> slower over write and larger area.  In normal
> high speed operation the behaviour is identical
> to (a), $f_{out}=f_{CK}/2$ on the falling edge.
> This is the basis of the TSPC and other
> prescalers.

Part (b) analysis of the pseudo-static keeper is also accurate. The final conclusion (divide-by-two frequency divider) matches the golden solution.

answers.question: How does the red inverter in Figure 12(b) affect the performance?

answer.text:
With the ideal switch the circuit is {\it ratio
less dynamic}. In Fig.12{\it a}

* $${\rm CK}=1~~{\rm CK}=0$$ : $${\rm CK}$$ closed
$${\rm \bar {CK}}$$ open

$$D\equiv Q\rightarrow {\rm Inv}_{1}\rightarrow B\tag
{1}$$
$$C$$ floating, $$Q$$ floating - held on $$C_{p}$$

* $${\rm CK}=0~~{\rm \bar {CK}}=1$$ : $${\rm CK}$$ open
$${\rm \bar {CK}}$$ closed

$$B\rightarrow C\rightarrow Q=\bar B\tag{2}$$
$$A$$ floating - held on $$C_{p}$$

i. e. a conventional 2 phase dynamic latch.
In normal high speed operation with $${\rm CK}\ne 0$$
and $${\rm CK}$$ not stopped it works with minimum
$$C$$, minimum power and minimum $${{t}_{p}}$$.
It has no d. c. operation. $${{f}_{{\rm min}}}$$ is
fixed by

$${{I}_{{\rm leak}}}{{T}_{{\rm max}}}<{{C}_{p}}\Delta V$$

typically $${{10}^{3}}-{{10}^{6}}{\rm Hz}$$, it is
very noise and charge sharing sensitive and it can
not be clock gated.

The $${\rm red}$$ $${\rm Inv}$$ is the conventional
{\it keeper, bleeder, trickle, weak staticizer}.
For $${\rm CK}=0$$

$${\rm Inv}_{1}+{\rm Inv}_{{\rm red}}$$

is a normal cross coupled static latch.

> {\it The master becomes pseudo static.}

For $${\rm CK}=0$$ $$A,B$$ are statically held.
For $${\rm CK}=1$$ the loop is closed through the
slave. The circuit remains dynamic on the slave side.
With a second keeper on $$C-Q$$ it becomes fully
static. Logically no change.

Normally $${{W}_{{\rm red}}}/{{L}_{{\rm red}}}\approx
1/5-1/10\,{{W}_{1}}/{{L}_{1}}$$, often with
$${{L}_{{\rm red}}}>{{L}_{{\rm min}}}$$, so that in
normal operation it can be over written by the
forward path.

* {\it D. C. operation:} $${{f}_{{\rm min}}}=0$$,
no refresh, clock can be stopped and gated, leakage
tolerant, charge sharing and noise margin essentially
that of a static latch.

* {\it A. C. operation:} To first order no change.
To second order:

$${{C}_{g}}+{{C}_{d}}$$ of $${\rm Inv}_{{\rm red}}$$

$$Q=D$$ must fight $${\rm Inv}_{{\rm red}}$$ through

answers.question:
In Figure 12(b), somebody answers:

> The red inverter acts as a keeper, forming a cross-coupled latch with `Inv1`.
> This removes the minimum clock frequency requirement due to leakage.

But the input of the red inverter is not tied to the output of `Inv1`.

Do you agree with this answer? What is the actual role of the red inverter?

answer.text:
With the usual notation

```
A\equiv Q_{3}/{\rm left\;of\;}S_{CK}\qquad 
B\equiv {\rm in\;}Inv_{1}/{\rm right\;of\;}S_{CK}
$$
$$
C\equiv {\rm out\;}Inv_{1}/{\rm left\;of\;}S_{\bar {CK}}
\qquad D\equiv {\rm in\;}Inv_{2}/{\rm right\;of\;}S_{\bar {CK}}
$$

$$C\stackrel{S_{\bar {CK}}}{=}D\stackrel{Inv_{2}}{\to}
E\stackrel{Inv_{3}}{\to}A\tag{1}$$

so that with $S_{\bar {CK}}$ closed

$$A = \bar{\bar C}=C\tag{2}$$

{\it a\/} is the conventional 2 phase dynamic divider.
$S_{CK}$ closed, $S_{\bar {CK}}$ open: $A=B$, $C$ is
driven by $Inv_{1}$ on the $C_{C}$ capacitance, $D$ is
floating on $C_{D}$. $S_{CK}$ open $S_{\bar {CK}}$ closed:
$C=D$, $C$ is driven by $Inv_{1}$ from the floating
$B$ on $C_{B}$, $A$ is driven from $C$ through (1).
$B$ for $CK=0$ and $D$ for $\bar {CK}=0$ are high
impedance dynamic nodes. Leakage on $C_{B},C_{D}$
destroys the state for $f_{CK}\to 0$. Minimum $f_{CK}$.

The conventional staticizer is a {\it weak\/} inverter
with

$${\rm in}=C\;\;{\rm out}=B\tag{3}$$

so that $Inv_{1}+{\rm keeper}$ is a $2T$ cross coupled
pair closing the loop $B\to C\to B$ when $S_{CK}$ is
open and holding $B$ on a low impedance. And a second
keeper $D\to A$ for the slave. That is {\it not\/} what
is drawn.

In Fig.12{\it b\/} as drawn

$${\rm in}_{R}=A\qquad {\rm out}_{R}=C \tag{4}$$

i. e. the $R$ inverter is {\it not\/} (3). With
$S_{CK}$ closed $A=B$ and (4) is

$$A=B\to C\;\;{\rm through\;}Inv_{1}\;\;{\rm and\;\;through\;\;}R
\tag{5}$$

in {\it parallel\/}, same sense, no cross coupling.
With $S_{CK}$ open $A$ is isolated from $B$ by
$S_{CK}$. $R$ does {\it not\/} drive $B$. The high
impedance node $B$ is left floating for $CK=0$ exactly
as in {\it a\/}. $D$ is left floating for $\bar {CK}=0$
exactly as in {\it a\/}. In no clock phase is the
floating $B$ or $D$ put on a low impedance feedback
loop.

What $R$ does do is to put $C$ on a low impedance at
all times:

* $CK=1$: $C$ driven by $Inv_{1}\parallel R$ from
$A=B$ - essentially double drive.

* $CK=0$: $S_{CK}$ open, $S_{\bar {CK}}$ closed,
$C=D$ is driven from $A$ through $R$,
$A$ is driven from $C$ through (1).

I. e. $C$ is made ``static''.

But the state of the divider is stored on $B$ and on
$D$. $B$ is still dynamic. $D$ is still dynamic for
$CK=1$. The circuit as a whole is still dynamic,
pseudo static at best, ratioed. Leakage on $C_{B}$
will still flip $Inv_{1}$ and leakage on $C_{D}$ will
still flip the slave. The $f_{CK,min}$ imposed by
junction and subthreshold leakage is {\it not\/}
removed. Stopping the clock with $CK=1$ leaves $D$
floating; stopping with $CK=0$ leaves $B$ floating.

Moreover with $S_{\bar {CK}}$ closed (2) holds and

$$C\stackrel{(1)}{\to}A\stackrel{R}{\to}\bar A =\bar C\tag{6}$$

on to the same physical node $C$. The loop

$$C\stackrel{Inv_{2}}{\to}\bar C\stackrel{Inv_{3}}{\to}
C\stackrel{R}{\to}\bar C\tag{7}$$

is a three inverter, odd, ring, not a latch. For
$CK=0$ $R$ fights $Inv_{1}$ which is trying to drive
$C=\bar B$ from the floating $B$. The circuit becomes
ratioed. With $R$ weak $Inv_{1}$ can overpower it for
$CK=1$ and the divider still divides, but $R$ is at
best a weak bleeder keeper for $C$, not a latch for
$B$. With $R$ strong the divider is functionally
destroyed by contention.

In particular $R+Inv_{2}+Inv_{3}$ is {\it not\/} a
two inverter latch. Reversed, ${\rm in}_{R}=C$,
${\rm out}_{R}=A$, $R$ would close $A\to C\to A$
through $Inv_{2}+Inv_{3}$ as a normal keeper for the
slave and, when $S_{CK}$ is closed $A=B$, as a keeper
for the master $B\to C\to B$. As drawn it is a
feed forward inverter in parallel with $Inv_{1}$ for
$CK=1$ and a contention driver for $CK=0$.

> {\it Proper staticization: $R: C\to B$, weak,
> and normally a second weak keeper $A\to D$. Then
> $B$ is held through $Inv_{1}+R$ for $CK=0$ and $D$
> is held through $Inv_{2}+Inv_{3}+$ keeper for
> $\bar {CK}=0$ and the divider is fully static with
> no $f_{min}$.}

It explicitly identifies the red inverter as a feedforward path that bypasses part of the latch chain, providing a parallel drive to C from A during CK=1 and a contention/controlling path during CK=0. It recognizes the tradeoff: pseudo-static behavior at best, does not remove the minimum clock frequency requirement since B and D remain dynamic nodes, and at low clock rates the feedforward can dominate/destroy intended latch behavior. The detailed analysis of why the keeper loop is broken and the ring-oscillator-like odd-inverter loop is correctly noted. This matches the golden solution's essential answer.

The analysis is detailed and consistent with the golden solution.

answers.question: How do we optimize the circuit of Figure 13 for the NF if Rin must remain equal to 50 Ohm?

answer.text:
With the usual $g_{m}r_{o}>>1$

$${\cal L}(s)\approx -g_{m}r_{o}\qquad 
g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}\qquad r_{o}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$$

$$R_{in}={R_{F}+r_{o}\over {1+g_{m}r_{o}}}\approx 
{{R_{F}}\over {1+g_{m}r_{o}}}+{1\over {g_{m}}}\tag{1}$$

$$A_{v}={V_{o}\over {V_{i}}}=-g_{m}r_{o}
{{1-1/g_{m}R_{F}}\over {1+r_{o}/R_{F}}}\approx -g_{m}r_{o}$$

$$A_{vs}={V_{o}\over {V_{s}}}=-{{r_{o}(g_{m}R_{F}-1)}
\over {R_{F}+R_{s}+r_{o}+g_{m}r_{o}R_{s}}}
\approx -{R_{F}\over {R_{s}}}\;\;{\rm for}\;\;g_{m}r_{o}R_{s}>>R_{F}$$

Put a current noise $4kT\gamma g_{m}df$ in parallel
with $r_{o}$ and a current noise $4kT/R_{F}df$ in
parallel with $R_{F}$ . With $G_{s}=1/R_{s}$,
$G_{F}=1/R_{F}$, $G_{o}=1/r_{o}$ and $D=G_{o}G_{s}+
G_{F}(G_{o}+G_{s}+g_{m})$

$$\eqalign{
{V_{o}\over {i_{n}}}&=-{{G_{s}+G_{F}}\over {D}}\cr
{V_{o}\over {i_{nF}}}&={{G_{s}+g_{m}}\over {D}}\cr
{V_{o}\over {V_{s}}}&=-{{G_{s}(g_{m}-G_{F})}\over {D}}}$$

so that, $D$ cancelling,

$$F=1+{{|V_{on}|^{2}+|V_{oF}|^{2}}\over {|V_{os}|^{2}}}
 =1+{{(G_{s}+G_{F})^{2}\gamma g_{m}+(G_{s}+g_{m})^{2}G_{F}}
\over {G_{s}^{2}(g_{m}-G_{F})^{2}R_{s}}}$$

$$F=1+{{\gamma g_{m}(R_{F}+R_{s})^{2}+R_{F}(1+g_{m}R_{s})^{2}}
\over {R_{s}(g_{m}R_{F}-1)^{2}}}\tag{2}$$

$$F\approx 1+{\gamma \over {g_{m}R_{s}}}+{R_{s}\over {R_{F}}}
{{(1+g_{m}R_{s})^{2}}\over {(g_{m}R_{F})^{2}}}+ \cdots $$

i. e. the conventional

$$ \overline{V_{n,in}^{2}}=4kT\gamma /g_{m}+4kTR_{F}/
(1+g_{m}r_{o})^{2}+ \cdots \tag{3}$$

referred to the $R_{s}=50\,{\rm \Omega }$ source.
For $g_{m}R_{F}>>1$

$$F\approx 1+{\gamma \over {g_{m}R_{s}}}+{1\over {g_{m}R_{F}}}
\left({1+g_{m}R_{s}\over {g_{m}R_{s}}}\right)^{2}+ \cdots \tag{4}$$

The $R_{F}$ noise is divided by the loop gain and the
MOS noise is $\propto 1/g_{m}$.

For $R_{s}$ fixed (2) is a monotone decreasing function
of $R_{F}$ for $g_{m}$ fixed,

$${{\partial F}\over {\partial R_{F}}}<0\qquad g_{m}R_{F}>1$$

and a monotone decreasing function of $g_{m}$ for
$R_{F}$ fixed.  The only way to increase $R_{F}$ and
$g_{m}$ and keep (1) constant is to increase the loop
gain $g_{m}r_{o}$.

From (1) with $R_{in}=R_{s}$

$$R_{F}=R_{s}(1+g_{m}r_{o})-r_{o}=R_{s}\left[1+a(y-1)\right]
\tag{5}$$

$$y=g_{m}R_{s}\qquad a=r_{o}/R_{s}\qquad g_{m}r_{o}=ay$$

$$g_{m}R_{F}-1=(y-1)(1+ay)\tag{6}$$

Putting (5)(6) in (2)

$$F=1+{{\gamma y\left[2+a(y-1)\right]^{2}
+\left[1+a(y-1)\right](1+y)^{2}}\over {(y-1)^{2}(1+ay)^{2}}}
\tag{7}$$

For the usual $r_{o}>>R_{s}$ or more generally for
$A_{v0}=g_{m}r_{o}>>1$, $1+ay\approx A_{v0}$,

$$F\approx 1+{\gamma \over {y}}+{(1+y)^{2}\over {A_{v0}y(y-1)}}
\tag{8}$$

$$F\approx 1+{\gamma \over {g_{m}R_{s}}}+{R_{s}\over {R_{F}}}
\;\;{\rm to\;first\;order}$$

In particular with $A_{v0}$ essentially constant for a
given technology, $g_{m}r_{o}\approx 2/\lambda V_{ov}$,
(8) is monotone decreasing in $y=g_{m}R_{s}$,

$${{\partial F}\over {\partial y}}=-{\gamma \over {y^{2}}}
+{1\over {A_{v0}}}{{1-3y}\over {y^{2}(y-1)^{2}}}(1+y)<0
\qquad y>1$$

so that

> {\it For $R_{in}=50\,{\rm \Omega }$ the noise figure is
> minimised by maximising the open loop gain $g_{m}r_{o}$
> and, from (5), maximising $R_{F}$.}

In ordinary language: make $g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}$ as
large as the power budget will allow and make $r_{o}$
as large as the technology will allow and re-choose

$$R_{F}=R_{in}(1+g_{m}r_{o})-r_{o}\approx R_{in}g_{m}r_{o}
\tag{9}$$

to keep $R_{in}=50\,{\rm \Omega }$.  Then from (3)(4)
both the $4kT\gamma g_{m}$ term $\propto 1/g_{m}$ and
the $4kTR_{F}$ term $\propto 1/R_{F}(1+g_{m}r_{o})^{2}$
go down.  Formally $F\rightarrow 1$ for
$g_{m}\rightarrow \infty $, $R_{F}\rightarrow \infty $,
in practice

$$F_{min}\approx 1+{\gamma \over {g_{m}R_{s}}}+{1\over {A_{v0}}}
\tag{10}$$

e. g. $\gamma \approx 1-1.5$, $A_{v0}\approx 10-20$,
$F\approx 1.2-2.0$, $1-3\,{\rm dB}$, for $g_{m}R_{s}\approx
2-5$.

For a {\it given} bias current $I_{D}=I_{D1}=I_{D2}$

$$g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}={2I_{D}\over {V_{ov1}}}+{2I_{D}\over {V_{ov2}}}$$

is maximised by the smallest $V_{ov}$, i. e. the largest
$W$ that still resonates with $R_{s}$ at the frequency of
interest, $R_{s}C_{gs}<1/\omega _{0}$, and by

$$g_{m1}\approx g_{m2}\qquad {W_{p}\over {W_{n}}}\approx
{\mu _{n}\over {\mu _{p}}}$$

so that the $g_{m}$ per mA is maximised.  $r_{o}$ is
maximised by non minimum $L$, $2-3\times L_{min}$, or by
cascoding, at the expense of $g_{m}$ and of headroom.
With $g_{m},r_{o}$ chosen (9) gives the $R_{F}$,
normally a few $10^{2}\,{\rm \Omega }$ to $1\,{\rm k\Omega }$,
to be realised in low noise poly, that restores
$R_{in}=50\,{\rm \Omega }$.

E. g. $R_{s}=50\,{\rm \Omega }$, $r_{o}=200\,{\rm \Omega }$,
$\gamma =1.5$:

$$\eqalign{
g_{m}=40\,{\rm mS}&:R_{F}=250\,{\rm \Omega },\;F\approx 4.6\,{\rm dB}\cr
g_{m}=100\,{\rm mS}&:R_{F}=850\,{\rm \Omega },\;F\approx 1.5\,{\rm dB}\cr
g_{m}=200\,{\rm mS}&:R_{F}=1.85\,{\rm k\Omega },\;F\approx 0.8\,{\rm dB}}$$

apart from $C_{gs}$ and supply limits.  In a power
constrained wide band design the optimum $W$ is the
largest $W$ for which $\omega _{0}R_{s}C_{gs}\approx 1$,
with $R_{F}$ given by (9) and a small series $L_{g}$ to
resonate $C_{gs}$ if necessary.  $C_{1}$ is a short at
$\omega _{0}$.  This is the usual shunt-shunt inverter
TIA/LNA optimum: maximum $g_{m}r_{o}$ per mW, maximum
$R_{F}$ consistent with $R_{in}=R_{s}$.

answers.question: Compute the input impedance of the circuit in Figure 14(a).

answer.text:
With the usual $r_{o}\gg R_{D}$ the small signal
circuit is, Fig.b, a $V$ amplifier

$$V_{o0}=-A_{0}V_{1}\qquad A_{0}>0\tag{1}$$

in series with $R_{D2}$ closed on $R_{F}$ in shunt -
shunt.

$$\eqalign{
M_{1}:&V_{X}=-g_{m1}R_{D1}^{\prime}V_{1}\qquad 
R_{D1}^{\prime}=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\cr
M_{2}-M_{3}:&i_{d3}=G_{m}V_{X}\cr
&G_{m}={{g_{m2}g_{m3}}\over {g_{m2}+g_{m3}+R_{SS}^{-1}}}
\approx {{g_{m}}\over {2}}{1\over {1+1/2g_{m}R_{SS}}}\cr}
\tag{2}$$

for $R_{SS}\rightarrow \infty $ and $g_{m2}=g_{m3}=g_{m}$

$$G_{m}=g_{m}/2\tag{3}$$

so that with $R_{D2}^{\prime}=R_{D2}\parallel r_{o3}$

$$V_{o}=G_{m}R_{D2}^{\prime}V_{X}
      =-g_{m1}R_{D1}^{\prime}G_{m}R_{D2}^{\prime}V_{1}
      =-A_{0}V_{1} \tag{4}$$

$$A_{0}=g_{m1}R_{D1}^{\prime}G_{m}R_{D2}^{\prime}
      ={{g_{m1}R_{D1}^{\prime}g_{m2}g_{m3}R_{D2}^{\prime}}
             {g_{m2}+g_{m3}+R_{SS}^{-1}}}\tag{5}$$

$$A_{0}\approx g_{m1}R_{D1}{{g_{m}R_{D2}}\over 2}\qquad 
r_{o}\to \infty ,\;R_{SS}\to \infty \tag{6}$$

is the open circuit, $R_{F}\to \infty $, voltage gain
from $P$ to the output.  Put $V_{1}=V_{P}$ and, at
low frequency $sC_{in}=0$,

$${\rm KCL}_{P}: I_{in}={{V_{1}-V_{o}}\over {R_{F}}}\tag{7}$$

$${\rm KCL}_{o}: {{V_{o}+A_{0}V_{1}}\over {R_{D2}^{\prime}}}
                +{{V_{o}-V_{1}}\over {R_{F}}}=0 \tag{8}$$

{\it i. e.} the Thevenin model of Fig.14b.  From (8)

$$V_{o}{{R_{F}+R_{D2}^{\prime}}\over {R_{F}R_{D2}^{\prime}}}
      =V_{1}{{1-A_{0}R_{F}/R_{D2}^{\prime}}\over {R_{F}}}$$

$$V_{o}=V_{1}{{R_{D2}^{\prime}-A_{0}R_{F}}\over 
                {R_{D2}^{\prime}+R_{F}}}\tag{9}$$

and from (7)

$$I_{in}={{V_{1}-V_{o}}\over {R_{F}}}
       ={{V_{1}}\over {R_{F}}}
         \left[1-{{R_{D2}^{\prime}-A_{0}R_{F}}\over 
                      {R_{D2}^{\prime}+R_{F}}}\right]
       =V_{1}{{1+A_{0}}\over {R_{F}+R_{D2}^{\prime}}}\tag{10}$$

$$\;R_{in0}\equiv \left.{{V_{1}}\over {I_{in}}}\right|_{C_{in}=0}
      ={{R_{F}+R_{D2}^{\prime}}\over {1+A_{0}}}\;
      ={{R_{F}+R_{D2}\parallel r_{o3}}\over 
             {1+g_{m1}R_{D1}^{\prime}G_{m}R_{D2}^{\prime}}}\tag{11}$$

which is $R_{in}$ with the feedback short circuit
loop gain in the denominator.  In the conventional
$R_{F}\gg R_{D2}^{\prime}$ , $A_{0}\gg 1$ form

$$R_{in0}\approx {{R_{F}}\over {A_{0}}}
        \approx {{R_{F}}\over {g_{m1}R_{D1}G_{m}R_{D2}}}\tag{12}$$

and for the normal $r_{o}\to \infty $, $R_{SS}\to \infty $,
$g_{m2}=g_{m3}=g_{m}$,

$$R_{in0}\approx {{R_{F}+R_{D2}}\over 
                {1+{\tfrac12}g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m}R_{D2}}}
        \approx {{2R_{F}}\over {g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m}R_{D2}}}\;\;
                R_{F}\gg R_{D2},\;A_{0}\gg 1 \tag{13}$$

apart from the $1/2$ due to the single ended
differential pair, $R_{in0}=(R_{F}+R_{D})/(1+g_{m}R_{D})$
for the one stage shunt - shunt stage.  With the
usual $Y$ feedback notation $R_{F}^{-1}$ the return
ratio with the input shorted is

$$T_{sc}\approx A_{0}{{R_{F}}\over {R_{F}+R_{D2}^{\prime}}}\tag{14}$$

so that $R_{in0}= (R_{F}+R_{D2}^{\prime})/(1+T_{sc})
(R_{F}+R_{D2}^{\prime})/R_{F}$.

Including $C_{in}$,

$$Z_{in}(s)=R_{in0}\parallel {1\over {sC_{in}}}
          ={{R_{in0}}\over {1+sC_{in}R_{in0}}}\tag{15}$$

so that at $s\to 0$, $Z_{in}\to R_{in0}$, Eq.11-13,
and for $|s|C_{in}R_{in0}\gg 1$, $Z_{in}\approx 1/sC_{in}$.
The closed loop transimpedance is

$$Z_{T}\equiv {{V_{o}}\over {I_{in}}}=-R_{F}{{A_{0}}\over {1+A_{0}}}
      {{R_{D2}^{\prime}}\over {R_{D2}^{\prime}+R_{F}/A_{0}}}
      \approx -R_{F}\qquad A_{0}\gg 1 \tag{16}$$

and the input pole is

$$\omega _{p,in}\approx {1\over {R_{in0}C_{in}}}
      \approx {{1+A_{0}}\over {(R_{F}+R_{D2}^{\prime})C_{in}}}
      \approx {{A_{0}}\over {R_{F}C_{in}}}\tag{17}$$

For the idealised block of Fig.14b this is normally
quoted as

$$R_{in}={{R_{F}+R_{D2}}\over {1+A}}\approx {R_{F}\over A}\tag{18}$$

with $A\equiv A_{0}$ given by (5)-(6).  Any $r_{o}$,
$R_{SS}$ and $g_{mb}$ can be absorbed in $R_{D1}^{\prime}$,
$R_{D2}^{\prime}$ and $G_{m}$.  E.G. $g_{m}\to g_{m}+g_{mb}$.

The derivation properly handles the output-side resistance in the feedback path, uses KCL rather than a simplistic loaded-gain approach, and arrives at the correct central conclusion.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in Figure 15 generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
With the usual abuse of notation the low
frequency noise on $V_{out}$ frequency
modulates the $LC$ tank. For
$f_{m}<< f_{0}$ :

$$V_{o}(t)=V_{0}\cos \left[\omega _{0}t+\phi _{n}(t)\right]$$

$$\omega _{0}= \frac{1}{\sqrt{L_{1}C_{tot}}}$$

$$C_{tot}=C_{B1}+C_{B2}+C_{v}(V_{cont}-V_{CM})+C_{gd,db}(V_{out})+...$$

$$V_{CM}\approx V_{out}-I_{VCO}R_{L1}$$

so that

$$K_{push}= \frac{\partial \omega _{0}}{\partial V_{out}}
      =2\pi K_{VDD}\;\;{\rm rad/s/V}$$

$$K_{VDD}= \frac{\partial f_{0}}{\partial V_{out}}\;\;{\rm Hz/V}
       \approx -\frac{1}{4\pi \sqrt{L_{1}C_{tot}^{3}}}
                \frac{\partial C_{tot}}{\partial V_{out}}$$

can be got to first order closed form from
$C_{v}(V)$ and $C_{db}(V)$ or normally
from $PSS$:

$$K_{VDD}= \left.\frac{\Delta f_{0}}{\Delta V_{out}}\right|_{V_{cont}}$$

measured with a $\Delta V_{out}\sim 10-50\,{\rm mV}$
sweep. It is $V_{cont}$ dependent and is
dominated by the $AM-PM$ conversion through
$M_{v1,2}$,

$$\frac{\partial C_{v}}{\partial V_{out}}=
 -\frac{\partial C_{v}}{\partial V_{cont}}$$

and through $C_{gd}+C_{db}(V_{DS})$ of $M_{1,2}$
and the Groszkowski effect
$\Delta \omega /\omega_{0}\propto \Delta A/A$.
Typical $10-100\,{\rm MHz/V}$.

For $f_{m}\ll f_{0}$ the inductor is a short
for the base band noise

$$Z_{L1}(j2\pi f_{m})=j2\pi f_{m}L_{1}\approx 0$$

so the $V_{out}$ noise appears as common mode
on $X,Y$.

Let

$$S_{v}(f)=S_{th}(f)\left|H_{LDO}(f)\right|^{2}\;\;
{\rm V^{2}/Hz\;one\;sided}$$

be the one sided PSD at the $V_{out}$ node.
For a white thermal floor $S_{th}=4kTR_{o,eq}$
flat to the $LDO$ closed loop $BW$,
$H_{LDO}(f)\approx 1/[1+jf/f_{p}]$ with
$f_{p}=1/2\pi R_{o}C_{o}$, plus $1/f$ noise
for $f<f_{c}$. For $f_{m}$ inside the $LDO$
$BW$, $S_{v}\approx S_{th}$.

Instantaneous frequency:

$$f(t)=f_{0}+K_{VDD}v_{n}(t)$$

$$\Delta \omega (t)=K_{push}v_{n}(t)$$

$$\phi _{n}(t)= \int \Delta \omega (t)dt
            =K_{push}\int v_{n}(t)dt$$

In Fourier domain for $f_{m}\ne 0$

$$\Phi _{n}(f_{m})=\frac{K_{push}}{j2\pi f_{m}}V_{n}(f_{m})
                =\frac{K_{VDD}}{jf_{m}}V_{n}(f_{m})$$

Hence one sided

$$S_{\phi}(f_{m})= \frac{K_{push}^{2}}{(2\pi f_{m})^{2}}S_{v}(f_{m})
                =\frac{K_{VDD}^{2}}{f_{m}^{2}}S_{v}(f_{m})
                \;\;{\rm rad^{2}/Hz}$$

$$S_{f}(f_{m})=K_{VDD}^{2}S_{v}(f_{m})\;\;{\rm Hz^{2}/Hz}$$

and for $|\phi _{n}|\ll 1$ the conventional
single side band ${\cal L}$,

$${\cal L}(f_{m})=\frac{S_{\phi}(f_{m})}{2}
               =\frac{K_{VDD}^{2}S_{v}(f_{m})}{2f_{m}^{2}}
               =\frac{K_{push}^{2}S_{v}(f_{m})}{2(2\pi f_{m})^{2}}$$

in linear units. In ${\rm dBc/Hz}$

$${\cal L}_{LDO}(f_{m})\approx 
10\log S_{v}(f_{m})+20\log K_{VDD}-20\log f_{m}-3\,{\rm dB}$$

$$=10\log S_{v}(f_{m})+20\log K_{push}-20\log 2\pi f_{m}-3\,{\rm dB}$$

For white $S_{v}=S_{th}$,

$${\cal L}_{LDO}\propto 1/f_{m}^{2}\;\;-20\,{\rm dB/dec}$$

If $S_{v}\propto 1/f_{m}$ for the $LDO$ flicker
noise, ${\cal L}\propto 1/f_{m}^{3}\;\;-30\,{\rm dB/dec}$.

With $H_{LDO}$,

$${\cal L}_{LDO}(f_{m})=
\frac{K_{VDD}^{2}S_{th}(f_{m})\left|H_{LDO}(f_{m})\right|^{2}}
     {2f_{m}^{2}}$$

to be added in power to the intrinsic
Leeson $VCO$ noise. In $PSS/PXF/PNoise$ this
is the $PM$ transfer from a small signal
source in series with $V_{out}$ to the
sideband at $f_{0}\pm f_{m}$.

E.G. $S_{th}^{1/2}=10\,{\rm nV/\sqrt{Hz}}$,
$S_{th}=10^{-16}{\rm V^{2}/Hz}$,
$K_{VDD}=50\,{\rm MHz/V}$:

$${\cal L}(1\,{\rm MHz})\approx 
\frac{(5\times 10^{7})^{2}10^{-16}}{2\times 10^{12}}
\approx 1.2\times 10^{-13}\approx -129\,{\rm dBc/Hz}$$

white, $-20\,{\rm dB/dec}$ to $f_{p}$ where
$H_{LDO}$ rolls off. Formally this is
$\Gamma_{supply}^{2}(i_{n}^{2}/\Delta f)/8\pi^{2}f_{m}^{2}q_{max}^{2}$
in Hajimiri's ISF language.

answers.question: We add CT to the tail node, as in Figure 16. What happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
With the conventional ${\cal H}$ analysis the
circuit is differential and

$${\cal H}_{P}(s)=0\tag {*}$$

for the ${\cal H}$ mode so that in first order
$C_{T}$ does nothing.  With a physical $I_{SS}$

$${\cal H}_{P}(s)={1\over {g_{m}+sC_{T}+Y_{SS}(s)}}$$

and the noise current $i_{n,SS}$ is commutated by
the ${\cal H}$ pair.  In the Hajimiri picture

$${\cal L}(\Delta \omega )\propto 
\sum_{n}c_{n}^{2}S_{i_{n,SS}}(n\omega _{0}\pm \Delta \omega )
\Gamma _{n}^{2}\tag{**}$$

where $\Gamma _{n}$ is the $n$th Fourier coefficient
of the impulse sensitivity function and $c_{n}$ is the
$n$th Fourier coefficient of the commutating function.
For the perfectly balanced circuit $c_{n}\ne 0$ only
for $n$ even and in particular the $n=2$ term,
$S_{i_{n,SS}}(2\omega _{0}\pm \Delta \omega )$,
down converted by $c_{2}\Gamma _{1}$, is normally the
dominant tail contribution to the $1/f^{2}$ floor.
Putting a $C_{T}$ from $P$ to ground puts the
admittance $sC_{T}$ in parallel with $Y_{SS}$ and

$$S_{i_{n,SS}}^{{\rm eff}}(2\omega _{0})=
S_{i_{n,SS}}(2\omega _{0})
\left|{Y_{SS}\over {Y_{SS}+2j\omega _{0}C_{T}}}\right|^{2}
\approx S_{i_{n,SS}}(2\omega _{0})
{1\over {1+\left(2\omega _{0}C_{T}/g_{m}\right)^{2}}}\tag{***}$$

for $Y_{SS}\approx g_{m}$ at $2\omega _{0}$.
In so far as ($**$) is concerned the wide band,
thermal, tail noise folded from $2\omega _{0}$ to
$\omega _{0}\pm \Delta \omega $ is low pass filtered
with the pole

$$\omega _{p}\approx {g_{m}\over {C_{T}}}\;\;,\;\;
\omega _{p}\approx {1\over {R_{SS}C_{T}}}{\rm \;for\;
a\;MOS\;tail}$$

and for $\Delta \omega <\omega _{p}<2\omega _{0}$
the $1/f^{2}$ contribution of the tail to

$${\cal L}(\Delta \omega )\approx 
10\log \left[{{kT\over {2Q^{2}P_{s}}}
\left({\omega _{0}\over {\Delta \omega }}\right)^{2}
\left(1+\gamma +{1\over 4}\gamma _{T}
{g_{mT}\over {g_{m}}}{1\over {1+(2\omega _{0}C_{T}R_{SS})^{2}}}
\right)\right] \tag{****}$$

can be made arbitrarily small.  In the limit
$C_{T}\to \infty $ the tail is a small signal ground
at $2\omega _{0}$ and, to first order, the tail
ceases to contribute to the thermal $1/f^{2}$ floor.
Normally $3-6\,{\rm dB}$ can be recovered in this way.

That is the {\it small signal\/} story.  Large signal
the common source node $P$ is not ground.  With
$I_{SS}$ ideal the differential pair steers $I_{SS}$
from side to side and

$$v_{P}(t)=V_{P0}-V_{0}\left|\sin \omega _{0}t\right|
+{\cal O}(V_{0}^{2}) \tag{\dag}$$

contains a large $2\omega _{0}$ component,
$I_{2\omega _{0}}\approx (2/\pi )I_{SS}$, flowing in
$Y_{SS}$.  Putting a naked $C_{T}$ to ground short
circuits that $2\omega _{0}$ current.  The second
harmonic is shorted, the common mode $Q$ is de-$Q$ed,
the pair spends a much larger fraction of the period
with $V_{ds}\approx 0$ in the triode region loading
the $LC$ tank and the available negative
$G_{m}=-g_{m}/2$ is made strongly frequency dependent.
More important, $C_{T}$ introduces a long memory,
$\tau _{P}=R_{SS}C_{T}$ or $C_{T}/g_{m}$, at the tail.
The oscillator becomes very asymmetric and the ISF
acquires a large d. c. average

$$\Gamma _{0}={1\over {2\pi }}\int_{0}^{2\pi }\Gamma (\theta )
d\theta \ne 0 \tag{\ddag}$$

so that the low frequency, $1/f$, noise of $I_{SS}$,
which ($***$) does {\it not\/} filter, is up converted
with the coefficient $\Gamma _{0}^{2}$,

$${\cal L}_{1/f^{3}}(\Delta \omega )\propto 
\Gamma _{0}^{2}{S_{1/f}( \Delta \omega )\over {\Delta \omega ^{2}}}
\tag{\S}$$

and, through the non linear $C_{gs}-C_{gd}-C_{db}$
of $M_{1}-M_{2}$ and/or any varactor in the tank,
AM to PM, Groszkowski, conversion

$${{\delta \omega _{0}}\over {\omega _{0}}}\approx
{1\over {2Q}}{{ \delta C_{T,{\rm eff}}}\over {C_{T,{\rm eff}}}}
\approx {1\over {2Q}}{{C_{T}}\over {C+C_{T}}}{{ \delta V_{P}}\over {V_{P}}}
\tag{\P}$$

converts the LF amplitude modulation produced by
$i_{n,SS}( \Delta \omega )$ flowing in $Z_{P}( \Delta
\omega )\approx 1/j\Delta \omega C_{T}$ into close in
phase modulation.  Formally the $1/f^{3}$ corner

$$\omega _{1/f^{3}}\approx \omega _{1/f}\,
{\Gamma _{0}^{2}\over {\Gamma _{1}^{2}}}\,
\left[1+\left(\omega _{p}/\Delta \omega \right)^{2}\right] \tag{\Vert}$$

is pushed out by essentially the amount the $1/f^{2}$
floor is pushed down.

In most practical technologies the second effect
dominates.  A large plain $C_{T}$ to ground as drawn
in Fig. 16 degrades the loaded $Q$, reduces the
swing for a given $I_{SS}$ and, because of ($\ddag $)-
($\Vert $), {\it increases\/} the close in $1/f^{3}$
phase noise, often by $5-10\,{\rm dB}$, while improving
the far out $1/f^{2}$ floor by at most $2-3\,{\rm dB}$.
Net measured ${\cal L}(\Delta \omega )$ is normally
worse.

The useful circuit is the Hegazi-Abidi tail filter,
{\it IEEE J. Solid State Circuits\/} {\bf 36}, 1928
(2001): $C_{T}$ is resonated with a (real or active)
inductor $L_{T}$ in series with $I_{SS}$,

$$\omega _{T}={1\over {\sqrt{L_{T}C_{T}}}}=2\omega _{0}\tag{**}$$

so that

$$Z_{P}(2\omega _{0})=j2\omega _{0}L_{T}+{1\over {j2\omega _{0}C_{T}}}
\parallel R_{SS}\to {\rm high}\tag{\dag\dag}$$

presents a high impedance to the $2\omega _{0}$
commutated current, preserving the $Q$ and the swing,
and a low impedance,
$Z_{P}(\Delta \omega )\approx 1/j\Delta \omega C_{T}$,
to wide band noise, filtering ($***$), and, with
$Z_{P}(0)=R_{SS}$, no LF memory, $\Gamma _{0}\to 0$.
With $L_{T}C_{T}$ tuned to $2\omega _{0}$ $6-10\,{\rm dB}$
improvement in both $1/f^{2}$ and $1/f^{3}$ ${\cal L}$
is routinely obtained.  Without $L_{T}$ the conventional
wisdom is: do not put a large naked $C_{T}$ on the
tail.  If a $C_{T}$ is used keep $\omega _{p}\gg
2\omega _{0}$, i. e. $C_{T}\ll g_{m}/2\omega _{0}$,
so that ($\dag $) is essentially undisturbed.

> {\it Remark:\/} In the text book first order
> analysis the answer is often phrased as ``$C_{T}$
> bypasses the noise of $I_{SS}$ to ground and the
> phase noise goes down by ($***$)-($****$)''.  That is
> correct for the thermal $1/f^{2}$ contribution with
> $C_{T}$ small enough not to disturb ($\dag $).  With
> the usual large $C_{T}\approx 10-100\,{\rm pF}$
> intended to be an a. c. ground the opposite is
> observed: the $1/f^{3}$ phase noise goes up.

minimax_m3.rationale: The answer demonstrates strong circuit understanding and correctly identifies that a 'naked' CT without LT degrades phase noise overall (increasing 1/f³ while modestly improving 1/f²). However, it misses the central point from the golden solution: the effect is nonmonotonic, with class-C-like switching in an intermediate range potentially improving phase noise before instability occurs at large CT. The answer treats it as a strict 'naked CT is bad' conclusion (monotonic degradation for large CT) rather than recognizing that an optimally chosen CT can improve phase noise in a specific range via class-C behavior, and instability at high CT. It also misses flicker noise upconversion from M1/M2 through the tail-node waveform change at small/moderate CT. The discussion is technically rich but largely one-sided and misses the nonmonotonic optimization framework that is the essential answer.

deepseek_v4_pro.rationale: The answer correctly identifies that adding CT to the tail node has a nonmonotonic effect on phase noise, mentioning both potential improvement (filtering tail noise) and degradation (flicker noise upconversion, triode loading, low-frequency instability). However, it overemphasizes the small-signal filtering benefit and concludes that a large plain CT degrades phase noise, which is only one side of the tradeoff. The golden solution emphasizes that CT is an optimization variable with possible class-C-like improvement in an intermediate range, which the answer does not adequately address. The answer also introduces a specific tail filter (Hegazi-Abidi) as the useful circuit, but the question is about the simple CT addition, and the answer's final recommendation to avoid large CT contradicts the golden solution's central point that CT must be optimized rather than simply avoided. Thus, the answer captures some relevant mechanisms but misses the key nonmonotonic optimization aspect.

answers.question: Estimate the oscillation frequency of the circuit in Figure 17.

answer.text:
With the usual weak coupling the circuit is two
identical parallel tuned circuits injection locked to
each other.  Put

$${\cal Y}_{T}=G_{p}+jB\qquad 
B=\omega C_{T}-1/\omega L\tag{1}$$

for one side, $C_{T}$ the total capacity to earth on
$X_{i},Y_{i}$,

$$C_{T}=C_{0}+C_{gs}+C_{gd}+C_{db}+C_{w}\approx 0.5-2\,{\rm pF}$$

$C_{0}$ the explicit tank capacity if any, $L$ the
one side inductance to $V_{DD}$, $G_{p}=1/R_{p}$,
$R_{p}=Q\omega _{0}L$, $Q\approx 5-10$,

$$\omega _{0}^{2}=1/LC_{T}\qquad f_{0}=\omega _{0}/2\pi \tag{2}$$

the conventional parallel resonance of one tank.
For the differential signal

$$V_{1}=X_{1}-Y_{1}\qquad V_{2}=X_{2}-Y_{2}$$

the small signal KCL on the two tanks is, with the
conventional $G_{m}=g_{m}/2$ differential
transconductance, $G_{mS}$ of the $I_{SS}$ pair,
$G_{m1}$ of the $I_{1}$ pair,

$$\eqalign{
{\cal Y}_{T}V_{1}&=G_{mS}V_{1}\pm G_{m1}V_{2}\cr
{\cal Y}_{T}V_{2}&=G_{mS}V_{2}\mp G_{m1}V_{1}\cr}\tag{3}$$

the upper sign for the straight connection, the lower
sign for the crossed connection of Fig.17.  In compact
form with

$${\cal Y}^{\prime}={\cal Y}_{T}-G_{mS}=G_{p}-G_{mS}+jB\tag{4}$$

$${\cal Y}^{\prime}V_{1}= \pm G_{m1}V_{2}\qquad 
  {\cal Y}^{\prime}V_{2}= \mp G_{m1}V_{1}\tag{5}$$

for the normal quadrature cross, and

$${\cal Y}^{\prime}V_{1}= G_{m1}V_{2}\qquad 
  {\cal Y}^{\prime}V_{2}= G_{m1}V_{1}\tag{6}$$

for the in phase connection.  E. {\it g.} for the
quadrature cross

$${\cal Y}^{\prime 2}+G_{m1}^{2}=0\tag{7}$$

$${\cal Y}^{\prime}= \pm jG_{m1}\tag{8}$$

i. {\it e.}

$$G_{p}-G_{mS}=0\tag{9}$$

$$B=\omega C_{T}-1/\omega L =\pm G_{m1}\tag{10}$$

in small signal $G_{mS}=g_{mS}/2$, $G_{m1}=g_{m1}/2$,
$g_{mS}=\sqrt{2k_{n}I_{SS}}$, $g_{m1}=\sqrt{2k_{n}I_{1}}$,
in large signal, hard switching,

$$G_{mS}\approx {2\over \pi}{I_{SS}\over \hat V}\qquad 
  G_{m1}\approx {2\over \pi}{I_{1}\over \hat V}\qquad 
  \hat V\approx {2\over \pi}I_{SS}R_{p}\tag{11}$$

the familiar $G_{mS}R_{p}\approx 1$, $2$ according to the
definition of $R_{p}$, start up condition.  (9) is the
usual start up condition, (10) is the frequency
condition.  I. {\it e.} the tank has to be detuned off
its parallel resonance by just enough susceptance to
give the $90^{{\rm o}}$ phase shift required for the
quadrature loop.  From (10)

$$\omega^{2}LC_{T}\mp G_{m1}L\omega -1=0\tag{12}$$

$$\omega_{q}^{\pm}={G_{m1}\over 2C_{T}}\pm
\sqrt{\left({G_{m1}\over 2C_{T}}\right)^{2}+{1\over LC_{T}}}
      =\omega_{0}\left[\sqrt{1+\left({G_{m1}\over
2\omega_{0}C_{T}}\right)^{2}}\pm{G_{m1}\over
2\omega_{0}C_{T}}\right] \tag{13}$$

the $+$ sign is the normally stable quadrature mode

$$V_{2}= \mp jV_{1}\qquad |V_{1}|=|V_{2}|\tag{14}$$

$X_{1}-Y_{1}$ in quadrature with $X_{2}-Y_{2}$, the $-$
sign the unstable in phase mode.  For the in phase
wiring (6)

$${\cal Y}^{\prime}= \pm G_{m1}\tag{15}$$

$$G_{p}-G_{mS}= \pm G_{m1}\qquad B=0\tag{16}$$

so that to first order the frequency stays at $\omega_{0}$
and the two modes $V_{2}= \pm V_{1}$ have different
thresholds $G_{mS}=G_{p}\mp G_{m1}$.

For the normal weak coupling design

$${G_{m1}\over \omega_{0}C_{T}}={G_{m1}R_{p}\over Q}
      \approx {I_{1}\over I_{SS}}{1\over Q}\ll 1\tag{17}$$

(13) can be linearised,

$$\omega_{q}\approx \omega_{0}\pm {G_{m1}\over 2C_{T}}
      =\omega_{0}\left[1\pm {G_{m1}\over 2\omega_{0}C_{T}}\right]
      =\omega_{0}\left[1\pm {G_{m1}R_{p}\over 2Q}\right] \tag{18}$$

$$\Delta\omega_{q}\approx \pm {g_{m1}\over 4C_{T}}\;\;
{\rm s.s.}\;\;\approx \pm {I_{1}\over \pi C_{T}\hat V}
      \approx \pm {I_{1}\over I_{SS}}{\omega_{0}\over 2Q}
      \;\;{\rm l.s.}\tag{19}$$

So that to ${\cal O}(Q^{-1})$ the circuit oscillates at
the free running frequency of one $LC$ tank,

$$f_{osc}\approx f_{0}={1\over 2\pi}{1\over \sqrt{LC_{T}}}$$

apart from the small coupling split (18)-(19).  With
$C_{T}$ taken as the differential capacity $C_{0}/2$ the
more familiar $f_{0}=1/2\pi\sqrt{L\,C_{0}/2}$ is often
quoted; with $C_{T}$ the one side capacity to ground it
is $1/2\pi\sqrt{LC_{T}}$.

In particular for $G_{m1}\to 0$ the conventional single
oscillator result is recovered.  For the usual
$I_{1}\approx 0.2-0.5\,I_{SS}$, $Q\approx 5-10$,

$${\Delta f_{q}\over f_{0}}\approx {1\over 2Q}{I_{1}\over I_{SS}}
      \approx 1-5\% \tag{20}$$

so that for all practical purposes

$$f_{osc}\approx {1\over 2\pi\sqrt{LC_{T}}}\tag{21}$$

is the quadrature frequency, the upper side band in
(13) being the stable quadrature mode for the cross
wiring of Fig.17, the lower side band the unstable
in phase mode and vice versa for the opposite cross.

E. {\it g.} for an on chip spiral $L\approx 1-5\,{\rm nH}$
and $C_{T}\approx 0.5-2\,{\rm pF}$

$$f_{0}\approx 1.5-7\,{\rm GHz}$$

e. {\it g.} $L=2\,{\rm nH}$, $C_{T}=1\,{\rm pF}$,
$R_{p}\approx 0.5\,{\rm k\Omega }$, $I_{SS}=2\,{\rm mA}$,
$I_{1}=0.5\,{\rm mA}$, $g_{mS}\approx 4\,{\rm mS}$,
$g_{m1}\approx 2\,{\rm mS}$, $G_{m1}\approx 1\,{\rm mS}$,

$$f_{0}\approx 3.6\,{\rm GHz}\qquad 
  \Delta f_{q}\approx {G_{m1}\over 4\pi C_{T}}\approx 80\,{\rm MHz}
      \approx 0.3\,{\rm GHz\;l.s.}$$

so that $f_{q}^{+}\approx 3.9\,{\rm GHz}$,
$f_{q}^{-}\approx 3.3\,{\rm GHz}$.  With no explicit
$C_{0}$, $C_{T}$ is the parasitic $C_{gs}+C_{gd}+C_{db}$
on $X_{i},Y_{i}$, typically a few $100\,{\rm fF}$, giving
$f_{0}$ in the $5-10\,{\rm GHz}$ range.  Any explicit
tank capacitor simply adds to $C_{T}$ in (2), (13).

In large signal notation (13) is often written as

$$\omega_{osc}\approx \omega_{0}\sqrt{1\pm k^{2}}\pm k\omega_{0},
\qquad k={G_{m1}\over \omega_{0}C_{T}}\approx {g_{m1}\over g_{mS}}{1\over Q}$$

or, with $g_{m}\propto \sqrt{I}$,

$$k\approx \sqrt{I_{1}/I_{SS}}/Q$$

so that the often quoted $\omega_{osc}\approx
\omega_{0}\sqrt{1+(I_{1}/I_{SS})^{2}}$ is recovered up to
the $Q$ factor.  Neglecting the ${\cal O}(k)$ correction
this is commonly abbreviated as $f_{osc}\approx
1/2\pi\sqrt{LC}$ with $L$ the one side inductance and $C$
the total tank capacity.  The circuit then provides two
differential outputs $V_{1},V_{2}$ of the same amplitude
and frequency (21), (13) in quadrature, $V_{2}= \pm
jV_{1}$, the sign depending on which of the two split
frequencies is selected.

minimax_m3.rationale: The candidate answer correctly derives the oscillation frequency starting from the tank resonance ω0 = 1/√(LC_T) and includes the coupling-induced frequency shift. Equation (18) gives Δω_q ≈ ±(G_m1/2C_T) = ±(g_m1/4C_T) (small-signal), and equation (19) gives Δω_q ≈ ±(I_1/I_SS)(ω_0/(2Q)) (large-signal), which match the golden solution's Δω = αω_0/(2Q) with α ≈ I_1/I_SS or α ≈ g_mc/g_m1. The sign ambiguity depending on coupling orientation is also acknowledged. The answer correctly warns that using only g_mc/(2C_node) is insufficient without the edge-of-oscillation assumption, and provides a complete design analysis with both topology (quadrature cross vs in-phase) and numerical examples. Minor notation differences (e.g., G_m1 vs g_mc) are secondary.

deepseek_v4_pro.rationale: The answer correctly starts from the tank resonance ω0=1/√(LC_T), derives the coupling-induced frequency shift Δω≈(G_m1/(2C_T))≈(I1/ISS)ω0/(2Q), and gives the final oscillation frequency as ω0 plus a small shift. It includes both the tank term and the coupling-shift term, matches the golden solution's required form, and correctly notes the edge-of-oscillation warning. Minor notation differences and the large-signal approximations are secondary.
